In ''[[Das Kapital]]'', Marx identified the commodity as the basic unit of capitalist organization. Marx described a "common denominator" among commodities, namely that they are products of labor and are related to each other by an [[exchange value]] (i.e., [[price]]).<ref name="commodities">{{Cite book|url=http://marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1867-c1/ch01.htm#S1|title=Chapter 1: Commodities – Capital, Volume 1|last=Marx|first=Karl|publisher=Penguin Classics|year=1992|isbn=978-0-14-044568-8}}</ref> By using the labor theory of value, [[Marxism|Marxists]] see a connection between labor and exchange value, in that commodities are exchanged depending on the [[socially necessary labor time]] needed to produce them.<ref name="valueprice">{{cite web|url=http://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1865/value-price-profit/|title=Value, Price, and Profit|last=Marx|first=Karl|access-date=10 March 2008}}</ref> However, due to the productive forces of industrial organization, laborers are seen as creating more exchange value during the course of the working day than the cost of their survival (food, shelter, clothing and so on).<ref name="wagelabour">{{cite web|url=http://marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1847/wage-labour/ch06.htm|title=Wage Labour and Capital|last=Marx|first=Karl|access-date=10 March 2008}}</ref> Marxists argue that capitalists are thus able to pay for this cost of survival while expropriating the excess labor (i.e. [[surplus value]]).<ref name="valueprice"/>

Marxists further argue that due to [[economic inequality]], the purchase of labor cannot occur under "free" conditions. Since capitalists control the [[means of production]] (e.g., factories, businesses, machinery, and so on) and workers control only their labor, the worker is naturally coerced into allowing their labor to be exploited.<ref name="competition">{{cite web|url=http://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1845/condition-working-class/ch05.htm|title=Competition – The Condition of the Working Class in England|last=Engels|first=Frederick|access-date=10 March 2008}}</ref> Critics argue that exploitation occurs even if the exploited consents, since the definition of exploitation is independent of consent. In essence, workers must allow their labor to be exploited or face starvation. Since some degree of unemployment is typical in modern economies, Marxists argue that wages are naturally driven down in free market systems. Hence, even if a worker contests their wages, capitalists can find someone from the [[reserve army of labor]] who is more desperate.<ref name="histmaterial">{{cite web|url=http://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1880/soc-utop/ch03.htm|title=Historical Materialism – Socialism: Utopian and Scientific|last=Engels|first=Frederick|access-date=10 March 2008}}</ref>

The act (or threat) of [[Strike action|striking]] has historically been an organized action to withhold labor from capitalists, without fear of individual retaliation.<ref name="tradesoc">{{cite web|url=http://www.marxists.org/archive/kautsky/1901/04/unions.htm|title=Trade Unions and Socialism|last=Kautsky|first=Karl|access-date=10 March 2008}}</ref> Some critics of capitalism, while acknowledging the necessity of [[trade union]]ism, believe that trade unions reform an already exploitative system, leaving the system of exploitation intact.<ref name="subterranean">{{Cite book|title=Subterranean Fire: A History of Working Class Radicalism in the United States|last=Smith|first=Sharon|publisher=[[Haymarket Books]]|year=2006|isbn=978-1-931859-23-3|page=320}}</ref><ref name="reformrevolution">{{cite web|url=http://marxists.org/archive/luxemburg/1900/reform-revolution/ch07.htm|title=Chapter VII: Co-operatives, Unions, Democracy – Reform or Revolution|last=Luxembourg|first=Rosa|access-date=10 March 2008}}</ref> [[Lysander Spooner]] argued that "almost all fortunes are made out of the capital and labour of other men than those who realize them. Indeed, large fortunes could rarely be made at all by one individual, except by his sponging capital and labour from others".<ref>Martin, James J. ''Men Against the State'', p. 173</ref>

Some [[Labor history (discipline)|labor historians]] and scholars have argued that [[unfree labor]]—by [[Slavery|enslaved people]], [[Indentured servitude|indentured servants]], [[Incarceration in the United States#Employment|prisoners]], or other coerced persons—is compatible with capitalist relations. [[Tom Brass]] argued that unfree labor is acceptable to capital.<ref>Cass, ''Towards a Comparative Political Economy of Unfree Labor'' (1999)</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=http://www.historycooperative.org/journals/llt/52/linden.html |title=Labour History as the History of Multitudes |journal=Labour/Le Travail |volume=52 |date=Fall 2003 |pages=235–244 |author=Marcel van der Linden |access-date=26 February 2008 |doi=10.2307/25149390 |jstor=25149390 |s2cid=43371533 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071217185826/http://www.historycooperative.org/journals/llt/52/linden.html |archive-date=17 December 2007|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Historian [[Greg Grandin]] argues that capitalism has its origins in slavery, saying that "[w]hen historians talk about the Atlantic market revolution, they are talking about capitalism. And when they are talking about capitalism, they are talking about slavery."<ref name="Grandin">{{Cite interview|last=Grandin|first=Greg|subject-link=Greg Grandin|interviewer=Alex Gourevitch|title=Capitalism and Slavery: An Interview with Greg Grandin|url=https://www.jacobinmag.com/2014/08/capitalism-and-slavery-an-interview-with-greg-grandin/|work=[[Jacobin (magazine)|Jacobin]]|date=1 August 2014|access-date=6 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406181935/https://www.jacobinmag.com/2014/08/capitalism-and-slavery-an-interview-with-greg-grandin/|archive-date=6 April 2018|url-status=live|quote=There's many ways this happens. Deceit, through [[contraband]], is absolutely key to the expansion of slavery in South America. When historians talk about the Atlantic market revolution, they are talking about capitalism. And when they are talking about capitalism, they are talking about slavery. And when they are talking about slavery, they are talking about corruption and crime. Not in a moral sense, in that the slave system was a crime against humanity. That it was. But it was also a crime in a technical sense: probably as many enslaved Africans came into South America as contraband, to avoid taxes and other lingering restrictions, as legally.}}</ref> Some scholars, including [[Edward E. Baptist]], [[Sven Beckert]], and [[Matthew Desmond]], assert that slavery was an integral component in the violent development of American and global capitalism.<ref>Edward E. Baptist. [https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/edward-e-baptist/the-half-has-never-been-told/9780465097685/?lens=basic-books ''The Half Has Never Been Told: Slavery And The Making Of American Capitalism''], {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150324174604/http://www.basicbooks.com/full-details?isbn=978-0465002962 |date=24 March 2015 }} [[Basic Books]], 2014. {{ISBN|046500296X}}.</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Slavery's Capitalism: A New History of American Economic Development|editor1-first=Sven|editor1-last=Beckert|editor2-first=Seth|editor2-last=Rockman|editor1-link=Sven Beckert|url=http://www.upenn.edu/pennpress/book/15556.html|publisher=[[University of Pennsylvania Press]]|year=2016|isbn=978-0-8122-2417-7|access-date=3 March 2019|archive-date=6 March 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306044324/http://www.upenn.edu/pennpress/book/15556.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last= Desmond|first=Matthew|date=August 14, 2019|title=In order to understand the brutality of American capitalism, you have to start on the plantation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2019/08/14/magazine/slavery-capitalism.html|website=[[The New York Times Magazine]]|location= |publisher= |access-date=February 19, 2025|quote=During slavery, "Americans built a culture of speculation unique in its abandon," writes the historian Joshua Rothman in his 2012 book, "Flush Times and Fever Dreams." That culture would drive cotton production up to the Civil War, and it has been a defining characteristic of American capitalism ever since. It is the culture of acquiring wealth without work, growing at all costs and abusing the powerless. It is the culture that brought us the Panic of 1837, the stock-market crash of 1929 and the recession of 2008. It is the culture that has produced staggering inequality and undignified working conditions. If today America promotes a particular kind of low-road capitalism — a union-busting capitalism of poverty wages, gig jobs and normalized insecurity; a winner-take-all capitalism of stunning disparities not only permitting but awarding financial rule-bending; a racist capitalism that ignores the fact that slavery didn't just deny black freedom but built white fortunes, originating the black-white wealth gap that annually grows wider — one reason is that American capitalism was founded on the lowest road there is.}}</ref> The Slovenian [[continental philosopher]] [[Slavoj Žižek]] posits that the new era of global capitalism has ushered in new forms of [[Slavery#Contemporary slavery|contemporary slavery]], including migrant workers deprived of basic civil rights on the [[Arabian Peninsula]], the total control of workers in Asian [[sweatshops]] and the use of forced labor in the exploitation of natural resources in [[Central Africa]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Žižek|first=Slavoj|date=2018|title=The Courage of Hopelessness: A Year of Acting Dangerously|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=POZFDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA29|publisher=Melville House|page=29|isbn=978-1-61219-003-7|access-date=11 July 2018|archive-date=27 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200727165255/https://books.google.com/books?id=POZFDwAAQBAJ&lpg=PP1&pg=PA29|url-status=live}}</ref>

Academics such as the [[Developmental psychology|developmental psychologist]] [[Howard Gardner]] have proposed the adoption of upper limits in individual wealth as "a solution that would make the world a better place".<ref name="alternet">{{cite web|url=http://www.alternet.org/economy/62507/|title=When the Rich Make Too Much: Is it Time for a Maximum Wage?|date=19 November 2009|publisher=alternet.org|access-date=11 January 2014}}</ref> [[Marxian economics|Marxian economist]] [[Richard D. Wolff]] postulates that capitalist economies prioritize profits and capital accumulation over the social needs of communities, and that capitalist enterprises rarely include the workers in the basic decisions of the enterprise.<ref>Frances Goldin, Debby Smith, Michael Smith (2014). ''Imagine: Living in a Socialist USA'', [[Harper Perennial]]. {{ISBN|0062305573}} pp. 49–50.</ref>

{{quote box
| quote = "Most people have no alternative but to sell their ability to work for a wage and inevitably be paid less than the value they produce. This is the capital order, the backbone of our society that we do not criticize or even discuss."
| source = — [[Clara Mattei]]{{sfn|Mattei|2026|page=[https://www.google.com/books/edition/Escape_from_Capitalism/3JNkEQAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=Clara%20mattei&pg=PA13&printsec= 13]}}
| width = 25%
| align = right
}}

Political economist Clara E. Mattei of the [[New School for Social Research]] demonstrates that the imposition of fiscal, monetary and industrial [[austerity]] policies meant to discipline labor by reinforcing hierarchal wage relations and therefore protect the capitalist system through wage repression and the weakening of collective bargaining power by workers can increase their exploitation while boosting the profits of the ownership class, which she says is one of the primary drivers of the "global inequality trend". As an example, Mattei shows that over the last four decades in the United States, the profit share of national output increased while labor's share plummeted, demonstrating a symmetrical relationship between owner profit and worker loss, in which the former took from the latter. She adds that "an increase in exploitation was also evident, with real wages grossly lagging behind labor productivity."{{sfn|Mattei|2022|pages=16–19}}

=== Imperialism, political oppression, and genocide ===

Near the start of the 20th century, [[Vladimir Lenin]] wrote that state use of military power to defend capitalist interests abroad was an inevitable corollary of monopoly capitalism.<ref name="marxists" /> He argued that capitalism needs imperialism to survive.<ref>Lenin's Selected Works, Progress Publishers, 1963, Moscow, Volume 1, pp. 667–766</ref> According to Lenin, the export of financial capital superseded the export of commodities; banking and industrial capital merged to form large financial cartels and trusts in which production and distribution are highly centralized; and [[monopoly capitalism|monopoly capitalists]] influenced state policy to carve up the world into spheres of interest. These trends led states to defend their capitalist interests abroad through military power.

According to anthropologist [[Jason Hickel]], capitalism requires the accumulation of excess wealth in the hands of economic elites for the purpose of large scale investment, continuous growth and expansion, and enormous amounts of cheap labor. As such, there was never and could never have been a gradual or peaceful transition to capitalism, and that "organized violence, mass impoverishment, and the destruction of self-sufficient subsistence economies" ushered in the capitalist era. Its emergence was fueled by [[Immiseration thesis|immiseration]] and extreme violence, including indigenous genocide, [[artificial scarcity]] and [[Famine|famines]], and mass slavery, that accompanied [[enclosure]] and [[colonization]], with colonized peoples becoming enslaved workers producing products that were then processed by European peasants, dispossessed by enclosure, who filled the factories in desperation as exploited cheap labor. Hickel adds that there was fierce resistance to these developments, as that the period 1500 to the 1800s, "right into the Industrial Revolution, was among the bloodiest, most tumultuous times in world history."<ref>{{cite book|last=Hickel|first=Jason|title=Less is More: How Degrowth Will Save the World|chapter=Capitalism: A Creation Story |year=2021|publisher=Windmill Books|pages=39–80|isbn=978-1-78609-121-5}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last = Hickel| first =Jason| title =The Divide: Global Inequality from Conquest to Free Markets|chapter=The Great Dispossession | publisher = [[W. W. Norton & Company]]| year =2018 |pages=76–82 | isbn =978-0-393-65136-2}}</ref>

Sociologist [[David Nibert]] argues that while capitalism "turned out to be every bit as violent and oppressive as the social systems dominated by the old aristocrats", it also included "an additional and pernicious peril—the necessity for continuous growth and expansion". As an example of this, Nibert points to the mass killing of [[bison hunting#19th-century bison hunts and near-extinction|millions of buffalo]] on the [[Great Plains]] and the subjugation and expulsion of the indigenous population by the U.S. military in the 19th century for the purpose of expanding ranching operations, and rearing livestock for profit.<ref>{{cite book |last= Nibert |first=David |editor1=Steven Best|editor2=Richard Kahn|editor3=Anthony J. Nocella II|editor4=Peter McLaren|editor1-link= Steven Best|editor4-link=Peter McLaren |date=2011|title=The Global Industrial Complex: Systems of Domination|chapter=Origins and Consequences of the Animal Industrial Complex |publisher=[[Rowman & Littlefield]] |pages=198–199|url= https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/global-industrial-complex-9780739136980/ |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3ZM3gTCIWb0C&pg=PA197|isbn=978-0-7391-3698-0}}</ref>

Capitalism and capitalist governments have also been criticized by socialists as [[oligarchic]] in nature,<ref>{{cite news|last=Gorman|first=Connor|date=14 January 2018|title=Guest Commentary: Capitalism is Economic Oligarchy, Socialism is Economic Democracy|url=http://www.davisvanguard.org/2018/01/guest-commentary-capitalism-economic-oligarchy-socialism-economic-democracy/|url-status=live|work=Davis Vanguard|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406144110/http://www.davisvanguard.org/2018/01/guest-commentary-capitalism-economic-oligarchy-socialism-economic-democracy/|archive-date=6 April 2018|access-date=6 April 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=O'Reilly|first=Jim|date=21 August 2016|title=Capitalism as Oligarchy: 5,000 Years of Diversion and Suppression|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GqkrvgAACAAJ|publisher=Jor|edition=1|isbn=978-0-692-51426-9|via=Google Books|access-date=6 April 2018|archive-date=27 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200727180953/https://books.google.com/books?id=GqkrvgAACAAJ|url-status=live}}</ref> due to the inevitable inequality.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Muller|first=Jerry Z.|title=Capitalism and Inequality: What the Right and the Left Get Wrong|url=https://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/2013-02-11/capitalism-and-inequality|url-access=registration|url-status=live|magazine=[[Foreign Affairs]]|type=Essay|publisher=[[Council of Foreign Relations]]|date=March–April 2013|volume=92|issue=2|issn=0015-7120|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406151044/https://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/2013-02-11/capitalism-and-inequality|archive-date=6 April 2018|access-date=6 April 2018|quote=Inequality is indeed increasing almost everywhere in the postindustrial capitalist world. But despite what many on the left think, this is not the result of politics, nor is politics likely to reverse it, for the problem is more deeply rooted and intractable than generally recognized. Inequality is an inevitable product of capitalist activity, and expanding equality of opportunity only increases it—because some individuals and communities are simply better able than others to exploit the opportunities for development and advancement that capitalism affords.}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Satherly|first=Dan|date=19 January 2015<!--Per the Newshub archive, but the oldest copy archived in Internet Archive from 11 March 2016 states 19 January-->|title=Inequality inevitable under capitalism – expert|url=https://www.newshub.co.nz/nznews/inequality-inevitable-under-capitalism---expert-2015012010|work=[[Newshub]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406153501/https://www.newshub.co.nz/nznews/inequality-inevitable-under-capitalism---expert-2015012010|archive-date=6 April 2018|access-date=6 April 2018}}</ref>

The [[military–industrial complex]], mentioned in [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]]'s presidential farewell address, appears to play a significant role in the American capitalist system. It may be one of the driving forces of American militarism and intervention abroad.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.commondreams.org/views/2016/10/25/doctrine-armed-exceptionalism|title=The Doctrine of Armed Exceptionalism|newspaper=Common Dreams|access-date=2 February 2017|language=en}}</ref> The United States has used military force and has encouraged and facilitated [[state terrorism]] and mass violence to entrench [[Neoliberalism|neoliberal]] capitalism in the [[Global South]], protect the interests of U.S. economic elites, and to crush any possible resistance to this entrenchment, especially during the [[Cold War]],<ref>{{cite book|last=Blakeley|first=Ruth|date=2009|title=State Terrorism and Neoliberalism: The North in the South|url=http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9780415462402/|publisher=[[Routledge]]|pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=rft8AgAAQBAJ&lpg=PA92&pg=PA85#v=onepage&q&f=false 85-96]|isbn=978-0-415-68617-4}}</ref><ref name="Bevins2020">{{cite book |last1=Bevins |first1=Vincent|author-link=Vincent Bevins |title=[[The Jakarta Method|The Jakarta Method: Washington's Anticommunist Crusade and the Mass Murder Program that Shaped Our World]]|date=2020 |publisher= [[PublicAffairs]]|pages=238–243|isbn= 978-1-5417-4240-6}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Prashad |first=Vijay |author-link=Vijay Prashad |date=2020 |title=Washington Bullets: A History of the CIA, Coups, and Assassinations |publisher=[[Monthly Review|Monthly Review Press]]|pages=83–88 |isbn=978-1-58367-906-7}}</ref> with significant cases being [[Military dictatorship in Brazil|Brazil]], [[Military dictatorship of Chile (1973–1990)|Chile]] and [[Transition to the New Order|Indonesia]].<ref name="Bevins2020"/><ref>[[Naomi Klein|Klein, Naomi]] (2008). ''[[The Shock Doctrine: The Rise of Disaster Capitalism]]'', [[Picador (imprint)|Picador]]. {{ISBN|0312427999}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=PwHUAq5LPOQC&pg=PA105 p. 105]</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Farid|first= Hilmar|date=2005|title=Indonesia's original sin: mass killings and capitalist expansion, 1965–66|journal=[[Inter-Asia Cultural Studies]] |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=3–16 |doi=10.1080/1462394042000326879|s2cid= 145130614}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Robinson|first=Geoffrey B.|date=2018|title=The Killing Season: A History of the Indonesian Massacres, 1965–66|url=https://press.princeton.edu/titles/11135.html|publisher=Princeton University Press|page=177|isbn=978-1-4008-8886-3}}</ref>

=== Inefficiency, irrationality, and unpredictability ===
Some opponents criticize capitalism's [[inefficiency]]. They note a shift from pre-industrial [[reuse]] and thriftiness before capitalism to a consumer-based economy that pushes "ready-made" materials.<ref name="isrwaste">{{cite web|url=http://www.isreview.org/issues/53/garbage.shtml|title=The Conquest of Garbage|last=Rogers|first=Heather|website=isreview.org|publisher=International Socialist Review (1997)|access-date=13 March 2008|archive-date=10 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210510142346/http://www.isreview.org/issues/53/garbage.shtml}}</ref> It is argued that a [[sanitation]] industry arose under capitalism that deemed trash valueless—a significant break from the past when much "waste" was used and reused almost indefinitely.<ref name="isrwaste" /> In the process, critics say, capitalism has created a profit-driven system based on selling as many products as possible.<ref name="natural">{{cite web|url=https://www.motherjones.com/news/feature/1997/03/hawken.html|title=Natural Capitalism|last=Hawken|first=Paul|access-date=13 March 2008}}</ref> Critics relate the "ready-made" trend to a growing garbage problem in which, as of 2008, 4.5&nbsp;pounds of trash are generated per person each day (compared to 2.7&nbsp;pounds in 1960).<ref name="epawaste">{{cite web|url=http://www.epa.gov/msw/facts-text.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030708002854/http://www.epa.gov/msw/facts-text.htm|archive-date=8 July 2003|title=Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) Pie Chart|last=U.S. EPA|access-date=13 March 2008}}</ref> [[Anti-capitalist]] groups with an emphasis on [[Conservation movement|conservation]] include [[eco-socialists]] and [[Social ecology (theory)|social ecologists]].

[[Planned obsolescence]] has been criticized as a wasteful practice under capitalism. By designing products to wear out faster than need be, new consumption is generated.<ref name="isrwaste" /> This would benefit corporations by increasing sales while at the same time generating excessive waste. A well-known example is the charge that Apple designed its [[iPod]] to fail after 18&nbsp;months.<ref name="ipod">{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2006/sep/30/news.consumernews|title=When your iPod isn't all that it's cracked up to be|last=Inman|first=Phillip|date=30 September 2006|access-date=13 March 2008|work=The Guardian|location=London}}</ref> Critics view planned obsolescence as wasteful and an inefficient use of resources.<ref name="obsolescence">{{cite web|url=http://www.davidmcminn.com/ngc/pages/obsol.htm|title=Planned Obsolescence: The Ultimate Economic Inefficiency|last=McMinn|first=David|access-date=13 March 2008}}</ref> Other authors such as [[Naomi Klein]] have criticized brand-based marketing for putting more emphasis on the company's name-brand than on manufacturing products.<ref name="kleininter">{{cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/persuaders/interviews/klein.html|title=Interview with Naomi Klein|last=PBS Frontline|website=[[PBS]]|date=9 November 2004|access-date=13 March 2008}}</ref>

Some economists, most notably [[Marxian economists]], argue that the system of perpetual capital accumulation leads to irrational outcomes and a misallocation of resources, as industries and jobs are created for the sake of making money rather than satisfying actual demands and needs.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BlEpAQAAMAAJ|title=Beyond the Profits System: Possibilities for a post-capitalist era|last=Shutt|first=Harry|date=2010|publisher=Zed Books|isbn=978-1-84813-417-1}}</ref>

==== Market failure ====
[[Market failure]] is a term used by economists to describe the condition where the allocation of goods and services by a market is not [[Efficiency (economics)|efficient]]. [[Keynesian economics|Keynesian economist]] [[Paul Krugman]] views this scenario in which individuals' pursuit of self-interest leads to bad results for society as a whole.<ref name="krugman">Krugman, Paul, Wells, Robin, ''Economics'', Worth Publishers, New York, (2006)</ref> [[John Maynard Keynes]] preferred [[economic interventionism]] by government to free markets.<ref name="keynes">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yVhBPgAACAAJ|title=The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money|last=Keynes|first=John Maynard|publisher=[[Palgrave Macmillan]]|year=2007|isbn=978-0-230-00476-4}}</ref> Some believe that the lack of [[perfect information]] and [[perfect competition]] in a free market is grounds for government intervention. Others perceive certain unique problems with a free market including: [[Monopoly|monopolies]], [[monopsony|monopsonies]], [[insider trading]] and [[price gouging]].<ref name="part6">{{cite web|url=http://www.chass.utoronto.ca/~reak/eco100/100_6.htm|title=Monopoly, Imperfect Competition, and Oligopoly|last=Rea|first=K.J.|access-date=11 March 2008|archive-date=12 June 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100612201706/http://www.chass.utoronto.ca/~reak/eco100/100_6.htm}}</ref>

=== Inequality ===
{{see also|Economic inequality|Social inequality}}
[[File:Day 9 Occupy Wall Street September 25 2011 Shankbone 25.JPG|thumb|A man at the protest event [[Occupy Wall Street]]]]
Critics argue that capitalism is associated with the unfair [[distribution of wealth]] and power; a tendency toward market monopoly or [[oligopoly]] (and government by [[oligarchy]]); imperialism, counter-revolutionary wars and various forms of economic and cultural exploitation; [[Political repression|repression]] of workers and [[trade union]]ists and phenomena such as [[social alienation]], economic inequality, unemployment and economic instability. Critics have argued that there is an inherent tendency toward oligopolistic structures when ''[[laissez-faire]]'' is combined with capitalist [[private property]]. Many socialists regard capitalism as irrational in that production and the direction of the economy are unplanned, creating many inconsistencies and internal contradictions, and thus should be controlled through [[competition law|public policy]].<ref>Brander, James A. Government policy toward business. 4th ed. Mississauga, Ontario: John Wiley & Sons Canada, Ltd., 2006. Print.</ref>

In the early 20th century, [[Vladimir Lenin]] argued that state use of military power to defend capitalist interests abroad was an inevitable corollary of monopoly capitalism.<ref name="marxists" />

In 2019, [[Marxian economics|Marxian Economist]] [[Richard D. Wolff]] argued that Capitalism is unstable, Capitalism is unequal, and fundamentally Undemocratic.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YJQSuUZdcV4|title=Capitalism vs. Socialism - Richard Wolff vs. Gene Epstein|website=YouTube|date=14 November 2019 |access-date= 25 Mar 2023}}</ref>

In a 1965 letter to [[Carlos Quijano]], editor of ''[[Marcha (newspaper)|Marcha]]'', a weekly newspaper published in Montevideo, Uruguay, [[Che Guevara]] wrote:
<blockquote>The laws of capitalism, which are blind and are invisible to ordinary people, act upon the individual without he or she being aware of it. One sees only the vastness of a seemingly infinite horizon ahead. That is how it is painted by capitalist propagandists who purport to draw a lesson from the example of [[John D. Rockefeller|Rockefeller]]—whether or not it is true—about the possibilities of individual success. The amount of poverty and suffering required for a [[Rockefeller family|Rockefeller]] to emerge, and the amount of depravity entailed in the accumulation of a fortune of such magnitude, are left out of the picture, and it is not always possible for the popular forces to expose this clearly.&nbsp;... It is a contest among wolves. One can win only at the cost of the failure of others.<ref name="Socialism and Man in Cuba">GUevara, Che (12 March 1965).[http://www.marxists.org/archive/guevara/1965/03/man-socialism.htm "From Algiers, for Marcha: The Cuban Revolution Today"]. Retrieved 19 August 2020.</ref></blockquote>
[[File:Total US family wealth timeline by wealth group.png|thumb|[[Wealth inequality in the United States]] increased from 1989 to 2013.<ref>{{cite news|title=Trends in Family Wealth, 1989 to 2013|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/51846|date=18 August 2016|work=[[Congressional Budget Office]]|access-date=31 July 2019|archive-date=11 November 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191111215339/https://www.cbo.gov/publication/51846|url-status=live}}</ref>]]

A modern critic of capitalism is [[Ravi Batra]], who focuses on inequality as a source of both immiserization and system failure. Batra popularised the concept "share of wealth held by the richest 1%" as an indicator of inequality and an important determinant of depressions in his best-selling books in the 1980s.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/01/06/books/best-sellers-from-1987-s-book-crop.html?pagewanted=all&src=pm|title=Best Sellers From 1987's Book Crop|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=6 January 1988 |access-date=13 October 2011|last1=McDowell |first1=Edwin }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=http://catalogue.nla.gov.au/Record/358815|title=Regular economic cycles: money, inflation, regulation and depressions, Venus Books, 1985|author=Ravi Batra|year=1990|publisher=Investment Library|isbn=978-1-86350-028-9|access-date=13 October 2011}}</ref> The scholars [[Kristen Ghodsee]] and Mitchell A. Orenstein suggest that left to its own devices, capitalism will result in a small group of economic elites capturing the majority of wealth and power in society.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ghodsee|first1=Kristen|last2=Orenstein|first2=Mitchell A.|date=2021|title=Taking Stock of Shock: Social Consequences of the 1989 Revolutions|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|page=192|doi=10.1093/oso/9780197549230.001.0001 |isbn=978-0-19-754924-7|quote=Without an accompanying welfare state in which social programs funded by a progressive income tax redistribute from the rich to the poor, capitalism can be a deeply unfair system where a small, well-connected elite captures a majority of the wealth and power, and not necessarily through meritocratic processes.}}</ref> Dylan Sullivan and [[Jason Hickel]] argue that [[poverty]] continues to exist in the contemporary global capitalist system despite it being highly productive because it is undemocratic and has maintained conditions of extreme inequality where masses of working people, who have no ownership or control over the means of production, have their labor power "appropriated by a ruling class or an external imperial power," and are cut off from common land and resources.{{sfn|Sullivan|Hickel|2023}} They further contend that capitalism needs significant levels of inequality as capital accumulation requires access to cheap labor, and lots of it, as without it the system would be crippled.<ref name="Monthly Review">{{Cite web |last1=Hickel |first1=Jason |last2=Sullivan|date=2023-07-01 |title=Capitalism, Global Poverty, and the Case for Democratic Socialism |url=https://monthlyreview.org/articles/capitalism-global-poverty-and-the-case-for-democratic-socialism/ |access-date=2025-04-28 |website=[[Monthly Review]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

Italian economist and academic [[Clara Mattei]] noted in her 2026 book ''Escape from Capitalism'' that in Mumbai's [[Dharavi]], one of the largest slums in the world, an estimated 2 million workers produce over $2 billion in wealth, with the majority of it ending up in the bank accounts of large American shareholders, and concluded that "this vast inequality illustrates the deep contradictions of our capitalist economy that must be fought."{{sfn|Mattei|2026|page=152}}

{{quote box
| quote = "Since value is produced only by workers, capitalists can extract, appropriate and accumulate the surplus part of this value only through exploitation. And exploitation, by definition, negates equality."
| source = — [[Jonathan Nitzan]] and [[Shimshon Bichler]].{{sfn|Nitzan|Bichler|2009|page=29}}
| width = 25%
| align = left
}}

In the United States, the shares of earnings and wealth of the households in the top 1 percent of the corresponding distributions are 21 percent (in 2006) and 37 percent (in 2009), respectively.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.levyinstitute.org/pubs/wp_589.pdf|title=Working Paper No. 589|publisher=Levyinstitute.org|access-date=23 February 2014}}</ref> Critics, such as Ravi Batra, argue that the capitalist system has inherent biases favoring those who already possess greater resources. The inequality may be propagated through inheritance and economic policy. Rich people are in a position to give their children a better education and inherited wealth, which can create or widen large differences in wealth between people who do not differ in ability or effort. One study shows that in the United States, 43.35% of the people in the ''[[Forbes]]'' magazine "400 richest individuals" list were already rich enough at birth to qualify.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.faireconomy.org/press/archive/Pre_1999/forbes_400_study.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060828223407/http://www.faireconomy.org/press/archive/Pre_1999/forbes_400_study.html|title=UFE - Press Room: BORN ON THIRD BASE: The Sources of Wealth of the 1996 Forbes 400|archive-date=28 August 2006|website=www.faireconomy.org}}</ref> Another study indicated that in the United States wealth, race and schooling are important to the inheritance of economic status, but that IQ is not a major contributor and the genetic transmission of IQ is even less important.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.umass.edu/preferen/gintis/intergen.pdf|title=The Inheritance of Inequality|access-date=23 February 2014}}</ref> Batra has argued that the tax and benefit legislation in the United States since the [[Presidency of Ronald Reagan|Reagan presidency]] has contributed greatly to the inequalities and economic problems and should be repealed.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.truth-out.org/occupy-wall-street-movement-and-coming-demise-crony-capitalism/1318341474|title="The Occupy Wall Street Movement and the Coming Demise of Crony Capitalism", ''Foreign Affairs'', October 11, 2011|author=Ravi Batra|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111013183247/http://www.truth-out.org/occupy-wall-street-movement-and-coming-demise-crony-capitalism/1318341474|archive-date=13 October 2011|access-date=13 October 2011}}</ref>

According to sociologist Thomas Volscho, the [[neoliberal]] revolution starting in the late 1970s resulted from a [[class conflict]] in which the [[Powell Memorandum|political mobilizations]] of an increasingly class-conscious capitalist elite "against the New Deal of the 1930s, War on Poverty programs from the 1960s, and the power of organized labor" dramatically increased both the political power of [[Wall Street]] and [[economic inequality]].{{sfn|Volscho|2015}}

=== {{Visible anchor|Market instability}} ===
Critics of capitalism, particularly Marxists, identify market instability as a permanent feature of the capitalist economy.<ref name="onfreetrade">{{cite web|url=http://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1888/free-trade/index.htm|title=On the Question of Free Trade|last=Engels|first=Frederick|access-date=11 March 2008}}</ref><ref name="isrcrisis">{{cite web|url=http://www.isreview.org/issues/32/crisis_theory.shtml|title=Marx's Theory of Economic Crisis|last=Easterling|first=Earl|publisher=International Socialist Review|access-date=13 March 2008|archive-date=27 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210227033442/https://isreview.org/issues/32/crisis_theory.shtml}}</ref> Marx believed that the unplanned and explosive growth of capitalism does not occur in a smooth manner, but is interrupted by periods of overproduction in which stagnation or decline occur (i.e. [[recessions]]).<ref name="communistmanifesto">{{cite web|url=http://marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1848/communist-manifesto/index.htm|title=The Communist Manifesto|last=Marx|first=Karl|access-date=11 March 2008}}</ref> In the view of Marxists, several contradictions in the capitalist [[mode of production]] are present, particularly the internal contradiction between anarchy in the sphere of capital (i.e. [[free market]]) and socialised production in the sphere of labor (i.e. [[industrialism]]).<ref name="anti-duhring">{{cite web|url=http://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1877/anti-duhring/ch24.htm|title=Part III: Socialism (Theoretical) – Anti-Duhring|last=Engels|first=Frederick|access-date=11 March 2008}}</ref> In ''[[The Communist Manifesto]]'', Marx and Engels highlighted what they saw as a uniquely capitalist juxtaposition of overabundance and poverty: "Society suddenly finds itself put back into a state of momentary barbarism. And why? Because there is too much civilization, too much means of subsistence, too much industry, too much commerce".<ref name="communistmanifesto" />

Some scholars blame the [[2008 financial crisis]] on the neoliberal capitalist model.{{refn|<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lavoie |first=Marc |title=Financialization, neo-liberalism, and securitization |journal=Journal of Post Keynesian Economics |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=215–233 |jstor=23469991 |date=Winter 2012–2013 |doi=10.2753/pke0160-3477350203|s2cid=153927517 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last= Stein|first=Howard|s2cid=26437908|date=25 July 2012|title=The Neoliberal Policy Paradigm and the Great Recession|journal=Panoeconomicus|volume=59 |issue= 4|pages= 421–440|doi=10.2298/PAN1204421S|quote=The role of deregulation and related neoliberal policies as a both a source of massive financialization of the economy and cause of the Great Recession is widely recognized in the literature (David M. Kotz 2009; Bill Lucarelli 2009; Joseph Stiglitz 2010; William Tabb 2012). Some authors aptly call it the 'crisis of neoliberal capitalism' (Kotz 2010).|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>Susan Braedley and Meg Luxton, ''[http://www.mqup.ca/neoliberalism-and-everyday-life-products-9780773536739.php Neoliberalism and Everyday Life] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141113184415/http://www.mqup.ca/neoliberalism-and-everyday-life-products-9780773536739.php |date=13 November 2014 }}'' ([[McGill-Queen's University Press]], 2010), {{ISBN|0773536922}}, [https://books.google.com/books?id=CvD-6GQWr04C&pg=PA3 p. 3] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150319082754/http://books.google.com/books?id=CvD-6GQWr04C&lpg=PP1&pg=PA3 |date=19 March 2015 }}</ref><ref>[[Manfred B. Steger]] and Ravi K. Roy. ''[https://global.oup.com/academic/product/neoliberalism-a-very-short-introduction-9780199560516?cc=us&# Neoliberalism: A Very Short Introduction]''. ([[Oxford University Press]], 2010.) {{ISBN|019956051X}}. p. 123.</ref><ref>[[Gérard Duménil]] and Dominique Lévy, [http://www.hup.harvard.edu/catalog.php?isbn=9780674072244 ''The Crisis of Neoliberalism''], {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161009082937/http://www.hup.harvard.edu/catalog.php?isbn=9780674072244 |date=9 October 2016 }} ([[Harvard University Press]], 2013), {{ISBN|0674072243}}</ref><ref>David M Kotz, ''[https://www.hup.harvard.edu/catalog.php?isbn=9780674980013 The Rise and Fall of Neoliberal Capitalism] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200212170646/https://www.hup.harvard.edu/catalog.php?isbn=978-0674980013 |date=12 February 2020 }}'' ([[Harvard University Press]], 2015), {{ISBN|0674725654}}</ref>}} Following the banking crisis of 2007, economist and former Chair of the [[Federal Reserve]], [[Alan Greenspan]] told the United States Congress on 23 October 2008 that "[t]his modern risk-management paradigm held sway for decades. The whole intellectual edifice, however, collapsed in the summer of last year",<ref>{{cite news|last=Andrews|first=Edmund L.|author-link=Edmund L. Andrews|date=23 October 2008|title=Greenspan Concedes Error on Regulation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/10/24/business/economy/24panel.html|url-status=live|department=Economy|work=The New York Times|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406173958/https://www.nytimes.com/2008/10/24/business/economy/24panel.html|archive-date=6 April 2018|access-date=6 April 2018|quote=He noted that the immense and largely unregulated business of spreading financial risk widely, through the use of exotic financial instruments called [[Derivative (finance)|derivatives]], had gotten out of control and had added to the havoc of today's crisis. As far back as 1994, Mr. Greenspan staunchly and successfully opposed tougher regulation on derivatives. But on Thursday, he agreed that the multitrillion-dollar market for [[credit default swap]]s, instruments originally created to insure bond investors against the risk of default, needed to be restrained. 'This modern risk-management paradigm held sway for decades,' he said. 'The whole intellectual edifice, however, collapsed in the summer of last year.'}}</ref> and that "I made a mistake in presuming that the self-interests of organizations, specifically banks and others, were such that they were best capable of protecting their own shareholders and their equity in firms&nbsp;... I was shocked".<ref>{{cite news|last1=Knowlton|first1=Brian|last2=Grynbaum|first2=Michael M.|date=23 October 2008|title=Greenspan 'shocked' that free markets are flawed|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/10/23/business/worldbusiness/23iht-gspan.4.17206624.html|url-status=live|department=International Business|work=The New York Times|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406175418/https://www.nytimes.com/2008/10/23/business/worldbusiness/23iht-gspan.4.17206624.html|archive-date=6 April 2018|access-date=6 April 2018|quote=Pressed by [[Henry Waxman|Waxman]], Greenspan conceded a more serious flaw in his own philosophy that unfettered free markets sit at the root of a superior economy. 'I made a mistake in presuming that the self-interests of organizations, specifically banks and others, were such as that they were best capable of protecting their own shareholders and their equity in the firms,' Greenspan said.&nbsp;... 'In other words, you found that your view of the world, your ideology, was not right, it was not working,' Waxman said. 'Absolutely, precisely,' Greenspan replied. "You know, that's precisely the reason I was shocked, because I have been going for 40 years or more with very considerable evidence that it was working exceptionally well.'}}</ref>

=== Property ===
[[Pierre-Joseph Proudhon]] and [[Friedrich Engels]] argue that the [[free market]] is not necessarily free, but weighted towards those who already own private property.<ref name="histmaterial"/><ref name="propertytheft">{{cite web|url=http://www.marxists.org/reference/subject/economics/proudhon/property/index.htm|title=What Is Property? An Inquiry Into the Principle of Right and Government|last=Proudhon|first=Pierre-Joseph|access-date=10 March 2008}}</ref> They view capitalist regulations, including the enforcement of [[private property]] on land and exclusive rights to natural resources, as unjustly [[Enclosure|enclosing]] upon what should be owned by all, forcing those without private property to sell their labor to capitalists and landlords in a market favorable to the latter, thus forcing workers to accept low wages to survive.<ref name="meaningmarx">{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/meaningofmarxism00dama|url-access=registration|title=The Meaning of Marxism|last=D'Amato|first=Paul|publisher=[[Haymarket Books]]|year=2006|isbn=978-1-931859-29-5|page=[https://archive.org/details/meaningofmarxism00dama/page/60 60]}}</ref> In his criticism of capitalism, Proudhon believed that the emphasis on private property is the problem. He argued that [[property is theft]], arguing that private property leads to despotism: "Now, property necessarily engenders despotism—the government of caprice, the reign of libidinous pleasure. That is so clearly the essence of property that, to be convinced of it, one need but remember what it is, and observe what happens around him. Property is the right to use and abuse".<ref name="propertytheft" /> Many left-wing anarchists, such as [[anarchist communist]]s, believe in replacing capitalist private property with a system where people can lay claim to things based on personal use and claim that "[private] property is the domination of an individual, or a coalition of individuals, over things; it is not the claim of any person or persons to the use of things" and "this is, usufruct, a very different matter. Property means the monopoly of wealth, the right to prevent others using it, whether the owner needs it or not".<ref>''Anarchist Essays'', pp. 22–23, 40. Freedom Press, London, 2000.</ref>

[[Mutualism (economic theory)|Mutualists]] and some anarchists support markets and private property, but not in their present form.<ref name="mutualiststudy">{{Cite book|title=Studies in Mutualist Political Economy|last=Carson|first=Kevin|publisher=BookSurge Publishing|year=2007|isbn=978-1-4196-5869-3}}</ref> They argue that particular aspects of modern capitalism violate the ability of individuals to trade in the absence of coercion. Mutualists support markets and private property in the product of labor, but only when these markets guarantee that workers [[worker cooperative|will realize for themselves]] the value of their labor.<ref name="propertytheft"/>

In recent times, most economies have extended private property rights to include such things as [[patents]] and [[copyrights]]. Critics see these so-called [[intellectual property]] laws as coercive against those with few prior resources. They argue that such regulations discourage the sharing of ideas and encourage nonproductive [[rent seeking]] behavior, both of which impose a [[deadweight loss]] on the economy and erect a prohibitive barrier to market entry.<ref name="copyright">{{cite web|url=http://cyber.law.harvard.edu/IPCoop/89land1.html|title=An Economic Analysis of Property Law|last1=Landes|first1=William M.|last2=Posner|first2=Richard A.|access-date=10 March 2008}}</ref> Not all pro-capitalists support the concept of copyrights, but those who do argue that compensation to the creator is necessary as an incentive.<ref name="copyright"/>

=== Environmental sustainability ===
{{see also|Degrowth|Steady-state economy}}
[[File:Gullfaks Alpha.jpg|thumb|[[Gullfaks oil field]] in the North Sea. As petroleum is a [[non-renewable resource|non-renewable natural resource]], the industry is faced with an inevitable eventual depletion of the world's oil supply.]]
Many aspects of capitalism have come under attack from the [[anti-globalization movement]], which is primarily opposed to [[corporate capitalism]]. [[Environmentalist]]s and scholars have argued that capitalism requires continual [[economic growth]] and that it will inevitably deplete Earth's finite natural resources and cause [[Holocene extinction|mass extinctions]] of animal and plant life.<ref>{{cite book|last=Hickel|first=Jason|author-link=Jason Hickel|title=Less is More: How Degrowth Will Save the World |year=2021|publisher=Windmill Books|pages=19–23|isbn=978-1-78609-121-5}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last = McMurty |first = John |title = The Cancer Stage of Capitalism |publisher = Pluto Press |year = 1999 |isbn = 978-0-7453-1347-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/georgemonbiot/2014/oct/01/george-monbiot-war-on-the-living-world-wildlife|title=It's time to shout stop on this war on the living world|last=Monbiot|first=George|author-link=George Monbiot|date=1 October 2014|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406160337/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/georgemonbiot/2014/oct/01/george-monbiot-war-on-the-living-world-wildlife|archive-date=6 April 2018|url-status=live|access-date=6 April 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Dawson|first=Ashley|author-link=Ashley Dawson|title=Extinction: A Radical History|date=2016|publisher=[[OR Books]]|url=http://www.orbooks.com/catalog/extinction-by-ashley-dawson/|page=41|isbn=978-1-944869-01-4|access-date=20 August 2016|archive-date=17 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160917203814/http://www.orbooks.com/catalog/extinction-by-ashley-dawson/|url-status=live}}</ref> Such critics argue that while [[neoliberalism]], the ideological backbone of contemporary globalized capitalism, has indeed increased global trade, it has also destroyed traditional ways of life, exacerbated inequality, increased global [[poverty]], and that environmental indicators indicate massive [[environmental degradation]] since the late 1970s.<ref name="Duménil">{{cite interview|last=Gérard|first=Duménil|subject-link=Gérard Duménil|interviewer=Paul Jay|type=Transcript|title=The crisis of neoliberalism|url=https://therealnews.com/stories/gdumenilneolib0216pt1|publisher=[[The Real News]]|date=30 March 2010|access-date=6 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406160817/https://therealnews.com/t2/index.php?Itemid=74&id=31&jumival=4962&option=com_content&task=view|archive-date=6 April 2018|url-status=live|quote=When we speak of neoliberalism, we speak of contemporary capitalism. Neoliberalism, it's a new stage of capitalism which began around 1980. It began in big countries like United Kingdom and the United States. Then it was implemented in Europe, and later in Japan, and later around the world in general. So this is a new phase of capitalism.}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Jones|first1=Campbell|last2=Parker|first2=Martin|last3=Ten Bos|first3= Rene|date= 2005|title=For Business Ethics |url= |location= |publisher=[[Routledge]] |page=101 |isbn=978-0-415-31135-9}}</ref><ref>Stephen Haymes, Maria Vidal de Haymes and Reuben Miller (eds), [http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9780415673440/ ''The Routledge Handbook of Poverty in the United States''], {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150617164555/http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9780415673440/ |date=17 June 2015 }} (London: Routledge, 2015), {{ISBN|0415673445}}, [https://books.google.com/books?id=qnHfBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA1 pp. 1–2] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200727162556/https://books.google.com/books?id=qnHfBQAAQBAJ&lpg=PP1&pg=PA1 |date=27 July 2020 }}.</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Udland|first=Myles|date=27 May 2016|title=IMF: The last generation of economic policies may have been a complete failure|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/imf-neoliberalism-warnings-2016-5|url-status=live|work=[[Business Insider]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406161633/https://www.businessinsider.com/imf-neoliberalism-warnings-2016-5|archive-date=6 April 2018|access-date=6 April 2018|quote=Neoliberalism—which IMF researchers Jonathan Ostry, Prakash Loungani, and Davide Furceri loosely define as the opening of economies to foreign capital along with a reduction in government debt burdens—has been the dominant trend in economic policymaking over the past 30 years.&nbsp;... But now it seems some at the IMF aren't so sure this tradition is all it's been cracked up to be. In their paper, Ostray, Loungani, and Furceri argue that these goals have both hampered the economic growth that neoliberalism champions and exacerbated the rise of inequality.}}</ref>
[[File:Climate Crisis National Day of Action Melbourne (49574102132).jpg|alt=Placard saying "capitalism equals climate crisis" at a demonstration.|thumb|A placard criticising capitalism held by a [[Climate change protests in Australia|climate change protester in Australia]]]]

Some scholars argue that the capitalist approach to [[environmental economics]] does not take into consideration the preservation of natural resources<ref>{{cite journal|last=Castro|first=Carlos J.|date=June 2004|title= Sustainable Development|journal=Organization & Environment|volume=17|issue=2|pages=195–225|doi=10.1177/1086026604264910|s2cid=143645829|issn=1086-0266}}</ref> and that capitalism creates three ecological problems: growth, technology, and consumption.<ref name="Jones 54–73">{{Cite journal|last=Jones|first=Andrew W.|date=March 2011|title=Solving the Ecological Problems of Capitalism: Capitalist and Socialist Possibilities|journal=Organization & Environment|language=en|volume=24|issue=1|pages=54–73|doi=10.1177/1086026611402010|bibcode=2011OrgEn..24...54J |s2cid=154749910|issn=1086-0266}}</ref> The growth problem results from the nature of capitalism, as it focuses around the pursuit of limitless [[economic growth]] and the accumulation of capital.<ref name="Jones 54–73" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bell |first1=Karen |title=Can the capitalist economic system deliver environmental justice? |journal=[[Environmental Research Letters]] |date=2015 |volume=10 |issue=12 |article-number=125017 |doi=10.1088/1748-9326/10/12/125017 |bibcode=2015ERL....10l5017B |doi-access=free|hdl=1983/5c7c9d17-dec3-4182-9d35-5efd75830ac8 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> The innovation of new technologies has an impact on the environmental future as they serve as a capitalist tool in which environmental technologies can result in the expansion of the system.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Harris|first=Jerry|date=1 January 2014|title=Can Green Capitalism Build a Sustainable Society?*|journal=Perspectives on Global Development and Technology|volume=13|issue=1–2|pages=43–60|doi=10.1163/15691497-12341288|issn=1569-1500}}</ref> Consumption is focused around the capital accumulation of commodities<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Koutoufaris-Malandrinos |first=Jason |date=2020-04-01 |title=Society as an accumulation of commodities |url=https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.4674264 |language=en |doi=10.5281/ZENODO.4674264}}</ref> and neglects the use-value of production.<ref name="Jones 54–73" /> Professor Radhika Desai, director of the Geopolitical Economy Research Group at the [[University of Manitoba]], contends that ecological crises such as [[climate change]], [[pollution]] and [[biodiversity loss]] occur when "capitalist firms compete to appropriate and plunder the free resources of nature and when this very appropriation and plunder forces working people to overexploit their ever-shrinking share of these resources."<ref>{{cite book |last=Desai|first=Radhika |date=2022 |title=Capitalism, Coronavirus and War: A Geopolitical Economy|location=|url=|publisher=[[Routledge]]|page=53|isbn=978-1-032-05950-1|doi=10.4324/9781003200000-2|s2cid=|quote=Ecological crises occur when capitalist firms compete to appropriate and plunder the free resources of nature and when this very appropriation and plunder forces working people to overexploit their ever-shrinking share of these resources leading to climate change, pollution and biodiversity loss.}}</ref>

One of the main modern criticisms of the [[sustainability]] of capitalism concerns the so-called commodity chains, or production/consumption chains.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.it-environment.org/publications/QITS%20report.pdf|title=de beste bron van informatie over it-environment. Deze website is te koop!|publisher=it-environment.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121202211947/http://www.it-environment.org/publications/QITS%20report.pdf|archive-date=2 December 2012|access-date=23 February 2014}}</ref><ref name="unpop">{{cite web|url=http://www.unpop.nl/inhoud/artikelen/Francken%20CRR%20sept%202006%20dublin.ppt|title=Geregistreerd via Argeweb|publisher=Unpop.nl|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928161519/http://www.unpop.nl/inhoud/artikelen/Francken%20CRR%20sept%202006%20dublin.ppt|archive-date=28 September 2007|access-date=11 January 2014}}</ref> These terms refer to the network of transfers of materials and commodities that is currently part of the functioning of the global capitalist system. Examples include high tech commodities produced in countries with low average wages by multinational firms and then being sold in distant high income countries; materials and resources being extracted in some countries, turned into finished products in some others and sold as commodities in further ones; and countries exchanging with each other the same kind of commodities for the sake of consumers' choice (e.g. Europe both exporting and importing cars to and from the United States). According to critics, such processes, all of which produce pollution and waste of resources, are an integral part of the functioning of capitalism (i.e., its "[[metabolism]]").<ref name="unu">{{cite web|url=http://www.unu.edu/unupress/unupbooks/80841e/80841E00.htm#Contents|title=Industrial metabolism: Restructuring for sustainable development|publisher=unu.edu|access-date=11 January 2014}}</ref>

Critics note that the statistical methods used in calculating [[ecological footprint]] have been criticized; some find the whole concept of counting how much land is used to be flawed, arguing that there is nothing intrinsically negative about using more land to improve living standards (rejection of the [[Intrinsicism|intrinsic]] value of nature).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://econpapers.repec.org/scripts/redir.pl?u=http://www.tinbergen.nl/discussionpapers/98105.pdf;h=repec:dgr:uvatin:19980105|title=EconPapers: Spatial Sustainability, Trade and Indicators|author=Jeroen C.J.M. van den Bergh and Harmen Verbruggen|date=28 September 1998|publisher=Econpapers.repec.org|access-date=18 January 2014}}{{Dead link|date=July 2019|bot=InternetArchiveBot|fix-attempted=yes}}</ref><ref name="usc">{{cite web|url=http://www-pam.usc.edu/volume1/v1i1a2print.html|title=Planning and Markets: Peter Gordon and Harry W. Richardson|publisher=-pam.usc.edu|access-date=11 January 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100627044350/http://www-pam.usc.edu/volume1/v1i1a2print.html|archive-date=27 June 2010}}</ref>

Under what anti-capitalists such as [[Murray Bookchin]] call the "grow or die" imperative of capitalism, they say there is little reason to expect hazardous consumption and production practices to change promptly. They also claim that markets and states invariably drag their feet on substantive environmental reform and are notoriously slow to adopt viable sustainable technologies.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.social-ecology.org/article.php?story=20031118113538865|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051225001752/http://www.social-ecology.org/article.php?story=20031118113538865|title=Institute for Social Ecology - What Is Social Ecology?|archive-date=25 December 2005|website=www.social-ecology.org}}</ref><ref name="monthlyreview">{{cite web|url=https://monthlyreview.org/articles/capitalisms-environmental-crisis-is-technology-the-answer/|title=Capitalism's Environmental Crisis – Is Technology the Answer?|date=December 2000|publisher=monthlyreview.org|access-date=11 January 2014}}</ref> [[Immanuel Wallerstein]], referring to the externalization of costs as the "dirty secret" of capitalism, claims that there are built-in limits to ecological reform and that the costs of doing business in the world capitalist economy are ratcheting upward because of deruralization and democratization.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://fbc.binghamton.edu:80/iwecol.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060128132537/http://fbc.binghamton.edu/iwecol.htm|title=I. Wallerstein, "Ecology and Capitalist Costs ofProduction: No Exit"|archive-date=28 January 2006|website=fbc.binghamton.edu}}</ref>

A team of Finnish scientists hired by the UN Secretary-General to aid the 2019 Global Sustainable Development Report asserts that capitalism as we know it is moribund, primarily because it focuses on short-term profits and fails to look after the long-term needs of people and the environment, which is being subjected to unsustainable exploitation. Their report goes on to link many seemingly disparate contemporary crises to this system, including environmental factors such as [[global warming]] and accelerated [[Holocene extinction|species extinctions]] and also societal factors such as rising [[economic inequality]], [[unemployment]], sluggish economic growth, rising debt levels, and impuissant governments unable to deal with these problems. The scientists say a new economic model, one which focuses on sustainability and efficiency and not profit and growth, will be needed as decades of robust economic growth driven by abundant resources and cheap energy are rapidly coming to a close.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/scientists-warn-the-un-of-capitalisms-imminent-demise/|title=Scientists Warn the UN of Capitalism's Imminent Demise|last=Ahmed|first=Nafeez|date=27 August 2018|work=Vice|access-date=30 August 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/entry/climate-change-capitalism-economy_us_5b87bf0ce4b0cf7b00326edc|title=We Cannot Fight Climate Change With Capitalism, Says Report|last=Paddison|first=Laura|date=31 August 2018|work=The Huffington Post|access-date=2 September 2018}}</ref> Another group of scientists contributing to the 2020 "Scientists warning on affluence" argue that a shift away from paradigms fixating on economic growth and the "profit-driven mechanism of prevailing economic systems" will be necessary to mitigate [[human impacts on the environment]], and suggest a range of ideas from the reformist to the radical, with the latter consisting of [[degrowth]], [[eco-socialism]] and [[eco-anarchism]].{{sfn|Wiedmann|Lenzen|Keyßer|Steinberger|2020}}

Some scientists contend that the rise of capitalism, which itself developed out of European [[imperialism]] and [[colonialism]] of the 15th and 16th centuries, marks the emergence of the [[Anthropocene]] epoch, in which human beings started to have significant and mostly negative impacts on the earth system.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Maslin|first1=Mark|last2=Lewis|first2=Simon|date=25 June 2020|title=Why the Anthropocene began with European colonisation, mass slavery and the 'great dying' of the 16th century|url=http://theconversation.com/why-the-anthropocene-began-with-european-colonisation-mass-slavery-and-the-great-dying-of-the-16th-century-140661|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200910163239/https://theconversation.com/why-the-anthropocene-began-with-european-colonisation-mass-slavery-and-the-great-dying-of-the-16th-century-140661|archive-date=10 September 2020|access-date=25 August 2020|website=[[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]]|language=en}}</ref> Others have warned that contemporary global capitalism "requires fundamental changes" to mitigate the worst environmental impacts, including the "abolition of perpetual economic growth, properly pricing [[Externality|externalities]], a rapid exit from fossil-fuel use, strict regulation of markets and property acquisition, reining in corporate lobbying, and the empowerment of women".<ref>{{cite news |last= Weston |first=Phoebe |date=13 January 2021 |title=Top scientists warn of 'ghastly future of mass extinction' and climate disruption |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2021/jan/13/top-scientists-warn-of-ghastly-future-of-mass-extinction-and-climate-disruption-aoe |work=[[The Guardian]] |location= |access-date=13 January 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bradshaw |first1=Corey J. A. |last2=Ehrlich |first2=Paul R. |last3=Beattie |first3=Andrew |last4=Ceballos |first4=Gerardo |last5=Crist |first5=Eileen |last6=Diamond |first6=Joan |last7=Dirzo |first7=Rodolfo |last8=Ehrlich |first8=Anne H. |last9=Harte |first9=John |last10=Harte |first10=Mary Ellen |last11=Pyke |first11=Graham |last12=Raven |first12=Peter H. |last13=Ripple |first13=William J. |last14=Saltré |first14=Frédérik |last15=Turnbull |first15=Christine |last16=Wackernagel |first16=Mathis |last17=Blumstein |first17=Daniel T. |date=2021 |title=Underestimating the Challenges of Avoiding a Ghastly Future |journal=Frontiers in Conservation Science |volume=1 |issue= |article-number=615419 |doi=10.3389/fcosc.2020.615419 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2021FrCS....1.5419B }}</ref> [[Jason Hickel]] writes that capitalism creates pressures for [[population growth]]: "more people means more labour, cheaper labour, and more consumers." He argues that continued population growth makes the challenge of sustainability even more difficult, but adds that even if the population leveled off, capitalism would get existing consumers to increase their consumption, as consumption rates have always outpaced population growth.<ref>{{cite book|last=Hickel|first=Jason|author-link=Jason Hickel|title=Less is More: How Degrowth Will Save the World |year=2021|publisher=Windmill Books|pages=110–111|isbn=978-1-78609-121-5}}</ref>

In 2024 a group of experts including [[Michael E. Mann]] and [[Naomi Oreskes]] published "An urgent call to end the age of destruction and forge a just and sustainable future". They conducted an extensive review of the existing scientific literature on the issue. They blamed the ecological crisis on "imperialism, extractive capitalism, and a surging population". They proposed a paradigm shift that replaces it with a socio-economic model prioritizing sustainability, resilience, justice, kinship with nature, and communal well-being. They described many ways to achieve the transition.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Earth at risk: An urgent call to end the age of destruction and forge a just and sustainable future |journal=PNAS Nexus |date=4 April 2024 |volume=3 |issue=4 |doi=10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae106  |doi-access=free|url=https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/3/4/pgae106/7638480?login=false |access-date=4 April 2024|pmc=10986754 |last1=Fletcher |first1=Charles |last2=Ripple |first2=William J. |last3=Newsome |first3=Thomas |last4=Barnard |first4=Phoebe |last5=Beamer |first5=Kamanamaikalani |last6=Behl |first6=Aishwarya |last7=Bowen |first7=Jay |last8=Cooney |first8=Michael |last9=Crist |first9=Eileen |last10=Field |first10=Christopher |last11=Hiser |first11=Krista |last12=Karl |first12=David M. |last13=King |first13=David A. |last14=Mann |first14=Michael E. |last15=McGregor |first15=Davianna P. |last16=Mora |first16=Camilo |last17=Oreskes |first17=Naomi |last18=Wilson |first18=Michael |article-number=pgae106 |pmid=38566756 }}</ref>

=== Profit motive ===
The majority of criticisms of the [[profit motive]] centre on the idea that it encourages [[selfishness]] and [[greed]], rather than serving the public good or necessarily increasing net wealth. Critics of the profit motive argue that companies disregard morals or public safety in the pursuit of profits. Capitalist firms seek to reduce spending to increase profits, often at the expense of workers, such as cutting wages, deskilling workers, mechanizing tasks and reducing workers to interchangeable parts, and [[Layoff|downsizing]], which causes [[unemployment]]. The reason the profit motive is harmful is the fundamental contradiction between the interests of capitalists and workers: capitalists want to pay their workers as little as possible and make them work as much as possible to increase profits. In contrast, workers want to be paid fairly and have their increased productivity result in fewer working hours. This fundamental contradiction, critics argue, shows how illogical capitalism is, as it is a system in which two classes have fundamentally opposite interests which create conflict.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/budding-wall-street-movement-gives-voice-to-anger-over-greed-corporations|title='Occupy Wall Street' Protests Give Voice to Anger Over Greed, Corporate Culture|date=5 October 2011|department=[[PBS NewsHour]]|publisher=PBS|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406122942/https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/budding-wall-street-movement-gives-voice-to-anger-over-greed-corporations|archive-date=6 April 2018|url-status=live|access-date=6 April 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/business/archive/2014/04/greed-is-good-a-300-year-history-of-a-dangerous-idea/360265/|title=Greed is Good: A 300-Year History of a Dangerous Idea|last=Rollert|first=John Paul|date=7 April 2014|website=The Atlantic|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406121500/https://www.theatlantic.com/business/archive/2014/04/greed-is-good-a-300-year-history-of-a-dangerous-idea/360265/|archive-date=6 April 2018|url-status=live|access-date=6 April 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Szalavitz|first=Maia|date=28 February 2012|title=Why the Rich Are Less Ethical: They See Greed as Good|url=https://healthland.time.com/2012/02/28/why-the-rich-are-less-ethical-they-see-greed-as-good/|department=Healthland|magazine=Time|access-date=6 April 2018|archive-date=6 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406121846/http://healthland.time.com/2012/02/28/why-the-rich-are-less-ethical-they-see-greed-as-good/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Why Greed Begets More Greed|last=Norton|first=Michael I.|author-link=Michael Norton (professor)|date=1 March 2014|journal=Scientific American|volume=25|issue=2|pages=24–25|doi=10.1038/scientificamericanmind0314-24}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last= Anderson|first=Elizabeth|author-link=Elizabeth S. Anderson|date=2023 |title=Hijacked: How Neoliberalism Turned the Work Ethic against Workers and How Workers Can Take It Back|location= |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|page=269|url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Hijacked/r9PQEAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PA269&printsec=frontcover|isbn= 978-1-009-27543-9}}</ref>

Recently, a compelling criticism of unmoderated capitalism has emerged: it prioritizes capital over human well-being, except where human well-being contributes to capital production. Critics argue that such a system tends to reward sociopathic behavior. Consequently, they contend that pure (unmoderated) capitalism is inherently unsuitable as a foundation for society. As pure capitalistic models develop, they foster an increase in sociopathic behavior, which ultimately degrades societal functioning, defined by the well-being of most of its members. The detrimental processes associated with excessive sociopathic behavior include the spread of disinformation, the implementation of policies that create severe economic inequalities, and the manipulation of legal and judicial systems to benefit capital flow without regard for the majority's welfare. In response to this criticism, some advocate for a moderated capitalism that promotes policies valuing human well-being. This approach creates reward structures that are not solely tied to capital. However, one counterargument is that in a global society with diverse economic models, pure capitalism might prevail over moderated capitalism in the long run because it generates more economic power.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Piketty |first=Thomas |title=Capital in the Twenty-First Century |publisher=Harvard University Press |year=2014 |isbn=978-0-674-43000-6 |location=Cambridge, MA |page= }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Wilkinson |first1=Richard |last2=Pickett |first2=Kate |title=The Spirit Level: Why More Equal Societies Almost Always Do Better |publisher=Allen Lane |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-84614-039-6 |location=London |page= }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Bakan |first=Joel |title=The Corporation: The Pathological Pursuit of Profit and Power |publisher=Free Press |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-7432-4746-7 |location=New York, NY |page= }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Chomsky |first=Noam |title=Profit Over People: Neoliberalism and Global Order |publisher=Seven Stories Press |year=1999 |isbn=978-1-888363-82-1 |location=New York, NY |page= }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Stiglitz |first=Joseph E. |title=The Price of Inequality: How Today's Divided Society Endangers Our Future |publisher=W.W. Norton & Company |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-393-08869-4 |location=New York, NY |page= }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Rodrik |first=Dani |title=The Globalization Paradox: Democracy and the Future of the World Economy |publisher=W.W. Norton & Company |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-393-07161-0 |location=New York, NY |page= }}</ref>

=== Comparison to slavery ===
{{Main|Critique of work|Wage slavery|Refusal of work}}

[[File:Pinkerton escorts hocking valley leslies.jpg|thumb|[[Pinkerton National Detective Agency|Pinkerton guards]] escort strikebreakers in [[Buchtel, Ohio]], 1884.]]
Wage labor has long been compared to slavery.<ref>''The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia''. Geoffrey W. Bromiley. Wm. B. Eerdmans Publishing, 1995. {{ISBN|0802837840}}. p. 543.</ref> As a result, the phrase "[[Labour economics#Wage slavery|wage slavery]]" is often utilized as a pejorative for wage labor.<ref>{{Harvnb|Roediger|2007a}}.<br />The term is not without its critics, as {{Harvnb|Roediger|2007b|p=247}}, notes: "[T]he challenge to loose connections of wage (or white) slavery to chattel slavery was led by [[Frederick Douglass]] and other Black, often fugitive, abolitionists. Their challenge was mercilessly concrete. Douglass, who tried out speeches in workplaces before giving them in halls, was far from unable to speak to or hear white workers, but he and [[William Wells Brown]] did sharply challenge metaphors of white slavery. They noted, for example, that their escapes from slavery had left job openings and wondered if any white workers wanted to take the jobs."</ref> Similarly, advocates of slavery looked upon the "comparative evils of Slave Society and of Free Society, of slavery to human Masters and slavery to Capital"<ref name="Fitzhugh 1857 xvi">{{Harvnb|Fitzhugh|1857|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=ECdb7EjiBnEC&pg=PR16 xvi]}}</ref> and proceeded to argue that wage slavery was actually worse than [[chattel slavery]].<ref>{{Harvnb|Carsel|1940}}.</ref> Slavery apologists like [[George Fitzhugh]] contended that workers only accepted wage labor with the passage of time as they became "familiarised and inattentive to the infected social atmosphere they continually inhale".<ref name="Fitzhugh 1857 xvi" /> Scholars have debated the exact relationship between wage labor, slavery, and capitalism at length, especially for the [[Antebellum South]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://networks.h-net.org/node/11465/pages/76870/capitalism-and-slavery-united-states-topical-guide|title=Capitalism and Slavery in the United States (Topical Guide)|last=Leccese|first=Stephen R.|date=28 July 2015|publisher=[[H-Net]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406205713/https://networks.h-net.org/node/11465/pages/76870/capitalism-and-slavery-united-states-topical-guide|archive-date=6 April 2018|url-status=live|access-date=6 April 2018}}</ref>

With the advent of the [[Industrial Revolution]], thinkers such as [[Pierre-Joseph Proudhon]] and [[Karl Marx]] elaborated the comparison between wage labor and slavery in the context of a critique of societal property not intended for active personal use<ref name="reformrevolution"/> while [[Luddite]]s emphasized the [[dehumanisation]] brought about by machines. Before the [[American Civil War]], Southern defenders of [[African American]] slavery invoked the concept of wage slavery to favorably compare the condition of their slaves to workers in the North.{{citation needed|date=January 2021}} The United States abolished slavery during the Civil War, but labor union activists found the metaphor useful. According to [[Lawrence B. Glickman|Lawrence Glickman]], in the [[Gilded Age]] "references abounded in the labor press, and it is hard to find a speech by a labour leader without the phrase".<ref>{{cite book|author=Lawrence B. Glickman|title=A Living Wage: American Workers and the Making of Consumer Society|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uaZeBhl2QLYC&pg=PA19|year=1999|publisher=Cornell UP|page=19|isbn=978-0-8014-8614-2|access-date=27 June 2015|archive-date=18 October 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151018024416/https://books.google.com/books?id=uaZeBhl2QLYC&pg=PA19|url-status=live}}</ref>

{{quote box
| quote = The slave, together with his labour-power, was sold to his owner once for all.&nbsp;... The [wage] labourer, on the other hand, sells his very self, and that by fractions.&nbsp;... He [belongs] to the capitalist class; and it is for him&nbsp;... to find a buyer in this capitalist class.<ref>{{Harvnb|Marx|1847|loc=[http://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1847/wage-labour/ch02.htm Chapter&nbsp;2]}}</ref>
