{{short description|International labor pool of workers}}
'''Global workforce''' refers to the international labor pool of workers, including those [[employment|employed]] by [[multinational corporation|multinational companies]] and connected through a global system of [[computer network|networking]] and [[Production (economics)|production]], [[foreign worker]]s, transient [[migrant worker]]s, [[remote work]]ers, those in [[export-oriented employment]], [[contingent workforce]] or other [[precarious work]].<ref>{{cite book | year=2006 | last1=James | first1=Paul | author-link= Paul James (academic) |first2=Robert |  last2=O’Brien | title=Globalization and Economy, Vol. 4: Globalizing Labour | url=https://www.academia.edu/4303461 | publisher= Sage Publications |location=London }}</ref> As of 2012, the global labor pool consisted of approximately 3 billion workers, around 200 million [[Unemployment|unemployed]].<ref name="ILO1">{{cite book | url=http://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---dgreports/---dcomm/---publ/documents/publication/wcms_202326.pdf | title=World of work report 2013: Repairing the economic and social fabric | publisher=International Labour Organisation, International Institute for Labour Studies | editor=Torres, Raymond | year=2013 | location=Geneva | isbn=978-9292510183}}</ref>
{{TOC left}}
{{Clear}}

==Structure of global labour==
=== New international division of labor ===
{{Main|New international division of labour}}

The global workforce, or international labor pool, reflects a new international division of labor that has been emerging since the late 1970s in the wake of other forces of [[globalization]].  The [[economic globalization|global economic]] factors driving the rise of [[multinational corporation]]s—namely, cross-border movement of [[good (economics)|good]]s, [[Tertiary sector of the economy|services]], [[technology]] and [[Capital (economics)|capital]]—are changing ways of thinking about labor and the structure of today's workforce.  With roots in the social processes surrounding the shift to [[standardization]] and [[industrialization]], [[post-industrial society]] in the Western world has been accompanied by industrialization in other parts of the world, particularly in [[Asia]]. As industrialization takes hold worldwide and more cultures move away from [[Traditional society|traditional]] practices in respect to work and labor, the ways in which [[employers]] think about and utilize labor are changing. Usually, barriers come into play such as different laws.

=== Labor supply ===
{{Main|Labor force}}

The global [[Labour supply|supply of labor]] almost doubled in absolute numbers between the 1980s and early 2000s, with half of that growth coming from Asia.<ref name="Freeman1"/> At the same time, the rate at which new workers entered the [[workforce]] in the Western world began to decline. The growing pool of global labor is accessed by employers in more advanced economies through various methods, including imports of goods, [[offshoring]] of production, and [[Human migration|immigration]].<ref name="IMF07">{{cite book |url=http://www.imf.org/external/Pubs/FT/WEO/2007/01/pdf/c5.pdf| title=World Economic Outlook Chapter 5: The Globalization of Labor | publisher=International Monetary Fund | year=2007 | isbn=978-0511760594}}</ref> [[Global labor arbitrage]], the practice of accessing the lowest-cost workers from all parts of the world, is partly a result of this enormous growth in the workforce. While most of the absolute increase in this global labor supply consisted of less-educated workers (those without higher education), the relative supply of workers with higher education increased by about 50 percent during the same period.<ref name="IMF07"/> From 1980 to 2010, the global workforce grew from 1.2 to 2.9 billion people. According to a 2012 report by the McKinsey Global Institute, this was caused mostly by developing nations, where there was a "farm to factory" transition. Non-farming jobs grew from 54 percent in 1980 to almost 73 percent in 2010. This industrialization took an estimated 620 million people out of poverty and contributed to the economic development of China, India and others.<ref name="MGI12"/> The Institute estimates that increased exports in developing countries contribute to one-fifth of non-farm jobs in those nations and that immigrants from developing countries contributed to 40 percent of the workforce in advanced ones. By 2008 foreign-born workers accounted for 17 percent of all STEM (science, technology, engineering and math) positions in the United States.<ref name="MGI12">{{cite journal |url=http://www.mckinsey.com/insights/employment_and_growth/the_world_at_work| title=The world at work: Jobs, pay and skills for 3.5 billion people | publisher=McKinsey Global Institute | date=June 2012|first1=Richard|last1=Dobbs|first2=Dominic|last2=Barton|first3=Anu|last3=Madgavkar|first4=Eric|last4=Labaye|first5=James|last5=Manyika|first6=Charles|last6=Roxburgh|first7=Susan|last7=Lund|first8=Siddarth|last8=Madhav}}</ref>

=== Employment and unemployment ===
[[Image:World Unemployment.gif|thumb|300px|[[Unemployment]] by country, 2010]]
{{Main|Employment}}

Employment is growing fastest in emerging and developing economies. Over the past 5 years, the incidence of long-term unemployment (the share of unemployed persons out of work for 12 months or more) has increased 60% in the
advanced and developing economies for which data exist. Global unemployment is expected to approach 208 million in 2015, compared with slightly over 200 million in 2012.<ref name="ILO1"/>

From January 2012 to January 2013, Italy experienced the largest increase in its unemployment rate (+2.1 percentage points), followed by the Netherlands (+1.0 percentage point), and France (+0.6 percentage point).  Over that same period, Canada experienced the largest decrease in its unemployment rate (−0.5 percentage points), followed by the United States (−0.4 percentage point).<ref>Bureau of Labor Statistics, U.S. Department of Labor, The Economics Daily, International unemployment rates, January 2013 on the Internet at http://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2013/ted_20130308.htm (visited October 28, 2014).</ref>

The number of people employed in [[precarious work]] (also called "vulnerable employment")— employment that is poorly paid, insecure, unprotected, and cannot support a household—has increased dramatically in recent decades. This includes [[Part-time job]]s, [[self-employment]] or [[freelancer]]s, [[remote work|homeworker]]s, fixed-term or [[temporary work]], on-call work, and other [[contingent workforce]] jobs.<ref name=FudgeOwens2006p3-28>{{cite book |editor1-first=Judy |editor1-last=Fudge |editor2=and Rosemary Owens|year=2006 |title=Precarious Work, Women and the New Economy: The Challenge to Legal Norms |pages=3–28 |series=Onati International Series in Law and Society |publisher=Hart |location=Oxford |isbn=978-1841136158}}</ref>

=== Demographic trends ===
[[File:Median age 2024 cia the world factbook.png|thumb|300px|[[Median]] age by country, 2024]]
{{Main|Demographics of the world}}

These numbers show that, globally, the structure of the workforce has been changing. In addition to the economic and social factors described above, a large part of this restructuring is also due to [[demographic]] factors, changes in the structure of the world's population.  In wealthier countries with more advanced economies, fewer people die from [[communicable disease]]s and, overall, [[life expectancy|life expectancies]] are much longer while [[birth rate]]s are lower.<ref>{{cite book | url=http://www.prb.org/pdf12/2012-population-data-sheet_eng.pdf | title=World Population Data Sheet | publisher=Population Reference Bureau | year=2012 | access-date=2013-07-08 | archive-date=2014-05-21 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140521191647/http://www.prb.org/pdf12/2012-population-data-sheet_eng.pdf | url-status=dead }}</ref> In these areas, the overall median age is rising (see [[List of countries by median age]]). The youngest populations, primarily those in [[Southeast Asia]] and [[Africa]], are those in which overall life expectancies are lower—many children and some adults still die from communicable diseases—but the birth rate is also high.

===Global worker mobility===
{{See also|International assignment}}
The movement of individuals across [[nation]]al, [[region]]al, [[cultural]], or [[linguistic]] boundaries has been referred to as "global mobility."  This global workforce mobility impacts an employer's ability to provide goods or services to users and consumers.<ref name="Selmer15">{{cite encyclopedia | title=Global Mobility | encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Quality and the Service Economy | publisher=Sage | author=Selmer, J., J. Lauring and T. Bjerregaard | editor=Su Mi Dahlgaard-Park| year=1015 | volume=1 | pages=255–57  | isbn=9781452256726}}</ref>  [[Management]] theory attempts to address these  movements of globally mobile individuals ranging from business [[expatriates]] to more recently identified groups such as self-initiated expatriates, international business travelers, international commuters, and "flexpatriates" (short-term assignees and international commuters).<ref name="Makela16">{{cite encyclopedia | title=Flexpatriates, short-term assignees and international commuters | encyclopedia=The Research Handbook of Expatriates (Forthcoming) | publisher=Edward Elgar | author=Makela, L., K. Sarenpaa and Y. McNulty |editor1=McNulty Y. |editor2=J. Selmer | year=2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | title=Addressing international mobility confusion – developing definitions and differentiations for self-initiated and assigned expatriates as well as migrants | author=Andresen, M. | journal=The International Journal of Human Resource Management | year=2014 | volume=25 | issue=16 | pages=2295–318 | doi=10.1080/09585192.2013.877058|display-authors=etal| hdl=1826/14776 | s2cid=143790254 | hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Global Mobility Journeys (GMJ): Global Mobility HR First |url=https://www.globalmobilityjourneys.com/ |access-date=2022-10-15 |website=Global Mobility Journeys |language=en}}</ref>

Movement of people across national borders is becoming increasingly common.  Traditionally, this has been described in terms of push and pull forces that drive [[migrant workers]] and [[immigration|immigrant laborers]] toward more developed countries. However, not all [[labor mobility]] is outward movement toward more advanced economies.  An increasing number of individuals move to less developed countries <ref>{{cite journal|last=Arp|first=Frithjof|date=2013|title=Typologies: What types of foreign executives are appointed by local organisations and what types of organisations appoint them?|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/256043899|journal=German Journal of Human Resource Management|volume=27|issue=3|pages=167–194|doi=10.1177/239700221302700302|s2cid=56210528 |hdl=10419/85280|hdl-access=free}}</ref> to provide new expertise <ref>{{cite journal|last=Arp|first=Frithjof|date=2014|title=Emerging giants, aspiring multinationals and foreign executives: Leapfrogging, capability building, and competing with developed country multinationals|journal=Human Resource Management|volume=53|issue=6|pages=851–876|doi=10.1002/hrm.21610|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/256012200}}</ref> or return their expertise to their country of origin. This includes a return movement or repatriation of internationally relocated individuals such as immigrants, [[refugee]]s, sojourners, [[retiree]]s, [[military]] personnel, international [[students]], or other expatriates.<ref>{{cite journal | title=Global mobility orientation and the success of self-initiated expatriates in Greater China. |author1=Lauring, J.  |author2=J. Selmer | journal=Asia Pacific Business Review | year=2014 | volume=20 | issue=4 | pages=523–40 | doi=10.1080/13602381.2013.847607|s2cid=154790453 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1 = Arp|first1 = Frithjof|last2 = Hutchings|first2 = Kate|last3 = Smith|first3 = Wendy A.|date = 2013|title = Foreign executives in local organisations: An exploration of differences to other types of expatriates|url = https://www.researchgate.net/publication/258951786|journal = Journal of Global Mobility|volume = 1|issue = 3|pages = 312–335|doi = 10.1108/JGM-01-2013-0006}}</ref>  Such movements of people may influence interstate relationships concerning politics, economics and culture.  Thus, global workforce mobility research is relevant to both host and home country policies.  From a focus on longer-term and assigned expatriation, current research is focusing on the drivers and dynamics of a range of new alternative forms of global mobility in the workforce.<ref name="Selmer15"/> Reviews on global workforce mobility have been recently published by [[Paula Caligiuri|Caligiuri and Bonache]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Caligiuri|first1=Paula|last2=Bonache|first2=Jaime|date=2016-01-01|title=Evolving and enduring challenges in global mobility|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1090951615000802|journal=Journal of World Business|language=en|volume=51|issue=1|pages=127–141|doi=10.1016/j.jwb.2015.10.001|issn=1090-9516|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and Collings and Sheeran.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Sheeran|date=2021-05-06|title=Research insights: Global mobility in a post-covid world|journal=The Irish Journal of Management|language=de|volume=39|issue=2|pages=77–84|doi=10.2478/ijm-2020-0002|s2cid=234345248 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

With the rise in [[remote work]] and [[Virtual team|virtual teams]] during and after the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], academics described a shift toward "the replacement of personal physical international interactions for work purposes with electronic personal online international interactions", summarized as "virtual global mobility".<ref name="Selmer2022">{{cite journal |last1=Selmer|first1=Jan|last2=Dickmann|first2=Michael|last3=Froese|first3=Fabian J.|last4=Lauring|first4=Jakob|last5=Reiche|first5=B. Sebastian|last6=Shaffer|first6=Margaret|title=The potential of virtual global mobility: implications for practice and future research|journal=Journal of Global Mobility|volume=10|issue=1|pages=1–13|year=2022|doi=10.1108/JGM-07-2021-0074|url=https://pure.au.dk/ws/files/353507877/Selmer_2022_The_potential_of_virtual_global_mobility.pdf|access-date=8 June 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Biswas |first=Tania |last2=Abdul Hadi |first2=Acil |date=2026-09-22 |title=Global crisis as catalyst: institutional changes and the rise of virtual global mobility |url=https://doi.org/10.1108/JGM-04-2026-0040 |journal=Journal of Global Mobility |pages=1–27 |doi=10.1108/JGM-04-2026-0040 |issn=2049-8799|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Implications ==

=== Social vulnerability ===

One issue related to the shift of employment to countries with an overall younger population has to do with the [[dependency ratio]] in differing countries. The dependency ratio is an age-population ratio of those typically not in the labor force (the dependent part) and those typically in the labor force (the productive part).  A high dependency ratio can cause serious problems for a country if a large proportion of a government's expenditure is on health, social security & education, which are most used by the youngest and the oldest in a population.  The fewer people of working age, the fewer the people who can support [[school]]s, retirement [[pension]]s, [[disability pension]]s and other assistances to the youngest and oldest members of a population, often considered the most [[social vulnerability|vulnerable]] members of [[society]].{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}}

=== Downward pressure on wages ===

Another issue can arise in regard to the capital-labor ratio in the [[world population|global population]]. Freeman (2010) holds that the new entrants to the global workforce since the 1980s brought little [[Capital (economics)|capital]] with them, either because they were poor or because the capital they had was of little economic value.<ref name="Freeman1">{{cite web |author=Freeman, Richard |url=http://www.theglobalist.com/StoryId.aspx?StoryId=4542 |title=What Really Ails Europe (and America): The Doubling of the Global Workforce |publisher=The Globalist |date=2010-03-05 |access-date=2013-07-06 |archive-date=2013-05-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130508182915/http://www.theglobalist.com/StoryId.aspx?StoryId=4542 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He estimates that the entry of [[China]], [[India]] and the [[Eastern Bloc]] into the global economy cut the global capital-labor ratio to around 55–60% of what it otherwise would have been. The capital-labor ratio, according to Freeman, is a critical determinant of the wages paid to workers and of the returns to capital. The more capital each worker has, the higher will be their productivity and pay. Even considering the high savings rate of new entrants—he cites [[World Bank]] estimates that China has a savings rate of 40% of GDP—he estimates it would take 30 or so years for the world to re-attain the capital-labor ratio among the countries that had previously made up the global economy.  This, along with the effects of the [[Great Recession]], could mean that downward pressure on [[wage]]s and [[Compensation of employees|compensation]], particularly in more advanced economies, will continue for the foreseeable future.

=== Race to the bottom ===
{{main|Race to the bottom}}

"Race to the bottom" is a phrase coined to describe the potential outcome of companies searching for the lowest-cost in all their business needs.  For example, lowest taxes and tariffs, land, materials, labor, etc. In terms of global labor arbitrage, the lowest-cost labor is often found in countries that have the fewest protections for workers.  Such protections, collectively known as [[labor rights]], include regulation of [[Child labour|child labor]], [[Occupational safety and health|workplace safety]], [[Working time|work hours]], [[minimum wage]]s, and the availability of [[collective bargaining]]. One potential outcome of widespread global labor arbitrage, then, is [[Exploitation of labour|exploitation]] and even [[2013 Savar building collapse|death]] of workers in countries that have the fewest protections. Another potential outcome is an [[Social undermining|undermining]] of the protections that are already in place in some countries; that is, a pressure to lower [[Domestic policy|domestic]] and, ultimately, [[international labor standards]].  One example of this is employer abuse of [[guest worker program]]s wherein employers act to sponsor [[guest worker]]s at lower wages in order to decrease the overall domestic standard wage for workers in a given occupation, such as with [[Information technology]] workers in the United States.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/rundown/2013/07/the-bogus-high-tech-worker-shortage-how-guest-workers-lower-us-wages.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130725174035/http://www.pbs.org/newshour/rundown/2013/07/the-bogus-high-tech-worker-shortage-how-guest-workers-lower-us-wages.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=July 25, 2013 | title=The Bogus High-Tech Worker Shortage: How Guest Workers Lower US Wages | publisher=PBS | date=24 July 2013 | access-date=25 July 2013 |author1=Salzman, Hal  |author2=B. Lindsay Lowell}}</ref>

=== Mitigating factors ===

However, other forces may mitigate these processes. Some observe that a growing number of [[multinational corporation|multinationals]], especially from wealthier areas, are starting to see the benefits of keeping more of their operations close to home. For many products, labor is a small and diminishing fraction of total costs. Long, complex [[supply chain]]s, it turns out, are likely riskier than many firms may have realized. For example, when an epidemic such as [[Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS)|SARS]] hits Asia or when an earthquake hits Japan, supply chains are disrupted. Also, as emerging economies boom, wages there are rising. The benefits of global labor arbitrage may disappear, particularly in [[secondary sector of the economy|basic manufacturing]] and especially in China, where wages have been rising the fastest.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.economist.com/business/2011/05/12/moving-back-to-america | title=Moving back to America: the dwindling allure of building factories offshore | newspaper=The Economist | date=12 May 2011 | access-date=8 July 2013}}</ref>

== Registered Employer (EOR) == 
This is a third-party organization that officially acts as the employer for employees on behalf of another company.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Employer of Record Explained: A Practical Guide for Global Teams|url=https://www.bamboohr.com/blog/employer-of-record-eor-guide|access-date=2025-11-22|work=www.bamboohr.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=What is an Employer of Record (EOR)? How It Works, Benefits|url=https://www.hireborderless.com/post/what-is-an-employer-of-record|access-date=2025-11-22|work=www.hireborderless.com}}</ref> The EOR takes on responsibility for legal and administrative employment matters such as payroll processing, tax payments, benefits administration, and compliance with local labor laws.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Employer of Record (EoR) explained: Hire globally without setting up local entities|url=https://zalaris.com/consulting/resources/blog/employer-of-record-eor-explained-hire-globally-without-setting-up-local-entities|access-date=2025-11-22|work=zalaris.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=What Is an Employer of Record (EOR)? A Full HR Guide|url=https://vensure.com/resources/blog/employer-of-record/|access-date=2025-11-22|work=vensure.com |date=4 November 2024 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=What is an Employer of Record?|url=https://www.nesfircroft.com/resources/blog/what-is-an-employer-of-record-/|access-date=2025-11-22|work=www.nesfircroft.com |date=18 September 2024 }}</ref> While the EOR handles these formalities, the client company controls the daily activities and work of the employees. This mechanism is often used by companies wishing to hire employees in regions where they do not have a registered legal entity.<ref>{{Cite web|title=What is an EOR? Meaning, purpose, and benefits|url=https://remote.com/blog/eor-peo/what-is-an-employer-of-record|access-date=2025-11-22|work=remote.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=EOR vs Entity Setup: How to Choose the Right Global Hiring Model for Your Business|url=https://workmotion.com/eor-vs-entity-setup/|access-date=2025-11-22|work=workmotion.com |date=11 November 2025 }}</ref>

EOR services are frequently utilized by companies seeking to hire employees in countries where they lack local subsidiaries. The EOR allows companies to operate in foreign markets while ensuring that all employment practices comply with local legislation. This arrangement also enables companies to avoid the complexities associated with establishing and maintaining a legal entity in each jurisdiction where they want to hire employees.{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}}

For many companies, establishing a legal entity in each new country is expensive, time-consuming, and often impractical. This is where the EOR becomes a strategic partner. Instead of building your own infrastructure, you can rely on a registered employer who acts as the official employer on paper. The EOR assumes legal and administrative responsibilities, while you manage the day-to-day work and objectives of the team.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Employer of record|url=https://rivermate.com/blog/what-is-an-employer-of-record|access-date=2025-11-22|work=rivermate.com |date=18 April 2024 }}</ref>
 
The EOR takes on responsibility for compliance with local labor laws, which vary from country to country and can be quite complex regulatory-wise. By managing these legal obligations, the EOR reduces the risks faced by companies when hiring employees abroad.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Global Employer of Record Market Research Report 2025|url=https://reports.valuates.com/market-reports/QYRE-Auto-7D9395/global-employer-of-record|access-date=2025-11-22|work=reports.valuates.com}}</ref>

* {{cite book | title=Digital Disconnect: How Capitalism Is Turning the Internet Against Democracy | publisher=The New Press | author=McChesney, Robert Waterman | year=2013 | isbn=978-1595588913}}
* {{cite book |title=Managing Diversity: Toward a Globally Inclusive Workplace |publisher=Sage Pubs. |author=Mor-Barak, Michàlle E. |year=2013 |isbn=978-1452242231 |author-link=Michàlle Mor Barak}}

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Glossary of economics
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}

This '''glossary of economics''' is a list of definitions containing terms and concepts used in economics, its sub-disciplines, and related fields.

{{compact TOC|side=yes|center=yes|nobreak=yes|num=yes|seealso=yes|refs=yes}}
{{Economics sidebar}}

== A ==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[absolute advantage]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''resource cost advantage'''.}}
{{defn|The ability of a party (whether an individual, firm, or country) to produce a greater quantity of a good, product, or service than competitors using the same amount of resources.}}

{{term|[[Absorption (economics)|absorption]]}}
{{defn|The total demand for all [[final good|final]] marketed [[goods and services]] by all [[Agent (economics)|economic agent]]s resident in an economy, regardless of the origin of the goods and services themselves<ref>{{cite book |title=Terms of Trade: Glossary of International Economics |last=Deardorff |first=Alan V. |author-link=Alan Deardorff |year=2006 |publisher=World Scientific Publishing |location=Hackensack |isbn=978-981-256-603-4 }}</ref>}}

{{term|abandonment of the gold standard}}
{{defn|The decision by a government to abandon a {{gli|monetary system}} in which the standard economic {{gli|unit of account}} is based on a fixed quantity of gold.}}

{{term|[[accelerator effect]]}}
{{defn|A positive effect on private fixed investment because of the growth of the market economy. Rising GDP usually implies that profit expectations and business confidence rise, encouraging businesses to build more factories and other buildings and to install more machinery.}}

{{term|[[adaptive expectations]]}}
{{defn|A hypothetical process by which people form expectations about what will happen in the future based on what has happened in the past.}}

{{term|[[AD–AS model]]}}
{{defn|A macroeconomic model that explains price level and output through the relationship of downward-sloping aggregate demand (AD) and upward-sloping aggregate supply (AS).}}

{{term|[[AD–IA model]]}}
{{defn|A macroeconomic model that explains inflation and output through the relationship of downward-sloping aggregate demand (AD) and  horizontal inflation adjustment (IA). The monetary policy rule (MPR) is assumed, which is that the central bank increases interest rates in response to increase in inflation and vice versa.}}

{{term|[[adverse selection]]}}
{{defn|A market situation where buyers and sellers have different information, and participants with key information participate selectively in trades at the expense of other parties.}}

{{term|[[advertising elasticity of demand|advertising elasticity of demand (AED)]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''advertising elasticity'''.}}
{{defn|Measures the sensitivity of a good's demand to a change in advertising.}}

{{term|[[agflation]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''agrarian inflation'''.}}
{{defn|An increase in the price of food and industrial agricultural crops when compared to the general rise in prices.}}

{{anchor|aggregate demand}}{{term|[[aggregate demand]] (AD)}}
{{ghat|Also called '''domestic final demand (DFD)''' or '''effective demand'''.}}
{{defn|The total {{gli|demand}} for goods and services in an economy.<ref>{{cite book | title = Exploring Economics | first1 = Robert | last1 = Sexton | first2 = Peter | last2 = Fortura | isbn = 978-0-17-641482-5 | year = 2005 | publisher = Nelson Education Limited | quote = This is the sum of the demand for all final goods and services in the economy. It can also be seen as the quantity of real GDP demanded at different price levels. | url = https://archive.org/details/exploringeconomi0000sext }}</ref> It specifies the amounts of goods and services that will be purchased at all possible price levels.<ref>{{cite book| last = O'Sullivan| first = Arthur| author-link = Arthur O'Sullivan (economist) |author2= Steven M. Sheffrin| title = Economics| publisher = Savvas Learning Company| year = 2022| location = Paramus, New Jersey | page = 307| url = https://www.savvas.com/index.cfm?locator=PS3jRm| isbn = 978-0-13-063085-8}}</ref> Aggregate demand can also be interpreted as the demand for the {{gli|gross domestic product}} of a country. It is often called {{gli|effective demand}}, though this term also has a distinct meaning.}}

{{anchor|aggregate supply}}{{term|[[aggregate supply]] (AS)}}
{{ghat|Also called '''domestic final supply (DFS)'''.}}
{{defn|The total {{gli|supply}} of goods and services in an economy.}}

{{term|[[aggregation problem]]}}
{{defn|The difficult problem of finding a valid way to treat an [[empirical]] or theoretical aggregate as if it reacted like a less-aggregated measure, say, about behavior of an individual {{gli|agent}} as described in general {{gli|microeconomics|microeconomic}} theory.<ref>Franklin M. Fisher  (1987).  "aggregation problem," ''[[The New Palgrave: A Dictionary of Economics]]'', v. 1, p. 54.  [Pp. 53–55.]</ref>}}

{{term|[[Agent (economics)|agent]]}}
{{defn|An actor or, more specifically, a [[decision maker]] in a {{gli|economic model|model}} of some aspect of the economy.}}

{{term|[[agricultural economics]]}}
{{defn|An applied field of {{gli|economics}} concerned with the application of economic theory in optimizing the production and distribution of food.}}

{{term|[[AK model]]}}
{{defn|A macroeconomic model that explains output through the relationship of [[total factor productivity]] and capital. It assumes that there is no diminishing return of capital.}}

{{term|[[Alchian–Allen effect]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''shipping the good apples out theorem''', or the '''third law of demand'''.}}
{{defn|When the prices of two substitute goods, such as high and low grades of the same product, are both increased by a fixed per-unit amount, consumption will shift toward the higher-grade product. This is because the added per-unit amount decreases the relative price of the higher-grade product.}}

{{term|[[Allais paradox]]}}
{{defn|A choice problem showing an inconsistency of actual observed choices with the independence axiom of expected utility theory.}}

{{term|[[allocative efficiency]]}}
{{defn|A state of the economy in which production represents consumer preferences; in particular, every good or service is produced up to the point where the last unit provides a marginal benefit to consumers equal to the marginal cost of producing. In the single-price model, at the point of allocative efficiency, price is equal to marginal cost.<ref>{{cite book | last = Markovits | first = Richard | title = Matters of Principle | publisher = [[New York University Press]] | location = New York City | year = 1998 | isbn = 978-0-8147-5513-6 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last = Markovits | first = Richard | title = Truth or Economics | publisher = [[Yale University Press]] | location = [[New Haven]] | year = 2008 | isbn = 978-0-300-11459-1 }}</ref>}}

{{term|[[alternative minimum tax]] (AMT)}}
{{defn|A tax imposed by the U.S. federal government in addition to the regular income tax for certain individuals, estates, and trusts. High-income taxpayers must calculate and pay the greater of the AMT or regular tax.<ref>[http://www.cbo.gov/ftpdocs/108xx/doc10800/01-15-AMT_Brief.pdf Calculating the Alternative Minimum Tax] Congressional Budget Office Economics and Budget Issue Brief, 2010, page 2. See Willis & Hoffman (2009) page __, and Pratt & Kulsrud (2010) Chapter 13.</ref>}}

{{term|[[ambiguity aversion]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''uncertainty aversion'''.}}
{{defn|Any preference for known risks over unknown risks.}}

{{term|[[American School (economics)|American school]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''national system'''.}}
{{defn|A school of thought based around industry protection, government investment in infrastructure, and a national bank.}}

{{term|[[Amoroso–Robinson relation]]}}
{{defn|An equation that describes the relation between [[price]], [[marginal revenue]], and [[price elasticity of demand]].}}

{{term|[[ancient economic thought]]}}
{{defn|The {{gli|economics|economic}} ideas proposed by [[ancient history|ancient]] thinkers, in the {{gli|history of economic thought}}.}}

{{term|[[Anglo-Saxon model]]}}
{{defn|A school of thought based around low levels of regulation and taxation, minimal public services, strong private property rights, contract enforcement, overall ease of doing business, and low barriers to free trade.}}

{{term|[[annual effective discount rate]] (AER)}}
{{defn|The amount of interest paid or earned as a percentage of the balance at the end of the annual period.}}

{{term|[[anti-rival good]]}}
{{defn|The opposite of a [[rival good]]. The more people share an anti-rival good, the more utility each person receives.}}

{{term|[[Competition law|antitrust law]]}}
{{ghat|Also called a '''competition law''' or '''anti-monopoly law'''.}}
{{defn|Any law that promotes or seeks to maintain [[market competition]] by regulating [[anti-competitive]] conduct by companies.<ref name="papers.ssrn.com">{{cite SSRN |title=The Role of Competition Law: An Asian Perspective|first1=Rita Yi Man|last1=Li|first2=Yi Lut|last2=Li|date=1 June 2013|ssrn = 2281756}}</ref><ref name="Taylor 2006 1">{{Cite book| last = Taylor| first = Martyn D.| title = International competition law: a new dimension for the WTO?| publisher = Cambridge University Press| year = 2006| page = 1| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=wTsfwxMvz_MC&q=competition+law| isbn = 978-0-521-86389-6 }}</ref> Competition law is implemented through public and private enforcement.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Cartel Damage Claims (CDC)|title=Cartel Damage Claims (CDC)|url=http://www.carteldamageclaims.com/|website=www.carteldamageclaims.com/|access-date=23 June 2014}}</ref> It is also known as "[[United States antitrust law|antitrust law]]" in the United States for historical reasons and as "anti-{{gli|monopoly}} law" in China<ref name="papers.ssrn.com"/> and Russia.}}

{{term|[[applied economics]]}}
{{defn|The application of [[economic theory]] and {{gli|econometrics}} in specific settings. As one of the two sets of fields of {{gli|economics}} (the other being the ''core''),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aeaweb.org/resources/students/|title=American Economic Association|website=www.aeaweb.org}}</ref> it is typically characterized by the application of the ''core'', i.e. economic theory and econometrics, to address practical issues in a range of fields.}}

{{term|[[appropriate technology]]}}
{{defn|A movement (and its manifestations) encompassing technological choice and application that is small-scale, [[Decentralization|decentralized]], [[labor-intensive]], [[efficient energy use|energy-efficient]], [[environmentally sound]], and [[localism (politics)|locally autonomous]].<ref name=BrownU>{{cite book|title=Appropriate Technology: Tools, Choices, and Implications|year=1999|publisher=Academic Press|location=New York|isbn=978-0-12-335190-6|pages=3, 270|author=Hazeltine, B.|author2=Bull, C.}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[arbitrage]]}}
{{defn|The practice of taking advantage of a price difference between two or more {{gli|market|markets}} by striking a combination of matching deals that capitalize upon the imbalance, with the profit being the difference between the {{gli|market price|market prices}}.}}

{{term|[[Arrow–Debreu model]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''Arrow–Debreu–McKenzie model''' or '''ADM model'''.}}
{{defn|A model that suggests there must be a set of prices such that aggregate supplies will equal aggregate demands for every commodity in the economy, given certain assumptions. It can be used to prove the existence of general equilibrium (or Walrasian equilibrium) of an economy.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal | last1 = Arrow | first1 = K. J. | last2 = Debreu | first2 = G. | year = 1954 | title = Existence of an equilibrium for a competitive economy | journal = Econometrica | volume = 22 | issue =3 | pages = 265–290 | doi = 10.2307/1907353 | jstor = 1907353 }}</ref>}}

{{term|[[Arrow-Debreu security]]}}
{{ghat|Also called a '''state-price security''', '''pure security''', or '''primitive security'''.}}
{{defn|A contract that agrees to pay one unit of a numeraire (a currency or a commodity) if a particular state occurs at a particular time in the future and pays zero numeraire in all the other states.}}

{{term|[[Arrow information paradox]] (AIP)}}
{{ghat|Also called '''Arrow's disclosure paradox'''.}}
{{defn|A problem faced by companies when considering the transfer of intellectual property. A company may wish to sell some information, but it cannot fully describe the capabilities of the information without effectively transferring the information for free.}}

{{term|[[Arrow's impossibility theorem]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''general possibility theorem''' or '''Arrow's paradox'''.}}
{{defn|When voters have three or more distinct options, no [[ranked voting]] [[electoral system]] can convert the ranked preferences of individuals into a community-wide (complete and transitive) ranking while also meeting the specified set of criteria: [[unrestricted domain]], [[non-dictatorship]], [[Pareto efficiency]], and [[independence of irrelevant alternatives]].}}

{{term|[[Associate's Degree]]}}
{{defn|An academic program taken at the undergraduate level and after secondary school, which is considered a two-year degree and can be obtained from a community college, junior college, or some four-year universities.}}

{{term|[[Atkinson–Stiglitz theorem]]}}
{{defn|Where the utility function is separable between labor and all commodities, no indirect taxes need be employed.}}

{{term|[[Aumann's agreement theorem]]}}
{{defn|If the probabilistic beliefs of agents who share a common prior and update their probabilistic beliefs by Bayes' rule, regarding a fixed event, are common knowledge then these probabilities must coincide. Thus, agents cannot have common knowledge of a disagreement over the posterior probability of a given event.}}

{{term|[[austerity]]}}
{{defn|A set of [[Political economy|political-economic]] policies that aim to reduce [[Government budget balance|government budget deficits]] through spending cuts, tax increases, or a combination of both.<ref name="ft_lexicon">{{cite web|url=http://lexicon.ft.com/Term?term=austerity-measure|title=Austerity measure|work=[[Financial Times]] Lexicon|access-date=1 March 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130322221836/http://lexicon.ft.com/Term?term=austerity-measure|archive-date=22 March 2013}}</ref><ref name="Traynor">{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2010/jun/11/europe-deficit-crisis-austerity-budgets|title=Austerity Europe: who faces the cuts|last=Traynor|first=Ian|author2=Katie Allen|date=11 June 2010|publisher=Guardian News|access-date=29 September 2010|location=London}}</ref><ref name="Wesbury">{{cite news|url=https://www.forbes.com/2010/07/26/government-spending-taxes-opinions-columnists-brian-wesbury-robert-stein.html |title=Government Austerity: The Good, Bad And Ugly |last=Wesbury |first=Brian S. |author2=Robert Stein |date=26 July 2010 |work=Forbes |access-date=29 September 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100929125657/http://www.forbes.com/2010/07/26/government-spending-taxes-opinions-columnists-brian-wesbury-robert-stein.html |archive-date=29 September 2010 |url-status=live }}</ref>}}

{{term|[[Austrian School]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|heterodox economics|heterodox}}<ref name="Austrian Economists: Boettke">{{Cite web|url=http://austrianeconomists.typepad.com/weblog/2008/05/is-austrian-eco.html|title=Is Austrian Economics Heterodox Economics?|last=Boettke |first=Peter|publisher=The Austrian Economists|access-date=2009-02-13| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090328232903/http://austrianeconomists.typepad.com/weblog/2008/05/is-austrian-eco.html| archive-date= 28 March 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref><ref name="Boettke and Leeson">{{Cite book|last=Boettke|first=Peter J.|author2=Peter T. Leeson|title=A Companion to the History of Economic Thought|editor=[[Warren Samuels]] |editor2=Jeff E. Biddle |editor3=John B. Davis|pages=446–52|chapter=28A: The Austrian School of Economics 1950–2000|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3H8gBQv5MysC&pg=PA445 |publisher=Blackwell Publishing |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-631-22573-7|author2-link=Peter T. Leeson}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.economist.com/briefing/2011/12/31/marginal-revolutionaries | title=Heterodox economics: Marginal revolutionaries | newspaper=The Economist | date=December 31, 2011 | access-date=February 22, 2012 | url-status=live | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120222004727/http://www.economist.com/node/21542174 | archive-date=February 22, 2012 }}</ref> [[Schools of economic thought|school of economic thought]] that is based on [[methodological individualism]]—the concept that social phenomena result from the motivations and actions of individuals.<ref>Carl Menger, Principles of Economics, online at {{cite web |url=https://www.mises.org/etexts/menger/principles.asp |title=Principles of Economics |date=18 August 2014 |access-date=2014-09-13 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140914004206/https://www.mises.org/etexts/menger/principles.asp |archive-date=2014-09-14 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/spr2015/entries/methodological-individualism/|title=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|first=Joseph|last=Heath|editor-first=Edward N.|editor-last=Zalta|date=1 May 2018|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|access-date=1 May 2018|via=Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}}</ref><ref name="Mises_Action">Ludwig von Mises.  [[Human Action]], p. 11, "Purposeful Action and Animal Reaction". Referenced 2011-11-23.</ref>}}

{{term|[[autarky]]}}
{{defn|The characteristic of being [[Self-sufficiency|self-sufficient]]; the term is usually applied to political states or their economic systems. Autarky is possible when an entity can survive or continue its activities without external assistance or [[international trade]]. If a self-sufficient economy also deliberately ''refuses'' all trade with the outside world, then it is called a '''closed economy'''.<ref>[http://www-personal.umich.edu/~alandear/glossary/c.html#ClosedEconomy|Deardorff's Glossary of International Economics] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071212072813/http://www-personal.umich.edu/~alandear/glossary/c.html |date=2007-12-12 }}.</ref>}}

{{term|[[automatic stabilizer]]}}
{{defn|A feature of the structure of modern government budgets, particularly {{gli|income tax|income taxes}} and {{gli|welfare|welfare spending}}, that acts to damp out fluctuations in {{gli|real gross domestic product|real GDP}}.<ref>{{cite book| last1 = O'Sullivan| first1 = Arthur| author-link = Arthur O'Sullivan (economist)| first2 = Steven M. | last2 = Sheffrin| title = Economics: Principles in Action| publisher = Savvas Learning Company | year = 2003| location = Paramus, New Jersey| page = 399| isbn = 978-0-13-063085-8}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[autonomous consumption]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''exogenous consumption'''.}} 
{{defn|The consumption expenditure that occurs when income levels are zero. Such consumption is considered autonomous of income only when expenditure on these {{gli|consumable|consumables}} does not vary with changes in income; generally, it may be required to fund necessities and debt obligations. If income levels are actually zero, this consumption counts as {{gli|dissaving}}, because it is financed by {{gli|loan|borrowing}} or using up {{gli|savings}}.}}

{{term|[[average cost]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''unit cost'''.}}
{{defn|A quantity equal to the {{gli|total cost}} divided by the number of goods produced (the output quantity, Q). It is also equal to the sum of {{gli|variable cost|variable costs}} (total variable costs divided by Q) plus {{gli|average fixed cost|average fixed costs}} (total {{gli|fixed cost|fixed costs}} divided by Q).}}

{{term|[[average fixed cost]]}}
{{defn|The {{gli|fixed cost|fixed costs}} (FC) of production divided by the quantity (Q) of {{gli|output}} produced. Fixed costs are those costs that must be incurred in fixed quantity regardless of the level of output produced.}}

{{term|[[average variable cost]]}}
{{defn|A firm's {{gli|variable cost|variable costs}} (labour, electricity, etc.) divided by the quantity of {{gli|output}} produced. Variable costs are those costs which vary with the output.}}

{{term|[[average tax rate]]}}
{{defn|The ratio of the total amount of {{gli|tax|taxes}} paid to the total {{gli|tax base}} (taxable income or spending), expressed as a percentage.<ref name="whatisthedif">{{cite web|url=http://www.fairtax.org/PDF/WhatIsTheDifferenceBetweenTaxRates.pdf|title=What is the difference between statutory, average, marginal, and effective tax rates?|publisher=Americans For Fair Taxation|access-date=2007-04-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070614190648/http://www.fairtax.org/PDF/WhatIsTheDifferenceBetweenTaxRates.pdf|archive-date=2007-06-14}}</ref>}}
{{glossaryend}}

== B ==
{{glossary}}

{{term|[[Backus–Kehoe–Kydland puzzle]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''Backus–Kehoe–Kydland consumption correlation puzzle''' or '''BKK puzzle'''.}}
{{defn|The observation that consumption is much less correlated across countries than output. According to theory we should observe that consumption is much more correlated across countries than output in an [[Arrow–Debreu model|Arrow–Debreu economy]].}}

{{term|[[Backus–Smith puzzle]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''Backus-Smith consumption-real exchange rate puzzle''' or '''consumption – real-exchange-rate anomaly'''.}}
{{defn|The observation that the correlations between consumption and real exchange rates are zero or negative. This is contrary to economic theory which predicts that with full risk sharing, relative consumption should be perfectly correlated with the real exchange rate.}}

{{term|[[backward advantage]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''advantage of backwardness''' or the '''latecomer's advantage'''.}}
{{defn|The advantage that a still-developing country has because it can take advantage of the technology/industry gap with a developed country by implementing a new technology or venturing into an industry that is new to its economy but mature in the developed country.}}

{{term|[[backward disadvantage]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''latecomer's disadvantage'''.}}
{{defn|The fact that it is easier for late-development countries to imitate technologies, but more difficult to imitate the system, because the reform will offend vested interests.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://duoweicn.dwnews.com/zh/CN-2018%E5%B9%B4040%E6%9C%9F/10007285.html|title=The "Period of Contradictions" Has Arrived, What's the next step?|author=|date=29 Nov 2018|work=[[Duowei News]]|archive-date=9 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210709181254/https://duoweicn.dwnews.com/zh/CN-2018%E5%B9%B4040%E6%9C%9F/10007285.html}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[backward induction]]}}
{{defn|The process of reasoning backward in time, from the end of a problem or situation, to determine a sequence of optimal actions. It proceeds by first considering the last time a decision might be made and choosing what to do in any situation at that time. Using this information, one can then determine what to do at the second-to-last time of decision. This process continues backward until one has determined the best action for every possible situation (i.e. for every possible [[information set (game theory)|information set]]) at every point in time.}}

{{term|[[balance of payments]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''balance of international payments''' and abbreviated '''B.O.P.''' or '''BoP'''.}}
{{defn|A record or summary of all economic transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world in a particular period of time (e.g. over a quarter of a year or, more commonly, over a year). These transactions are made by individuals, firms and government bodies. Thus the balance of payments includes all external visible and non-visible transactions of a country.}}

{{term|[[balance of trade]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''commercial balance''' or '''net exports (NX)'''.}}
{{defn|The difference between the monetary value of a nation's {{gli|export|exports}} and {{gli|import|imports}} over a certain period.<ref>{{cite book |last1=O'Sullivan |first1=Arthur |author-link=Arthur O'Sullivan (economist) |first2=Steven M. |last2=Sheffrin |title=Economics |publisher=Savvas Learning Company |year=2022 |location=Paramus, New Jersey |page=462 |isbn=978-0-13-063085-8}}</ref> Sometimes a distinction is made between a balance of trade for goods versus one for services. "Balance of trade" can be a misleading term because trade measures a ''flow'' of exports and imports over a given period of time, rather than a ''balance'' of exports and imports at a given point in time. Also, balance of trade does not necessarily imply that exports and imports are "in balance" with each other or anything else.}}

{{term|[[balanced budget]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|budget}} in which {{gli|revenue|revenues}} equal {{gli|expenditure|expenditures}}. Thus, neither a {{gli|budget deficit}} nor a {{gli|budget surplus}} exists (the accounts "balance"). The term may also refer more generally to a budget that has no budget deficit but could possibly have a budget surplus.<ref>{{cite book| last1 = O'Sullivan| first1 = Arthur| author-link = Arthur O'Sullivan (economist)| first2 = Steven M. | last2 = Sheffrin| title = Economics| publisher = Savvas Learning Company| year = 2022| location = Paramus, New Jersey| pages = 376, 403| isbn = 978-0-13-063085-8}}</ref> A cyclically balanced budget is a budget that is not necessarily balanced year-to-year, but is balanced over the {{gli|economic cycle}}, running a surplus in boom years and running a deficit in lean years, with these offsetting over time.}}

{{term|bank}}
{{defn|A financial institution that accepts {{gli|deposit account|deposits}} from the public and creates {{gli|demand deposit|credit}}.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bank of England |work=Rulebook Glossary |url=http://www.prarulebook.co.uk/rulebook/Glossary/Rulebook/0/B |date=1 January 2014 |access-date=13 July 2018 |archive-date=13 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180713043152/http://www.prarulebook.co.uk/rulebook/Glossary/Rulebook/0/B }}</ref> Lending activities can be performed either directly or indirectly through [[capital market]]s. Due to their importance in the financial stability of a country, banks are [[Banking regulation|highly regulated]] in most countries. Most nations have institutionalized a system known as [[fractional reserve banking]], under which banks hold liquid assets equal to only a portion of their current liabilities. In addition to other regulations intended to ensure liquidity, banks are generally subject to [[minimum capital requirement]]s based on an international set of capital standards, known as the [[Basel Accords]].}}

{{term|[[bank rate]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''discount rate''' in American English.}}
{{defn|The rate of interest which a central bank charges on its loans and advances to a commercial bank.}}

{{term|bankruptcy}}
{{defn|The inability to pay {{gli|debt}} due to loss of income, increased spending, or an unforeseen financial crisis.}}

{{term|[[bargaining model of war]]}}
{{defn|A method of representing the potential gains and losses and ultimate outcome of war between two actors as a [[bargaining]] interaction.<ref name="Coyne Mathers 2011">{{cite book |last1=Coyne |first1=C.J. |last2=Mathers |first2=R.L. |title=The Handbook on the Political Economy of War |publisher=Edward Elgar Publishing Limited |series=Elgar Original Reference Series |year=2011 |isbn=978-1-84980-832-3 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-rSF4xEMhDwC&pg=PA19 |access-date=11 July 2018 |page=19}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[barriers to entry]]}}
{{defn|In theories of {{gli|competition}} in economics, a cost that must be incurred by a new entrant into a {{gli|market}} that incumbents do not have or have not had to incur.<ref name="entryBarriersInEconomicAndAntitrustAnalysis">{{cite web|url=http://authors.library.caltech.edu/11284/1/MCAaer04.pdf|title=When Are Sunk Costs Barriers to Entry? |website=caltech.edu|access-date=3 May 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=http://archive.wikiwix.com/cache/20160327112428/http://authors.library.caltech.edu/11284/1/MCAaer04.pdf|archive-date=27 March 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.micronomics.com/articles/UCLA_Law_Institute_Barriers_to_Entry_Final.pdf|title=Antitrust Aspects of Barriers to Entry|website=micronomics.com|access-date=3 May 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170517011312/http://www.micronomics.com/articles/UCLA_Law_Institute_Barriers_to_Entry_Final.pdf|archive-date=17 May 2017}}</ref> Because barriers to entry protect incumbent firms and restrict competition in a market, they can contribute to distortionary prices and are therefore most important when discussing {{gli|antitrust}} policy. Barriers to entry often cause or aid the existence of {{gli|monopoly|monopolies}} or give companies {{gli|market power}}.}}

{{term|[[barter]]}}
{{ghat|also called '''direct exchange'''.}}
{{defn|In {{gli|trade}}, a system of {{gli|exchange}} in which participants in a {{gli|transaction}} directly exchange {{gli|good|goods}} or {{gli|service|services}} for other goods or services without using a {{gli|medium of exchange}}, such as {{gli|money}}.<ref>{{cite book |last = O'Sullivan |first = Arthur |author2= Steven M. Sheffrin |title = Economics |publisher = Savvas Learning Company |year= 2022 |page= 243 |isbn= 978-0-13-063085-8}}</ref> Economists distinguish barter from {{gli|gift economy|gift economies}} in many ways; barter, for example, features immediate [[Reciprocity (cultural anthropology)|reciprocal exchange]] that is not delayed in time. Barter usually takes place on a [[Bilateral trade|bilateral]] basis, but may be [[Multilateral exchange|multilateral]] (i.e. mediated through a {{gli|trade exchange}}). In most [[developed countries]], barter usually only exists parallel to monetary systems to a very limited extent. Market actors use barter as a replacement for money as the method of exchange in times of [[monetary crisis]], such as when {{gli|currency}} becomes unstable (e.g. by {{gli|hyperinflation}} or a {{gli|deflationary spiral}}) or simply unavailable for conducting {{gli|commerce}}.}}

{{term|[[base erosion and profit shifting]] (BEPS)}}
{{defn|Corporate tax planning strategies used by multinationals to "shift" profits from higher-tax jurisdictions to lower-tax jurisdictions or no-tax locations.}}

{{term|Baxter-Stockman neutrality of exchange rate regime puzzle}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''exchange rate disconnect puzzle'''.}}
{{defn|The unexpectedly weak relationship between the exchange rate and any other macroeconomic variable.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Obstfeld |first1=Maurice |last2=Rogoff |first2=Kenneth |date=2000-07-03 |title=The Six Major Puzzles in International Macroeconomics: Is There a Common Cause? |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/0sx02651 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[Beckstrom's law]]}}
{{defn|"The value of a network equals the net value added to each user's transactions conducted through that network, summed over all users."}}

{{term|[[behavioral economics]]}}
{{defn|The branch of {{gli|economics}} that studies the effects of psychological, cognitive, emotional, cultural and social factors on the economic [[decision making|decisions]] of individuals and institutions and how those decisions vary from those implied by classical theory.<ref name="ssrn.com">{{cite journal|ssrn=2040946|title=A Behavioral Framework for Securities Risk|publisher =SSRN|last = Lin|first = Tom C. W. |date = 16 April 2012|journal = Seattle University Law Review}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[Bellman equation]]}}
{{defn|The dynamic programming equation associated with [[discrete-time]] optimization problems.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kirk |first1=Donald E. |title=Optimal Control Theory: An Introduction |date=1 January 2004 |publisher=Courier Corporation |isbn=978-0-486-43484-1 |page=70 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fCh2SAtWIdwC&pg=PA70 |language=en}}</ref> It writes the "value" of a decision problem at a certain point in time in terms of the payoff from some initial choices and the "value" of the remaining decision problem that results from those initial choices.}}

{{term|[[bequest motive]]}}
{{defn|Seeks to provide an economic justification for the phenomenon of [[intergenerational]] transfers of {{gli|wealth}}; in other words, to explain why people leave money behind when they die.}}

{{term|[[Bertrand competition]]}}
{{defn|A model of competition that describes interactions among producers that set prices and their consumers that choose quantities at the prices set.}}

{{term|[[Bertrand–Edgeworth model]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|microeconomics|microeconomic}} model of price-setting oligopoly which studies what happens when there is a homogeneous product (i.e. consumers want to buy from the cheapest seller) where there is a limit to the output of firms which they are willing and able to sell at a particular price. This differs from the Bertrand competition model where it is assumed that firms are willing and able to meet all demand. The limit to output can be considered a physical capacity constraint which is the same at all prices (as in [[Francis Ysidro Edgeworth|Edgeworth]]'s work) or to vary with price under other assumptions.}}

{{term|[[Bertrand paradox (economics)|Bertrand paradox]]}}
{{defn|A situation in which two players (firms) reach a state of Nash equilibrium where both firms charge a price equal to marginal cost.}}

{{term|[[biflation]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''mixflation'''.}}
{{defn|A state of the economy in which the processes of inflation and [[deflation]] occur simultaneously in different parts of the economy.<ref name="NW">{{cite web |last1=Summers |first1=Nick |title=What Is 'Biflation'? |url=https://www.newsweek.com/what-biflation-71855 |website=[[Newsweek]] |access-date=10 August 2021 |language=en |date=16 August 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Biflation |url=https://www.collinsdictionary.com/submission/9109/Biflation |publisher=[[Collins Dictionary]] |access-date=10 August 2021}}</ref> }}

{{term|[[big push model]]}}
{{defn|A concept in {{gli|development economics}} or {{gli|welfare economics}} that emphasizes that a firm's decision whether to industrialize or not depends on its expectation of what other firms will do. It assumes {{gli|economies of scale}} and [[oligopoly|oligopolistic]] market structure and explains when industrialization would happen.}}

{{term|[[Birmingham school (economics)|Birmingham school]]}}
{{defn|A school of thought based around opposing the gold standard, advocating for expansionary monetary policy, and belief in underconsumption.}}

{{term|[[Bishop–Cannings theorem]]}}
{{defn|A [[theorem]] in [[evolutionary game theory]] that states that (i) all members of a mixed [[evolutionarily stable strategy]]  have the same payoff, and (ii) that none of these can also be a pure ESS.<ref name="BandC78">{{Cite journal |last1=Bishop |first1=D.T. |last2=Cannings |first2=C. |date=1978 |title=A generalized war of attrition |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0022519378903041 |journal=Journal of Theoretical Biology |language=en |volume=70 |issue=1 |pages=85–124 |doi=10.1016/0022-5193(78)90304-1|pmid=564432 |bibcode=1978JThBi..70...85B |url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term|[[Black–Scholes model]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''Black–Scholes–Merton model'''.}} 
{{defn|A mathematical model for the dynamics of a [[financial market]] containing [[Derivative (finance)|derivative]] investment instruments. From the [[partial differential equation]] in the model, known as the [[Black–Scholes equation]], one can deduce the '''Black–Scholes formula''', which gives a theoretical estimate of the price of [[option style|European-style]] [[option (finance)|options]] and shows that the option has a unique price regardless of the risk of the security and its expected return (instead replacing the security's expected return with the [[risk-neutral]] rate). The formula led to a boom in options trading and provided mathematical legitimacy to the activities of the [[Chicago Board Options Exchange]] and other options markets around the world.<ref name="mackenzie">{{cite book|title= An Engine, Not a Camera: How Financial Models Shape Markets|last= MacKenzie|first= Donald|author-link= Donald Angus MacKenzie|year= 2006|publisher= MIT Press|location= Cambridge, MA|isbn= 978-0-262-13460-6|url= https://archive.org/details/enginenotcamerah00mack_0}}</ref> It is widely used, although often with adjustments and corrections, by options market participants.<ref name="bodie-kane-marcus">{{cite book |title= Investments|last= Bodie|first= Zvi|author-link=Zvi Bodie |author2=Alex Kane|author3=Alan J. Marcus|year= 2008|publisher= McGraw-Hill/Irwin|location= New York|edition=7th|isbn=978-0-07-326967-2 }}</ref>{{rp|751}}}}

{{term|[[board of governors]]}}
{{defn|The main governing body that directs the operations of the United States {{gli|Federal Reserve System}}. Its seven members supervise the 12 Federal Reserve Districts.}}

{{term|[[Bond (finance)|bond]]}}
{{defn|In {{gli|finance}}, an instrument of indebtedness of the bond issuer to the holders. The most common types of bonds include [[municipal bond]]s and [[corporate bond]]s. The bond is a {{gli|debt}} {{gli|security}}, under which the issuer owes the holders a debt and (depending on the terms of the bond) is obliged to pay them {{gli|interest}} (the {{gli|coupon}}) or to repay the principal at a later date, termed the {{gli|maturity}} date.<ref>{{Cite book| last = O'Sullivan| first = Arthur|author2=Sheffrin, Steven M.| title = Economics: Principles in action| publisher = Savvas Learning Company| year = 2022| location = Upper Saddle River, New Jersey| pages = 197, 507| url = https://www.savvas.com/index.cfm?locator=PS3jRm| isbn = 978-0-13-063085-8}}</ref> Interest is usually payable at fixed intervals (semiannual, annual, or sometimes monthly). Very often the bond is negotiable, that is, the ownership of the instrument can be transferred in the secondary market. This means that once the transfer agents at the bank medallion stamp the bond, it is highly liquid on the secondary market.<ref>[http://www.moneycontrol.com/pehlakadam/bonds.php Bonds], accessed: 2012-06-08</ref>}}

{{term|[[Bondareva–Shapley theorem]]}}
{{defn|Describes a necessary and sufficient condition for the non-emptiness of the core of a cooperative game in characteristic function form.}}

{{term|[[boots theory]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''Sam Vimes theory of socioeconomic unfairness'''.}} 
{{defn|Purchasing cheap, low-quality goods may become more expensive in the long run because they must be replaced more frequently. For example, purchasing expensive, high-quality boots may be cheaper over a long time because cheaper boots would quickly wear out and require replacement.}}

{{term|[[borrower]]}}
{{defn|See ''{{gli|debtor}}''.}}

{{term|[[bounded rationality]]}}
{{defn|The idea that [[rationality]] is limited when individuals [[decision-making|make decisions]], and under these limitations, rational individuals will select a decision that is [[satisficing|satisfactory]] rather than optimal.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sent |first1=Esther-Mirjam |title=Rationality and bounded rationality: you can't have one without the other |journal=The European Journal of the History of Economic Thought |date=October 31, 2017 |volume=25 |issue=6 |pages=1370–1386 |doi=10.1080/09672567.2018.1523206 |doi-access=free|hdl=2066/199920 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>}}

{{term|[[Braess's paradox]]}}
{{defn|The observation that adding one or more roads to a road network can slow down overall traffic flow through it.}}

{{term|[[Brander–Spencer model]]}}
{{defn|An economic model in international trade that illustrates a situation where a government can subsidize domestic firms to help them in their competition against foreign producers and in doing so enhances national welfare.}}

{{term|[[break-even (economics)|break-even]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''break-even point (BEP)'''.}}
{{defn|The point at which total {{gli|cost}} and total {{gli|revenue}} are equal, i.e. "even". There is no net loss or gain, and one has "broken even", though {{gli|opportunity cost|opportunity costs}} have been paid and {{gli|capital}} has received the risk-adjusted, expected return. In short, all costs that must be paid are paid, and there is neither profit nor loss.<ref name='R000000'>{{cite book | last = Levine | first = David | author-link = David K. Levine |author2= Michele Boldrin | title = Against Intellectual Monopoly | publisher = Cambridge University Press | date = 2008-09-07 | page = 312 | url = http://www.dklevine.com/general/intellectual/againstfinal.htm | isbn = 978-0-521-87928-6 }}</ref><ref>Tapang, Bienvenido, and Lorelei Mendoza. ''Introductory Economics.'' University of the Philippines, Baguio.</ref>}}

{{term|[[Bretton Woods system]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|monetary system}} which established the rules for commercial and financial relations among the United States, Canada, Western Europe, Australia, and Japan after the 1944 Bretton Woods Agreement. The Bretton Woods system was the first example of a fully {{gli|representative money|negotiated}} monetary order intended to govern monetary relations among independent states. The chief features were an obligation for each country to adopt a monetary policy that maintained its external {{gli|exchange rate|exchange rates}} within 1 percent by tying its currency to gold and the ability of the {{gli|International Monetary Fund|IMF}} to bridge temporary {{gli|balance of payments|imbalances of payments}}; there was also a need to address the lack of cooperation among other countries and to prevent [[competitive devaluation]] of the currencies.}}

{{term|[[budget]]}}
{{defn|The itemization of an individual's or firm's total income and total expenses for a set period of time, usually a month or a year.}}

{{term|[[Deficit spending|budget deficit]]}}
{{ghat|Also simply called '''spending'''.}}
{{defn|The amount by which spending exceeds {{gli|revenue}} over a particular period of time; it is the opposite of {{gli|budget surplus}}. The term may be applied to the budget of a government, private company, or individual.}}

{{term|[[budget set]]}}
{{ghat|Also called an '''opportunity set'''.}}
{{defn|The set of all possible consumption bundles that an individual can afford, given the {{gli|price|prices}} of goods and the individual's {{gli|income}} level. The budget set is bounded above by the [[Budget constraint|budget line]]. Graphically speaking, all the consumption bundles that lie inside and on the budget constraint form the budget set. By most definitions, budget sets must be [[Compact set|compact]] and [[Convex set|convex]].}}

{{term|[[Engel curve|budget share Engel curve]]}}
{{defn|Describes how the proportion of household income spent on a good or service varies with income.}}

{{term|[[budget surplus]]}}
{{defn|A budget's revenues in excess of its expenditures.}}

{{term|[[buffer stock scheme]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''intervention storage''' or the '''ever-normal granary'''.}}
{{defn|An attempt to use [[commodity]] storage for the purposes of [[price stability|stabilising prices]] in an entire economy or an individual (commodity) market. Specifically, [[commodities]] are bought when a [[Economic surplus|surplus]] exists in the economy, stored, and are then sold from these stores when [[economic shortage]]s in the economy occur.<ref name="Morrow1980">{{cite book|last=Morrow|first=Daniel T.|title=The economics of the international stockholding of wheat|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=czEts2pPxq4C|year=1980|publisher=International Food Policy Research Institute|isbn=978-0-89629-019-8}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[bullionism]]}}
{{defn|An economic theory that defines wealth by the amount of [[precious metal]]s owned.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kindleberger |first1=Charles P. |title=A Financial History of Western Europe |date=3 June 2015 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-136-80578-3 |page=33 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tgzICQAAQBAJ&pg=PA33 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[business cycle]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''economic cycle''' or '''trade cycle'''.}}
{{defn|The downward and upward movement of {{gli|gross domestic product}} (GDP) around its long-term growth trend.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Madhani | first1 = P. M. | year = 2010 | title = .Rebalancing Fixed and Variable Pay in a Sales Organization: A Business Cycle Perspective | journal = [[Compensation & Benefits Review]] | volume = 42 | issue = 3| pages = 179–189 | doi=10.1177/0886368709359668| s2cid = 154281029 | url = https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm/SSRN_ID2389986_code765212.pdf?abstractid=1562551&mirid=1 }}</ref> The length of a business cycle is the period of time containing a single boom and contraction in sequence. These fluctuations typically involve shifts over time between periods of relatively rapid economic growth ({{gli|economic expansion|expansions}} or {{gli|boom|booms}}) and periods of relative stagnation or decline ({{gli|contraction|contractions}} or {{gli|recession|recessions}}).}}

{{term|[[business economics]]}}
{{defn|A branch of {{gli|applied economics}} which uses [[economic theory]] and quantitative methods to analyze [[Business|business enterprises]] and the factors contributing to the diversity of organizational structures and the relationships of firms with labour, {{gli|capital}} and product markets.<ref name="Moschandreas">Moschandreas, Maria (2000). ''Business Economics'', 2nd Edition, Thompson Learning,  [https://books.google.com/books?id=ncVfjhTULyAC&pg=PA410 Description] and chapter-preview [https://books.google.com/books?id=ncVfjhTULyAC&pg=PR5 links].</ref>}}

{{term|[[business sector]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''corporate sector''' or sometimes simply '''business'''.}}
{{defn|The part of the {{gli|economy}} made up by [[company|companies]].<ref>Longman Business English Dictionary</ref> It is generally considered a subset of the [[Sovereign state|domestic]] economy,<ref>But compare {{cite book| last1=Keese| first1=Mark| last2=Salou| first2=Gérard| last3= Richardson| first3=Pete| title=The measurement of output and factors of production for the business sector in OECD countries: the OECD business sector database| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Zzm5AAAAIAAJ| series=OECD Department of Economics and Statistics working papers| volume=99| publisher=Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development| date=1991| page=i| access-date=2015-06-07| quote=[...] recent work of the OECD Economics and Statistics Department to construct an international Business Sector Data Base (BSDB) for use in a wide variety of analyses of production and supply issues [...].}}</ref> excluding the economic activities of general government, of private households, and of non-profit organizations serving individuals.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bls.gov/bls/glossary.htm |title=BLS Information |date=February 28, 2008 |work=Glossary |publisher=U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Division of Information Services |access-date=2009-05-05}}</ref>}}
