==C==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[Cambridge capital controversy]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''the capital controversy''' or '''the two Cambridges debate'''.}}
{{defn|A dispute between proponents of two differing theoretical and mathematical positions in economics concerning the nature and role of [[capital (economics)|capital]] goods and a critique of the [[Neoclassical economics|neoclassical]] vision of aggregate production and distribution.<ref name=tche>Tcherneva (2011)</ref>}}

{{term|[[Cambridge equation]]}}
{{defn|Relates money demand, price level, and real national income in the Cambridge quantity theory of money.}}

{{term|[[cameralism]]}}
{{defn|A German science of [[public administration]] in the 18th and early 19th centuries that aimed at strong management of a centralized economy for the benefit mainly of the [[State (polity)|state]].<ref name="oxford-dict">{{cite web |title=Definition of cameralism in English |url=https://en.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/cameralism |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190101002814/https://en.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/cameralism |archive-date=January 1, 2019 |website=Oxford Dictionaries |publisher=Oxford University Press |quote=An economic theory prevalent in 18th-cent. Germany, which advocated a strong public administration managing a centralized economy primarily for the benefit of the state.}}</ref> }}

{{term|[[Emissions trading|cap and trade (CAT)]]}}
{{defn|A market-based approach to limiting negative externalities (for example, pollution) by providing economic [[incentive]]s for reducing the production of said negative externalities.<ref name="stavins01">{{Cite journal |first=Robert N. |last=Stavins |date=November 2001 |access-date=2010-05-20 |title=Experience with Market-Based Environmental Policy Instruments |url=http://www.rff.org/documents/RFF-DP-01-58.pdf |journal=Discussion Paper 01-58 |publisher=Resources for the Future |location=Washington, D.C. |quote=Market-based instruments are regulations that encourage behavior through market signals rather than through explicit directives regarding pollution control levels or methods |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110501113141/http://www.rff.org/documents/RFF-DP-01-58.pdf |archive-date=2011-05-01 }}</ref> A central authority or [[government agency|governmental]] body allocates or sells a limited number (a "cap") of permits that allow the creation of a specific negative externality over a set time period. Permit owners are then allowed to sell these permits to others.}}

{{term|[[capacity utilization]]}}
{{defn|The extent to which an enterprise or a nation uses its installed [[productive capacity]]. It is the relationship between {{gli|output}} that ''is'' produced with the installed equipment and the potential output which ''could'' be produced with it if capacity was fully used.}}

{{term|[[Capital (economics)|capital]]}}
{{defn|Any asset that can enhance one's power to perform economically useful work. '''Capital goods''', '''real capital''', or [[capital asset]]s are already-produced, [[durable good]]s or any non-financial asset that is used in {{gli|production}} of {{gli|good|goods}} or {{gli|service|services}}.<ref name="Boulding">{{cite web|last1=Boulding|first1=Kenneth E.|title=Capital and interest|url=http://www.britannica.com/topic/capital-economics|website=Encyclopedia Britannica|access-date=July 22, 2017|language=en}}</ref> Capital is distinct from land (or [[non-renewable resources]]) in that capital can be increased by human labor. At any given moment in time, total [[physical capital]] may be referred to as the '''capital stock''' (which is not to be confused with the {{gli|stock|capital stock}} of a business entity).}}

{{term|[[capital account]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''capital and financial account'''}}
{{defn|Reflects net change in ownership of national assets. A surplus in the capital account means money is flowing into the country, and the inbound flows effectively represent borrowings or sales of assets. A deficit in the capital account means money is flowing out of the country, and it suggests the nation is increasing its ownership of foreign assets.}}

{{term|[[capital accumulation]]}}
{{defn|Any net addition to existing wealth and/or a redistribution of wealth. Capital accumulation is the dynamic that motivates the pursuit of [[Profit (economics)|profit]], involving the investment of money or any financial asset with the goal of increasing the initial monetary value of said asset as a financial return.}}

{{term|[[capital cost]]}}
{{defn|A fixed, one-time {{gli|expenditure|expense}} incurred on the purchase of {{gli|real property|land}}, buildings, construction, and equipment used in the production of goods or in the rendering of services. In other words, it is the total cost needed to bring a project to a commercially operable status. Whether a particular cost is capital or not depends on many factors, such as accounting, [[tax law]]s, and [[Materiality (auditing)|materiality]].}}

{{term|[[capital flight]]}}
{{defn|Occurs when money or assets rapidly flow out of a country due to an event of economic consequence. Such events may include an increase in {{gli|tax|taxes}} on {{gli|capital}} or capital holders or the government of the country [[default (finance)|defaulting]] on its debt that disturbs investors and causes them to lower their valuation of the assets in that country or otherwise to lose confidence in its economic strength.}}

{{term|[[capital formation]]}}
{{defn|Any method for increasing the amount of [[Capital (economics)|capital]] owned or under one's control, or any method in using or mobilizing capital resources for investment purposes. Capital formation also sometimes refers to a specific statistical concept, also known as [[net investment]], which measures the net additions to the (physical) capital [[stock and flow|stock]] of a country (or an economic sector) in an accounting interval. Capital formation is also sometimes a modern general term for [[capital accumulation]], referring to the total "stock of capital" that has been formed, or to the growth of this total capital stock.<ref>Yanovsky, M.: ''Anatomy of Social Accounting Systems'', London; Chapman & Hall, 1965.</ref>}}

{{term|[[capital gain]]}}
{{defn|The [[Profit (economics)|profit]] earned on the sale of an [[asset]] which has increased in value over the holding period. An asset may include [[tangible property]], a car, a business, or [[intangible property]] such as [[share capital|shares]].}}

{{term|[[capital good]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|durable good}} that is used in the production of goods or services. Capital goods are one of the three types of producer goods, the other two being land and labour, which are also known collectively as primary {{gli|factors of production}}. This classification originated with {{gli|classical economics}} and has remained the dominant method for classification.}}

{{term|[[capital intensity]]}}
{{defn|The amount of fixed or real [[Capital (economics)|capital]] present in relation to other [[factors of production]], especially labor. At the level of either a production process or the aggregate economy, it may be estimated by the capital to labor ratio, such as from the points along a capital/labor [[isoquant]].}}

{{term|[[capitalism]]}}
{{defn|An [[economic system]] based on the [[private ownership]] of the [[means of production]] and their operation for [[Profit (economics)|profit]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Zimbalist |last2=Sherman |last3=Brown |first1=Andrew |first2=Howard J. |first3=Stuart |title=Comparing Economic Systems: A Political-Economic Approach |publisher=[[Harcourt College Publishing]] |date=October 1988 |isbn=978-0-15-512403-5 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/comparingeconomi0000zimb_q8i6/page/6 6–7] |quote=Pure capitalism is defined as a system wherein all of the means of production (physical capital) are privately owned and run by the capitalist class for a profit, while most other people are workers who work for a salary or wage (and who do not own the capital or the product). |url=https://archive.org/details/comparingeconomi0000zimb_q8i6/page/6}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Rosser |first1=Mariana V. |last2=Rosser |first2=J Barkley |title=Comparative Economics in a Transforming World Economy |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |date=23 July 2003 |isbn=978-0-262-18234-8 |page=7 |quote=In capitalist economies, land and produced means of production (the capital stock) are owned by private individuals or groups of private individuals organized as firms.}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first=Chris |last=Jenks |title=Core Sociological Dichotomies |quote=Capitalism, as a mode of production, is an economic system of manufacture and exchange which is geared toward the production and sale of commodities within a market for profit, where the manufacture of commodities consists of the use of the formally free labor of workers in exchange for a wage to create commodities in which the manufacturer extracts surplus value from the labor of the workers in terms of the difference between the wages paid to the worker and the value of the commodity produced by him/her to generate that profit. |location=London; Thousand Oaks, CA; New Delhi. |publisher=[[SAGE Publishing]] |page=383}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=The Challenge of Global Capitalism: The World Economy in the 21st Century |last=Gilpin |first=Robert |isbn=978-0-691-18647-4 |oclc=1076397003 |date=5 June 2018|publisher=Princeton University Press }}</ref> Central characteristics of capitalism include [[capital accumulation]], [[competitive market]]s, [[price system]]s, [[private property]], [[Property rights (economics)|property rights]] recognition, [[voluntary exchange]], and [[wage labor]].<ref>Heilbroner, Robert L. [http://www.dictionaryofeconomics.com/article?id=pde2008_C000053 "Capitalism"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171028232506/http://www.dictionaryofeconomics.com/article?id=pde2008_C000053 |date=28 October 2017 }}. {{term|[[cartel]]}}
{{defn|Any group of firms that colludes and acts as a single coordinated whole to restrict output and drive up prices.}}

{{term|[[cash]]}}
{{defn|Money in the physical form of currency, such as [[banknote]]s and [[coin]]s.}}


{{term|[[cash crop]]}}
{{defn|A cash crop, also called profit crop, is an agricultural crop which is grown to sell for profit. It is typically purchased by parties separate from a farm.}}

{{term|[[central bank]]}}
{{ghat|Also called a '''reserve bank''' or '''monetary authority'''.}} 
{{defn|An institution that manages the {{gli|currency}}, {{gli|money supply}}, and {{gli|interest rate|interest rates}} of an entire state or nation. Central banks also usually oversee the [[commercial bank|commercial banking system]] of their respective countries. In contrast to a commercial bank, a central bank possesses a {{gli|monopoly}} on increasing the {{gli|monetary base}} in the state, and usually also prints the national currency,<ref>{{Cite web  |url= http://www.bankofcanada.ca/2013/11/5-and-10-bank-note-issue-2/|title=$5 and $10 Bank Note Issue|author=Bank of Canada|access-date=7 November 2013}}</ref> which usually serves as the state's legal tender. Central banks also act as a "[[lender of last resort]]" to the banking sector during times of financial crisis. Most central banks usually also have supervisory and regulatory powers to ensure the solvency of member institutions, prevent [[bank run]]s, and prevent reckless or fraudulent behavior by member banks.}}

{{term|[[Certificate of Deposit]] (CD or COD)}}
{{defn|A savings instrument that usually earns more {{gli|interest}} than a savings account but is bound by limits set within a contract.}}

{{term|[[ceteris paribus]]}}
{{defn|A phrase or clause often loosely translated as "holding all else constant." It does not imply that no other things will in fact change; rather, it isolates the effect of one particular change.}}

{{term|[[charitable giving]]}}
{{defn|A gift of cash or property made to a nonprofit organization to help it accomplish its goals, for which the donor receives nothing of value in return. In the U.S. however, some charitable giving is tax deductible.}}

{{term|[[chartalism]]}}
{{defn|A [[Heterodox economics|heterodox]] theory of money that argues that money originated historically with states' attempts to direct economic activity rather than as a spontaneous solution to the problems with [[barter]] or as a means with which to tokenize debt,<ref>{{cite book|last1=Graeber|first1=David|title=Debt: The First 5000 Years|date=12 July 2011|publisher=Melville House |isbn=978-1-933633-86-2|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/debtfirst5000yea00grae}}</ref> and that [[fiat currency]] has value in exchange because of sovereign power to levy [[taxes]] on economic activity payable in the currency they issue.}}

{{term|[[check (money)]]}}
{{defn|A check is a written, dated, and signed draft that directs a bank to pay a specific sum of money to the bearer. The person or entity writing the check is known as the payor or drawer, while the person to whom the check is written is the payee.}}

{{term|[[Chicago school of economics|Chicago school]]}}
{{defn|A [[Neoclassical economics|neoclassical]] school of thought once based around rational expectations, monetarism, and free market supremacy.}}

{{term|[[Choice]] (CD or COD)}}
{{defn|Making a decision when facing multiple possible options.}}

{{term|[[choice modelling]]}}
{{defn|A method of modelling the decision process of an individual or segment via revealed or stated preferences.}}

{{term|[[circular flow of income]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''circular flow model'''.}}
{{defn|A model of the economy in which the major exchanges are represented as flows of {{gli|money}}, {{gli|good|goods}} and {{gli|service|services}}, etc. between {{gli|agent|economic agents}}. The flows of money and goods exchanged in a closed circuit correspond in value, but run in the opposite direction. The circular flow analysis is the basis of [[national accounts]] and hence of {{gli|macroeconomics}}.}}

{{term|[[Circulation (currency)|circulation]]}}
{{defn|The continuous movement of goods, services, and money within an economy.}}

{{term|[[citizen's dividend]]}}
{{defn|A proposed set of regular payments to all citizens from revenue raised by leasing or taxing the monopoly of valuable land and other natural resources. It is based on the Georgist principle that the natural world is the common property of all people.}}

{{term|[[classical economics]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''classical political economy'''.}}
{{defn|A [[school of thought]] in economics that flourished, primarily in [[Kingdom of Great Britain|Britain]], in the late 18th and early-to-mid 19th century. Its main thinkers are held to be [[Adam Smith]], [[Jean-Baptiste Say]], [[David Ricardo]], [[Thomas Robert Malthus]], and [[John Stuart Mill]]. These economists produced a theory of [[Market economy|market economies]] as largely self-regulating systems, governed by natural laws of production and exchange (famously captured by Adam Smith's metaphor of the [[invisible hand]]).}}

{{term|[[classical general equilibrium model]]}}
{{defn|A model that aims to describe the economy by aggregating the behavior of individuals and firms.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Burgstaller |first=André |date=1989 |title=A Classical Model of Growth, Expectations and General Equilibrium |journal=Economica |volume=56 |issue=223 |pages=373–393 |doi=10.2307/2554284 |jstor=2554284 |issn=0013-0427}}</ref> Note that the classical [[general equilibrium]] model is unrelated to [[classical economics]], and was instead developed within [[neoclassical economics]] beginning in the late 19th century.<ref>{{Cite book |last=McKenzie |first=Lionel W. |title=Classical general equilibrium theory |date=2002 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=0-262-13413-6 |location=Cambridge, Mass. |oclc=49226070}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[club good]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''artificially scarce goods''', '''toll goods''', '''collective goods''' or '''quasi-public goods'''.}}
{{defn|A good that is [[excludability|excludable]] but [[non-rivalrous]], at least until reaching a point where [[:wikt:congestion|congestion]] occurs.}}

{{term|[[Coase conjecture]]}}
{{defn|A model in which a monopolist must sell its product at a low price because it is effectively in competition with itself over multiple periods. It is assumed that the monopolist sells a durable good to a market where resale is impossible, faces an infinite time horizon, faces consumers who have different valuations, and does not know individuals' valuations.}}

{{term|[[Coase theorem]]}}
{{defn|States that if the provision of a good or service results in an externality and trade in that good or service is possible, then bargaining will lead to a [[Pareto efficiency|Pareto efficient]] outcome regardless of the initial allocation of property. This requires sufficiently low [[transaction costs]] in the bargaining and exchange process.}}

{{term|[[cobweb model]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''cobweb theory'''.}}
{{defn|A model which describes cyclical [[supply and demand]] in a market where the amount produced must be chosen before prices are observed. Producers' [[Expected value|expectation]]s about prices are assumed to be based on observations of previous prices. It explains why [[price]]s may be subjected to periodic fluctuations in certain types of [[Market (economics)|market]]s.}}

{{term|[[collateral loan]]}}
{{defn|Also known as a secured loan, it is a loan where the borrower pledges an asset to a financial institution to access funds. The asset, called collateral, protects the lender from possible defaulting as they would take ownership in case of default.}}

{{term|[[collective action]]}}
{{defn|Any action taken together [[Advocacy group|by a group of people]] whose [[goal]] is to enhance their condition and achieve a common objective.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/1917157/collective-action-problem|title=collective action problem – collective action|website=Encyclopædia Britannica}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[collective action problem]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''social dilemma'''}}
{{defn|A situation in which all individuals would be better off cooperating but fail to do so because of conflicting interests between individuals that discourage joint action.<ref>{{Cite book|chapter-url=http://www.oxfordreference.com/view/10.1093/acref/9780199670840.001.0001/acref-9780199670840-e-223|title=Collective action problem – Oxford Reference|volume=1|language=en|doi=10.1093/acref/9780199670840.001.0001|access-date=2018-04-11|isbn=978-0-19-967084-0|chapter=Collective action problem|publisher=Oxford University Press|date=2018-01-18|editor1-last=Brown|editor1-first=Garrett|editor2-first=Iain|editor2-last=McLean|editor3-first=Alistair|editor3-last=McMillan}}</ref><ref>Erhard Friedberg, "Conflict of Interest from the Perspective of the Sociology of Organized Action" in ''Conflict of Interest in Global, Public and Corporate Governance'', Anne Peters & Lukas Handschin (eds), Cambridge University Press, 2012</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Allison | first1 = S. T. | last2 = Beggan | first2 = J. K. | last3 = Midgley | first3 = E. H. | year = 1996 | title = The quest for "similar instances" and "simultaneous possibilities": Metaphors in social dilemma research | doi =10.1037/0022-3514.71.3.479 | journal = Journal of Personality and Social Psychology | volume = 71 | issue = 3| pages = 479–497 }}</ref>}}

{{term|[[collusion]]}}
{{defn|A deceitful agreement or secret cooperation between two or more parties to limit open competition by deceiving, misleading or defrauding others of their legal right.}}

{{term|[[command economy]]}}
{{defn|An economy in which the government directs all economic activity.}}

{{term|[[commercial agriculture]]}}

{{term|[[commodity]]}}
{{defn|An economic good or service that has full or substantial [[fungibility]]: that is, the market treats instances of the good as equivalent or nearly so with no regard to who produced them.}}

{{term|[[communism]]}}
{{defn|An ideology centered around [[common ownership]] of the [[means of production]], distribution, and exchange that allocates products to everyone in the society based on need.<ref>{{cite book |last=Ely |first=Richard T |title=French and German socialism in modern times |date=1883 |publisher=[[Harper & Brothers]] |location=New York |pages=35–36 |oclc=456632 |quote=All communists without exception propose that the people as a whole, or some particular division of the people, as a village or commune, should own all the means of production—land, houses, factories, railroads, canals, etc.; that production should be carried on in common; and that officers, selected in one way or another, should distribute among the inhabitants the fruits of their labor.}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Bukharin |first1=Nikolai |title=[[The ABC of Communism]] |last2=Preobrazhensky |first2=Yevgeni |date=1922 |publisher=[[Communist Party of Great Britain]] |location=London, England |pages=72–73, § 20 |translator-last1=Paul |translator-first1=Cedar |chapter=Distribution in the communist system |author1-link=Nikolai Bukharin |author2-link=Yevgeni Preobrazhensky |access-date=18 August 2021 |orig-date=1920 |translator-last2=Paul |translator-first2=Eden |translator-link1=Cedar Paul |translator-link2=Eden Paul |chapter-url=https://www.marxists.org/archive/bukharin/works/1920/abc/ABC-of-Communism.pdf#page=67 |via=[[Marxists Internet Archive]]}}</ref><ref name="Steele p.43">{{cite book |last=Steele |first=David R. |date=1992 |title=From Marx to Mises: Post-Capitalist Society and the Challenge of Economic Calculation |publisher=Open Court Publishing Company |isbn=978-0-87548-449-5 |page=43 |quote= One widespread distinction was that socialism socialised production only while communism socialised production and consumption.}}</ref>}}
{{term|[[comparative advantage]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''opportunity cost advantage'''.}}
{{defn|The ability to produce most efficiently given all of the other products that could be produced.}}

{{term|[[compensating differential]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''compensating wage differential''' or '''equalizing difference'''.}}
{{defn|The additional amount of income that a given worker must be offered to motivate them to accept a given undesirable job, relative to other jobs that worker could perform.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kaufman |first1=Bruce E. |first2=Julie L. |last2=Hotchkiss |year=2005 |chapter=Education, Training, and Earnings Differentials: The Theory of Human Capital |title=The economics of labor markets |edition=5th |publisher=Harcourt College Publishers |isbn=978-0-324-28879-7 }}</ref><ref name="Rosen">{{cite book |last=Rosen |first=Sherwin |year=1986 |chapter=The theory of equalizing differences |editor1-first=Orley |editor1-last=Ashenfelter |editor2-first=Richard |editor2-last=Layard |title=The Handbook of Labor Economics |volume=1 |pages=641–692 |location=New York |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-444-87856-4 }}</ref>}}

{{term|Competition (CD or COD)}}
{{defn|The presence in a market of independent buyers and sellers competing with one another and the freedom of buyers and sellers to enter and leave the market.}}

{{term|[[competition law]]}}
{{ghat|Also called an '''antitrust law''' or '''anti-monopoly law'''.}}
{{defn|Any law that promotes or seeks to maintain [[market competition]] by regulating [[anti-competitive]] conduct by companies.<ref name="papers.ssrn.com"/><ref name="Taylor 2006 1"/>}}

{{term|[[competitive market]]}}
{{defn|A market in which many sellers compete against each
other to attract customers. Each seller has an incentive to sell at the lowest
price possible to attract customers, so prices tend to be driven so low that
the sellers can just barely make a profit.}}

{{term|[[complementary goods]]}}
{{defn|{{gli|good|Goods}} that are bought and used together.}}

{{term|[[complex multiplier]]}}
{{defn|The multiplier by which a change in autonomous expenditure changes the equilibrium income in an economy.}}

{{term|[[compound interest]]}}
{{defn|The addition of {{gli|interest}} to the principal sum of a {{gli|loan}} or {{gli|deposit}}; it is often interpreted as "interest on interest". Compound interest is the result of reinvesting interest, rather than paying it out, so that interest in the next period is then earned on the principal sum plus any previously accumulated interest. Contrast ''{{gli|simple interest}}''.}}

{{term|[[computable general equilibrium]] (CGE)}}
{{ghat|Also called '''applied general equilibrium (AGE)'''.}}
{{defn|A class of economic models that use actual economic data to estimate how an economy might react to changes in policy, technology, or other external factors.}}

{{term|[[concentration ratio]]}}
{{defn|The sum of the percentage market shares of (a pre-specified number of) the largest firms in an industry, which is used to quantify [[market concentration]] in an industry.}}

{{term|[[conspicuous consumption]]}}
{{defn|The consumer practice of buying and using goods of a higher quality, [[price]], or in greater quantity than practical.<ref>Phillips, Ronnie J.  2014 April 22. "[https://www.britannica.com/topic/conspicuous-consumption Conspicuous consumption]." ''Encyclopedia Britannica''.</ref>}}

{{term|[[conspicuous consumption|conspicuous compassion]]}}
{{defn|The ostentatious use of charity meant to enhance the [[reputation]] and social prestige of the donor.<ref name="West 2004">{{cite book |last=West |first=Patrick |title=Conspicuous Compassion: Why Sometimes It Really Is Cruel To Be Kind |location=London |publisher=Civitas, Institute for the Study of Civil Society |year=2004 |isbn=978-1-903386-34-7 }}</ref>}}

{{term|consumer}}
{{defn|A member of a household that spends on goods and services.}}

{{term|[[consumer choice]]}}
{{defn|A theory of {{gli|microeconomics}} that relates {{gli|preference|preferences}} to consumption expenditures and to [[supply and demand|consumer demand curves]]. It analyzes how consumers maximize the desirability of their consumption as measured by their preferences subject to limitations on their expenditures, by maximizing {{gli|utility}} subject to a consumer {{gli|budget constraint}}.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.ecnmy.org/learn/your-home/consumption/what-is-consumer-choice-theory/|title=What is 'consumer choice theory'? — Economy|work=Economy|access-date=2017-05-31|language=en-GB}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[consumer confidence]]}}
{{defn|An {{gli|economic indicator}} that measures the degree of optimism that {{gli|consumer|consumers}} feel about the overall state of the {{gli|economy}} and their [[Personal finance|personal financial]] situation.}}

{{term|[[consumer credit]]}}
{{defn|A loan afforded to a consumer for the payment of goods and services which they will have to repay to the lender over time usually plus interest.}}

{{term|[[consumer price index]] (CPI)}}
{{defn|Measures changes in the price level of [[market basket]] of [[Goods|consumer goods]] and [[Services marketing|services]] purchased by households.
The CPI is a statistical estimate constructed using the prices of a sample of representative items whose prices are collected periodically. Sub-indices and sub-sub-indices are computed for different categories and sub-categories of goods and services, being combined to produce the overall index with weights reflecting their shares in the total of the consumer expenditures covered by the index. It is one of several [[price index|price indices]] calculated by most national statistical agencies. The annual percentage change in a CPI is used as a measure of {{gli|inflation}}. A CPI can be used to index (i.e. adjust for the effect of inflation) the real value of wages, salaries, and pensions; to regulate prices; and to deflate monetary magnitudes to show changes in real values. In most countries, the CPI, along with the population census, is one of the most closely watched national economic statistics.}}

{{term|[[consumer surplus]]}}
{{defn|the difference between the maximum price a consumer is willing to pay and the actual price they do pay. If a consumer is willing to pay more for a unit of a good than the current asking price, they are getting more benefit from the purchased product than they would if the price was their maximum willingness to pay. They are receiving the same benefit, the obtainment of the good, with a smaller cost as they are spending less than they would if they were charged their maximum willingness to pay.<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia | doi=10.1057/978-1-349-95121-5_626-2| chapter=Consumer Surplus| encyclopedia=The New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics| pages=1–7| year=2008| last1=Slesnick| first1=Daniel T.| isbn=978-1-349-95121-5}}</ref> }}

{{term|[[consumerism]]}}
{{defn|Economic policies which emphasize {{gli|consumption}}.}}
  
{{term|[[Consumption (economics)|consumption]]}}
{{defn|According to [[mainstream economics|mainstream economists]], only the final purchase of {{gli|good|goods}} and {{gli|service|services}} by individuals constitutes consumption, while other types of expenditure—in particular, [[fixed investment]], [[intermediate consumption]], and government spending—are placed in separate categories (see ''{{gli|consumer choice}}''). Other economists define consumption much more broadly, as the aggregate of all economic activity that does not entail the design, production and marketing of goods and services (e.g. the selection, adoption, use, disposal and recycling of goods and services).}}

{{term|[[consumption function]]}}
{{defn|A mathematical function which describes a relationship between {{gli|consumption}} and {{gli|disposable income}}.<ref>Algebraically, this means <math>C = f(Y_{d})</math> where <math>f \colon \mathbb{R}^{+} \to \mathbb{R}^{+}</math> is a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] that [[Map (mathematics)|maps]] levels of disposable income <math>Y_{d}</math>—income after government intervention, such as taxes or transfer payments—into levels of consumption <math>C</math>.</ref><ref>{{cite book |first=John |last=Lindauer |author-link=John Lindauer |title=Macroeconomics |location=New York |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |edition=Third |year=1976 |isbn=978-0-471-53572-0 |pages=40–43 }}</ref> The concept is believed to have been introduced into {{gli|macroeconomics}} by [[John Maynard Keynes]] in 1936, who used it to develop the notion of a [[Fiscal multiplier|government spending multiplier]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hall |first1=Robert E. |author-link=Robert Hall (economist) |last2=Taylor |first2=John B. |author2-link=John B. Taylor |chapter=Consumption and Income |pages=63–67 |title=Macroeconomics: Theory, Performance, and Policy |location=New York |publisher=W. W. Norton |year=1986 |isbn=978-0-393-95398-5 }}</ref>}}

{{term|[[contract curve]]}}
{{defn|In [[microeconomics]], the '''contract curve''' is the set of points representing final allocations of two goods between two people that could occur as a result of mutually beneficial trading between those people given their initial allocations of the goods. All the points on this locus are [[Pareto efficient]] allocations, meaning that from any one of these points there is no reallocation that could make one of the people more satisfied with his or her allocation without making the other person less satisfied. The contract curve is the subset of the Pareto efficient points that could be reached by trading from the people's initial holdings of the two goods.}}

{{term|[[contract theory]]}}
{{defn|The study of how economic actors can and do construct contractual arrangements, generally in the presence of [[asymmetric information]]. Because of its connections with both [[agency (law)|agency]] and [[incentive]]s, contract theory is often categorized within a field known as [[law and economics]].}}

{{term|[[Convergence (economics)|convergence]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''catch-up effect'''.}}
{{defn|The hypothesis that poorer [[Economic system|economies]]' per capita incomes will tend to grow at faster rates than richer economies.}}

{{term|[[Convexity in economics|convexity]]}}
{{defn|In the [[Arrow–Debreu model]] of [[general equilibrium|general economic equilibrium]], agents have convex {{gli|budget set|budget sets}} and [[convex preferences]]: at {{gli|equilibrium}} prices, the budget [[supporting hyperplane|hyperplane supports]] the best attainable [[indifference curve]].<ref name="Newman1987d" >{{harvtxt|Newman|1987d}}</ref> The [[profit (economics)|profit function]] is the [[convex conjugate]] of the [[Cost curve|cost function]].<ref name="Newman, Peter p. 1">Newman, Peter (1987c). "Convexity". In Eatwell, John; Milgate, Murray; Newman, Peter (eds.). The New Palgrave: A Dictionary of Economics (first ed.). Palgrave Macmillan. p. 1. {{doi|10.1057/9780230226203.2282}}. {{ISBN|9780333786765}}.</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Newman |first=Peter |author-link=Peter Kenneth Newman |chapter=Duality |title=The New Palgrave: A Dictionary of Economics |editor1-first=John |editor1-last=Eatwell |editor2-first=Murray |editor2-last=Milgate |editor3-first=Peter |editor3-last=Newman |editor3-link=Peter Kenneth Newman |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan |year=1987d |edition=first |doi=10.1057/9780230226203.2412<!-- SNAFU at NP? 30 Jan 2011--> |page=1 |chapter-url=http://www.dictionaryofeconomics.com/article?id=pde1987_X000626 |isbn=978-0-333-78676-5}}</ref> [[Convex analysis]] is the standard tool for analyzing textbook economics.<ref name="Newman, Peter p. 1" /> Non‑convex phenomena in economics have been studied with [[subgradient|nonsmooth analysis]], which generalizes [[convex analysis]].<ref>Khan, M. Ali (2008). "Perfect competition". In Durlauf, Steven N.; Blume, Lawrence E., ed. (eds.). The New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics (Second ed.). Palgrave Macmillan. pp. 354–365. {{doi|10.1057/9780230226203.1267}}. {{ISBN|978-0-333-78676-5}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[coordination good]]}}
{{defn|A [[good (economics)|good]] created by the coordination of people within [[civil society]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/08/16/opinion/16iht-edmesquita.html|title=An open economy, a closed society|first1=Bruce Bueno de |last1=Mesquita|author1-link=Bruce Bueno de Mesquita|first2=George W.|last2=Downs|author2-link=George W. Downs (political scientist)|date=August 17, 2005|work=New York Times}}</ref> Coordination goods are non-[[Rivalry (economics)|rivalrous]], but may be partially [[Excludability|excludable]] through the means of withholding cooperation from a non-cooperative state.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://faculty.ucc.edu/egh-damerow/global_commons.htm|title=Global Commons, Collective Goods, Free Riders, and Destruction of the Commons|access-date=2014-12-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304023511/http://faculty.ucc.edu/egh-damerow/global_commons.htm|archive-date=2016-03-04}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[corporate tax]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''corporation tax''' or '''company tax'''.}}
{{defn|A type of [[direct tax]] levied on the income or capital of corporations and other similar legal entities.}}

{{term|corporation}}
{{defn|A type of business organization owned by many people but treated by law as though it were an individual person; it can own property, pay taxes, make contracts, and contribute to political causes.}}

{{term|[[cost]]}}
{{defn|no=1|The value of {{gli|money}} that is used up to produce a {{gli|good}} or deliver a {{gli|service}}, and hence is no longer available for further use. In business, the cost may be one of acquisition, in which case the amount of money expended to acquire a good or service is counted as the cost; in this case, money is the input that is gone to acquire the thing. This acquisition cost may be the sum of the cost of production as incurred by the original producer and of further costs of transaction as incurred by the acquirer over and above the {{gli|price}} paid to the producer. Usually, the price designated by the producer also includes a mark-up for {{gli|profit}} over the cost of production.}}
{{defn|no=2|More generally, a [[performance metric]] that is totaling up as a result of a process or as a differential for the result of a [[Decision making|decision]].<ref>{{cite book| last1 = O'Sullivan| first1 = Arthur| author-link = Arthur O'Sullivan (economist)| first2 = Steven M. | last2 = Sheffrin| title = Economics| publisher = Savvas Learning Company| year = 2022| location = Paramus, New Jersey| page = 16| isbn = 978-0-13-063085-8}}</ref> Hence cost is the metric used in the standard [[Business process modelling|modeling]] paradigm applied to economic [[Business process|processes]]. Costs (pl.) are often further described based on their timing or their applicability.}}

{{term|[[cost curve]]}}
{{defn|A graph of the [[costs of production]] as a function of total quantity produced. In a {{gli|free market}} economy, {{gli|productive efficiency|productively efficient}} firms optimize their production process by minimizing cost consistent with each possible level of production, and the result is a cost curve; and {{gli|profit maximization|profit maximizing}} firms use cost curves to decide output quantities. There are various types of cost curves, all related to each other, including total and average cost curves; marginal ("for each additional unit") cost curves, which are equal to the [[Differentiation (mathematics)|differential]] of the total cost curves; and variable cost curves. Some are applicable to the [[short run]], others to the [[long run]].}}

{{term|[[cost of living]]}}
{{defn|The {{gli|cost}} of maintaining a certain [[standard of living]]. Changes in the cost of living over time are often operationalized in a [[cost-of-living index]]. Cost of living calculations are also used to compare the cost of maintaining a certain standard of living in different geographic areas. Differences in cost of living between locations can also be measured in terms of {{gli|purchasing power parity}} rates.}}

{{term|[[cost overrun]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''cost increase''' or '''budget overrun'''.}}
{{defn|A situation involving unexpected incurred {{gli|cost|costs}}. A cost overrun occurs when an underestimation of the actual cost during budgeting results in costs that are in excess of budgeted amounts.}}

{{term|[[cost the limit of price]]}}
{{defn|A maxim indicating a (prescriptive) version of the [[labor theory of value]]. It suggests that the price of a good should be equal to its cost, implying that [[profit (economics)|profit]], [[renting|rent]], and interest could be considered unjust economic arrangements.}}

{{term|[[Cournot competition]]}}
{{defn|A model used to describe an industry structure in which companies compete on the amount of output they will produce, which they decide on independently of each other and at the same time.}}

{{term|[[cost-benefit analysis]] (CBA)}}
{{ghat|Sometimes called '''benefit costs analysis (BCA)'''.}}
{{defn|A systematic approach to estimating the strengths and weaknesses of alternative options (for example in {{gli|transaction|transactions}}, activities, or functional business requirements). It is often used to determine the option or options that provide the best approach to achieve benefits while preserving savings.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=David|first1=Rodreck|last2=Ngulube|first2=Patrick|last3=Dube|first3=Adock|title=A cost-benefit analysis of document management strategies used at a financial institution in Zimbabwe: A case study|journal=SA Journal of Information Management|date=16 July 2013|volume=15|issue=2|doi=10.4102/sajim.v15i2.540|doi-access=free}}</ref> Cost-benefit analysis may be used to compare potential (or completed) courses of actions, or estimate (or evaluate) the value against {{gli|cost|costs}} of a single decision, project, or policy. Common areas of application include commercial transactions, functional business decisions, policy decisions (especially [[government policy]]), and project investments.}}

{{term|[[cost-of-production theory of value]]}}
{{defn|The theory that the {{gli|price}} of an object or condition is determined by the sum of the {{gli|cost}} of the resources that went into producing it. The cost can comprise any of the {{gli|factors of production}} (including labor, capital, or land) as well as [[Effect of taxes and subsidies on price|taxation]].}}

{{term|[[cost-push inflation]]}}
{{defn|A purported type of inflation caused by increases in the cost of important [[good (economics)|goods]] or services where no suitable alternative is available. As businesses face higher prices for underlying inputs, they are forced to increase prices of their outputs.}}

{{term|[[credit bureau]]}}
{{defn|An agency that tracks the {{gli|credit}}, employment, and housing history of {{gli|consumer|consumers}} and assigns them a {{gli|credit score}}.}}

{{term|credit card}}
{{defn|A [[payment card]] issued to users (cardholders) to enable the cardholder to pay a {{gli|merchant}} for {{gli|good|goods}} and {{gli|service|services}} based on the cardholder's promise to the [[credit card issuer|card issuer]] to pay them at a later time for the cost of the good or service plus other agreed-upon fees and charges.<ref>{{cite book| last = O'Sullivan| first = Arthur| author-link = Arthur O'Sullivan (economist)|author2=Steven M. Sheffrin| title = Economics| publisher = Savvas Learning Company| year = 2003| location = Upper Saddle River, New Jersey| page = 261| isbn = 0-13-063085-3|type=Textbook}}</ref> The card issuer (usually a bank) creates a [[revolving account]] and grants a {{gli|line of credit}} to the cardholder, from which the cardholder can borrow money for payment to a merchant or as a [[cash advance]].}}

{{term|[[credit score]]}}
{{defn|A numerical value assigned to a person's potential ability to repay {{gli|debt}}. A good credit score in the United States is approximately 700.}}

{{term|[[credit rating]]}}
{{defn|An evaluation of the [[credit risk]] of a prospective {{gli|debtor}} (an individual, business, company, or government), predicting their ability to pay back the debt, and an implicit forecast of the likelihood of the debtor [[Default (finance)|defaulting]] on the debt.<ref>{{cite book| last = Kronwald| first = Christian| title = Credit Rating and the Impact on Capital Structure| publisher = Druck und Bingdung| year = 2009| location = Norderstedt, Germany| page = 3| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=CzjS5YV5nK8C&q=%22credit%20rating%22| isbn = 978-3-640-57549-7}}</ref> Credit rating represents an evaluation of a [[credit rating agency]] of the qualitative and quantitative information for the prospective debtor, including information provided by the prospective debtor and other non-public information obtained by the credit rating agency's analysts. A subset of credit rating called credit reporting or {{gli|credit score}} is a numeric evaluation of an individual's credit worthiness, which is conducted by a {{gli|credit bureau}} or [[consumer credit reporting agency]].}}

{{term|[[credit union]]}}
{{defn|A {{gli|financial institution}} that is usually local and owned by its members.}}

{{term|[[creditor]]}}
{{defn|A person or a firm that lends money to a {{gli|debtor|borrower}}.}}

{{term|[[crisis theory]]}}
{{defn|A set of theories concerning the causes<ref>"[https://www.marxists.org/archive/hilferding/1910/finkap/ch17.htm The causes of crises"] in [[Rudolf Hilferding]] [1910] [https://www.marxists.org/archive/hilferding/1910/finkap/ ''Finance Capital. A Study of the Latest Phase of Capitalist Development''. Part IV. ''Finance capital and crises''].</ref> and consequences of the [[Tendency of the rate of profit to fall|tendency for the rate of profit to fall]] in a [[capitalism|capitalist system]].}}

{{term|[[criticism of capitalism]]}}
{{defn|A critique of [[political economy]] that involves the rejection of, or dissatisfaction with the economic system of [[capitalism]] and its outcomes.}}

{{term|[[critique of work]]}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|[[cross elasticity of demand]] (XED)}}
{{defn|Measures the sensitivity of a good's demand to the price of a different good.}}

{{term|[[Crowding out (economics)|crowding out]]}}
{{defn|A phenomenon that occurs when increased government involvement in a sector of a {{gli|market economy}} substantially affects the remainder of the market, either on the {{gli|supply}} or {{gli|demand}} side of the market.}}

{{term|[[crowding-in effect]]}}
{{defn|An increase in private investment that results from government spending. It occurs because public investment makes the private sector more productive, as well as because government spending may have a stimulative effect on the economy.}}

{{term|[[cultural economics]]}}
{{defn|The branch of {{gli|economics}} that studies the relationship between culture and economic outcomes. Here, "culture" is defined by shared beliefs and preferences of respective groups. {{term|currency}}
{{defn|{{gli|money|Money}} in any form when in actual use or circulation as a {{gli|medium of exchange}}, especially circulating [[banknote]]s and [[coin]]s.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia | url = http://www.thefreedictionary.com/currency | title = Currency | dictionary = The Free Dictionary}}</ref><ref name=Bernstein>{{cite book |last =Bernstein |first =Peter |author-link =Peter L. Bernstein |title=A Primer on Money, Banking and Gold | edition = 3rd |year=2008 |orig-date=1965 |publisher=Wiley |location=Hoboken, NJ  |isbn=978-0-470-28758-3 |oclc = 233484849 |chapter= 4–5}}</ref> A more general definition is that a currency is a "{{gli|monetary system|system}}" of money (monetary units) in common use, especially within a particular nation.}}

{{term|[[Current account (balance of payments)|current account]]}}
{{defn|A country's current account is one of the two components of its [[balance of payments]], the other being the [[capital account]] (also known as the financial account). The current account consists of the [[balance of trade]], net ''primary income'' or ''factor income'' (earnings on foreign investments minus payments made to foreign investors) and net cash transfers, that have taken place over a given period of time. The current account balance is one of two major measures of a country's foreign trade (the other being the [[net capital outflow]]). A current account surplus indicates that the value of a country's net foreign assets (i.e. assets less liabilities) grew over the period in question, and a current account deficit indicates that it shrank. Both government and private payments are included in the calculation. It is called the current account because {{gli|good|goods}} and {{gli|service|services}} are generally consumed in the current period.<ref name="Ecological Economics">''Ecological Economics: Principles And Applications''. Herman E. Daly, Joshua Farley; Island Press, 2003</ref><ref name="IMF_2012">{{cite web|url=http://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/basics/current.htm| title=Current Account Deficits: Is There a Problem?| publisher=International Monetary Fund| date=28 March 2012| access-date=24 December 2015| author1=Ghosh, Atish| author2=Ramakrishnan, Uma}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[cyclical unemployment]]}}
{{defn|{{gli|unemployment|Unemployment}} resulting from the {{gli|business cycle}}. It is unpredictable.}}
