==D==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[DAD–SAS model]]}}
{{defn|A macroeconomic model based on the AD-AS model, but examining the relationship between inflation and income, rather than price level and income. DAD is short for Dynamic Aggregate Demand, and SAS is short for Surprise Aggregate Supply.}}

{{term|[[dead cat bounce]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''sucker rally'''.}} 
{{defn|A small, brief recovery in the price of a declining asset.<ref>{{cite web |title=Definition of dead-cat bounce {{!}} Dictionary.com |url=https://www.dictionary.com/browse/dead-cat-bounce |website=www.dictionary.com |access-date=30 April 2022 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[deadweight loss]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''excess burden''' or '''allocative inefficiency'''.}} 
{{defn|A loss of {{gli|economic efficiency}} that occurs when the free-market {{gli|economic equilibrium|equilibrium}} for a {{gli|good}} or {{gli|service}} is not achieved. Deadweight loss can be caused by {{gli|monopoly}} pricing in the case of {{gli|artificial scarcity}}, an {{gli|externality}}, a [[effect of taxes and subsidies on price|tax or subsidy]], or a compulsory {{gli|price ceiling}} or {{gli|price floor}} such as a {{gli|minimum wage}}.}}

{{term|[[Debreu's representation theorems]]}}
{{defn|A set of [[preference representation theorem]]s proved by [[Gerard Debreu]]. They specify some conditions on the preference relation that guarantee the existence of a representing utility function.}}

{{term|[[debt]]}}
{{defn|Total money owed.}}

{{term|[[debit card]]}}
{{defn|A debit card is a payment card that allows you to make purchases and withdraw cash from your bank account. Debit cards are also known as "check cards." They look and work similarly to credit cards, but they use money that's already in your checking account instead of money you borrow.}}

{{term|[[debtor]]}}
{{defn|An entity that owes a {{gli|debt}} to another entity. The entity may be an individual, a firm, a government, a company, or another [[legal person]]. The [[counterparty]] to which the debt is owed is called a {{gli|creditor}}. When the counterparty of the arrangement is a {{gli|bank}}, the debtor is more often referred to as a {{gli|borrower}}.}}

{{term|[[deficit spending]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''budget deficit''' or simply '''deficit'''.}}
{{defn|The amount by which spending exceeds {{gli|revenue}} over a particular period of time; it is the opposite of {{gli|budget surplus}}. The term may be applied to the budget of a government, private company, or individual.}}

{{term|[[deflation]]}}
{{defn|A decrease in the general {{gli|price index|price level}} of goods and services.<ref>Robert J. Barro and Vittorio Grilli (1994), ''European Macroeconomics'', chap. 8, p. 142. {{ISBN|0-333-57764-7}}</ref> Deflation occurs when the {{gli|inflation}} rate falls below 0% (a negative inflation rate); though inflation reduces the value of {{gli|currency}} over time, deflation increases it. This allows more goods and services to be bought than before with the same amount of currency. Deflation is distinct from {{gli|disinflation}}, which occurs when the inflation rate decreases but is still positive.<ref>{{Cite book| last1 = O'Sullivan | first1 = Arthur | author-link = Arthur O'Sullivan (economist) | first2 = Steven M. | last2 = Sheffrin | author-link2 = Steven M. Sheffrin | title = Economics | publisher = Savvas Learning Company | year = 2022 | location = Paramus, New Jersey | page = 343 | isbn = 978-0-13-063085-8}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[deflator]]}}
{{defn|A value that allows data to be measured over time in terms of some [[base period]], usually through a {{gli|price index}}, to distinguish between changes in the money value of a {{gli|gross national product}} (GNP) that come from a change in prices, and changes from a change in physical output. It is the measure of the price level for some quantity. A deflator serves as a price index in which the effects of inflation are nulled.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bls.gov/bls/glossary.htm|title=BLS Information |date=February 28, 2008|work=Glossary|publisher=U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Division of Information Services |access-date=2009-05-05}}</ref><ref name="umweb">{{cite web|url=http://www-personal.umich.edu/~alandear/glossary/d.html|title=Deardorff's Glossary of International Economics|work=D|publisher=umweb|access-date=2009-05-10}}</ref><ref name="orbex">{{cite web|url=https://www.orbex.com/en/glossary|title=Orbex Financial Glossary|date=November 30, 2014|work=Glossary|publisher=Orbex|access-date=2014-12-02}}</ref> It is the difference between real and nominal GDP.<ref name="forex">{{cite web|url=http://euro.uz/forex/41.htm |title=The forex quick guide for beginners and private traders |year=2008 |publisher=Forex |access-date=2009-05-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141130031015/http://euro.uz/forex/41.htm |archive-date=November 30, 2014 }}</ref><ref name="nationalstat">{{cite web|url=http://www.statistics.gov.uk/about/glossary/economic_terms.asp|title=Economic terms|date=7 January 2004|work=Glossary|publisher=National Statistics|access-date=2009-05-10|archive-url=http://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/20110907093405/http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/guide-method/geography/beginner-s-guide/glossary/glossary-u.html|archive-date=2011-09-07}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[deleveraging]]}}
{{defn|A reduction in debt. At the [[microeconomics|micro-economic]] level, it is measured as the reduction of the [[leverage ratio]], or the percentage of [[debt]] in the [[balance sheet]] of a single economic entity, such as a household or a firm. At the [[macroeconomics|macro-economic]] level, it is usually measured as a decline of the total debt to [[nominal GDP|GDP]] ratio in the [[national accounts]].}}

{{term|[[demand]]}}
{{defn|The whole range of quantities that a person or group with a given income and preferences demands at various prices.}}

{{term|[[demand curve]]}}
{{defn|A line on a graph that represents how much of a good or service buyers are going to consume at various prices.}}

{{term|[[demand deposit]]}}
{{defn|Demand deposits, bank money or scriptural money are funds held in [[demand deposit account]]s in [[commercial banks]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/bank+money |title=Bank Money: Merriam-Webster Dictionary |publisher=www.merriam-webster.com |access-date=19 August 2009 }}</ref> These account balances are usually considered money and form the greater part of the narrowly defined [[money supply]] of a country.<ref name=Krugman>[[Paul Krugman|Krugman, Paul R.]], and Robin Wells. Economics. New York: Worth, 2006. Print.</ref>}}

{{term|[[demand shock]]}}
{{defn|A sudden event that increases or decreases {{gli|demand}} for {{gli|good|goods}} or {{gli|service|services}} temporarily.}}

{{term|[[demand-pull inflation]]}}
{{defn|A purported type of inflation caused by an increase in aggregate demand greater than the increase in aggregate supply. As real gross domestic product rises and unemployment falls, the economy moves along the [[Phillips curve]] and prices increase.}}

{{term|[[demographic economics]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''population economics'''.}}
{{defn|The application of economic analysis to [[demography]], the study of human populations, including [[population size|size]], [[population growth|growth]], density, [[population distribution|distribution]], and [[vital statistics (government records)|vital statistics]].<ref name="economic demography">{{cite encyclopedia |doi=10.1057/9780230226203.0428 |entry=Economic Demography |title=The New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics |year=2008 |last1=Kelley |first1=Allen C. |last2=Schmidt |first2=Robert M. |pages=1–12 |isbn=978-0-333-78676-5 |location=London |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |pmid=12342564 |first=Bernard M. S. |last=van Praag |author-link=Bernard van Praag |journal=Journal of Population Economics |jstor=20007247 |year=1988 |title=The notion of population economics |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=5–16 |doi=10.1007/bf00171507}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[dependent care plan]]}}
{{defn|A pre-tax account used to pay for either child or adult care while a married couple works, looks for work, or studies.}}

{{term|[[depreciation]]}}
{{defn|The gradual decrease in the economic value of the {{gli|capital stock}} of a firm, nation, or other entity, either through physical depreciation, obsolescence, or changes in the demand for the services of the capital in question. If the capital stock is <math>K_t</math> in one period <math>t</math>, [[gross investment|gross (total) investment]] spending on newly produced capital is <math>I_t</math> and depreciation is <math>D_t</math>, the capital stock in the next period, <math>K_{t+1}</math>, is <math>K_t + I_t - D_t</math>. The net increment to the capital stock is the difference between gross investment and depreciation, and is called {{gli|net investment}}.}}

{{term|[[Depression (economics)|depression]]}}
{{defn|A sustained, long-term decrease in economic activity in one or more economies. It is a more severe economic downturn than a {{gli|recession}}, which is a slowdown in economic activity over the course of a normal {{gli|business cycle}}.}}

{{term|[[deregulation]]}}
{{defn|The process of removing or reducing economic regulations, or the total repeal of governmental [[Economic regulation|regulation of the economy]]. It became common in advanced industrial economies in the 1970s and 1980s, as a result of new trends in economic thinking about the inefficiencies of [[government regulation]], and the risk that regulatory agencies would be controlled by the regulated industry to its benefit, and thereby hurt consumers and the wider economy.}}

{{term|[[Diamond–Dybvig model]]}}
{{defn|A [[Model (economics)|model]] of [[bank run]]s and related [[financial crisis|financial crises]]. The model shows how banks' mix of illiquid assets (such as business or mortgage loans) and liquid liabilities (deposits which may be withdrawn at any time) may give rise to self-fulfilling panics among depositors.}}

{{term|[[differentiated Bertrand competition]]}}
{{defn|A variation of [[Bertrand competition]] where each firm produces a somewhat differentiated product, and consequently faces a demand curve that is downward-sloping for all levels of the firm's price. This provides a solution to the [[Bertrand paradox (economics)]].}}

{{term|[[diminishing marginal utility]]}}
{{defn|A situation where each additional, or marginal, unit of a good or service that is consumed brings less utility than the previous unit.}}

{{term|[[diminishing returns]]}}
{{defn|The decrease in the {{gli|marginalism|marginal}} (incremental) output of a {{gli|production}} process as the amount of a single {{gli|factors of production|factor of production}} is incrementally increased, while the amounts of all other factors of production stay constant. The law of diminishing returns states that in all productive processes, adding more of one factor of production while holding all others constant ("''[[ceteris paribus]]''"), will at some point yield lower incremental per-unit returns.<ref name=Samuelson2001p110>{{cite book |first1=Paul A. |last1=Samuelson |author1-link=Paul Samuelson |first2=William D. |last2=Nordhaus |title=Microeconomics |publisher=McGraw-Hill |year=2001 |isbn=0-07-118066-4 |page=110 |edition=17th}}</ref> It does not imply that adding more of a factor will decrease the ''total'' production, a condition known as '''negative returns''', though in practice this is common.}}

{{term|[[discounting]]}}
{{defn|A mechanism in which a [[debtor]] obtains the right to delay [[payment]]s to a [[creditor]], for a defined period of time, in exchange for a charge or [[fee]].<ref name="Finance_Discount">See "Time Value", "Discount", "Discount Yield", "Compound Interest", "Efficient Market", "Market Value" and "Opportunity Cost" in Downes, J. and Goodman, J. E. ''Dictionary of Finance and Investment Terms'', Baron's Financial Guides, 2003.</ref>  Essentially, the party that owes money in the present purchases the right to delay the payment until some future date.<ref name="Economics_Discount">See "Discount", "Compound Interest", "Efficient Markets Hypothesis", "Efficient Resource Allocation", "Pareto-Optimality", "Price", "Price Mechanism" and "Efficient Market" in Black, John, ''Oxford Dictionary of Economics'', Oxford University Press, 2002.</ref>}}

{{term|[[discrete choice]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''qualitative choice'''.}}
{{defn|A set of models that describe, explain, and predict choices between two or more [[discrete variable|discrete]] alternatives, such as entering or not entering the [[labor market]], or choosing between modes of transport. These models examine situations in which the potential outcomes are discrete, such that the optimum is not characterized by standard first-order conditions.}}

{{term|[[discretionary income]]}}
{{defn|Money available after one pays {{gli|tax|taxes}} and all other necessary expenses like housing and transportation.}}

{{term|[[disequilibrium macroeconomics]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''non-Walrasian theory''', '''equilibrium with rationing''', the '''non-market clearing approach''', and '''non-tâtonnement theory'''.}}
{{defn|A tradition of research centered on the role of [[Disequilibrium (economics)|disequilibrium]] in economics.}}

{{term|[[disinflation]]}}
{{defn|A decrease in the rate of {{gli|inflation}}; a slowdown in the rate of increase of the general {{gli|price index|price level}} of goods and services in an economy's {{gli|gross domestic product}} over time. It is the opposite of {{gli|reflation}}. Disinflation is also distinct from {{gli|deflation}}, which occurs when the inflation rate is negative.}}

{{term|[[dispersed knowledge]]}}
{{defn|The notion that no single [[Agent (economics)|agent]] has information as to all of the factors which influence [[prices]] and [[Production (economics)|production]] throughout the system.<ref>{{Cite journal|jstor=1809376|title = The use of knowledge in society|last = Hayek|first = Friedrich|date = 1 September 1945|journal = The American Economic Review|volume = 35|issue=4|pages = 519–530|issn = 0002-8282}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[Disposable and discretionary income|disposable income]]}}
{{defn|Money available after one pays {{gli|tax|taxes}}; income available for personal consumption and saving.}}

{{term|[[disposition effect]]}}
{{defn|The tendency to sell an asset that has accumulated in value and resist selling an asset that has declined in value.}}

{{term|[[dissaving]]}}
{{defn|Negative {{gli|saving}}, which occurs when spending is greater than {{gli|disposable income}}. This spending may be financed by already accumulated savings, such as money in a {{gli|savings account}}, or it can be {{gli|loan|borrowed}}.}}

{{term|[[Distribution (economics)|distribution]]}}
{{defn|The way total {{gli|output|economic output}}, {{gli|income}}, or {{gli|wealth}} is distributed among individuals or among the {{gli|factors of production}} (such as {{gli|labor}}, {{gli|land}}, and {{gli|capital}}).<ref>[[Paul A. Samuelson]] and [[William Nordhaus|William D. Nordhaus]] (2004). ''[[Economics (textbook)|Economics]]'', 18th ed., [end] Glossary of Terms, "Distribution."</ref> In general theory and the [[national income and product accounts]], each unit of output corresponds to a unit of income.}}

{{term|[[dividends]]}}
{{defn|Payments by a corporation of all or part of its profit to its stockholders (the corporate owners).}}

{{term|[[dividend imputation]]}}
{{defn|A [[corporate tax]] system in which some or all of the tax paid by a company may be attributed, or [[imputation (economics)|imputed]], to the shareholders by way of a [[tax credit]] to reduce the income tax payable on a distribution.}}

{{term|divorce}}
{{defn|The dissolution of a marriage, which in many countries, is considered a contract of property which is shared among the spouses.}}

{{term|[[Dixit–Stiglitz model]]}}
{{defn|A model of [[monopolistic competition]] which formalises consumers' preferences for product variety by using a [[Constant elasticity of substitution|CES]] function.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Dixit | first1 = Avinash K. | last2 = Stiglitz | first2 = Joseph E. |author-link1 = Avinash Dixit | title = Monopolistic competition and optimum product diversity | journal = The American Economic Review | volume = 67 | issue = 3 | pages = 297–308 | publisher = American Economic Association  | date = June 1977 | jstor = 1831401 }}</ref> In the model, variety preference is inherent within the assumption of [[monotone preferences|monotonic preferences]] because a consumer with such preferences prefers to have an average of any two bundles of goods as opposed to extremes.}}

{{term|[[dollar auction]]}}
{{defn|A non-[[zero sum]] [[sequential game]] that illustrates a [[paradox]] brought about by traditional [[rational choice theory]] in which players are compelled to make an ultimately [[irrational]] decision based completely on a sequence of apparently [[rationality|rational]] choices made throughout the game.<ref name="shubik">[[#Shubik|Shubik: 1971]]. p. 109</ref>}}

{{term|[[Domar serfdom model]]}}
{{defn|A mid-to-late 20th century model that develops a hypothesis concerning the causes of agricultural slavery or serfdom in historical societies.}}

{{term|[[Dorfman-Steiner theorem]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''Dorfman–Steiner condition'''.}}
{{defn|A theorem which specifies the optimal level of advertising that a firm should undertake.}}

{{term|[[double marginalization]]}}
{{defn|A [[Externality|vertical externality]] that occurs when two firms with market power (i.e., not in a situation of [[perfect competition]]), at different vertical levels in the same [[supply chain]], apply a mark-up to their prices.<ref>Gabrielsen, Tommy., Johansen, Bjorn Olav., Shaffer, Greg. (2018). Double Marginalization and the Cost of Shelf Space, Konkurransetilsynet</ref> This is caused by the prospect of facing a steep demand curve slope, prompting the firm to mark-up the price beyond its marginal costs.<ref>Badasyan, Narine., Goeree, Jacob K., Hartmann, Monica., Holt, Charles., Morgan, John., Rosenblat, Tanya., Servatka, Maros., Yandell, Dirk. (2005). ''Vertical Integration of Successive Monopolists: A Classroom Experiment'', National Science Foundation and the University of Virginia Bankard Fund.</ref>}}

{{term|[[Doughnut (economic model)|doughnut economics]]}}
{{defn|A visual framework for [[sustainable development]] – shaped like a [[doughnut]] or [[lifebuoy|lifebelt]] –  combining the concept of [[planetary boundaries]] with the complementary concept of social boundaries.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Raworth |first=Kate |url=https://www-cdn.oxfam.org/s3fs-public/file_attachments/dp-a-safe-and-just-space-for-humanity-130212-en_5.pdf |title=A Safe and Just Space for Humanity: Can We Live within the Doughnut? |date=2012 |series=Oxfam Discussion Papers |author-link=Kate Raworth}}</ref> The name derives from the shape of the diagram, i.e. a disc with a hole in the middle.}}

{{term|[[Downs–Thomson paradox]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''Pigou–Knight–Downs paradox'''.}} 
{{defn|A paradox that states that the equilibrium speed of car traffic on a road network is determined by the average door-to-door speed of equivalent journeys taken by [[public transportation|public transport]] or the next best alternative. Although consistent with [[economic theory]], it is a paradox in that it contradicts the common expectation that improvements in the road network will reduce [[traffic congestion]].}}

{{term|[[dual-sector model]]}}
{{ghat|Also called the '''Lewis model'''.}} 
{{defn|A model in [[Development economics|developmental economics]] that explains the growth of a developing economy in terms of a [[labour (economics)|labour]] transition between two sectors, the subsistence or traditional agricultural sector and the capitalist or modern industrial sector.}}

{{term|[[Duggan–Schwartz theorem]]}}
{{defn|A result about [[voting system]]s designed to choose a nonempty set of winners from the preferences of certain individuals, where each individual ranks all candidates in order of preference.}}

{{term|[[duopoly]]}}
{{defn|A situation in which there are exactly two suppliers for a particular good or service.}}

{{term|[[dynamic discrete choice]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''DDC models''' or'''discrete choice models of dynamic programming'''.}}
{{defn|Models that simulate an agent's choices over discrete options that have future implications. Rather than assuming observed choices are the result of static utility maximization, observed choices in DDC models are assumed to result from an agent's maximization of the [[present value]] of utility, generalizing the [[utility theory]] upon which [[discrete choice]] models are based.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Michael P. |last1=Keane |author-link1=Michael Keane (economist) |first2=Kenneth I. |last2=Wolpin |author-link2=Kenneth Wolpin |title=Empirical applications of discrete choice dynamic programming models |journal=Review of Economic Dynamics |volume=12 |number=1 |pages=1–22 |date=2009 |doi=10.1016/j.red.2008.07.001}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[dynamic stochastic general equilibrium]] (DSGE)}}
{{ghat|Also abbreviated '''DGE''' and '''SDGE'''.}} 
{{defn|A method in {{gli|macroeconomics}} that attempts to explain economic phenomena, such as {{gli|economic growth}} and {{gli|business cycle|business cycles}}, and the effects of {{gli|economic policy}}, through {{gli|econometrics|econometric models}} based on applied [[general equilibrium theory]] and [[microfoundations|microeconomic principles]].}}
{{glossaryend}}

==E==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[Easterlin paradox]]}}
{{defn|A finding in [[happiness economics]] which states that at a point in time happiness varies directly with income both among and within nations, but over time happiness does not trend upward as income continues to grow: while people on higher incomes are typically happier than their lower-income counterparts at a given point in time, higher incomes don't produce greater happiness over time.<ref name="Easterlin1974">{{cite book|last=Easterlin|year=1974|chapter=Does Economic Growth Improve the Human Lot? Some Empirical Evidence|editor1=Paul A. David|editor2=Melvin W. Reder|title=Nations and Households in Economic Growth: Essays in Honor of Moses Abramovitz|location=New York|publisher=Academic Press, Inc.|chapter-url=http://graphics8.nytimes.com/images/2008/04/16/business/Easterlin1974.pdf}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[ecological model of competition]]}}
{{defn|A reassessment of the nature of competition in the economy which models the economy on [[biology]] (growth, change, death, evolution, [[survival of the fittest]], complex inter-relationships, non-linear relationships) rather than physics.}}

{{term|[[econometrics]]}}
{{defn|The application of [[statistical methods]] to economic data to give [[empirical]] content to economic relationships.<ref name="Pesaran">[[M. Hashem Pesaran]] (1987). "Econometrics," ''[[The New Palgrave: A Dictionary of Economics]]'', v. 2, p. 8 [pp. 8–22]. Reprinted in J. Eatwell ''et al.'', eds. (1990). ''Econometrics: The New Palgrave'', [https://books.google.com/books?id=gBsgr7BPJsoC&dq=econometrics&pg=PA1=false p. 1] [pp. 1–34].  [http://www.dictionaryofeconomics.com/article?id=pde2008_E000007&edition=current&q=Econometrics&topicid=&result_number=2 Abstract] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120518001558/http://www.dictionaryofeconomics.com/article?id=pde2008_E000007&edition=current&q=Econometrics&topicid=&result_number=2 |date=18 May 2012 }} ([[The New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics|2008]] revision by J. Geweke, J. Horowitz, and H. P. Pesaran).</ref> More precisely, it is "the quantitative analysis of actual economic phenomena based on the concurrent development of theory and observation, related by appropriate methods of inference".<ref>[[Paul Samuelson|P. A. Samuelson]], [[Tjalling Koopmans|T. C. Koopmans]], and [[Richard Stone|J. R. N. Stone]] (1954). "Report of the Evaluative Committee for ''Econometrica''," ''Econometrica'' 22(2), p. 142. [p [https://www.jstor.org/pss/1907538 pp. 141]–146], as described and cited in Pesaran (1987) above.</ref>}}

{{term|[[economic base analysis]]}}
{{defn|A theory that posits that activities in an area divide into two categories: basic and nonbasic. Basic industries are those exporting from the region and bringing wealth from outside, while nonbasic (or service) industries support basic industries.}}

{{term|[[economic calculation problem|economic calculation problem (ECP)]]}}
{{defn|A criticism of using [[economic planning]] as a substitute for [[Market (economics)|market-based]] allocation of the [[factors of production]].<ref name="Mises">{{cite book|title=Economic calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth|last=Von Mises|first=Ludwig|author-link=Ludwig von Mises|year=1990|publisher=[[Mises Institute]]|url=https://mises.org/sites/default/files/Economic%20Calculation%20in%20the%20Socialist%20Commonwealth_Vol_2_3.pdf}}</ref><ref>Hayek, Friedrich (1935). "The Nature and History of the Problem"; "The Present State of the Debate". ''Collectivist Economic Planning''. pp. 1–40, 201–243.</ref> It is argued that economy planning necessarily leads to an irrational and inefficient [[allocation of resources]].}}

{{term|[[economic cost]]}}
{{defn|The combination of  losses of any goods that have a value attached to them by any one individual.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Phillips|first=Ulrich B.|date=1905|title=The Economic Cost of Slaveholding in the Cotton Belt|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_political-science-quarterly_1905-06_20_2/page/256|journal=Political Science Quarterly|volume=20|issue=2|pages=257–275|doi=10.2307/2140400|issn=0032-3195|jstor=2140400|hdl=2027/hvd.32044082042185|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref name=mbw>{{Cite web |title=What is economic cost? Definition, comparisons, and examples |work=Market Business News |access-date=2019-07-16 |url=https://marketbusinessnews.com/financial-glossary/economic-cost/ |archive-date=2022-10-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221022164654/https://marketbusinessnews.com/financial-glossary/economic-cost/ }}</ref> Economic cost is used as means to compare the prudence of one course of action with that of another.}}

{{term|[[economic democracy]]}}
{{ghat|Also called a '''democratic economy'''.}}
{{defn|A [[Socioeconomics|socioeconomic]] philosophy that proposes to shift ownership<ref>{{cite web |url=https://bcdi.nyc/economic-democracy#:~:text=Economic%20democracy%20is%20a%20system,cooperation%2C%20democracy%2C%20and%20sustainability. |title=What is Economic Democracy? |website=bcdi |access-date=31 May 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://thenextsystem.org/node/204 |title=Economic Democracy: An Ethically Desirable Socialism That Is Economically Viable|last=Schweickart |first=David |website= The Next System |date=March 2016 |access-date=31 May 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/opendemocracyuk/economic-democracy-in-21st-century/ |title=Economic democracy in the 21st Century |last=Malleson |first=Tom |date=2014 |website=Open Democracy |access-date=28 May 2023}}</ref> and decision-making power from [[Shareholder|corporate shareholders]] and [[Management|corporate managers]] (such as a board of directors) to a larger group of [[stakeholder theory|public stakeholders]] that includes workers, consumers, suppliers, communities and the broader public.}}

{{term|[[economic development]]}}
{{defn|Broad improvement in the economic well-being or [[quality of life]] of a nation, region, or community, often but not necessarily as a consequence of {{gli|economic growth}}.}}

{{term|[[economic efficiency]]}}
{{defn|A variety of concepts which denote some situation where desired outputs (such as [[utility]]) are maximized given available inputs. This can include [[allocative efficiency]], [[distributive efficiency]], [[dynamic efficiency]], [[financial market efficiency]], [[Kaldor–Hicks efficiency]], [[operational efficiency]], [[Pareto efficiency]], and [[productive efficiency]].}}

{{term|[[economic equilibrium]]}}
{{defn|A situation in which economic forces such as {{gli|supply and demand}} are balanced and in which, in the absence of external influences, the values of economic variables do not change. For example, in the standard textbook model of {{gli|perfect competition}}, equilibrium occurs at the point at which quantity demanded and quantity supplied are equal.<ref>{{cite book |author-link=Hal Varian |first=Hal R. |last=Varian |title=Microeconomic Analysis |edition=3rd |publisher=Norton |location=New York |year=1992 |isbn=0-393-95735-7 |url=https://archive.org/details/microeconomicana00vari_0 }}</ref> '''Market equilibrium''' in this case is a condition in which a market price is established through competition such that the amount of goods or services sought by [[Law of supply and demand|buyers]] is equal to the amount of goods or services produced by [[Law of supply and demand|sellers]]. This price is often called the '''competitive price''' or {{gli|market clearing}} price and will tend not to change unless demand or supply changes, and the quantity is called the "competitive quantity" or market clearing quantity. However, the concept of equilibrium in economics also applies to {{gli|imperfect competition|imperfectly competitive}} markets, where it takes the form of a {{gli|Nash equilibrium}}.}}

{{term|[[economic growth]]}}
{{defn|An increase in the inflation-adjusted {{gli|market value}} of the goods and services produced by an {{gli|economy}} over time. It is conventionally measured as the percent rate of increase in real {{gli|gross domestic product}}, or real GDP.<ref>[http://www.statista.com/statistics/197039/growth-of-the-global-gross-domestic-product-gdp/ Statistics on the Growth of the Global Gross Domestic Product (GDP) from 2003 to 2013], IMF, October 2012.</ref>}}

{{term|[[economic indicator]]}}
{{defn|Any measurable unit of the economy which helps economists assess the past or make predictions about the future, such as {{gli|unemployment rate}} and {{gli|gross domestic product}}.}}

{{term|[[economic interdependence]]}}
{{defn|The existence of necessary relationships between different sectors of the economy and how the decisions and actions of one will impact the others.}}

{{term|[[economic methodology]]}}
{{defn|The study of methods, especially the scientific method, in relation to {{gli|economics}}, including principles underlying economic reasoning.}}

{{term|[[economic model]]}}
{{defn|A theoretical construct representing an economic process by a set of variables and a set of logical and/or quantitative relationships between them. Economic models are usually simplified, often [[Mathematical model|mathematical]], frameworks designed to illustrate complex processes. Frequently, economic models posit [[Coefficient of regression|structural parameters]]. A model may have various [[exogenous variable]]s, and those variables may change to create various responses by economic variables. Methodological uses of models include investigation, theorizing, and fitting theories to the world.<ref>[[Mary S. Morgan]], 2008 "models," ''[[The New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics]]'', 2nd Edition, [http://www.dictionaryofeconomics.com/article?id=pde2008_M000391 Abstract].<br/>&nbsp;&nbsp; Vivian Walsh 1987. "models and theory," ''The New Palgrave: A Dictionary of Economics'', v. 3, pp. 482–83.</ref>}}

{{term|[[economic rent]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''economic profits'''.}}
{{defn|Any monies collected by a firm above and beyond what is required to keep an entrepreneur owner interested in continuing in business.}}

{{term|[[economic sector]]}}
{{defn|A category of economic activity.}}

{{term|[[economic security]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''financial security'''.}}
{{defn|The condition of having stable income or other resources to support a [[standard of living]] now and in the foreseeable future. It includes probable continued [[solvency]], predictability of the future [[cash flow]] of a person or other [[Economic Entity]], such as a country, and employment security or [[job security]].}}

{{term|[[economic shortage]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''excess demand'''.}}
{{defn|A situation in which the {{gli|demand}} for a particular {{gli|good}} or {{gli|service}} exceeds its {{gli|supply}} within a particular {{gli|market}}. A shortage is the opposite of a {{gli|economic surplus|surplus}}.}}

{{term|[[economic surplus]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''excess supply'''.}}
{{defn|A situation in which the {{gli|supply}} of a {{gli|good}} or {{gli|service}} exceeds its {{gli|demand}} within a particular {{gli|market}}, often as a result of the current {{gli|price}} being below the {{gli|economic equilibrium}}.}}

{{term|[[economic system]]}}
{{ghat|Also called an '''economic order'''.<ref>Daniel J. Cantor, Juliet B. Schor, ''Tunnel Vision: Labor, the World Economy, and Central America'', South End Press, 1987, p. 21: "By economic system or economic order, we mean the principles, laws, institutions, and understandings business is conducted."</ref>}}
{{defn|A system of {{gli|production}}, {{gli|resource allocation}}, and {{gli|distribution}} of {{gli|goods and services}} within a society or a given geographic area. It includes the combination of the various institutions, agencies, entities, decision-making processes, and patterns of {{gli|consumer|consumption}} that comprise the economic structure of a given community. As such, an economic system is a type of [[social system]]. The {{gli|mode of production}} is a related concept.<ref>{{cite book|last=Gregory and Stuart|first=Paul and Robert|title=The Global Economy and its Economic Systems|publisher=South-Western College Pub|year=2013|isbn=978-1-285-05535-0|page=30|quote=Economic system – A set of institutions for decision making and for the implementation of decisions concerning production, income, and consumption within a given geographic area.}}</ref> All economic systems have three basic questions to ask: what to produce, how to produce it, and in what quantities and who receives the output of production.}}

{{term|[[economics]]}}
{{defn|The [[social science]] that studies the {{gli|production}}, {{gli|distribution}}, and {{gli|consumption}} of {{gli|goods and services}} within {{gli|economy|economies}}.<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Krugman | first1 = Paul | author-link = Paul Krugman | last2 = Wells | first2= Robin | title = Economics | publisher =Worth Publishers | edition =3rd | date =2012 | page = 2 | isbn =978-1-4641-2873-8 }}</ref>}}

{{term|[[economies of agglomeration]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''agglomeration effects'''.}}
{{defn|The major subfield of [[urban economics]] which explains how urban agglomeration occurs in locations where cost savings can naturally arise.<ref name=":0b">{{Cite journal |last1=Ellison |first1=Glenn |last2=Glaeser |first2=Edward L. |date=May 1999 |title=The Geographic Concentration of Industry: Does Natural Advantage Explain Agglomeration? |journal=The American Economic Review |volume=89 |issue=2 |pages=311–316 |doi=10.1257/aer.89.2.311 |jstor=117127 }}</ref> This term is most often discussed in terms of economic firm productivity. However, agglomeration effects also explain some social phenomenon, such as large proportions of the population being clustered in cities and major urban centres.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Puga |first=Diego |date=3 February 2010 |title=The magnitude and causes of agglomeration economies |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1467-9787.2009.00657.x |journal=Journal of Regional Science |volume=50 |issue=1 |pages=203–219 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9787.2009.00657.x |bibcode=2010JRegS..50..203P |s2cid=17848032 |via=Wiley Online Library|url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term|[[economies of scale]]}}
{{defn|The cost advantages that enterprises obtain as a result of the increased efficiency offered by a certain scale of operation (typically measured by amount of {{gli|output}} produced), with cost per unit of output decreasing with increasing scale. At the basis of economies of scale there may be technical, statistical, organizational, or related factors to the degree of market control.}}

{{term|[[economies of scope]]}}
{{defn|The cost advantages that enterprises obtain as a result of the increased efficiency offered by variety rather than by volume, with cost per unit of {{gli|output}} decreasing with increasing variety.<ref name=hbr>{{cite news|author1=Joel D. Goldhar|author2=Mariann Jelinek|title=Plan for Economies of Scope|url=https://hbr.org/1983/11/plan-for-economies-of-scope|work=Harvard Business Review|date=November 1983}}</ref> In economics, "scope" is synonymous with broadening production through diversified products. For example, a gas station that sells gasoline can also sell soda, milk, baked goods, etc. through their customer service representatives, which may make the sale of gasoline more efficient.<ref name=econ>{{cite news|title=Economies of scale and scope|url=https://www.economist.com/news/2008/10/20/economies-of-scale-and-scope|newspaper=The Economist|date=October 20, 2008}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[economist]]}}
{{defn|A practitioner in the discipline of {{gli|economics}}.}}

{{term|[[economy]]}}
{{defn|An area of the {{gli|production}}, {{gli|distribution}}, {{gli|trade}}, and {{gli|consumption}} of {{gli|good|goods}} and {{gli|service|services}} by different agents. In its broadest sense, an economy may be defined as "a social domain that emphasizes the practices, discourses, and material expressions associated with the production, use, and management of resources".<ref>{{Cite book | last1= James | first1= Paul | author-link= Paul James (academic) | last2= with Magee | first2= Liam | last3= Scerri | first3= Andy | last4= Steger | first4= Manfred B. | title= Urban Sustainability in Theory and Practice: Circles of Sustainability | url= https://www.academia.edu/9294719 | year= 2015 | publisher= Routledge | location= London | page=53| isbn= 978-1-315-76574-7 }}</ref>}}

{{term|[[Edgeworth box]]}}
{{ghat|Also called an '''Edgeworth-Bowley box'''.}}
{{defn|A graphical representation of a market with just two commodities, ''X'' and ''Y'', and two consumers. The dimensions of the box are the total quantities Ω<sub>''x''</sub> and Ω<sub>''y''</sub> of the two goods.}}

{{term|[[Edgeworth paradox]]}}
{{defn|A situation in which two players cannot reach a state of equilibrium with pure strategies, i.e. each charging a stable price. It was proposed to solve the [[Bertrand paradox (economics)|Bertrand paradox]].}}

{{term|[[Edgeworth's limit theorem]]}}
{{defn|A theorem stating that the [[Core (game theory)|core]] of an economy shrinks to the set of [[Walrasian equilibria]] as the number of [[Agent (economics)|agents]] increases to infinity. That is, among all possible outcomes which may result from [[free market]] exchange or [[barter]] between groups of people, while the precise location of the final settlement (the ultimate division of goods) between the parties is not uniquely determined, as the number of traders increases, the set of all possible final settlements converges to the set of Walrasian equilibria.}}

{{term|[[effective demand|effective demand (ED)]]}}
{{defn|The [[demand]] for a product or service which occurs when purchasers are constrained in a different market.}}

{{term|[[efficiency dividend]]}}
{{defn|An annual reduction in resources available to an organization.<ref>{{cite web|title=efficiency dividend|url=http://www.businessdictionary.com/definition/efficiency-dividend.html|website=www.businessdictionary.com|publisher=WebFinance Inc|access-date=5 January 2015|archive-date=30 December 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141230162748/http://www.businessdictionary.com/definition/efficiency-dividend.html}}</ref>  It is usually applied as a percentage of operational (running) costs.}}

{{term|[[efficiency wage]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''efficiency earnings'''.}}
{{defn|Originally referred to the wage per efficiency unit of labor.<ref name="EOL">{{Cite book |last=Marshall |first=Alfred |title=Principles of Economics |publisher=Macmillan and Co., Ltd. |year=1920 |edition=8th |location=London |chapter=Earnings of Labour Book VI Chapter III |doi=10.1057/9781137375261_45}}</ref> Marshallian efficiency wages are those calculated with efficiency or ability exerted being the unit of measure rather than time.<ref name="EOL" /> Today, efficiency wage refers to the idea that higher wages may increase the efficiency of the workers by various channels, making it worthwhile for the employers to offer wages that exceed a [[Market clearing|market-clearing]] level.}}

{{term|[[efficient envy-free division]]}}
{{ghat|Also called a '''PEEF division'''.}}
{{defn|A [[fair division|division of resources]] among agents that is both [[Pareto efficient]] (PE) and [[envy-free]] (EF).}}

{{term|[[efficient market hypothesis|efficient market hypothesis (EMH)]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''efficient market theory (EMT)'''.}}
{{defn|A hypothesis that states that [[asset]] prices reflect all available information. A direct implication is that it is impossible to "beat the market" consistently on a risk-adjusted basis since market prices should only react to new information.}}

{{term|[[price elasticity of demand|elastic demand]]}}
{{defn|{{gli|demand|Demand}} that is sensitive to changes in {{gli|price}}, such that changes in price have a relatively large effect on the quantity of the good demanded. Contrast ''{{gli|inelastic demand}}''.}}

{{term|[[Elasticity (economics)|elasticity]]}}
{{defn|The measurement of the proportional change of an economic variable in response to a change in another. Colloquially, elasticity is often interpreted as how easy it is for a supplier or consumer to change their behavior and substitute another good, the strength of an incentive over choices per the relative {{gli|opportunity cost}}.}}

{{term|[[elasticity of complementarity]]}}
{{defn|Measures the sensitivity of relative factor prices to a change in relative inputs.}}

{{term|[[elasticity of intertemporal substitution|elasticity of intertemporal substitution (EIS)]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''intertemporal elasticity of substitution (IES)'''.}}
{{defn|Measures the sensitivity of the [[Economic growth|growth rate]] of [[consumption (economics)|consumption]] to the [[real interest rate]].<ref>[https://www.jstor.org/pss/1833112 Robert Hall, JPE]</ref>}}

{{term|[[elasticity of substitution]]}}
{{defn|Measures the sensitivity of the relative use of two goods to a change in their relative prices.}}

{{term|[[electronic funds transfer|electronic funds transfer (EFT)]]}}
{{defn|The digital transfer of money from one bank account to another, usually through computer-based systems, without the involvement of bank staff.}}

{{term|[[Elliott wave principle]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''Elliott wave theory'''.}}
{{defn|A form of [[technical analysis]] that [[Trader (finance)|financial traders]] use to analyze financial [[Stock market cycles|market cycles]] and forecast [[market trend]]s by identifying extremes in investor psychology and price levels, such as highs and lows, by looking for patterns in prices.
}}

{{term|[[Ellsberg paradox]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''Ellsberg's paradox'''.}}
{{defn|A [[paradox]] in which people's decisions are inconsistent with [[subjective expected utility]] theory. It is generally taken to be evidence of [[ambiguity aversion]], in which a person tends to prefer choices with quantifiable risks over those with unknown, incalculable risks.}}

{{term|[[employee benefits]]}}
{{defn|Any forms of compensation to an employee in addition to wages or salary for example, parental leave and vacation pay.}}

{{term|[[endogenous growth theory]]}}
{{defn|A theory that economic growth is primarily the result of [[Endogeneity (econometrics)|endogenous]] and not external forces.<ref>{{cite journal |journal = [[The Journal of Economic Perspectives]] |volume= 8 |issue= 1 |year= 1994 |first= P. M. |last= Romer |title= The Origins of Endogenous Growth |author-link= Paul Romer |pages =3–22 |jstor=2138148 |doi=10.1257/jep.8.1.3 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Endogenous growth theory holds that investment in [[human capital]], [[innovation]], and knowledge are significant contributors to economic growth. The theory also focuses on [[positive externalities]] and [[spillover effects]] of a knowledge-based economy which will lead to economic development.}}

{{term|[[Exogenous and endogenous variables|endogenous variable]]}}
{{defn|A variable whose measure is determined by the model.}}

{{term|[[energy modeling]]}}
{{defn|The process of building [[computer model]]s of [[energy system]]s in order to analyze them.}}

{{term|[[Engel curve]]}}
{{defn|Describes how household expenditure on a particular good or service varies with household income.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chai |first1=A. |last2=Moneta |first2=A. |year=2010 |title=Retrospectives: Engel Curves |journal=[[Journal of Economic Perspectives]] |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=225–240 |doi= 10.1257/jep.24.1.225 |doi-access= free|hdl=10072/34021 |url=https://www.iris.sssup.it/bitstream/11382/347390/1/9_ChaiMoneta10.pdf |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name="bare_url">{{cite book | chapter-url = https://www2.bc.edu/arthur-lewbel/palengel.pdf | author = Lewbel, A | date = 2007 | chapter = Engel Curves | title = The New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[engineering economics]]}}
{{defn|Previously known as engineering economy, is a subset of economics concerned with the use and "...application of economic principles"<ref name="Dharmaraj2009">Dharmaraj, E.. Engineering Economics. Mumbai, IN: Himalaya Publishing House, 2009. ProQuest ebrary. Web. 9 November 2016.</ref> in the analysis of engineering decisions.<ref name="Morris1960">Morris, W. Thomas. (1960). Engineering economy: the analysis of management decisions. Homewood, Ill.: R. D. Irwin.</ref>}}

{{term|[[entrepreneurship]]}}
{{defn|The efforts by a person, known as an '''entrepreneur''', in organizing resources for the creation of something new or taking risks to create new innovations and production.}}

{{term|[[envelope theorem]]}}
{{defn|A major result about the differentiability properties of the [[value function]] of a parameterized optimization problem.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Kim C. |last=Border |year=2019 |title=Miscellaneous Notes on Optimization Theory and Related Topics |journal=Lecture Notes |publisher=California Institute of Technology |page=154 |url=https://paperzz.com/doc/7000652/miscellaneous-notes-on-optimization-theory-and-related-to...}}</ref> As we change parameters of the objective, the envelope theorem shows that, in a certain sense, changes in the decision variable(s) of the objective do not contribute to the change in the objective function.}}

{{term|[[environmental economics]]}}
{{defn|A sub-field of economics concerned particularly with environmental issues.}}

{{term|[[equal opportunity]]}}
{{defn|A state of fairness in which job applicants are treated similarly, unhampered by artificial barriers or prejudices or preferences, except when particular distinctions can be explicitly justified.<ref>Paul de Vries (September 12, 2011), "equal opportunity", Blackwell Reference, retrieved September 12, 2011</ref>}}

{{term|[[wikt:Equilibrium|equilibrium]]}}
{{defn|The point at which quantity demanded and quantity supplied are equal and both consumer and producer are satisfied.}}

{{term|[[equilibrium price]]}}
{{defn|The {{gli|market price}} at which both the supplier and consumer will trade and both are satisfied.}}

{{term|[[Equity (economics)|equity]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''economic equality'''.}}
{{defn|The concept or idea of fairness in economics, particularly in regard to {{gli|taxation}} or {{gli|welfare economics}}. More specifically, it may refer to [[Equal opportunity|equal life chances]] regardless of identity, to provide all citizens with a basic and equal minimum of income, goods, and services or to increase funds and commitment for redistribution.<ref name=ODI2>Kate Bird 2009. [http://blogs.odi.org.uk/blogs/main/archive/2009/11/24/building_fair_future.aspx Building a fair future: why equity matters] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721182208/http://blogs.odi.org.uk/blogs/main/archive/2009/11/24/building_fair_future.aspx |date=2011-07-21 }}. London: Overseas Development Institute</ref>}}

{{term|[[equity home bias puzzle]]}}
{{defn|The fact that individuals and institutions in most countries hold only modest amounts of foreign [[Equity (finance)|equity]], and tend to strongly favor company stock from their home nation. This finding is regarded as puzzling, since ample evidence shows [[Portfolio (finance)|equity portfolios]] obtain substantial benefits from [[Diversification (finance)|diversification]] into global stocks.}}

{{term|[[equity premium puzzle]]}}
{{defn|The inability of an important class of [[economic model]]s to explain the average equity risk premium provided by a diversified portfolio of [[equities]] over that of [[government bond]]s, which has been observed for more than 100 years.}}

{{term|[[ergodicity economics]]}}
{{defn|A research programme aimed at reworking the theoretical foundations of [[economics]] around the concept of [[ergodicity]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Ergodicity Economics: About – London Mathematical Laboratory |url=http://lml.org.uk/research/economics/ |access-date=2 October 2024}}</ref> The programme's main goal is to understand how traditional economic theory, framed in terms of the ''[[expected value|expectation values]]'', changes when replacing expectation value with time averages.}}

{{term|[[Eurosclerosis]]}}
{{defn|A pattern of high unemployment and slow job creation in Europe during the 1970s and 1980s that may have resulted from government over-regulation and overly generous social benefits policies.}}

{{term|[[excess burden of taxation]]}}
{{defn|The economic loss that society suffers as a result of the distortions caused by taxes or subsidies.}}

{{term|[[excess supply]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''economic surplus'''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.amosweb.com/cgi-bin/awb_nav.pl?s=wpd&c=dsp&k=excess+supply|title=AmosWEB is Economics: Encyclonomic WEB*pedia|website=www.amosweb.com}}</ref>}}
{{defn|A situation in which the quantity of a good or service supplied is more than the quantity demanded,<ref>{{cite book| last1 = O'Sullivan| first1 = Arthur| author-link = Arthur O'Sullivan (economist)| first2 = Steven M. | last2 = Sheffrin| title = Economics| publisher = Savvas Learning Company| year = 2022| location = Paramus, New Jersey| page = 128| isbn = 978-0-13-063085-8}}</ref> and the price is above the {{gli|economic equilibrium|equilibrium}} level determined by {{gli|supply and demand}}; that is, the quantity of the product that producers wish to sell exceeds the quantity that potential buyers are willing to buy at the prevailing price. It is the opposite of an {{gli|shortage|economic shortage}}.}}

{{term|[[exchange rate]]}}
{{defn|The rate at which one {{gli|currency}} is exchanged for another. It is also commonly regarded as the value of one country's currency relative to another currency.<ref>{{cite book| last = O'Sullivan| first = Arthur| author-link = <!-- Arthur O'Sullivan -->|author2=Steven M. Sheffrin| title = Economics| publisher = Savvas Learning Company| year = 2022| location = Paramus, New Jersey| page = 458| url = https://www.savvas.com/index.cfm?locator=PS3jRm| isbn = 978-0-13-063085-8}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[exchange rate regime]]}}
{{defn|Any method a [[monetary authority]] of a country or [[currency union]] may use to manage the [[currency]] in relation to other currencies and the [[foreign exchange market]].}}

{{term|[[exchange-traded fund]]}}
{{defn|A group of securities that are traded in an exchange market.}}

{{term|[[excludability]]}}
{{defn|The degree to which a [[Goods|good]], [[Service (economics)|service]], or [[resource]] can be limited to only paying customers, or conversely, the degree to which a supplier, producer, or other managing body (e.g. a government) can prevent [[Consumption (economics)|consumption]] of a good.}}

{{term|[[exogenous growth model]]}}
{{defn|See ''[[Glossary of economics#solow–swan model|Solow-Swan model]]''.}}

{{term|[[Exogenous and endogenous variables|exogenous variable]]}}
{{defn|A variable whose measure is determined outside the model and is imposed on the model.}}

{{term|[[expected utility hypothesis]]}}
{{defn|A foundational assumption in [[mathematical economics]] concerning [[decision theory|decision making]] under [[uncertainty]]. It postulates that [[rational agent]]s maximize utility, meaning the subjective desirability of their actions, choosing between risky prospects by comparing expected utility values (i.e. the weighted sum of adding the respective utility values of payoffs multiplied by their probabilities).}}

{{term|[[expeditionary economics]]}}
{{defn|An emerging field of economic enquiry that focuses on the rebuilding and reconstructing of economies in post-conflict nations and providing support to disaster-struck nations. It focuses on the need for good [[economic planning]] on the part of developed nations to help prevent the creation of failed states. It also emphasizes the need for the structuring on new firms to rebuild national economies.<ref name="Expeditionary Economics: A New Model for Post-Conflict Countries">{{cite web |url=http://www.milkeninstitute.org/events/gcprogram.taf?function=detail&EvID=2305&eventid=gc10 |title=Expeditionary Economics: A New Model for Post-Conflict Countries |work=Milken Institute |access-date=March 29, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130307193918/http://www.milkeninstitute.org/events/gcprogram.taf?function=detail&EvID=2305&eventid=GC10 |archive-date=March 7, 2013 }}</ref>}}

{{term|[[expenditure function]]}}
{{defn|Any function which gives the minimum amount of money an individual needs to spend to achieve some level of [[utility]], given a [[utility function]] and the prices of the available goods.}}

{{term|[[experimental economics]]}}
{{defn|The application of [[Experiment|experimental methods]]<ref>Including [[statistical]], [[econometric]], and [[computational economics|computational]]. On the latter see [[Alvin E. Roth]], 2002. "The Economist as Engineer: Game Theory, Experimentation, and Computation as Tools for Design Economics," ''Econometrica'', 70(4), pp. [http://kuznets.fas.harvard.edu/~aroth/papers/engineer.pdf 1341–1378] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040414102216/http://kuznets.fas.harvard.edu/~aroth/papers/engineer.pdf |date=2004-04-14 }}.</ref> to study economic questions.}}

{{term|[[externality]]}}
{{defn|A cost or benefit that falls not on the person(s) directly involved in an activity, but on others. Externalities can be positive or negative.}}

{{term|[[extreme poverty]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''deep poverty''', '''abject poverty''', '''absolute poverty''', '''destitution''', or '''penury'''.}}
{{defn|The most severe type of [[poverty]], defined by the [[United Nations]] as "a condition characterized by severe deprivation of basic human needs, including food, safe [[drinking water]], sanitation facilities, health, shelter, [[education]], and [[information]]. It depends not only on income but also on access to services".<ref>United Nations. [https://web.archive.org/web/2019*/https://www.un.org/documents/ga/conf166/aconf166-9.htm "Report of the World Summit for Social Development"], 6–12 March 1995. (archived from [https://www.un.org/documents/ga/conf166/aconf166-9.htm the original] on 4 July 2019)</ref>}}

{{term|finance}}
{{defn|The study of {{gli|money}} and how it is used. Specifically, it deals with the questions of how an individual, company, or government acquires the money needed—called {{gli|capital}} in the company context—and how they then spend or invest that money.<ref name="freedictionary">[https://financial-dictionary.thefreedictionary.com/finance "Finance"] Farlex Financial Dictionary. 2012</ref>
<!-- Participants in the [[market (economics)|market]] aim to price assets based on their risk level, fundamental value, and their expected [[rate of return]]. --> Finance is often split into three areas: [[personal finance]], [[corporate finance]], and [[public finance]]. At the same time, ''finance'' is about the overall "system", i.e. the [[financial market]]s that allow the flow of money, via investments and other {{gli|financial instrument|financial instruments}}, between and within these areas; this "flow" is facilitated by the {{gli|financial services}} sector. A major focus within finance is thus [[investment management]]—called [[money management]] for individuals, and [[asset management]] for institutions—and finance then includes the associated activities of [[securities trading]], [[investment bank]]ing, [[financial engineering]], and [[risk management]].}}

{{term|[[free market]] (enterprise)}}
{{defn|An {{gli|economic system}} in which the {{gli|price|prices}} for [[goods and services]] are self-regulated by the {{gli|open market}} and by {{gli|consumer|consumers}}. In a free market, the laws and forces of [[supply and demand]] are free from any intervention by a [[Forms of government|government]] or other authority and from all forms of economic privilege, {{gli|monopoly|monopolies}}, and {{gli|artificial scarcity|artificial scarcities}}.<ref>Popper, Karl (1994). The Open Society and Its Enemies. Routledge Classics. {{ISBN|978-0-415-61021-6}}.</ref> Proponents of the concept of the free market contrast it with a [[regulated market]] in which a government intervenes in supply and demand through various methods such as {{gli|tariff|tariffs}} used to restrict trade and to protect the local economy. In an idealized [[free-market economy]], prices for goods and services are set freely by the forces of supply and demand and are allowed to reach their point of {{gli|economic equilibrium|equilibrium}} without intervention by government policy.}}

{{term|[[Keynesian economics]]}}
{{ghat|Also called '''Keynesianism'''.}}
{{defn|A diverse set of {{gli|macroeconomics|macroeconomic}} theories about how in the {{gli|short run}} (and especially during {{gli|recession|recessions}}) economic {{gli|output}} can be strongly influenced by the total amount of spending that occurs within an economy, known as {{gli|aggregate demand}}. Keynesian economists generally argue that because aggregate demand is often unstable and behaves erratically, it does not necessarily or predictably equal the {{gli|aggregate supply}}, which can cause {{gli|market economy|market economies}} to experience inefficient macroeconomic outcomes in the form of {{gli|recession|recessions}} (when demand is low) and {{gli|inflation}} (when demand is high), and that these outcomes can be mitigated by {{gli|monetary policy}} actions by a {{gli|central bank}} and {{gli|fiscal policy}} actions by a government authority, which can help stabilize output over the {{gli|business cycle}}.}}

{{defn|A theory in {{gli|macroeconomics}} which postulates that lowering tax rates, decreasing government regulation, and allowing free trade is the most effective way to foster economic growth because greater supplies of goods and services at lower prices cause employment to increase and consumers to spend more. Contrast ''{{gli|demand-side economics}}''.}}

{{term|[[Economic surplus|surplus]]}}
{{defn|A situation in which supply is greater than demand, usually as the result of high prices.}}

{{term|[[want]]}}
{{defn|Wants are often distinguished from needs. A need is something that is necessary for survival (such as food and shelter), whereas a want is simply something that a person would like to have. Some economists have rejected this distinction and maintain that all of these are simply wants, with varying levels of importance. {{term|wealth}}
{{defn|The [[abundance (economics)|abundance]] of [[Value (economics)|valuable]] [[financial asset]]s or [[property|physical possessions]] which can be converted into a form that can be used for [[financial transaction|transactions]]. This includes the core meaning as held in the originating old English word ''weal'', which is from an [[Indo-European languages|Indo-European]] word stem.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://dictionary.reference.com/browse/weal|title=weal|work=[[The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language]]|edition=4th|publisher=Houghton Mifflin Company|access-date=February 21, 2009}}</ref> The modern concept of wealth is of significance in all areas of {{gli|economics}}, especially for {{gli|economic growth|growth economics}} and {{gli|development economics}}, yet the meaning of wealth is context-dependent. Individuals or companies possessing a substantial {{gli|net worth}} are often referred to as ''wealthy''. Net worth is defined as the current value of one's {{gli|asset|assets}} less {{gli|liability|liabilities}} (excluding the principal in trust accounts).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://movies2.nytimes.com/books/first/s/stanley-millionaire.html|title=The Millionaire Next Door|website=movies2.nytimes.com|access-date=2018-09-27}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[wealth effect]]}}

"wealth effect," ''[[The New Palgrave: A Dictionary of Economics]]'', v. 4, pp. 883–4.<br/>&nbsp;&nbsp; • {{cite web|url=http://www.portfolio.com/views/blogs/odd-numbers/2008/06/17/in-praise-of-the-wealth-effect|title=In Praise of the Wealth Effect – Economics Blog – Zubin Jelveh – Odd Numbers – Portfolio.com|publisher=portfolio.com|access-date=2009-04-20|last=Jelveh|first=Zubin}}</ref> Usually the wealth effect is positive: spending changes in the same direction as perceived wealth.}}

{{term|welfare}}
{{defn|A type of government support for the citizens of that society. Welfare may be provided to people of any income level, as with [[social security]] (and is then often called a [[social safety net]]), but it is usually intended to ensure that people can meet their basic human needs such as food and shelter. Welfare attempts to provide a minimal level of [[well-being]], usually either a free- or a subsidized-supply of certain goods and social services, such as [[universal healthcare|healthcare]], education, and [[vocational training]].<ref name="Modern Thought Third Edition 1999 p. 919">''The New Fontana Dictionary of Modern Thought'' Third Edition (1999), Allan Bullock and Stephen Trombley Eds., p. 919.</ref>}}

{{term|[[Yield (finance)|yield]]}}
{{defn|In {{gli|finance}}, the yield on a {{gli|security}} is the amount of cash (in percentage terms) that returns to the owners of the security, in the form of interest or dividends received from it. Normally, it does not include the price variations, distinguishing it from the total {{gli|return}}. Yield applies to various stated rates of return on stocks (common and preferred, and [[Convertible bond|convertible]]), fixed income instruments (bonds, notes, bills, strips, zero coupon), and some other investment type insurance products (e.g. {{gli|annuity|annuities}}).}}

==Z==
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[Zelder paradox]]}}
{{defn|}}

{{term|[[zero-sum game]]}}
{{defn|In [[game theory]] and [[economic theory]], a zero-sum game is a [[Mathematical model|mathematical representation]] of a situation in which each participant's gain or loss of [[utility]] is exactly balanced by the losses or gains of the utility of the other participants. If the total gains of the participants are added up and the total losses are subtracted, they will sum to zero. Thus, [[Fair cake-cutting|cutting a cake]], where taking a larger piece reduces the amount of cake available for others as much as it increases the amount available for that taker, is a zero-sum game if all participants value each unit of cake equally (see {{gli|marginal utility}}).}}
{{glossaryend}}
