A December 2013 ''[[Associated Press]]'' survey of three dozen economists',<ref name="AP">{{Cite web|url=http://www.nbcnews.com/businessmain/widening-income-gap-hurting-economy-survey-says-2D11767020|title=Widening income gap is hurting the economy, survey says|date=December 18, 2013|website=NBC News|language=en|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref> a 2014 report by [[Standard and Poor's]]<ref name="S&P">{{Cite web|url=https://www.huffpost.com/|title=HuffPost - Breaking News, U.S. and World News|last=Boak|first=Josh|date=August 5, 2014|website=www.huffpost.com|language=en|access-date=October 9, 2019}}</ref> and economists [[Gar Alperovitz]], [[Robert Reich]], [[Joseph Stiglitz]], [[Branko Milanovic]] and [[Robert J. Gordon|Robert Gordon]] agree about the harms of inequality.

The majority of respondents in the ''[[Associated Press]]'' survey agreed that widening income disparity was harming the US economy. They argue that wealthy Americans are receiving higher pay, but they spend less per dollar earned than middle-class consumers, whose incomes have largely stagnated.<ref name="AP" />

The S&P report concluded that diverging income inequality had slowed the recovery and could contribute to future boom-and-bust cycles, given increasing personal debt levels. Higher levels of income inequality increase political pressures, discouraging trade, investment, hiring, and social mobility.<ref name="S&P" />

Alperovitz and Reich argued that concentration of wealth does not leave sufficient purchasing power for the economy to function effectively.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://therealnews.com/|title=The Real News Network {{!}} Independent, Fact-Based Journalism|last=Alperovitz|first=Gar|date=January 26, 2014|website=The Real News Network|language=en-US|access-date=October 9, 2019}}</ref>{{failed verification|date=October 2019}}<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.truthdig.com/articles/the-war-on-the-poor-and-middle-class-families/|title=The War on the Poor and Middle-Class Families|last=Reich|first=Robert|author-link=Robert Reich|date=February 8, 2014|website=Truthdig|language=en|access-date=October 9, 2019}}</ref>

Stiglitz argued that wealth and income concentration lead the economic elite to protect themselves from redistributive policies by weakening the state, which lessens public investments – roads, technology, education, etc. – that are essential for economic growth.<ref>{{Cite interview|last=Stiglitz|first=Joseph|interviewer=Ben Chu|title=Stiglitz: the full transcript|url=http://blogs.independent.co.uk/2012/07/02/stiglitz-the-full-transcript/|access-date=September 8, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120910120437/http://blogs.independent.co.uk/2012/07/02/stiglitz-the-full-transcript/|archive-date=September 10, 2012|newspaper=The Independent|date=July 2, 2012|author-link=Joseph Stiglitz}}</ref><ref name="Stiglitz-the-price" />{{rp|85}}<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dynan|first1=Karen|last2=Skinner|first2=Jonathan|last3=Zeldes|first3=Stephen|date=September 2000|title=Do the Rich Save More?|journal=Journal of Political Economy|location=Cambridge, MA|volume=112|issue=2|doi=10.3386/w7906|pages=397–444|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Milanovic stated that while traditionally economists thought inequality was good for growth, "When physical capital mattered most, savings and investments were key. Then it was important to have a large contingent of rich people who could save a greater proportion of their income than the poor and invest it in physical capital. But now that human capital is scarcer than machines, widespread education has become the secret to growth", and that while "broadly accessible education" is difficult to achieve under inequality, education tends to reduce income gaps.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2011/09/milanovic.htm|title=Finance and Development|date=September 2011|website=Finance and Development|language=en-US|access-date=October 9, 2019|volume=48|issue=3}}</ref>

Gordon wrote that such issues as 'rising inequality; factor price equalization stemming from the interplay between globalization and the Internet; the twin educational problems of cost inflation in higher education and poor secondary student performance; the consequences of environmental regulations and taxes ..." make economic growth harder to achieve.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gordon|first=Robert|date=August 2012|title=Is U.S. Economic Growth Over? Faltering Innovation Confronts the Six Headwinds|url=http://www.nber.org/papers/w18315.pdf|journal=National Bureau of Economic Research|language=en|location=Cambridge, MA|article-number=w18315|doi=10.3386/w18315|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In response to the [[Occupy movement in the United States|Occupy movement]], legal scholar [[Richard A. Epstein|Richard Epstein]] defended inequality in a free market society, maintaining that "taxing the top one percent even more means less wealth and fewer jobs for the rest of us." According to Epstein, "the inequalities in wealth ... pay for themselves by the vast increases in wealth", while "forced transfers of wealth through taxation ... will destroy the pools of wealth that are needed to generate new ventures".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hoover.org/research/three-cheers-income-inequality|title=Three Cheers for Income Inequality|last=Epstein|first=Richard A.|date=November 8, 2011|website=Hoover Institution|language=en|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

According to a 2020 study by the [[RAND Corporation]], the typical worker, defined in the study as a "Full-Year, Full-Time, Prime-Aged Worker",<ref name="priceedwards" /> makes $42,000 less than they would have if income inequality had not increased over the last four decades. The study also shows that white working-class males and rural workers who work full-time have been the hardest hit, while the higher-income earners captured the vast majority of economic growth over the same time period.<ref>{{cite news |last=Picchi |first=Aimee |date=September 14, 2020 |title=The price of inequality? Lost annual income of $42,000 for typical worker, study finds |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/income-inqequality-42k-lost-anually/ |work=[[CBS News]] |access-date=September 14, 2020}}</ref> The total wealth difference would have exceeded $50 trillion by early 2020, an amount that would have led to a more prosperous economy and a healthier, more financially secure population. The report concludes that the American economy's radical inequality is hindering economic growth, as the benefits are mainly enjoyed by those at the top, while the majority, responsible for the bulk of [[consumer spending]], which constitutes 67% of GDP, are left behind.<ref name="priceedwards">{{Cite book |last1=Price |first1=Carter |last2=Edwards |first2=Kathryn |url=https://www.rand.org/content/dam/rand/pubs/working_papers/WRA500/WRA516-1/RAND_WRA516-1.pdf |title=Trends in Income From 1975 to 2018 |date=September 2020 |publisher=RAND Corporation |language=en |doi=10.7249/wra516-1|s2cid=224943152 }}</ref>

==== Financial crises ====
Income inequality was cited as one of the causes of the [[Great Depression]] by Supreme Court Justice [[Louis D. Brandeis]] in 1933. In his dissent in the ''[[Louis K. Liggett Co. v. Lee]]'' (288 U.S. 517) case, he wrote: "Other writers have shown that, coincident with the growth of these giant corporations, there has occurred a marked concentration of individual wealth; and that the resulting disparity in incomes is a major cause of the existing depression."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/288/517/case.html|title=Louis K. Liggett Co. v. Lee: 288 U.S. 517 (1933) :: Justia U.S. Supreme Court Center|work=Justia Law}}</ref>

Rajan argued that "systematic economic inequalities, within the United States and around the world, have created deep financial 'fault lines' that have made [financial] crises more likely to happen than in the past".<ref name="Lo">{{cite web|url=http://www.argentumlux.org/documents/JEL_6.pdf|title=Reading About the Financial Crisis: A 21-Book Review|last=Lo|first=Andrew W.|year=2012|publisher=Journal of Economic Literature .|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130113032210/http://www.argentumlux.org/documents/JEL_6.pdf|archive-date=January 13, 2013|access-date=November 27, 2013}}</ref><ref name="KOEHN">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/08/01/business/01shelf.html|title=A Call to Fix the Fundamentals (Review of ''Fault Lines: How Hidden Fractures Still Threaten the World Economy'' by Raghuram G. Rajan)|last=Koehn|first=Nancy F.|date=July 31, 2010|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=November 20, 2013}}</ref>

==== Monopoly, labor, consolidation, and competition ====
Greater income inequality can lead to [[Monopoly|monopolization]], resulting in fewer employers requiring fewer workers.<ref name="Pigou">{{cite book|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=26kAAwAAQBAJ|title=The Economics of Welfare|last1=Pigou|first1=Arthur C.|publisher=Macmillan and Co.|year=1932|isbn=978-1-137-37563-6|edition=4th|location=London|language=en|chapter=Part I, Chapter VIII|access-date=October 12, 2019|archive-date=August 3, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200803133107/https://books.google.com/books?id=26kAAwAAQBAJ}}</ref><ref name="Lynn">{{cite journal|last1=Lynn|first1=Barry C.|last2=Longman|first2=Phillip|date=March–April 2010|title=Who Broke America's Jobs Machine?|url=http://www.washingtonmonthly.com/features/2010/1003.lynn-longman.html|journal=Washington Monthly|volume=March/April 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140812211534/http://www.washingtonmonthly.com/features/2010/1003.lynn-longman.html|archive-date=August 12, 2014|access-date=August 11, 2014}}</ref> Remaining employers can [[Consolidation (business)|consolidate]] and take advantage of the relative lack of competition.<ref name="Castells-Quintana" /><ref name="Lynn" />

==== Aggregate demand ====
Income inequality is claimed to lower [[aggregate demand]], leading to large segments of formerly middle-class consumers unable to afford as many goods and services.<ref name="Pigou" /> This pushes production and overall employment down.<ref name="Castells-Quintana" />

=== Income mobility ===
{{further|Socio-economic mobility in the United States}}The ability to move from one income group into another ([[Economic mobility|income mobility]]) is a measure of economic opportunity. A higher probability of upward income mobility would theoretically help mitigate income inequality, as each generation has a better chance of achieving higher income.

Several studies indicated that higher income inequality is associated with lower income mobility. In other words, income brackets tend to be increasingly "sticky" as income inequality increases. This is described by the [[Great Gatsby curve]].<ref name="Krueger2012" /><ref name="KSS2007">{{cite web|url=http://www.columbia.edu/~wk2110/bin/mobility-short.pdf|title=Uncovering the American Dream:  Inequality and Mobility in Social Security Earnings Data since 1937 Figure 4B|last1=Kopczuk|first1=Wojciech|last2=Saez|first2=Emmanuel|date=September 15, 2007|last3=Song|first3=Jae}}</ref> Noah summarized this as "you can't really experience ever-growing income inequality without experiencing a decline in [[Horatio Alger]]-style upward mobility because (to use a frequently-employed metaphor) it's harder to climb a ladder when the rungs are farther apart."<ref name="Noah2">{{Cite magazine|url=https://newrepublic.com/article/99651/white-house-heres-why-you-have-care-about-inequality|title=White House: Here's Why You Have To Care About Inequality|last=Noah|first=Timothy|date=January 13, 2012|magazine=The New Republic|access-date=October 10, 2019|issn=0028-6583}}</ref>

==== Over lifetimes ====
A 2013 [[Brookings Institution]] study claimed that income inequality was increasing and becoming permanent, sharply reducing [[social mobility]].<ref name="BrookingsPerm">{{cite web|url=http://www.brookings.edu/about/projects/bpea/latest-conference/2013-spring-permanent-inequality-panousi|title=Inequality Rising and Permanent Over Past Two Decades|last1=Panousi|first1=Vasia|last2=Vidangos|first2=Ivan|date=Spring 2013|work=Brookings Papers on Economic Activity|publisher=Brookings Institution|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130408151547/http://www.brookings.edu/about/projects/bpea/latest-conference/2013-spring-permanent-inequality-panousi|archive-date=April 8, 2013|access-date=March 23, 2013|last3=Ramnath|first3=Shanti|last4=DeBacker|first4=Jason|last5=Heim|first5=Bradley}}</ref> A 2007 study found the top population in the United States "very stable" and that income mobility had not "mitigated the dramatic increase in annual earnings concentration since the 1970s."<ref name="KSS2007" />

Krugman argued that while in any given year, some people with low incomes will be "workers on temporary layoff, small businessmen taking write-offs, farmers hit by bad weather" – the rise in their income in succeeding years is not the same 'mobility' as poor people rising to middle class or middle income rising to high income. It's the mobility of "the guy who works in the college bookstore and has a real job by his early thirties."<ref name="debate">{{Cite web|url=https://prospect.org/api/content/6c28c58a-5dc6-57b9-8bab-f5992e79ce2b/|title=The Rich, the Right, and the Facts: Deconstructing the Income Distribution Debate|last=Krugman|first=Paul|date=December 19, 2001|website=The American Prospect|language=en-us|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref><!--How does this relate to change in inequality? Instead it seems like a critique of IE as a measurement. These same factors affect workers in every country. Mobility may be overestimated for these reasons, but it would be overestimated everywhere, without necessarily affecting comparisons among countries.-->

<blockquote>Studies by the [[Urban Institute]] and the [[US Treasury]] have both found that about half of the families who start in either the top or the bottom quintile of the income distribution are still there after a decade, and that only 3 to 6% rise from bottom to top or fall from top to bottom.<ref name="debate" /></blockquote>On the issue of whether most Americans stay in the same income bracket over time, the 2011 CBO distribution of income study reported:<blockquote>Household income measured over a multi-year period is more equally distributed than income measured over one year, although only modestly so. Given the fairly substantial movement of households across income groups over time, it might seem that income measured over a number of years should be significantly more equally distributed than income measured over one year. However, much of the movement of households involves changes in income that are large enough to push households into different income groups but not large enough to greatly affect the overall distribution of income. Multi-year income measures also show the same pattern of increasing inequality over time as is observed in annual measures.<ref name="cbo">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/54646|title=The Distribution of Household Income, 2015 {{!}} Congressional Budget Office|website=www.cbo.gov|date=November 8, 2018 |access-date=2019-10-09}}</ref></blockquote>In other words,<blockquote>many people who have incomes greater than $1 million one year fall out of the category the next year – but that's typically because their income fell from, say, $1.05 million to .95 million, not because they went back to being middle class.</blockquote>Disagreements about the correct procedure for measuring income inequality continue to be a topic of debate among economists, including a panel discussion at the 2019 American Economic Association annual meeting.

==== Between generations ====
[[File:The Great Gatsby Curve.png|thumb|The [[Great Gatsby curve]] showing intergenerational economic immobility on the vertical axis and increasing inequality on the horizontal axis for several different countries]]
Several studies found the ability of children from poor or middle-class families to rise to upper income – known as "upward relative intergenerational mobility" – is lower in the US than in other developed countries.<ref name="DeParle">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/01/05/us/harder-for-americans-to-rise-from-lower-rungs.html|title=Harder for Americans to Rise From Lower Rungs|last=DeParle|first=Jason|date=January 4, 2012|work=The New York Times|access-date=October 10, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Krueger and Corak found lower mobility to be linked to income inequality.<ref name="Gatsby">{{cite web|url=http://milescorak.com/2012/01/12/here-is-the-source-for-the-great-gatsby-curve-in-the-alan-krueger-speech-at-the-center-for-american-progress/|title=Here is the source for the "Great Gatsby Curve" in the Alan Krueger speech at the Center for American Progress on January 12 - Economics for public policy|last=Corak|first=Miles|date=January 12, 2012|work=Economics for public policy}}</ref><ref name="Krueger2012" />

In their [[Great Gatsby curve]],<ref name="Gatsby" /> Labor economist Miles Corak found a negative [[correlation]] between inequality and social mobility. The curve plotted intergenerational income mobility, the likelihood that someone will match their parents' relative income level, and inequality for various countries.<ref name="Krueger2012" />

The connection between income inequality and low mobility can be explained by the lack of access to and preparation for schools that are crucial for high-paying jobs; lack of health care may lead to obesity and diabetes and limit education and employment.<ref name="DeParle" />

Krueger estimated that "the persistence in the advantages and disadvantages of income passed from parents to the children" will "rise by about a quarter for the next generation as a result of the rise in inequality that the U.S. has seen in the last 25 years."<ref name="Krueger2012" />

=== Poverty ===
{{main|Poverty in the United States}}
Greater income inequality can increase the market income poverty rate, as income shifts from lower to higher brackets. Jared Bernstein wrote, "If less of the economy's market-generated growth – i.e., before taxes and transfers kick in – ends up in the lower reaches of the income scale, either there will be more poverty for any given level of GDP growth, or there will have to be a lot more transfers to offset inequality's poverty-inducing impact." The [[Economic Policy Institute]] (EPI) estimated that greater income inequality added 5.5% to the poverty rate between 1979 and 2007, other factors equal. Income inequality was the largest driver of the change in the poverty rate, with economic growth, family structure, education, and race other important factors.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://economix.blogs.nytimes.com/2014/01/13/poverty-and-inequality-in-charts/?_r=0#more-171464|title=Poverty and Inequality, in Charts|last=Bernstein|first=Jared|date=January 13, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://billmoyers.com/2014/01/17/we-would-have-eliminated-poverty-entirely-by-now-if-inequality-hadnt-skyrocketed/|title=We Would Have Eliminated Poverty Entirely by Now if Inequality Hadn't Skyrocketed|last=Bruenig|first=Matt|date=January 17, 2014|website=BillMoyers.com|language=en-US|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref> An estimated 11.8% of Americans lived in poverty in 2018,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2019/demo/p60-266.html|title=Income and Poverty in the United States: 2018|website=www.census.gov|language=EN-US|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref> versus 16% in 2012 and 26% in 1967.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/economy/study-us-poverty-rate-decreased-over-past-half-century-thanks-to-safety-net-programs/2013/12/09/9322c834-60f3-11e3-94ad-004fefa61ee6_story.html|title=Study: U.S. poverty rate decreased over past half-century thanks to safety-net programs|last=Goldfarb|first=Zachary A.|date=December 9, 2013|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=October 10, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0190-8286}}</ref><!--Why not the other way around? Which is exogenous? Are both? E.g., poverty declined continuously 2007-2019. (See below.) Was that driven by declines in inequality? Might both be subject to some other cause?--> The [[poverty threshold]] in the United States was at $12,880 for a single-person household and $26,246 for a family of four in 2021.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2015/07/22/what-it-means-to-be-poor-by-global-standards/ |title=What it means to be poor by global standards |author=Rakesh Kochhar |website=[[Pew Research Center]] |date=July 22, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://aspe.hhs.gov/2021-poverty-guidelines |title=2021 Poverty Guidelines |website=aspe.hhs.gov |access-date=April 27, 2023}}</ref> 0.25% of the U.S. population lived below the international poverty line of $2.15 per day in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fact Sheet: An Adjustment to Global Poverty Lines |url=https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/factsheet/2022/05/02/fact-sheet-an-adjustment-to-global-poverty-lines#:~:text=The%20new%20international%20poverty%20line,be%20living%20in%20extreme%20poverty. |access-date=April 27, 2023 |website=World Bank}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Country Profile: United States |url=https://pip.worldbank.org/country-profiles/USA |access-date=April 27, 2023 |website=World Bank}}</ref>

A rise in income disparities weakens skills development among people with a poor educational background in terms of the quantity and quality of education attained.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Cingano|first=Federico|year=2014|title=Trends in Income Inequality and its Impact on Economic Growth|journal=OECD Social, Employment and Migration Working Papers|doi=10.1787/5jxrjncwxv6j-en|doi-access=free}}</ref><!--always?-->

=== Debt ===
Income inequality may be the driving factor in growing household debt,<ref name="denial">{{Cite magazine|url=https://newrepublic.com/article/109157/conservative-inequality-denialism|title=Conservative Inequality Denialism|last=Noah|first=Timothy|date=October 25, 2012|magazine=The New Republic|access-date=October 10, 2019|issn=0028-6583}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://newamerica.net/publications/policy/the_way_forward|title=The Way Forward|last1=Alpert|first1=Daniel|last2=Hockett|first2=Robert|date=October 10, 2011|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120711200159/http://newamerica.net/publications/policy/the_way_forward|archive-date=July 11, 2012|last3=Roubini|first3=Nouriel}}</ref> as high earners bid up the price of real estate and middle income earners go deeper into debt trying to maintain a middle class lifestyle.<ref name="plumer">{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/wonkblog/wp/2013/03/27/trickle-down-consumption-how-rising-inequality-can-leave-everyone-worse-off/|title='Trickle-down consumption': How rising inequality can leave everyone worse off|last=Plumer|first=Brad|date=March 27, 2013|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=March 27, 2013}}</ref> Between 1983 and 2007, the top 5 percent saw their debt fall from 80 cents for every dollar of income to 65 cents, while the bottom 95 percent saw their debt rise from 60 cents for every dollar of income to $1.40.<ref name="denial" /> Krugman found a strong correlation between inequality and household debt during the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.<ref name="crises" />

Twenty-first century college costs have risen much faster than income, resulting in an increase in [[Student debt|student loan debt]] from $260 billion in 2004 to $1.6 trillion in 2019Q2.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/SLOAS|title=Student Loans Owned and Securitized|date=January 1, 2006|website=FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis}}</ref> From 1995 to 2013, outstanding education debt grew from 26% of average yearly income to 58%, for households with net worth below the 50th percentile.<ref name="YellenOct14">{{cite news|url=http://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/yellen20141017a.htm|title=Perspectives on Inequality and Opportunity from the Survey of Consumer Finances|last=Yellen|first=Janet|access-date=October 17, 2014}}</ref>

=== Democracy and society{{anchor|Impact on democracy and society}} ===
{{See also|Democratic backsliding}}[[File:Merely recognizing a fact - Ehrhart. LCCN2011648858.jpg|thumb|Political cartoon from the [[Progressive Era]], when wealth concentration was similar to that of the present, shows how the concentration of wealth in a few hands leads to the extinguishing of [[individualism]], initiative, ambition, [[Meritocracy|untainted success]], and [[independence]].]]
Bernstein and Krugman assessed the concentration of income as variously "unsustainable"<ref name="CBO Report Shows Rich Got Richer">{{Cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2011-10-31/cbo-report-shows-rich-got-richer-as-did-most-americans-view|title=CBO Report Shows Rich Got Richer, As Did Most Americans: View|date=October 31, 2011|publisher=businessweek.com}}</ref> and "incompatible"<ref name="Oligarchy">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/11/04/opinion/oligarchy-american-style.html|title=Oligarchy, American Style|last=Krugman|first=Paul|date=November 3, 2011|work=The New York Times|access-date=October 10, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> with democracy. Political scientists [[Jacob S. Hacker]] and [[Paul Pierson]] quoted a warning by Greek-Roman historian [[Plutarch]]: "An imbalance between rich and poor is the oldest and most fatal ailment of all republics."<ref name="Hacker.p75">{{Cite book|title=Winner-take-all politics: how washington made the rich richer–and turned its back on the middle class|last1=Hacker|first1=Jacob S.|last2=Pierson|first2=Paul|date=2014|publisher=Simon & Schuster|isbn=978-1-4165-9384-3|page=75|oclc=892939587|author-link2=Paul Pierson}}</ref> Some academic researchers alleged that the US political system risks drifting towards [[oligarchy]], through the influence of corporations, the wealthy and other special interest groups.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Gilens|first1=Martin|last2=Page|first2=Benjamin I.|date=2014|title=Testing Theories of American Politics: Elites, Interest Groups, and Average Citizens|journal=[[Perspectives on Politics]]|volume=12|issue=3|pages=564–581|doi=10.1017/S1537592714001595|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Capital in the Twenty-First Century|last=Piketty|first=Thomas|date=2017|publisher=Belknap Press|isbn=978-0-674-97985-7|page=514|quote=the risk of a drift towards oligarchy is real and gives little reason for optimism about where the United States is headed.|author-link=Thomas Piketty|title-link=Capital in the Twenty-First Century}}</ref>

==== Political polarization ====
Rising income inequality has been linked to [[political polarization]].<ref name="SA2020"/><ref>Josh Harkinson (September 13, 2013). [https://www.motherjones.com/mojo/2013/09/chart-washington-gridlock-income-inequality Chart: Washington Gridlock Linked to Income Inequality]. ''[[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]].'' Retrieved September 16, 2013.</ref> Krugman wrote in 2014, "The basic story of political polarization over the past few decades is that, as a wealthy minority has pulled away economically from the rest of the country, it has pulled one major party along with it ... Any policy that benefits lower- and middle-income Americans at the expense of the elite – like health reform, which guarantees insurance to all and pays for that guarantee in part with taxes on higher incomes – will face bitter Republican opposition."<ref name="The New York Times-2014" /> He used environmental protection as another example, which became a partisan issue only after the 1990s.<ref name="The New York Times-2014">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/11/28/opinion/paul-krugman-pollution-and-politics.html|title=Pollution and Politics|date=November 28, 2014|work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Krugman: Income Inequality Pricks 'Conscience' |language=en |work=NPR.org |url=https://www.npr.org/2007/10/09/15119040/krugman-income-inequality-pricks-conscience |access-date=2022-09-22}}</ref> Evidence suggests the impact of national income inequality on regional economic divergence as one potential reason for the link between inequality and political polarization.<ref name = Manduca>{{cite journal| title = The Contribution of National Income Inequality to Regional Economic Divergence | last1 = Manduca | first1 = Robert | year=2019| journal = Social Forces | volume = 98| issue = 2 | pages = 622–648 |url = https://academic.oup.com/sf/article-abstract/98/2/622/5418441 | doi = 10.1093/sf/soz013}}</ref>

As income inequality increased, polarization in the [[United States House of Representatives|House of Representatives]], measured by voting records, increased as well. Inequality increased the influence of the rich on the regulatory, legislative, and electoral processes.<ref name="Bonica 103–124">{{Cite journal|last1=Bonica|first1=Adam|last2=McCarty|first2=Nolan|last3=Poole|first3=Keith T|last4=Rosenthal|first4=Howard|date=August 1, 2013|title=Why Hasn't Democracy Slowed Rising Inequality?|journal=[[Journal of Economic Perspectives]]|volume=27|issue=3|pages=103–124|doi=10.1257/jep.27.3.103|s2cid=154547751|issn=0895-3309|doi-access=free}}</ref> McCarty, Pool and Rosenthal wrote in 2007 that Republicans had then moved away from redistributive policies that would reduce income inequality, whereas earlier, they had supported redistributive policies such as the EITC. Polarization thus completed a feedback loop, increasing inequality.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://themonkeycage.org/2011/10/18/polarization-and-inequality/|title=Polarization and Inequality|last=Voeten|author-link1=Erik Voeten|first=Erik|date=October 18, 2011|work=The Monkey Cage}}</ref>

The IMF warned in 2017 that rising income inequality within Western nations, in particular the United States, could result in further political polarization.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/imf-g20-inequality/imf-calls-for-fiscal-policies-that-tackle-rising-inequality-idUSL2N1ML16B|title=IMF calls for fiscal policies that tackle rising inequality|last=Dunsmuir|first=Lindsay|date=October 11, 2017|work=[[Reuters]]|access-date=August 2, 2018}}</ref>

==== Political inequality ====
Several economists and political scientists have argued that income inequality translates into political inequality, for example, when politicians have financial incentives to accommodate special interest groups. Researchers such as [[Larry Bartels]] found that politicians are significantly more responsive to the political opinions of the wealthy, even when controlling for a range of variables including educational attainment and political knowledge.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Unequal Democracy: The Political Economy of the New Gilded Age|last=Bartels|first=Larry|publisher=Princeton University Press|year=2008|isbn=978-1-4008-2835-7|pages=270–80}}</ref><ref name="EIPR">{{Cite web|url=https://www.russellsage.org/sites/all/files/u4/Bartels%20EIPR.pdf|title=Economic Inequality and Political Representation|last=Bartels|first=Larry|date=November 2002|publisher=Russell Sage|access-date=July 1, 2016}}</ref>

==== Class system ====
A ''class system'' is a society organized around the division of the population into groups having a permanent status that determines their relation to other groups.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sociologyguide.com/social-stratification/class-system.php|title=Class System, Medieval Class System, Social Class System, What Are The Different Classes In The Class System, Social Stratification, Sociology Guide|website=www.sociologyguide.com|access-date=October 29, 2019}}</ref> Such groups may be defined by income, religion and/or other characteristics. Class warfare is thus conflict between/among such classes.

Investor [[Warren Buffett]] said in 2006, "There's class warfare, all right, but it's my class, the rich class, that's making war, and we're winning." He advocated much higher taxes on the wealthiest Americans.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/11/26/business/yourmoney/26every.html|title=In Class Warfare, Guess Which Class Is Winning|last=Stein|first=Ben|date=November 26, 2006|work=The New York Times|access-date=October 10, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

[[George Packer]] wrote, "Inequality hardens society into a [[class system]] ... Inequality divides us from one another in schools, in neighborhoods, at work, on airplanes, in hospitals, in what we eat, in the condition of our bodies, in what we think, in our children's futures, in how we die. Inequality makes it harder to imagine the lives of others."<ref name="Packer">{{Cite news|url=https://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/united-states/2011-10-11/broken-contract|title=The Broken Contract|last=Packer|first=George|journal=Foreign Affairs: America and the World|date=November–December 2011|access-date=October 10, 2019|publisher=[[Foreign Affairs]]|language=en-US|issn=0015-7120}}</ref>

In recent US history, the class conflict has taken the form of the "1% versus the 99%" issue, particularly as reflected in the [[Occupy movement in the United States|Occupy movement]] and struggles over tax policy and redistribution. The movement spread to [[List of Occupy movement protest locations|600 communities]] in 2011. Its main political slogan – "[[We are the 99%]]" – referenced its dissatisfaction with the era's income inequality.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2013/04/barack-obama-class-warrior-90052.html|title=Obama, GOP fight the class war|last1=Martin|first1=Jonathan|last2=Harris|first2=John F.|website=POLITICO|date=April 15, 2013 |language=en|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

==== Political change ====
Increasing inequality is both a cause and effect of [[political change]], according to journalist [[Hedrick Smith]]. The result was a political landscape dominated in the 1990s and 2000s by business groups, specifically "political insiders" – former members of Congress and government officials with an inside track – working for "Wall Street banks, the oil, defense, and pharmaceutical industries; and business trade associations." In the decade or so before the Great Divergence, middle-class-dominated reformist grassroots efforts – such as the [[civil rights movement]], [[Environmental movement in the United States|environmental movement]], [[consumer movement]], labor movement – had considerable political impact.<ref name=":0">{{cite book|title=Who stole the American dream?|last=Smith|first=Hedrick|date=2013|publisher=Random House Trade Paperbacks|isbn=978-0-8129-8205-3|pages=xviii–xix|oclc=856903936}}</ref>

World trade significantly expanded in the 1990s and thereafter, with the creation of the [[World Trade Organization]] and the negotiation of the [[North American Free Trade Agreement]]. These agreements and related policies were widely supported by business groups and economists such as Krugman<ref>{{cite journal|last=Krugman|first=Paul|date=1993|title=The Uncomfortable Truth about NAFTA: It's Foreign Policy, Stupid|journal=Foreign Affairs|volume=72|issue=5|pages=13–19|doi=10.2307/20045808|issn=0015-7120|jstor=20045808}}</ref> and Stiglitz.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.minneapolisfed.org/publications/the-region/interview-with-joseph-e-stiglitz|title=Interview with Joseph E. Stiglitz {{!}} Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis|website=www.minneapolisfed.org|access-date=October 29, 2019|archive-date=October 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191029013228/https://www.minneapolisfed.org/publications/the-region/interview-with-joseph-e-stiglitz}}</ref> One outcome was greatly expanded foreign outsourcing, which has been argued to have hollowed out the middle class.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Davidson|first=Paul|date=2013|title=Income Inequality and Hollowing Out the Middle Class|journal=Journal of Post Keynesian Economics|volume=36|issue=2|pages=381–383|doi=10.2753/PKE0160-3477360209|s2cid=153945956}}</ref>

Stiglitz later argued that inequality may explain political questions – such as why America's infrastructure (and other public investments) are deteriorating,<ref name="Stiglitz-the-price"/>{{rp|92}} or the country's recent relative lack of reluctance to engage in military conflicts such as the [[Iraq War]]. Top-earning families have the money to buy their own education, medical care, personal security, and parks. They showed little interest in helping pay for such things for the rest of society, and have the political influence to make sure they don't have to. The relatively few children of the wealthy who joined the military may have reduced their concern about going to war.<ref name="Joseph E. Stiglitz">{{cite magazine|url=https://www.vanityfair.com/news/2011/05/top-one-percent-201105|title=Of the 1%, by the 1%, for the 1%|last=Stiglitz|first=Joseph E.|magazine=Vanity Fair|language=en|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

Milanovic argued that globalization and immigration caused US middle-class wages to stagnate, fueling the rise of [[Populism|populist]] political candidates.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://qz.com/626076/the-hidden-economics-behind-the-rise-of-donald-trump/|title=The hidden economics behind the rise of Donald Trump|last=Phillips|first=Matt|date=March 2016 }}</ref> Piketty attributed the victory of [[Donald Trump]] in the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential election]], to "the explosion in economic and [[geographic inequality]] in the United States over several decades and the inability of successive governments to deal with this."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2016/nov/16/globalization-trump-inequality-thomas-piketty|title=We must rethink globalization, or Trumpism will prevail|last=Piketty|first=Thomas|date=November 16, 2016|work=The Guardian|access-date=October 10, 2019|issn=0261-3077|author-link=Thomas Piketty}}</ref>

==== Health ====

{{quote box
| quote =After rising for a century, average life expectancy in the U.S. is now declining. And for those in the bottom 90% of the income distribution, real (inflation-adjusted) wages have stagnated: the income of a typical male worker today is around where it was 40 years ago.| source = —[[Joseph Stiglitz]]<ref>{{cite web| last= Stiglitz |first=Joseph | date =May 13, 2019| title=Three decades of neoliberal policies have decimated the middle class, our economy, and our democracy|url=https://www.marketwatch.com/story/three-decades-of-neoliberal-policies-have-decimated-the-middle-class-our-economy-and-our-democracy-2019-05-13|access-date=December 9, 2019 |publisher= [[MarketWatch]]}}</ref>
| width = 340px}}

Using statistics from 23 developed countries and the 50 states of the US, British researchers [[Richard G. Wilkinson]] and [[Kate Pickett]] found a correlation that remains after accounting for ethnicity,<ref>{{Cite book|url={{google books |plainurl=y |id=WJbtCAAAQBAJ|page= 177}}|title=The Spirit Level: Why Greater Equality Makes Societies Stronger|last1=Wilkinson|first1=Richard|last2=Pickett|first2=Kate|date=May 3, 2011|publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA|isbn=978-1-60819-341-7|page=177|language=en}} A study confined to [[non-Hispanic whites]] in US and [[England]] also showed the effect.</ref> national culture<ref>Countries of similar cultures and different levels of equality – [[Spain]] and [[Portugal]] – showed differences in the index, while countries with very different cultures and ways of achieving equality – [[Nordic countries]] and [[Japan]] – charted closer to each other. {{harvnb|Wilkinson|Pickett|2011|p=183}}</ref> and occupational classes or education levels.<ref>The effect was worse among the lower class/education level in high inequality countries, but continued through all occupational classes and was still significant among the highest. {{harvnb|Wilkinson|Pickett|2011|pp=178–79}}</ref> Their findings place the United States as the most unequal and ranks poorly on social and health problems among developed countries.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.equalitytrust.org.uk/resources/slides|title=The Spirit Level|last1=Wilkinson|first1=Richard|last2=Pickett|first2=Kate|work=equalitytrust.org.uk|access-date=September 12, 2012|archive-date=May 31, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150531014956/http://www.equalitytrust.org.uk/resources/slides}}</ref> The authors argue inequality creates psychosocial [[Stress (psychological)|stress]] and [[Social status|status]] anxiety that lead to social ills.<ref name="thinktanks">{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2010/aug/14/the-spirit-level-equality-thinktanks|title=The Spirit Level: how 'ideas wreckers' turned book into political punchbag|last=Booth|first=Robert|date=August 13, 2010|work=The Guardian|access-date=October 10, 2019|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

A 2009 study attributed one in three deaths in the United States to high levels of inequality.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://billmoyers.com/2014/04/19/high-inequality-results-in-more-us-deaths-than-tobacco-car-crashes-and-guns-combined/|title=High Inequality Results in More US Deaths Than Tobacco, Car Crashes and Guns Combined|last=Holland|first=Joshua|date=April 19, 2014|website=BillMoyers.com|language=en-US|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref> According to [[The Earth Institute]], [[life satisfaction]] in the US has been declining over several decades, which they attributed to increasing inequality, lack of social trust and loss of faith in government.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.earth.columbia.edu/sitefiles/file/Sachs%20Writing/2012/World%20Happiness%20Report.pdf|title=World Happiness Report|last1=Helliwell|first1=John|last2=Layard|first2=Richard|publisher=[[The Earth Institute]]|access-date=October 1, 2013|last3=Sachs|first3=Jeffrey|page=8}}</ref>

A 2015 study by [[Angus Deaton]] and [[Anne Case]] found that income inequality could be a driving factor in a marked increase in deaths among white males between the ages of 45 and 54 in the period 1999 to 2013.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thenation.com/article/now-white-people-are-dying-from-our-terrible-economic-policies-too/|title=Now White People Are Dying From Our Terrible Economic Policies, Too|last=Chen|first=Michelle|journal=The Nation|date=November 6, 2015|access-date=October 10, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0027-8378|archive-date=September 18, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190918103422/https://www.thenation.com/article/now-white-people-are-dying-from-our-terrible-economic-policies-too/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://jacobinmag.com/2015/11/case-deaton-study-death-rate-health-care|title=How Class Kills|last=Gaffney|first=A. W.|date=November 8, 2015|website=jacobinmag.com|language=en-US|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref> So-called "[[deaths of despair]]", including [[Suicide in the United States|suicide]] and drug/alcohol related deaths, which have been pushing down life expectancy since 2014, reached record levels in 2017. Some researchers assert that income inequality, a shrinking middle class, the weakening labor union influence, and stagnant wages have been significant factors in this development.<ref>{{cite news|last=Woodward|first=Aylin|date=November 30, 2019|title=Life expectancy in the US keeps going down, and a new study says America's worsening inequality could be to blame|url=https://www.businessinsider.my/us-life-expectancy-declined-for-third-year-in-a-row-2019-11/|work=[[Business Insider]]|access-date=January 3, 2020|archive-date=December 18, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191218004240/https://www.businessinsider.my/us-life-expectancy-declined-for-third-year-in-a-row-2019-11/}}</ref> In their 2020 book ''Deaths of Despair and the Future of Capitalism'', Case and Deaton put forth the argument that in the United States, [[globalization]] and technological advancement dramatically shifted political power away from labor and towards capital by empowering corporations and weakening [[labor union]]s much more so than in peer countries such as those of Western Europe. As such, other rich countries, while facing their own challenges associated with globalization and technological change, did not experience a "long-term stagnation of wages, nor an epidemic of deaths of despair."<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Case A, Deaton A |date=2020 |title=Deaths of Despair and the Future of Capitalism |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y3n_DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA9 |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]]|page=9 |isbn=978-0-691-19078-5}}</ref>

According to the Health Inequality Project, the wealthiest American men live 15 years longer than the poorest. For American women, the life expectancy gap is 10 years.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://newrepublic.com/article/153870/inequality-death-america-life-expectancy-gap|title=The Gross Inequality of Death in America|last=Karma|first=Roge|date=May 10, 2019|magazine=The New Republic|access-date=June 15, 2019}}</ref> People in the richest 25 percent of the population studied across the United States and Europe were 40 percent less likely to die during the study period than those in the poorest quarter, according to a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://theconversation.com/americans-die-earlier-at-all-wealth-levels-even-if-wealth-buys-more-years-of-life-in-the-us-than-in-europe-253620|title=Americans die earlier at all wealth levels, even if wealth buys more years of life in the US than in Europe|first1=Irene N.|last1=Papanicolas|first2=Sara|last2=Machado|date=April 9, 2025|website=The Conversation}}</ref>

====Political extremism and violence====
A 2020 paper published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' posits that there is a correlation between economic inequality, poor economic conditions, and increased rates of political violence and [[right-wing extremism]].<ref name="SA2020"/> A 2019 study of mass shootings published in ''[[BMC Public Health]]'' found that communities with rising levels of income inequality are at an increased risk of [[Mass shootings in the United States|mass shootings]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kwon |first1=Roy |last2=Cabrera |first2=Joseph F. |date=September 20, 2019 |title=Income inequality and mass shootings in the United States|url= |journal=[[BMC Public Health]]|volume=19 |issue= 1|page=1147 |doi=10.1186/s12889-019-7490-x|pmid=31537201 |pmc=6753615 |quote=There is strong evidence in this study to suggest the recent growth of income inequality is significantly associated with mass shootings in the United States. Specifically, this evidence indicates that a one standard deviation increase in the growth of income inequality augments the number of mass shootings by 0.43 to 0.57. |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==== Financing of social programs ====
Krugman argues that the long-term funding problems of [[Social Security (United States)|Social Security]] and [[Medicare (United States)|Medicare]] can be blamed in part on rising inequality, as well as on changes such as longer life expectancy. The source of funding for these programs is [[Payroll taxes#Social Security and Medicare taxes|payroll taxes]], which are traditionally levied as a percent of salary up to a cap. Payroll taxes do not capture income from capital or income above the cap. Higher inequality thereby reduces the taxable pool.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://krugman.blogs.nytimes.com/2012/12/28/policy-implications-of-capital-biased-technology-opening-remarks/|title=Policy Implications of Capital-Biased Technology: Opening Remarks|last=Krugman|first=Paul|date=December 28, 2012|website=Paul Krugman Blog|publisher=New York Times|language=en-US|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

Had inequality remained stable, increased payments would have covered about 43% of the projected [[Social Security (United States)|Social Security]] shortfall over the next 75 years.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://cepr.net/blogs/cepr-blog/the-impact-of-the-upward-redistribution-of-wage-income-on-social-security-solvency|title=The Impact of the Upward Redistribution of Wage Income on Social Security|last=Baker|first=Dean|date=February 12, 2013|website=cepr.net|publisher=Center for Economic and Policy Research|language=en|access-date=October 10, 2019|archive-date=October 10, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191010015310/http://cepr.net/blogs/cepr-blog/the-impact-of-the-upward-redistribution-of-wage-income-on-social-security-solvency}}</ref>

==== Justice ====
Classical liberal economists such as [[Friedrich Hayek]] maintained that because individuals are diverse and different, state intervention to redistribute income is inevitably arbitrary and incompatible with the rule of law, and that "what is called 'social' or distributive' justice is indeed meaningless within a spontaneous order". Those who would use the state to redistribute, "take freedom for granted and ignore the preconditions necessary for its survival".<ref>{{Cite book|title=Law, Legislation and Liberty, Volume 2|last=Hayek|first=F. A.|date=1977|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-32083-0|volume=2:chapter=The Mirage of Social Justice|location=Chicago|page=33|doi = 10.7208/chicago/9780226321257.001.0001}}</ref><ref name="Hayek, Friedrich A 1960">{{Cite book|title=The Constitution of Liberty.|last=Hayek, F.A.|isbn=978-1-315-83208-1|page=231|oclc=1058964407}}</ref>

== Public attitudes ==
Americans are not generally aware of the extent of inequality or recent trends.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.salon.com/2012/06/14/weve_been_brainwashed/|title=We've been brainwashed|last=Stiglitz|first=Joe|date=June 14, 2012|website=Salon|access-date=October 9, 2019}}</ref> In 1998 a Gallup poll found 52% of Americans agreeing that the gap between rich and the poor was a problem that needed to be fixed, while 45% regarded it as "an acceptable part of the economic system".

A December 2011 Gallup poll found a decline in the number of Americans who rated reducing the gap in income and wealth between the rich and the poor as extremely or very important (21 percent of Republicans, 43 percent of independents, and 72 percent of Democrats).<ref name="tnr">{{Cite magazine|url=https://newrepublic.com/article/98655/obama-2012-income-inequality-gallup|title=Why Obama's New Populism May Sink His Campaign|last=Galston|first=William|date=December 17, 2011|magazine=The New Republic|access-date=October 10, 2019|issn=0028-6583}}</ref> Only 45% see the gap as in need of fixing, while 52% do not. However, there was a large difference between Democrats and Republicans, with 71% of Democrats calling for a fix.<ref name="tnr" />

In 2012, surveys found the issue ranked below issues such as growth and equality of opportunity, and ranked relatively low in affecting voters "personally".<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://newrepublic.com/article/103075/obama-populism-tnr-symposium|title=Why the President's Campaign Shouldn't Focus on Inequality|last=Galston|first=William|date=May 3, 2012|magazine=The New Republic|access-date=October 10, 2019|issn=0028-6583}}</ref>

A January 2014 poll found 61% of Republicans, 68% of Democrats, and 67% of independents accept that income inequality in the US had grown over the last decade.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2014/01/23/pew-poll-obama-wealth-gap-sotu/4777385/|title=Poll: United we stand on wealth gap|last1=Page|first1=Susan|last2=Breitman|first2=Kendall|date=January 23, 2014|website=USA Today|language=en|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref> The poll indicated that 69% of Americans supported the government doing "a lot" or "some" to address income inequality and that 73% of Americans supported raising the minimum wage from $7.25 to $10.10 per hour.<ref name="people-press.org">{{cite web|url=http://www.people-press.org/2014/01/23/most-see-inequality-growing-but-partisans-differ-over-solutions/|title=Most See Inequality Growing, but Partisans Differ over Solutions|date=January 23, 2014|work=Pew Research Center for the People and the Press}}</ref>

Surveys found that Americans were comparable to citizens of other nations in what they considered acceptable equality, but were more accepting of the level they thought it should be.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Osberg|first1=Lars|author-link=Lars Osberg|last2=Smeeding|first2=Timothy|year=2006|title=Fair Inequality? Attitudes Toward Pay Differentials: The United States in Comparative Perspective|journal=[[American Sociological Review]]|volume=71|issue=3|pages=450–73|doi=10.1177/000312240607100305|s2cid=145216360}}</ref> [[Dan Ariely]] and [[Michael Norton (professor)|Michael Norton]] found in a 2011 study that US citizens significantly underestimated wealth inequality.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Norton|first1=M. I.|last2=Ariely|first2=D.|date=January 2011|title=Building a Better America – One Wealth Quintile at a Time|url=http://www.people.hbs.edu/mnorton/norton%20ariely%20in%20press.pdf|journal=[[Perspectives on Psychological Science]]|volume=6|issue=6|pages=9–12|doi=10.1177/1745691610393524|pmid=26162108|s2cid=2013655}}</ref>

== States and cities ==
[[File:Gini Index US Counties 2010.jpg|thumb|This Gini Index map shows regional and county-level variation in pre-tax income inequality Gini index. The 2010 Gini index value range from 20.7 for [[Loving County, Texas|Loving County]] ([[Texas]]) to 64.5 to [[East Carroll Parish, Louisiana|East Carroll Parish]] ([[Louisiana]]).<ref name="uscb2012">{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/prod/2012pubs/acsbr10-18.pdf|title=Household Income Inequality Within U.S. Counties: 2006–2010|last=Bee|first=Adam|date=February 2012|publisher=Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170722060603/https://www.census.gov/prod/2012pubs/acsbr10-18.pdf|archive-date=July 22, 2017|access-date=December 7, 2017}}</ref>]]
The US household income Gini of 46.8 in 2009<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/newsroom/releases/archives/income_wealth/cb10-144.html|title=Income, Poverty and Health Insurance Coverage in the United States: 2009|work=Newsroom|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160203130251/http://www.census.gov/newsroom/releases/archives/income_wealth/cb10-144.html|archive-date=February 3, 2016|access-date=December 7, 2017}}</ref> [[List of U.S. states by Gini coefficient|varied significantly between states]]: after-tax income inequality in 2009 was greatest in [[Texas]] and lowest in [[Maine]].<ref name="Daniel H. Cooper, Byron F. Lutz, and Michael G. Palumbo">{{cite web|url=http://www.bos.frb.org/economic/ppdp/2011/ppdp1107.pdf|title=Quantifying the Role of Federal and State Taxes in Mitigating Income Inequality|last1=Cooper|first1=Daniel H.|last2=Lutz|first2=Byron F.|date=September 22, 2011|publisher=Federal Reserve, Boston, United States|last3=Palumbo|first3=Michael G.|access-date=July 30, 2012|archive-date=August 3, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120803160558/http://www.bos.frb.org/economic/ppdp/2011/ppdp1107.pdf}}</ref> Income inequality grew from 2005 to 2012 in more than 2 out of 3 metropolitan areas.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/govbeat/wp/2014/08/11/income-inequality-seems-to-be-rising-in-more-than-2-in-3-metro-areas/|title=Income inequality seems to be rising in more than 2 in 3 metro areas|last1=Chokshi|first1=Niraj|date=August 11, 2014|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=September 13, 2014}}</ref>

The states of [[Utah]], [[Alaska]], and [[Wyoming]] have a market income Gini coefficient that is 10% lower than the average, while the [[Washington, D.C.|District of Columbia]], and [[Puerto Rico]] have a market income Gini coefficient that is 10% higher than the average.

After-tax, the Federal Reserve estimated that 34 US states have a Gini index between 30 and 35, with Maine having the lowest.<ref name="Daniel H. Cooper, Byron F. Lutz, and Michael G. Palumbo" />

At the county and municipality levels, the 2010 market income Gini index ranged from 21 to 65, according to Census Bureau estimates.<ref name="uscb2012" />
