== International comparisons ==
[[File:GINI index World Bank up to 2018.png|alt=|thumb|Income [[gini coefficient]] map according to the [[World Bank]] (2018).<ref>{{Cite web|title=GINI index (World Bank estimate) {{!}} Data|url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SI.POV.GINI?view=map|access-date=July 23, 2020|website=data.worldbank.org}}</ref> Higher Income Gini Index for a nation in this map implies more income inequality among its people.]]
The United States has the highest level of income inequality in the [[Western world]], according to a 2018 study by the [[United Nations Special Rapporteur]] on extreme poverty and human rights. The United States has forty million people living in poverty, and more than half of these people live in "extreme" or "absolute" poverty. Income inequality has increased in recent decades, and large tax cuts that disproportionately favor the very wealthy are predicted to increase U.S. income inequality further.<ref name="upi.com"/>

Actual income inequality and public views about the need to address the issue are directly related in most developed countries, but not in the US, where income inequality is larger, but the concern is lower.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2013/12/06/the-u-s-s-high-income-gap-is-met-with-relatively-low-public-concern/|title=The U.S.'s high income gap is met with relatively low public concern|date=December 6, 2013|work=Pew Research Center}}</ref> Excluding retirees, US market income inequality is comparatively high (rather than moderate), and the level of redistribution is moderate (not low). These comparisons indicate Americans shift from reliance on market income to reliance on income transfers later in life, although less fully than in other developed countries.<ref name="newyorker.com" /><ref name="LIS1">{{cite web|url=http://www.gc.cuny.edu/CUNY_GC/media/CUNY-Graduate-Center/PDF/Centers/LIS/LIS-Center-Research-Brief-1-2015.pdf?ext=.pdf|title=Income Inequality in the U.S. in Cross-National Perspective|date=April 2015|publisher=Luxembourg Income Study Center|access-date=May 5, 2015|archive-date=May 5, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150505061328/http://www.gc.cuny.edu/CUNY_GC/media/CUNY-Graduate-Center/PDF/Centers/LIS/LIS-Center-Research-Brief-1-2015.pdf?ext=.pdf}}</ref>

International comparisons vary. In 2019 the CIA ranked the US 39th-worst among 157 countries measured by Gini.<ref name="CIA Factbook-2007">{{cite web|url=https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/fields/2172.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070613005439/https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/fields/2172.html|archive-date=June 13, 2007|title=Field Listing – Distribution of family income – Gini index|date=June 14, 2007|work=CIA Factbook|access-date=June 20, 2007}}</ref> While inequality increased after 1981 in two-thirds of OECD countries,<ref name="OECD2008">{{cite web|url=http://www.oecd.org/dataoecd/45/42/41527936.pdf|title=Growing Unequal? Income distribution and poverty in OECD countries (summary)|year=2008|publisher=OECD}}</ref> most are in the more equal end of the spectrum. The European Union measured 30.8.<ref name="CIA Factbook-2007" />

The US Gini rating (after taxes and transfers<ref name="OECDstats">{{cite web|url=http://www.compareyourcountry.org/inequality?cr=oecd&cr1=oecd&lg=en&page=0|title=Compare your country|work=compareyourcountry.org}}</ref>) puts it among those of less developed countries. The US is more unequal than or on par with countries such as Mozambique, Peru, Cameroon, Guyana, and Thailand.<ref name="CIA Factbook-2007" />

Across Europe, the ratio of post-tax income of the top 10% to that of the bottom 50% changed only slightly between the mid-1990s and 2019.<ref name="The Economist-2019" />

Comparative data are available from databases such as the [[Luxembourg Income Study]] (LIS) or the OECD Income Distribution database (OECD IDD), or, when including developing countries, from the World Bank's Povcalnet database, or the World Income Inequality Database (WIID),<ref><!-- World Income Inequality Database (WIID)-->{{cite Q|Q122442727}}</ref> maintained by the United Nations University [[World Institute for Development Economics Research]] (UNU-WIDER), or the [[World Inequality Database]] (WID).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nolan|first1=Brian|last2=Valenzuela|first2=Luis|date=July 11, 2019|title=Inequality and its discontents|journal=Oxford Review of Economic Policy|language=en|volume=35|issue=3|pages=396–430|doi=10.1093/oxrep/grz016|issn=0266-903X}}</ref>

=== Reasons for relative performance ===
[[File:Income inequality - share of income earned by top 1%25 1975 to 2015.png|thumb|Share of income of the top 1% for selected developed countries, 1975 to 2015]]
One 2013 study indicated that US market income inequality was comparable to that of other developed countries but was the highest among 22 developed countries after taxes and transfers. This implies that public policy choices, rather than market factors, drive U.S. income inequality disparities relative to other developed nations.<ref name="NYTRattner1">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/11/17/opinion/inequality-unbelievably-gets-worse.html|title=Inequality, Unbelievably, Gets Worse|last=Rattner|first=Steven|date=November 2014|work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.newyorker.com/online/blogs/johncassidy/2013/11/inequality-and-growth-what-do-we-know.html|title=American Inequality in Six Charts|last=Cassidy|first=John|date=November 18, 2013|magazine=The New Yorker}}</ref>

Inequality may be higher than official statistics indicate in some countries because of unreported income. Europeans hold higher amounts of wealth offshore than Americans.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://money.cnn.com/2004/04/06/news/newsmakers/worldswealthiestupdate/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040409005339/http://money.cnn.com/2004/04/06/news/newsmakers/worldswealthiestupdate/|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 9, 2004|title=Who's really the world's richest?|date=April 6, 2004|website=money.cnn.com|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2011/11/02/opinion/europe-shadow-economies/index.html|title=Tax evasion is a national pastime afflicting southern Europe|last=Lister|first=Tim|date=November 2, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120229233243/http://articles.cnn.com/2011-11-02/opinion/opinion_europe-shadow-economies_1_tax-evasion-tax-collection-tax-rates?_s=PM:OPINION|archive-date=February 29, 2012|work=CNN}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://articles.businessinsider.com/2012-01-12/europe/30618761_1_tax-evasion-tax-man-tax-revenue|title=Low-Income Italians Own An Awful Lot Of Supercars, Private Jets And Yachts|date=January 12, 2012|work=Business Insider|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121212053411/http://articles.businessinsider.com/2012-01-12/europe/30618761_1_tax-evasion-tax-man-tax-revenue|archive-date=December 12, 2012}}</ref>

Leonhardt and Quealy, in 2014, described three key reasons why other industrialized countries improved their real median income relative to the US over the 2000-2010 period. In the US:<ref name="NYT2014a">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/04/23/upshot/the-american-middle-class-is-no-longer-the-worlds-richest.html|title=The American Middle Class Is No Longer the World's Richest|last1=Leonhardt|first1=David|date=April 22, 2014|work=The New York Times|access-date=October 10, 2019|last2=Quealy|first2=Kevin|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

* educational attainment has risen more slowly;
* companies pay relatively lower wages to the middle class and poor, with top executives making relatively more;
* the government redistributes less from the rich to the poor.

As of 2012, the U.S. had the weakest [[social safety net]] among developed nations.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kenworthy|first1=Lane|year=1999|title=Do Social-Welfare Policies Reduce Poverty? A Cross-National Assessment|url=http://www.u.arizona.edu/~lkenwor/sf99-poverty.htm|journal=Social Forces|volume=77|issue=3|pages=1119–39|doi=10.1093/sf/77.3.1119|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080706151209/http://www.u.arizona.edu/~lkenwor/sf99-poverty.htm|archive-date=July 6, 2008}}{{cite journal|last1=Bradley|first1=D.|last2=Huber|first2=E.|last3=Moller|first3=S.|last4=Nielsen|first4=F.|last5=Stephens|first5=J. D.|year=2003|title=Determinants of Relative Poverty in Advanced Capitalist Democracies|journal=American Sociological Review|volume=68|issue=1|pages=22–51|doi=10.2307/3088901|jstor=3088901|s2cid=144289954 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.epi.org/publication/ib339-us-poverty-higher-safety-net-weaker/|title=U.S. poverty rates higher, safety net weaker than in peer countries|last1=Gould|first1=Elise|last2=Wething|first2=Hilary|date=July 24, 2012|website=Economic Policy Institute|language=en-US|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

=== 2014 ===
In 2014, Canadian middle-class incomes moved higher than those in the US; in some European nations, citizens received higher raises than their American counterparts.<ref name="NYT2014a" /> As of that year, only the wealthy had seen pay increases since the Great Recession, while average American workers had not.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2014-08-19/only-rich-know-wage-gains-with-no-raises-for-u-s-workers.html|title=Only Rich Know Wage Gains With No Raises for U.S Workers|last1=Ito|first1=Ki|date=August 19, 2014|newspaper=Bloomberg L.P.|access-date=August 23, 2014|last2=Katz|first2=Ian|last3=Kolet|first3=Ilan}}</ref>

== Policy responses ==
Debate continues over whether a public policy response is appropriate to income inequality. For example, Federal Reserve Economist Thomas Garrett wrote in 2010: "It is important to understand that income inequality is a byproduct of a well-functioning capitalist economy. Individuals' earnings are directly related to their productivity ... A wary eye should be cast on policies that aim to shrink the income distribution by redistributing income from the more productive to the less productive simply for the sake of 'fairness.'"<ref name="not-so-bad">{{cite web|url=https://www.stlouisfed.org/publications/inside-the-vault/spring-2010/us-income-inequality-its-not-so-bad|title=U.S. Income Inequality: It's Not So Bad|last=Garrett|first=Thomas A.|date=Spring 2010|publisher=Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis|access-date=March 13, 2019|archive-date=March 17, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190317051151/https://www.stlouisfed.org/publications/inside-the-vault/spring-2010/us-income-inequality-its-not-so-bad}}</ref> Alternatively, bipartisan political majorities have supported redistributive policies such as the EITC.

Economists have proposed various approaches to reducing income inequality. For example, then Federal Reserve Chair [[Janet Yellen]] described four "building blocks" in a 2014 speech. These included expanding resources available to children, affordable higher education, business ownership, and inheritance.<ref name="YellenOct14" /> That year, the [[Center for American Progress]] recommended tax reform, further subsidizing healthcare and higher education and strengthening unions as appropriate responses.<ref name="CAPMCS" />

Improved [[infrastructure]] could address both the causes and the effects of inequality. E.g., workers with limited mobility could use improved mass transit to reach higher-paying jobs further from home and to access beneficial services at lower cost.<ref name="Grusky-2013">{{cite news|url=http://www.bostonreview.net/BR37.2/ndf_david_b_grusky_inequality.php|title=What to Do about Inequality|last=Grusky|first=David B.|date=March–April 2013|newspaper=Boston Review|access-date=April 6, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130420175636/http://www.bostonreview.net/BR37.2/ndf_david_b_grusky_inequality.php|archive-date=April 20, 2013}}</ref>

Public policy responses addressing effects of income inequality include: [[tax incidence]] adjustments and strengthening [[social safety net]] provisions such as [[Temporary Assistance for Needy Families|welfare]], [[Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program|food stamps]], [[Social Security (United States)|Social Security]], [[Medicare (United States)|Medicare]] and [[Medicaid]].

Proposals that address the causes of inequality include education reform and limiting/taxing [[rent-seeking]].<ref name="Grusky-2013" /> Other reforms include raising the minimum wage, tax reform,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/12/30/us/politics/for-solution-to-income-stagnation-republicans-and-democrats-revise-their-playkohtml|title=For Solution to Income Stagnation, Republicans and Democrats Revise Their Playbooks|date=December 30, 2014|work=The New York Times}}</ref> and increased stock ownership at lower income levels via a deferred investment program.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kausik |first=B. N. |date=2022-05-03 |title=Income Inequality, Cause and Cure |journal=Challenge |volume=65 |issue=3–4 |pages=93–105 |doi=10.1080/05775132.2022.2046883 |arxiv=2201.10726 |s2cid=246285783 |issn=0577-5132}}</ref>

Surveys of American Economic Association members since the 1970s have shown that professional economists generally agree with the statement that "Redistribution of income is a legitimate role for the U.S. Government", and since the 1990s, that "The distribution of income in the U.S. should be more equal."{{refn|name=EconomistsConsensus|<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kearl|first1=J. R.|last2=Pope|first2=Clayne L.|last3=Whiting|first3=Gordon C.|last4=Wimmer|first4=Larry T.|year=1979|title=A Confusion of Economists?|journal=American Economic Review|publisher=American Economic Association|volume=69|issue=2|pages=28–37|jstor=1801612}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Alston |first1=Richard M. |last2=Kearl |first2=J.R. |author-link2=James R. Kearl |last3=Vaughan |first3=Michael B. |title=Is There a Consensus Among Economists in the 1990's? |date=May 1992 |journal=[[The American Economic Review]] |volume=82 |issue=2 |pages=203–209 |jstor=2117401 |url=http://www.weber.edu/wsuimages/AcademicAffairs/ProvostItems/global.pdf |archive-date=April 8, 2017 |access-date=April 27, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170408191354/http://www.weber.edu/wsuimages/AcademicAffairs/ProvostItems/global.pdf }}</ref><ref name="Fuller & Geide-Stevenson 2003" /><ref name="Fuller & Geide-Stevenson 2011" /><ref name="Geide-Stevenson La Parra-Perez" />}}

=== Education ===
Children from higher-income families often attend higher-quality [[private school]]s or are [[Home-schooling|home-schooled]]. Better teachers raise students' educational attainment and future earnings, but they tend to prefer school districts that educate higher-income children.<ref name="YellenOct14" />

=== Parenting assistance ===

Economist Richard V. Reeves and other researchers point out the "[[parenting gap]]" between high-income and low-income families. High-income families tend to have the resources to pay for assistance such as child care and tutors, and, having had economically successful ancestors, have culturally inherited the skills needed to raise economically successful children. Based on studies of economic outcomes, Reeves recommends that many governments fund [[home visiting]] programs that assist parents in raising healthy children who succeed in school and later obtain better-paying jobs.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://think.kera.org/2017/07/19/redefining-rich-not-just-the-1/ |date=July 19, 2017 |title=Redefining "Rich": Not Just The 1% |publisher=[[KERA-FM]]}} (audio interview with Richard V. Reeves)</ref>

=== Healthcare ===
{{See also|Poverty and health in the United States}}
[[File:1b-ACA Distribution in 2014.png|right|thumb|The distributional impact of the Affordable Care Act (ACA or Obamacare) during 2014. The ACA raised taxes mainly on the top 1% to fund approximately $600 in benefits on average for the bottom 40% of families.]]
Increasing public funding for services such as healthcare can reduce after-tax inequality. The [[Affordable Care Act]] reduced income inequality for calendar year 2014:<ref name="CBO_Dist14" />

* "households in the lowest and second quintiles [the bottom 40%] received an average of an additional $690 and $560 respectively, because of the ACA ..."
* "Most of the burden of the ACA fell on households in the top 1% of the income distribution, and relatively little fell on the remainder of households in that quintile. Households in the top 1% paid an additional $21,000, primarily because of the net investment income tax and the additional Medicare tax."

=== Public welfare and infrastructure spending ===
OECD asserted that public spending is vital in reducing the [[wealth gap]].<ref name="OECD13">{{Cite web|url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/wealth-gap-widens-austerity-inequlity_n_3275538|title=Dire Warning About Rich-Poor Divide|date=May 14, 2013|website=HuffPost|language=en|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref> [[Lane Kenworthy]] advocates incremental reforms in the direction of the [[Nordic model|Nordic social democratic model]], claiming that this would increase economic security and opportunity.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/united-states/2013-12-06/americas-social-democratic-future|title=America's Social Democratic Future|last=Kenworthy|first=Lane|journal=Foreign Affairs: America and the World|date=January 6, 2014|access-date=October 10, 2019|publisher=Foreign Affairs|language=en-US|issn=0015-7120|author-link=Lane Kenworthy}} See also: {{Cite book|url={{google books |plainurl=y |id=eVTSAQAAQBAJ}}|title=Social Democratic America|last=Kenworthy|first=Lane|date=February 2014|publisher=OUP USA|isbn=978-0-19-932251-0|language=en}}</ref>

Eliminating social safety nets can discourage [[entrepreneurs]] by exacerbating the consequences of business failure, turning a temporary setback into financial ruin.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/business/archive/2012/02/the-entrepreneur-state-safety-nets-for-startups-capitalism-for-corporations/253211/|title=The Entrepreneur State: Safety Nets for Startups, Capitalism for Corporations|last=Thompson|first=Derek|date=February 17, 2012|newspaper=The Atlantic}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thesocietypages.org/socimages/2011/11/10/start-ups-and-safety-nets/|title=Start-ups and Safety Nets - Sociological Images|last=Livingston|first=Jay|date=November 10, 2011|work=The Society Pages|language=en|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

=== Taxes ===
[[File:1960- Tax rates of richest versus low income people - US.svg |thumb|Total effective tax rates (includes ''all'' taxes: federal+state income tax, sales tax, property tax, etc) for the richest Americans declined by 2018 to a level beneath that of the bottom 50% of earners,<ref name=CBSnews_20191017>{{cite news |last1=Picchi |first1=Aimee |title=America's richest 400 families now pay a lower tax rate than the middle class |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/americas-richest-400-families-pay-a-lower-tax-rate-than-the-middle-class/ |agency=CBS News |date=17 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240511050359/https://www.cbsnews.com/news/americas-richest-400-families-pay-a-lower-tax-rate-than-the-middle-class/ |archive-date=11 May 2024 |url-status=live }} (Chart labeled "Effective tax rates by income".) Analysis by economists Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman.</ref> contributing to net income inequality. Analysis by economists Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman.]]
[[File:US overall tax burden in 2024.webp|thumb|Overall [[tax burden]] in the US in 2024]]
[[File:Tax_proposals_of_2020_US_presidential_candidates.jpg|thumb|Proposed tax plan payment rates by income group as a percentage of income, including mandatory health insurance, of four [[2020 United States presidential election]] candidates]]

Income taxes provide one mechanism for addressing after-tax inequality. Increasing the effective progressivity of income taxes reduces the gap between higher and lower incomes. However, taxes paid may not reflect statutory rates because (legal) tax avoidance strategies can offset higher rates.

Piketty called for a 90% wealth tax to address the situation.<ref name="The Economist-2019" />

==== Tax expenditures ====
{{Taxation|Economics}}
Tax expenditures (i.e., exclusions, deductions, preferential tax rates, and tax credits) affect the after-tax income distribution. The benefits of tax expenditures, such as income exclusions for employer-sponsored health insurance premiums and deductions for mortgage interest, are distributed unevenly across the income spectrum.

As of 2019, the US Treasury listed 165 federal income tax expenditures. The largest as employer health insurance deductions, followed by net imputed rental income, capital gains (except agriculture, timber, iron ore, and coal), and defined contribution employer pension plans.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/tax-policy/tax-expenditures|title=Tax Expenditures {{!}} U.S. Department of the Treasury|website=home.treasury.gov|access-date=October 31, 2019}}</ref>

Understanding how each tax expenditure is distributed across the income spectrum can inform policy choices.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/economy/richest-20-percent-get-half-the-overall-savings-from-tax-breaks-cbo-says/2013/05/29/645f75c6-c894-11e2-9245-773c0123c027_story.html|title=Richest 20 percent get half the overall savings from U.S. tax breaks, CBO says|last=Montgomery|first=Lori|date=May 29, 2013|via=www.washingtonpost.com}}</ref>

A 2019 study by the economists Saez and Zucman found the effective total tax rate (including state and local taxes, and government fees) for the bottom 50% of U.S. households was 24.2% in 2018, whereas for the wealthiest 400 households it was 23%.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2019/10/08/first-time-history-us-billionaires-paid-lower-tax-rate-than-working-class-last-year/|title=For the first time in history, U.S. billionaires paid a lower tax rate than the working class last year|last=Ingraham|first=Christopher|date=October 8, 2019|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=October 9, 2019}}</ref>

=== Corporate taxes ===
Economist [[Dean Baker]] argued that corporate income tax policies have multiple effects. Increased corporate profits increase inequality by distributing dividends (mostly to higher-income people). Taxing profits reduces this effect, but it may also reduce investment, thereby reducing employment. It also encourages payers to (often successfully) lobby for increased tax expenditures, which offset the reduction in inequality and push corporations to adjust their behavior to exploit them. Professional lobbying and accounting firms that generally pay well get more business, at the expense of other workers.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cepr.net/index.php/blogs/beat-the-press/how-to-think-about-the-corporate-income-tax|title=How to Think About the Corporate Income Tax|last=Baker|first=Dean|date=August 26, 2014|publisher=Center for Economic and Policy Research|access-date=November 16, 2014|archive-date=November 29, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129054044/http://www.cepr.net/index.php/blogs/beat-the-press/how-to-think-about-the-corporate-income-tax}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cepr.net/index.php/blogs/beat-the-press/subverting-the-inversions-more-thoughts-on-ending-the-corporate-tax|title=Subverting the Inversions: More Thoughts on Ending the Corporate Income Tax|last=Baker|first=Dean|date=August 26, 2014|publisher=Center for Economic and Policy Research|access-date=November 16, 2014|archive-date=November 29, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129053922/http://www.cepr.net/index.php/blogs/beat-the-press/subverting-the-inversions-more-thoughts-on-ending-the-corporate-tax}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cepr.net/index.php/blogs/beat-the-press/more-cheap-thoughts-on-the-corporate-income-tax|title=More Cheap Thoughts on the Corporate Income Tax|last=Baker|first=Dean|date=August 29, 2014|publisher=Center for Economic and Policy Research|access-date=November 26, 2014|archive-date=November 29, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129054042/http://www.cepr.net/index.php/blogs/beat-the-press/more-cheap-thoughts-on-the-corporate-income-tax}}</ref>

===Minimum wages===
{{main|Minimum wage in the United States}} 
''The Economist'' states that as inequality rises, political will to help low-paid workers increases, and minimum wages may not be as bad as some believe.<ref>{{cite news|date=December 14, 2013|title=The logical floor - The logical floor - Moderate minimum wages do more good than harm. They should be set by technocrats not politicians |url=https://www.economist.com/news/leaders/21591593-moderate-minimum-wages-do-more-good-harm-they-should-be-set-technocrats-not|newspaper=The Economist | quote=Scepticism about the merits of minimum wages remains this newspaper's starting-point. But as income inequality widens and workers' share of national income shrinks, the case for action to help the low-paid grows. Addressing the problem through subsidies for the working poor is harder in an era of austerity, when there are many other pressing claims on national coffers. Other policy options, such as confiscatory taxes, are unattractive. Nor is a moderate minimum wage as undesirable as neoclassical purists suggest. }}</ref>

In a blog post on the [[Economic Policy Institute]]'s site, they say that raising the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour would decrease income inequality.<ref name="EPI_CBOStudy">{{cite journal|date=July 9, 2019|title=The Effects on Employment and Family Income of Increasing the Federal Minimum Wage|url=https://www.epi.org/blog/low-wage-workers-will-see-massive-gains-from-minimum-wage-hike-cbo-finds/#}}</ref>

=== Basic income ===
{{Main|Basic income in the United States}}
A public [[basic income]] provides each individual with a fixed sum from the government, regardless of age, employment, wealth, or education. People who support basic income as a way to reduce income inequality include the [[Green Party of the United States|Green Party]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gp.org/committees/platform/2010/economic-justice.php|title=The Green Party of the United States|work=gp.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110619111124/http://www.gp.org//committees/platform/2010/economic-justice.php|archive-date=June 19, 2011}}</ref>

=== Economic democracy ===
{{Main|Economic democracy}}
Economic democracy is a [[Socioeconomics|socioeconomic]] philosophy that proposes shifting decision-making power from corporations to a broader group of [[Stakeholder theory|public stakeholders]], including workers, customers, suppliers, neighbours, and the broader public.

Economists [[Richard D. Wolff]] and Gar Alperovitz claim that such policies would improve equality.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://billmoyers.com/segment/richard-wolff-on-capitalisms-destructive-power/|title=Richard Wolff on Curing Capitalism|website=BillMoyers.com|language=en-US|access-date=October 10, 2019}} See also: {{Cite book|url=https://www.democracyatwork.info/|title=Democracy at Work (d@w)|last=Wolff|first=Richard D.|author-link=Richard D. Wolff|year=2012|website=Democracy at Work (d@w)|publisher=Haymarket Books|isbn=978-1-60846-247-6|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://programs.wypr.org/podcast/11-20-13-mk-asantes-memoir-buck-and-gar-alperovitz-using-democracy-reduce-inequality|title=MK Asante's Memoir "Buck" and Gar Alperovitz on Using Democracy to Reduce Inequality|date=November 20, 2013|publisher=[[WYPR]]|access-date=January 29, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/whatthenmustwedo0000alpe|title=What Then Must We Do?: Straight Talk about the Next American Revolution|last=Alperovitz|first=Gar|year=2013|publisher=Chelsea Green Publishing|isbn=978-1-60358-504-0|url-access=registration}}</ref>

=== Monetary policy ===
{{Main|Monetary policy of the United States}}
Monetary policy is responsible for balancing [[inflation]] and [[unemployment]]. It can be used to stimulate the economy (e.g., by lowering interest rates, which encourages borrowing and spending, creates additional jobs, and puts upward pressure on inflation) or to tighten it, with the opposite effects. Former Fed Chair [[Ben Bernanke]] wrote in 2015 that monetary policy affects income and wealth inequality in multiple ways, but that responsibility lies primarily in other areas:<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.brookings.edu/blogs/ben-bernanke/posts/2015/06/01-monetary-policy-and-inequality|title=Monetary policy and inequality|last=Bernanke|first=Ben S.|date=June 1, 2015|work=The Brookings Institution}}</ref>

* Stimulus reduces inequality by creating or preserving jobs, which mainly helps the middle and lower classes who derive more of their income from labor than the wealthy.
* Stimulus inflates the prices of financial assets (owned mainly by the wealthy), but also employment, housing, and the value of small businesses (owned more widely).
* Stimulus increases inflation and/or lowers interest rates, which helps debtors (mainly the middle and lower classes) while hurting creditors (mainly the wealthy), because they are paid back with cheaper dollars or reduced interest.

== Measurement ==
[[File:U.S. Income and Net Worth Distribution.png|thumb|U.S. family pre-tax income and net worth distribution for 2013 and 2016, from the Federal Reserve [[Survey of Consumer Finances]]<ref name="fed2017sept">{{cite web|url=https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/scf17.pdf|title=Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2013 to 2016: Evidence from the Survey of Consumer Finances|date=September 2017|publisher=[[Federal Reserve Bulletin]]|volume=103|issue=3|pages=4, 13}} See: [[Survey of Consumer Finances]] and {{Cite web|url=https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scfindex.htm|title=Federal Reserve Board - Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF)|website=Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System|language=en|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>]]
Various methods measure income inequality. Different sources prefer [[Gini coefficient]]s or [[Income inequality metrics#Ratio of percentiles|ratio of percentiles]], etc. [[United States Census Bureau|Census Bureau]] studies on household<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/hhes/www/income/histinc/p60no231_tablea3.pdf|title=US Census Bureau. (2005). Historical Income Tables – Income Equality.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070626183417/http://www.census.gov/hhes/www/income/histinc/p60no231_tablea3.pdf <!-- Bot retrieved archive -->|archive-date=June 26, 2007|access-date=June 20, 2007}}</ref> and individual income<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/hhes/www/income/histinc/ie2.html|title=US Census Bureau. (2006). Measures of Individual Earnings Inequality for Full-Time, Year-Round Workers by Sex: 1967 to 2005.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070617054703/http://www.census.gov/hhes/www/income/histinc/ie2.html <!-- Bot retrieved archive -->|archive-date=June 17, 2007|access-date=June 21, 2007}}</ref> show lower levels<ref>a gini index increase of 15% as opposed to CBO's increase in gini index of 33% (cbo "Trends in Distribution" study p. 7)</ref> than some other sources,<ref>Saez and Piketty, and the CBO</ref> but do not break out the highest-income households (99%+) where most change has occurred.<ref name="debate" /><ref name="cbo.px" />{{rp|6–7}}<ref>A 2010 census study showed the top 20 percent of Americans earned 49.4% of the nation's income, compared with the 3.4% earned by the ~15% of Americans living below the poverty line. This earnings ratio of 14.5 to 1 was an increase from the 13.6 to 1 ratio just two years earlier, and a significant rise from the historic low of 7.69 to 1 in 1968</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.salon.com/news/feature/2010/09/28/us_census_recession_s_impact_1|title=Associated Press. (September 28, 2010).|date=September 28, 2010 |access-date=March 20, 2011}}</ref>

One review describes six possible techniques for estimating American real median income growth. Estimates for the 1979-2014 period ranged from a decline of 8% (Piketty and Saez 2003) to an increase of 51% (CBO).<ref name="The Economist-2019" />

Two commonly cited estimates are the CBO and [[Emmanuel Saez]]. These differ in their sources and methods. Using 2011 IRS data, Saez claimed that the share of "market income less transfers" received by the top 1% was about 19.5%.<ref name="Striking it Richer">{{cite web|url=http://elsa.berkeley.edu/~saez/saez-UStopincomes-2012.pdf|title=Striking it Richer: The Evolution of Top Incomes in the United States|last=Saez|first=Emmanuel|date=September 3, 2013|publisher=[[University of California Berkeley]]|access-date=September 18, 2014}}</ref> The CBO uses both IRS data and Census data in its computations and reported a lower "pre-tax" figure for the top 1% of 14.6%.<ref name="CBOInc&Tax2014" />

=== Census Bureau data ===
[[File:U.S. Real Before Tax Median Family Income 2001-2016.png|right|thumb|U.S. median family income from 2001 to 2016 (real, measured in 2016 dollars), with comparative statistics, from the Fed Survey of Consumer Finances. The top decile and bottom quintile had real increases in income comparing 2001 and 2016, while the 20th to 80th percentiles had decreases. For all families, the median was $54,100 in 2001 and $52,700 in 2016, a slight decline. Note this differs from real median household income, which hit a record level in 2016.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scfindex.htm|title=Federal Reserve Board - Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF)|website=Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System}}</ref>]]
The Census Bureau ranks all households by household income based on its surveys and then divides them into quintiles. The highest-ranked household in each quintile provides the upper income limit for that quintile.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.law.upenn.edu/live/files/2934-autengeeturner-perspectives-on-mobility-inequality |title=New Perspectives On Income Mobility and Inequality |first1=Gerald |last1=Auten |first2=Geoffrey |last2=Gee |first3=Nicholas |last3=Turner |publisher=National Tax Journal |date=December 2013 |access-date=October 11, 2014 |archive-date=January 21, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160121012135/https://www.law.upenn.edu/live/files/2934-autengeeturner-perspectives-on-mobility-inequality }}</ref> Census data reflects market income without adjustments, and is not amenable to adjustment for taxes and transfers. Because census data do not capture changes within individual households, they are not suitable for studying income mobility.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.stlouisfed.org/publications/inside-the-vault/spring-2010/us-income-inequality-its-not-so-bad|title=U.S. Income Inequality: It's Not So Bad|last=Garrett|first=Thomas A.|date=April 1, 2010|website=www.stlouisfed.org|access-date=October 10, 2019|archive-date=September 17, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190917050102/https://www.stlouisfed.org/publications/inside-the-vault/spring-2010/us-income-inequality-its-not-so-bad}}</ref>{{blockquote|A major gap in the measurement of income inequality is the exclusion of [[capital gains]], profits made on increases in the value of investments. Capital gains are excluded for purely practical reasons. The Census doesn't ask about them, so they can't be included in inequality statistics.

Obviously, the rich earn much more from investments than the poor. As a result, real levels of income inequality in America are much higher than the official Census Bureau figures would suggest.|[[Salvatore Babones]]<ref name=Babones />}}

[[Gary Burtless]] noted that for this reason census data overstated the income losses that middle-income families suffered in the Great Recession.<ref name="brookings.edu">{{Cite web|url=https://www.brookings.edu/opinions/income-growth-and-income-inequality-the-facts-may-surprise-you/|title=Income Growth and Income Inequality: The Facts May Surprise You|last=Burtless|first=Gary|date=January 6, 2014|website=Brookings|language=en-US|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

=== Internal Revenue Service data ===
Saez and Piketty pioneered the use of IRS data to analyze income distribution in 1998.

=== GDP distribution ===
[[File:Private sector workers earnings compared to GDP.webp|thumb|300px|Private sector workers earnings compared to GDP <br /> 
Private sector workers made ~$2 trillion or about 29.6% of all money earned in Q3 2023 (before taxes)
{{legend|#8CD181|Quarterly [[GDP]] not Annualized|outline=#1DB100}}
{{legend|#73C9FF|Private Sector Workers Total Earnings|outline=#00A2FF}}
]]
Another approach attempts to allocate GDP to individuals, to compensate for the 40% of GDP that does not appear on tax returns. One source of the disagreement is the growth of tax-free retirement accounts, such as [[pension funds]], [[Individual Retirement Account|IRAs]], and [[401K]]s. Another source is tax evasion, whose distribution is also disputed.<ref name="The Economist-2019" />

=== Income measures: pre-and post-tax ===
Inequality can be measured before and after the effects of taxes and transfer payments, such as social security and unemployment insurance.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/prod/2004pubs/p20-550.pdf|title=Educational Attainment in the United States: 2003. ''US Census Bureau''.|last=Stoops|first=N.|date=June 2004|access-date=June 21, 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032006/hhinc/new01_001.htm|title=Selected Characteristics of Households, by Total Money Income in 2005.|year=2006|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070626072233/http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032006/hhinc/new01_001.htm|archive-date=June 26, 2007|access-date=June 21, 2007}}</ref>

Measuring inequality after accounting for taxes and transfers reduces observed inequality, because both the income tax system and transfer systems are designed to do so. The impacts of those policies vary as the policy regime changes. CBO reported in 2011 that: "The equalizing effect of transfers declined over the 1979–2007 period primarily because the distribution of transfers became less progressive. The equalizing effect of federal taxes also declined over the period, in part because the amount of federal taxes shrank as a share of market income and in part because of changes in the progressivity of the federal tax system."<ref name="cbo.gov"/>

CBO income statistics show the growing importance of these items. In 1980, in-kind benefits and employer and government spending on health insurance accounted for just 6% of the after-tax incomes of households in the middle one-fifth of the distribution. By 2010, these in-kind income sources represented 17% of middle-class households' after-tax income. Post-tax income items are increasing faster than pre-tax items. As a result of these programs, the spendable incomes of poor and middle-class families have been better insulated against recession-driven losses than the incomes of Americans in the top 1%. Incomes in the middle and at the bottom of the distribution have fared better since 2000 than incomes at the very top.<ref name="brookings.edu" />

Continuing increases in transfers, e.g., resulting from the Affordable Care Act, reduced inequality, while tax changes in the [[Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017]] had the opposite effect.

CBO incorporates capital gains.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbo.gov/system/files/115th-congress-2017-2018/workingpaper/53345-workingpaper.pdf|title=CBO's New Framework for Analyzing the Effects of Means-Tested Transfers and Federal Taxes on the Distribution of Household Income|last=Perese|first=Kevin|publisher=Congressional Budget Office}}</ref>

=== Demographic issues ===
Comparisons of household income over time should control for changes in average age, family size, number of breadwinners, and other characteristics. Measuring [[Personal Income in the United States|personal income]] ignores dependent children, but household income also has problems – a household of ten has a lower [[Standard of living in the United States|standard of living]] than one of two people, though their incomes may be the same.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Datta|first1=Gautam|last2=Meerman|first2=Jacob|date=December 1980|journal=Review of Income and Wealth|language=en|volume=26|issue=4|pages=401–418|doi=10.1111/j.1475-4991.1980.tb00175.x|issn=0034-6586|title=Household Income or Household Income per Capita in Welfare Comparisons}}</ref> People's earnings tend to rise over their working lifetimes, so point-in-time estimates can be misleading. (A world in which each person received a lifetime of income on their 21st birthday and no income thereafter would have an extremely high Gini, even if everyone received the same amount. Real-world incomes also tend to be spiky, although not to that extreme.)<ref name="wsjmyths">{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10000872396390444100404577643691927468370|title=Consumption and the Myths of Inequality|last1=Hassett|first1=Kevin A.|date=October 24, 2012|work=Wall Street Journal|access-date=October 10, 2019|last2=Mathur|first2=Aparna|language=en-US|issn=0099-9660}}</ref> Some 11% of households eventually appear in the 1% at some point.<ref name="The Economist-2019" /> The inequality between a recent college graduate and a 55-year-old at the peak of their career is not an issue if the graduate has the same career path.

Conservative researchers and organizations have focused on the limitations of household income as a measure of the standard of living to refute claims that income inequality is growing, excessive, or a problem.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cato.org/pubs/pas/pa586.pdf|title=Has U.S. Income Inequality Really Increased?. ''Cato Institute''.|last=Reynolds|first=A.|date=January 8, 2007|access-date=June 20, 2007}}</ref>

According to a 2004 analysis of income quintile data by [[The Heritage Foundation]], inequality is less after adjusting for household size. The aggregate share of income held by the upper quintile (the top-earning 20 percent) decreases by 20.3% when figures are adjusted for household size.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.heritage.org/Research/Taxes/bg1791.cfm|title=Two Americas, One Rich, One Poor? Understanding Income Inequality In the United States|last1=Rector|first1=R.|last2=Herderman|first2=R. Jr.|date=August 24, 2004|publisher=Heritage Foundation|url-status=unfit|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070613152949/http://www.heritage.org/Research/Taxes/bg1791.cfm|archive-date=June 13, 2007|access-date=June 20, 2007}}</ref>

However, the Pew Research Center found that household income declined less than individual income in the twenty-first century because those who could no longer afford separate housing moved in with relatives, creating larger households with more earners.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pewsocialtrends.org/2011/10/03/fighting-poverty-in-a-bad-economy-americans-move-in-with-relatives/|title=Fighting Poverty in a Bad Economy, Americans Move in with Relatives|last1=Rakesh|first1=Kochhar|last2=Cohn|first2=D'Vera|date=October 3, 2011|website=Pew Research Center's Social & Demographic Trends Project|language=en-US|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref> A 2011 CBO study adjusted for household size so that its quintiles contain an equal number of people, not an equal number of households.<ref name="cbo.px" />{{rp|2}} CBO found income distribution over a multi-year period "modestly" more equal than annual income,<ref name="cbo.px" />{{rp|4}} confirming earlier studies.<ref name="Aron-Dine & Sherman">{{cite web|url=http://www.cbpp.org/cms/?fa=view&id=957|title=New CBO Data Show Income Inequality Continues to Widen: After-tax-income for Top 1 Percent Rose by $146,000 in 2004.|last1=Aron-Dine|first1=A.|last2=Sherman|first2=A.|date=January 23, 2007|access-date=November 24, 2007}}</ref>

According to Noah, adjusting for demographic factors such as increasing age and smaller households indicates that income inequality is less extreme but growing faster than it would be without the adjustment.<ref name="denial" />

=== Gini index ===
{{further|Gini coefficient|List of U.S. states by income equality}}The Gini coefficient was developed by Italian [[Statistics|statistician]] and [[Sociology|sociologist]] [[Corrado Gini]] and published in his 1912 paper ''Variability and Mutability'' ({{langx|it|Variabilità e mutabilità}}).<ref>Gini, C. (1909). "Concentration and dependency ratios" (in Italian). English translation in ''Rivista di Politica Economica'', '''87''' (1997), 769–789.</ref>

Gini ratings can be used to compare inequality (by race, gender, and employment) within and between jurisdictions, using a variety of income measures and data sources, with differing results.<ref name="OECD1">{{cite web|url=http://stats.oecd.org/Index.aspx?QueryId=26068|title=Income distribution – Inequality: Income distribution – Inequality – Country tables|year=2012|publisher=OECD|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120205101233/http://stats.oecd.org/Index.aspx?QueryId=26068|archive-date=February 5, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Kakwani|first=N. C.|date=April 1977|title=Applications of Lorenz Curves in Economic Analysis|journal=Econometrica|volume=45|issue=3|pages=719–28|doi=10.2307/1911684|jstor=1911684}}</ref><ref name="imf2000">{{cite web|url=http://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/wp/2000/wp0062.pdf|title=Income Distribution and Tax and Government Social Spending Policies in Developing Countries|last1=Chu|first1=K.|last2=Gupta|first2=Davoodi|date=March 2000|publisher=International Monetary Fund}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Chen|last2=Caminada|first2=Koen|last3=Goudswaard|first3=Kees|date=July–September 2012|title=The redistributive effect of social transfer programmes and taxes: A decomposition across countries|journal=International Social Security Review|volume=65|issue=3|pages=27–48|doi=10.1111/j.1468-246X.2012.01435.x|s2cid=154029963|hdl=1887/3207160|hdl-access=free}}</ref> For example, the Census Bureau's official market Gini for the US was 47.6 in 2013, up from 45.4 in 1993.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/income-poverty-and-health-insurance-coverage-in-the-united-states-2013-275285621.html|title=Income, Poverty and Health Insurance Coverage in the United States: 2013|author=U.S. Census Bureau|date=September 16, 2014|work=prnewswire.com}}</ref> By contrast, OECD's US adjusted compensation Gini was 37 in 2012.<ref name="Babones">{{Cite web|url=https://inequality.org/research/unequal-americas-income-distribution/|title=U.S. Income Distribution: Just How Unequal?|last=Babones|first=Salvatore|date=February 14, 2012|website=Inequality.org|publisher=[[Institute for Policy Studies]]|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

===Consumer spending===

In 2024, the top 10% of earners (over $250,000) accounted for about half (49.7%) of US consumer spending.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.wsj.com/economy/consumers/us-economy-strength-rich-spending-2c34a571 |title=The U.S. Economy Depends More Than Ever on Rich People |publisher=The Wall Street Journal |author=Rachel Louise Ensign |date=February 23, 2025 }}</ref>

== Other indicators of inequality ==
Income, however measured, is only one indicator of equality. Others include equality of opportunity, consumption, and wealth.

=== Opportunity ===
Economist [[Thomas Sowell]], and former Congressman and [[Speaker of the United States House of Representatives|Speaker of the House]] [[Paul Ryan]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ricochet.com/200078/archives/paul-ryan-on-income-inequality-and-upward-mobility/|title=Paul Ryan on Income Inequality and Upward Mobility|date=November 28, 2011|website=Ricochet|language=en-US|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref> argued that more important than [[Equality of outcome|equality of results]] is [[equality of opportunity]]. This measures the degree to which individuals have the chance to succeed, despite their original circumstances.

Economic connectedness, or the extent to which individuals form social relationships across socioeconomic lines, has been identified as a significant factor in economic mobility. Research from the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] highlights how communities with greater cross-class interaction tend to exhibit higher levels of upward mobility, as these social connections provide access to job opportunities, educational resources, and economic knowledge. Studies analyzing large-scale data have demonstrated that low-income individuals with more high-income connections are more likely to experience economic advancement. This research suggests that, beyond traditional measures such as income distribution and wealth concentration, disparities in social capital contribute to broader patterns of inequality in the United States.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.amacad.org/economic-connectedness/what-why|title=Econcomic Connectedness|date=2024|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|language=en-US|access-date=February 11, 2025}}</ref>

=== Consumption ===
Other researchers argued that income is less important than consumption. Two individuals (or other units) who consume the same amount have similar outcomes despite differences in their incomes. Consumption inequality is also less extreme. Will Wilkinson wrote, "the run-up in consumption inequality has been considerably less dramatic than the rise in income inequality".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cato.org/pubs/pas/pa640.pdf|title=Thinking Clearly About Economic Inequality|last=Wilkinson|first=Will|year=2009|publisher=Cato Institute}}</ref> According to Johnson, Smeeding, and Tory, consumption inequality was lower in 2001 than in 1986.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Johnson|last2=Smeeding|last3=Tory|date=April 2005|title=Economic Inequality|journal=Monthly Labor Review}}</ref><ref name="wsjmyths" /><ref name="hidden">{{cite news|url=http://opinionator.blogs.nytimes.com/2013/01/30/the-hidden-prosperity-of-the-poor/?src=me&ref=general|title=The Hidden Prosperity of the Poor|last=Edsall|first=Thomas B.|date=January 30, 2013|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=January 2, 2013}}</ref> Other studies have not found consumption inequality less dramatic than household income inequality.<ref name="denial" /><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Attanasio|first1=Orazio|last2=Hurst|first2=Erik|last3=Pistaferri|first3=Luigi|year=2012|title=The Evolution of Income, Consumption, and Leisure Inequality in The US, 1980–2010|journal=NBER Working Paper No. 17982|doi=10.3386/w17982|ssrn=2035781|doi-access=free}}</ref> A CBO study found consumption data not capturing consumption by high-income households as well as it does their incomes,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-09-22 |title=How Inflation Has Affected Households at Different Income Levels Since 2019 {{!}} Congressional Budget Office |url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/58503 |access-date=2022-09-23 |website=www.cbo.gov |language=en}}</ref>{{Clarify|date=October 2019}} though it found that household consumption numbers are less unequal than household income.<ref name="cbo.px" />{{rp|5}}

Others dispute the importance of consumption, pointing out that if middle- and lower-income households are consuming more than they earn, it is because they are saving less or going further into debt.<ref name="ignore" /> Alternatively, higher-income persons may be consuming less than their income, saving/investing the balance.

=== Wealth ===
{{Main|Wealth inequality in the United States}}
{{multiple image
| total_width       = 450
| title             = Net personal wealth in the U.S. since 1962
| image1            = 1962- Net personal wealth - average in percentile ranges - linear scale - US.svg
| caption1          = The average personal wealth of people in the top 1% is more than a thousand times that of people in the bottom 50%.<ref name=WID_through_2021/>
| image2            = 1962- Net personal wealth - average in percentile ranges - logarithmic scale - US.svg
| caption2          = The logarithmic scale shows how wealth has increased for all percentile groups, though moreso for wealthier people.<ref name=WID_through_2021>{{cite web |title=Evolution of wealth indicators, USA, 1913-2019 |url=https://wid.world/country/usa/ |website=WID.world |publisher=World Inequality Database |access-date=September 6, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230705011218/https://wid.world/country/usa/ |archive-date=July 5, 2023 |date=2022 |url-status=live }}</ref>
}}

[[Distribution of wealth|Wealth inequality]] refers to the distribution of net worth (i.e., what is owned minus what is owed) as opposed to annual income. Wealth is affected by movements in the prices of assets, such as stocks, bonds, and real estate, which fluctuate in the short term. Income inequality has significant effects on long-term shifts in wealth inequality. Wealth inequality is increasing:

* The top .1% owned approximately 22% of the wealth in 2012, versus 7% in 1978. The top 1% share of wealth was at or below 10% from 1950 to 1987.<ref name="eml.berkeley.edu" /><ref name="Joseph E. Stiglitz" /> A conflicting estimate found that they held some 15%.<ref name="The Economist-2019" />
* The top 400 Americans had a net worth of $2 trillion in 2013, more than the bottom 50%. Their average net worth was $5 billion.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2013/09/16/400-richest-americans-now-worth-2-trillion.html|title=400 richest Americans now worth $2 trillion|last=Frank|first=Robert|website=[[CNBC]] |date=September 16, 2013}}</ref>
* The lower 50% of households held 3% of the wealth in 1989 and 1% in 2013. Their average net worth in 2013 was approximately $11,000.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/yellen20141017a.htm|title=FRB: Speech with Slideshow – Yellen, Perspectives on Inequality and Opportunity from the Survey of Consumer Finances|date=October 17, 2014|work=federalreserve.gov}}</ref>
* The threshold for the wealthiest 1% was approximately $8.4 million, measured for the 2008–2010 period. Nearly half the top 1% by income were also in the top 1% by wealth.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://economix.blogs.nytimes.com/2012/01/17/measuring-the-top-1-by-wealth-not-income/NYT-Measuring|title=the top 1% by wealth, not income-January 2013|date=January 1, 2012}}{{Dead link|date=November 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> In 2010, the wealthiest 5% of households owned approximately 72% of financial wealth, while the bottom 80% of households had 5%.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www2.ucsc.edu/whorulesamerica/power/wealth.html|title=Who Rules America: Wealth, Income, and Power|work=ucsc.edu}}</ref>
*The top 1% controlled 38.6% of the country's wealth in 2016.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://money.cnn.com/2017/09/27/news/economy/inequality-record-top-1-percent-wealth/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170927232001/http://money.cnn.com/2017/09/27/news/economy/inequality-record-top-1-percent-wealth/index.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 27, 2017|title=Record inequality: The top 1% controls 38.6% of America's wealth|last=Egan|first=Matt|date=September 27, 2017|work=CNN Money|access-date=December 9, 2019}}</ref>

Much of the wealth gain came to those in the top 1%. Those between the top 1 percent and top 5 percent controlled a smaller percentage of wealth than before.<ref name="gabriel-zucman.eu" /><ref>{{cite news|date=November 6, 2014|title=Forget the 1%|url=https://www.economist.com/news/finance-and-economics/21631129-it-001-who-are-really-getting-ahead-america-forget-1|newspaper=The Economist}}</ref>{{Clarify|date=October 2019}}

=== Education and family structure ===
{{multiple image | total_width=450
| image1=20230810 Ivy-Plus admission rates vs parent income percentile.svg |caption1=[[Ivy League|Ivy-Plus]] university admissions rates vary with the income of the students' parents, with the acceptance rate of the top 0.1% income percentile being almost twice as much as other students.<ref name="OpportunityInsights_202307">{{Cite web |last1=Chetty |first1=Raj |last2=Deming |first2=David J. |last3=Friedman |first3=John N. |date=July 2023 |title=Diversifying Society's Leaders? The Determinants and Consequences of Admission to Highly Selective Colleges |url=https://opportunityinsights.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/CollegeAdmissions_Nontech.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230731024342/https://opportunityinsights.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/CollegeAdmissions_Nontech.pdf |archive-date=July 31, 2023 |publisher=Opportunity Insights |page=2}} Figure 3. "Ivy-Plus" refers to [[Ivy League]] schools plus others with similar prestige, rankings, or selectivity.</ref>
| image2=Going up or down advertisement.jpg |caption2=A 1916 ad for a vocational school appealed to Americans' belief in the possibility of self-betterment, as well as threatening economic insecurity through lack of education.
}}
Another form of inequality is the [[Educational inequality|different level and quality of education]] available to students. School quality and educational outcomes vary dramatically depending on whether a student attends a [[Private school|private]] school, a [[charter school]], or an effective [[State school|public school]]. Many students have no choice but to attend dysfunctional public schools, where fewer achieve [[Educational stage|grade level performance]].<ref name="Lee and Orfield">{{Cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Chungmei |last2=Gary |first2=Gary |author-link2=Gary Orfield |year=2005 |title=Why Segregation Matters: Poverty and Educational Inequality |url=https://civilrightsproject.ucla.edu/research/k-12-education/integration-and-diversity/why-segregation-matters-poverty-and-educational-inequality |journal=The Civil Rights Project |series=Harvard University |pages=1–47}}</ref>

Pundit [[David Brooks (journalist)|David Brooks]]<ref>"David Brooks." Contemporary Authors Online. Detroit: Gale, 2012. Biography In Context. Web. November 7, 2013.</ref> argued that in the 1970s, high school and college graduates had "very similar family structures", while later high school grads were much less likely to get married, and much more likely to smoke, be obese, get divorced, and/or become a [[single parent]].<ref name="Brooks">{{Cite news |last=Brooks |first=David |author-link=David Brooks (journalist) |date=October 31, 2011 |title=The Wrong Inequality |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/11/01/opinion/brooks-the-wrong-inequality.html |access-date=October 10, 2019 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>
"The zooming wealth of the top one percent is a problem, but it's not nearly as big a problem as the tens of millions of Americans who have dropped out of high school or college. It's not nearly as big a problem as the 40 percent of children who are born out of wedlock. It's not nearly as big a problem as the nation's stagnant human capital, its stagnant social mobility and the disorganized social fabric for the bottom 50 percent."<ref name="Brooks" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Kristof |first=Nicholas |date=2012-02-08 |title=White Underclass |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/02/09/opinion/kristof-the-decline-of-white-workers.html |access-date=2019-10-10 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

=== Hollowing out of the Middle Class ===
Hollowing out of the middle class refers to its loss in income share beginning with [[Reaganomics]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=UCTV, University of California Television |url=https://www.uctv.tv/index.aspx?aspxerrorpath=/shows/The-Coming-Collapse-of-the-Middle-Class-Higher-Risks-Lower-Rewards-and-a-Shrinking-Safety-Net-with-Elizabeth-Warren-12620%20.%20https:/www.google.com/books/edition/The_Vanishing_Middle_Class_new_epilogue/A29RDwAAQBAJ |access-date=2022-09-22 |website=www.uctv.tv |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Temin |first=Peter |date=2018-01-18 |title=The Vanishing Middle Class |volume=1 |doi=10.7551/mitpress/9780262036160.001.0001|isbn=978-0-262-03616-0 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pattnayak |first=Satya |date=July 2012 |title=Book Review: Joseph E. Stiglitz, The Price of Inequality: How Today's Divided Society Endangers Our Future |journal=International Studies |volume=49 |issue=3–4 |pages=452–453 |doi=10.1177/0020881714534542 |s2cid=156981646 |issn=0020-8817}}</ref> The middle class is defined as the middle 20% of the income distribution, i.e., those between the 40th and 60th percentile. In 1980, the middle class earned 17% of total income in the United States.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Figure 1.2. The share of total income received by the top one percent is the highest in the OECD |doi=10.1787/888933302367 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Historical Income Tables: Households |url=https://www.census.gov/data/tables/time-series/demo/income-poverty/historical-income-households.html |access-date=2022-09-22 |website=Census.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Madden |first=Janice F. |title=Changes in Income Inequality within U.S. Metropolitan Areas |date=2000-05-01 |publisher=W.E. Upjohn Institute |doi=10.17848/9780585301785 |isbn=978-0-585-30178-5}}</ref> However, by 2019 its share decreased to 14%, a drop of 3%. Another way to see this is that in 1980, the share of the middle class was the same as that of the top 5%, but by 2019, the top 5% was 9 percentage points ahead of the middle class.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Komlos |first=John |date=2019-01-11 |title=Foundations of Real-World Economics |doi=10.4324/9781315099972|isbn=978-1-315-09997-2 |s2cid=186859234 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Schlesinger |first=Jill |title=Muddled in the middle class |url=https://independenttribune.com/ap/business/muddled-in-the-middle-class/article_1e378cb9-f809-5fcc-8128-4c2ce847e158.html |access-date=2022-09-22 |website=The Independent Tribune |language=en |archive-date=September 22, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220922175836/https://independenttribune.com/ap/business/muddled-in-the-middle-class/article_1e378cb9-f809-5fcc-8128-4c2ce847e158.html }}</ref>

== Opinions of notable individuals ==
Although some spoke out in favor of moderate inequality as a form of [[Economic incentive|incentive]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/does-u-s-economic-inequality-have-a-good-side|title=Does U.S. Economic Inequality Have a Good Side?|date=October 26, 2011|work=PBS NewsHour}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://blogs.lse.ac.uk/politicsandpolicy/archives/39215|title=Lower levels of inequality are linked with greater innovation in economies|last1=Hopkin|first1=Jonathan|author-link=Jonathan Hopkin|last2=Lapuente|first2=Victor|date=January 25, 2014|publisher=[[London School of Economics]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140211171400/http://blogs.lse.ac.uk/politicsandpolicy/archives/39215|archive-date=February 11, 2014|last3=Moller|first3=Lovisa}}</ref> others warned against excessive levels of inequality, including [[Robert J. Shiller]], (who called rising economic inequality "the most important problem that we are facing now today"),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.huffpost.com/|title=Income Inequality Is 'Most Important Problem|last=Shiller|first=Robert|date=October 15, 2013|website=www.huffpost.com|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref> former [[Federal Reserve]] [[Chair of the Federal Reserve|Board chairman]] [[Alan Greenspan]], ("This is not the type of thing which a democratic society – a [[Capitalism|capitalist]] [[Democracy|democratic]] society – can really accept without addressing"),<ref name="Noah2"/> and [[President of the United States|President]] [[Barack Obama]] (who referred to the widening income gap as the "defining challenge of our time").<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/obama-set-to-speak-on-income-gap-between-rich-and-poor|title=Obama says income inequality is defining challenge for U.S.|date=December 4, 2013|website=PBS NewsHour|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

[[United Nations special rapporteur]] [[Philip Alston]], following a fact-finding mission to the United States in December 2017, said in his report that "the United States already leads the developed world in income and wealth inequality, and it is now moving full steam ahead to make itself even more unequal."<ref>{{cite report|url=https://undocs.org/A/HRC/38/33/ADD.1|title=Report of the Special Rapporteur on extreme poverty and human rights on his mission to the United States of America|last=Alston|first=Philip|date=May 4, 2018|publisher=[[Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights]]|page=19|access-date=October 17, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://apnews.com/2f11091232a349f39cfe2e80e8c46545|title=UN expert calls US income inequality 'a political choice'|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|date=June 4, 2018|work=[[Associated Press]]|access-date=October 19, 2019}}</ref>

[[Alan Krueger]] summarized research studies in 2012, stating that as income inequality increases:<ref name="Krueger2012" />

* Income shifts to the wealthy, who tend to consume less of each marginal dollar, slowing consumption and therefore economic growth;
* Income mobility falls: parents' income better predicts their children's income;
* Middle and lower-income families borrow more to maintain their consumption, a contributing factor to financial crises; and
* The wealthy gain more political power, which results in policies that further slow economic growth.

Many economists claim that America's growing income inequality is "deeply worrying",<ref name="Noah2"/> unjust,<ref name="Richer" /> a danger to democracy/social stability,<ref name="Hacker.p75" /><ref name="CBO Report Shows Rich Got Richer" /><ref name="Oligarchy" /> or a sign of national decline.<ref name="Packer" /> [[Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences|Nobelist]] [[Robert Shiller]] after receiving the award stated, "The most important problem that we are facing now today, I think, is rising inequality in the United States and elsewhere in the world."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.stltoday.com/business/local/rising-inequality-most-important-problem-says-nobel-winning-economist/article_a5065957-05c3-5ac0-ba5b-dab91c22973a.html|title=Rising inequality 'most important problem,' says Nobel-winning economist|last=Christoffersen|first=John|date=October 14, 2013|newspaper=St. Louis Post-Dispatch|access-date=October 19, 2013}}</ref> Piketty warned, "The egalitarian pioneer ideal has faded into oblivion, and the [[New World]] may be on the verge of becoming the Old Europe of the twenty-first century's [[Economic globalization|globalized economy]]."<ref name="Piketty">{{cite journal|last=Cassidy|first=John|date=March 31, 2014|title=Forces of Divergence Is surging inequality endemic to capitalism? (review of ''Capital in the Twenty-first Century'' by Thomas Piketty)|url=https://www.newyorker.com/arts/critics/books/2014/03/31/140331crbo_books_cassidy?currentPage=all|journal=New Yorker|access-date=March 31, 2014}}</ref> [[Angus Deaton]] asserts that the prevailing orthodoxy which promotes the idea of unfettered free markets and limited government intervention helped to establish a predatory [[capitalist]] system in the US that enriches [[corporations]] and the wealthy at the expense of the [[Working class in the United States|working class]].<ref>{{cite news |last=McGreal|first=Chris |date=October 7, 2023 |title=Angus Deaton on inequality: 'The war on poverty has become a war on the poor'|url=https://www.theguardian.com/inequality/2023/oct/07/angus-deaton-interview-book-economics-in-america|work=The Guardian |location= |access-date=October 11, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Deaton |first=Angus |author-link=Angus Deaton |url= |title=Economics in America: An Immigrant Economist Explores the Land of Inequality |date=2023 |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |isbn=978-0691247625 |page=x|quote=I have come to understand the extent to which state and federal government in the United States often work, not to protect ordinary people but to help rich predators make ordinary people poorer.}}</ref>

Others claim that the increase is not significant,<ref name="heritage">{{Cite web|url=https://www.heritage.org/taxes/report/two-americas-one-rich-one-poor-understanding-income-inequality-the-united-states|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170420165336/http://www.heritage.org/taxes/report/two-americas-one-rich-one-poor-understanding-income-inequality-the-united-states|url-status=unfit|archive-date=April 20, 2017|title=Two Americas: One Rich, One Poor? Understanding Income Inequality in the United States|last=Hederman|first=Rea|website=[[The Heritage Foundation]]|language=en|access-date=October 9, 2019}}</ref> that America's economic growth and/or equality of opportunity should be the primary focus,<ref name="Sowell">{{Cite web|url=http://www.jewishworldreview.com/cols/sowell020700.asp|title=Perennial Economic Fallacies|last=Sowell|first=Thomas|date=February 7, 2000|website=www.jewishworldreview.com|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref> that rising inequaity is a global phenomenon that would be foolish to try to change through US domestic policy,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052970204653604577249852320654024|title=A Look at the Global One Percent|last=Meltzer|first=Allan H.|date=March 9, 2012|work=Wall Street Journal|access-date=October 10, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0099-9660}}</ref> that it "has many economic benefits and is the result of ... a well-functioning economy",<ref name="not-so-bad"/> and has or may become an excuse for "class-warfare rhetoric".<ref name="heritage" /> They argue against "[[redistribution of wealth]]", instead advocating for "sound economic policy to reduce poverty [which] would lift people out of poverty (increase their productivity) while not reducing the well-being of wealthier individuals".<ref name="not-so-bad" />
