Another 4.5 million women working in factories, usually in unskilled positions, up 112%.<ref name=":3" /> The aviation industry saw the highest increase in female workers during the war. By 1943 310,000 women worked there, or 65% of the industry's workforce.<ref name=":2" />

While women's wages rose more relative to men's during this period, real wages did not increase due to higher wartime income taxes.<ref name="Goldin 2013">{{cite journal|last=Goldin|first=Claudia|author-link=Claudia Goldin|author2=Claudia Olivetti |title=Shocking labor supply: A reassessment of the role of World War II on US women's labor supply|journal=National Bureau of Economic Research|year=2013|volume=w18676}}</ref> Although jobs that had been previously closed to women opened up, demographics such as African American women who had already been participating more fully experienced less change. Their husbands' income effect was historically even more positive than white women's. During the war, African American women engagement as domestic servants decreased from 59.9% to 44.6%, but Karen Anderson in 1982 characterized their experience as "last hired, first fired."<ref name="Anderson 1982">{{cite journal|last=Anderson|first=Karen Tucker|title=Last hired, first fired: Black women workers during World War II|journal=The Journal of American History|year=1982|volume=69|issue=1|pages=82–97|doi=10.2307/1887753|jstor=1887753}}</ref>

At the end of the war, most of the munitions-making jobs ended. Many factories were closed; others retooled for civilian production. In some jobs, women were replaced by returning veterans who did not lose seniority because they were in service. However, the number of women at work in 1946 was 87% of the number in 1944, leaving 13% left the labor force to become housewives.<ref>D'Ann Campbell, ''Women at War with America: Private Lives in a Patriotic Era'' (Harvard University Press, 1984), pp 225–226.</ref>

===Walter Reuther and UAW===
{{Main|United Auto Workers}}
The [[Flint sit-down strike|Flint Sit-Down Strike]] of 1936–37 was the decisive event in the formation of the [[United Auto Workers|United Auto Workers Union]] (UAW).
During the war [[Walter Reuther]] took control of the UAW, and soon led major strikes in 1946. He ousted the Communists from the positions of power, especially at the Ford local. He was one of the most articulate and energetic leaders of the CIO, and of the merged [[AFL–CIO|AFL-CIO]]. Using brilliant negotiating tactics he leveraged high profits for the Big Three automakers into higher wages and superior benefits for UAW members.<ref>Nelson Lichtenstein, ''Walter Reuther: The most dangerous man in Detroit'' (U of Illinois Press, 1997).</ref>

===PAC and politics of 1940s===
New enemies appeared for the labor unions after 1935. Newspaper columnist [[Westbrook Pegler]] was especially outraged by the New Deal's support for powerful labor unions that he considered morally and politically corrupt. Pegler saw himself a populist and muckraker whose mission was to warn the nation that dangerous leaders were in power. In 1941 Pegler became the first columnist ever to win a [[Pulitzer Prize]] for reporting, for his work in exposing [[racketeering]] in Hollywood labor unions, focusing on the criminal career of [[William Morris Bioff]]. Pegler's popularity reflected a loss of support for unions and liberalism generally, especially as shown by the dramatic Republican gains in the 1946 elections, often using an anti-union theme.<ref>Susan M. Hartman, ''Truman and the 80th Congress'' (1971)</ref>

====Strike wave of 1945====
{{Main|Strike wave of 1945–1946}}
With the end of the war in August 1945 came a [[Strike wave of 1945–1946|wave of major strikes]], mostly led by the CIO. In November, the UAW sent their 180,000 GM workers to the picket lines; they were joined in January 1946 by a half-million steelworkers, as well as over 200,000 electrical workers and 150,000 packinghouse workers. Combined with many smaller strikes a new record of strike activity was set.<ref name="Ziegler, pp. 212">Ziegler, ''CIO'' pp. 212–13</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Griffith|first=Barbara S.|title=The Crisis of American Labor: Operation Dixie and the Defeat of the CIO|url=https://archive.org/details/crisisofamerican0000grif|url-access=registration|year=1988|publisher=Temple University Press|isbn=978-0877225034}}</ref>

The results were mixed, with the unions making some gains, but the economy was disordered by the rapid termination of war contracts, the complex reconversion to peacetime production, the return to the labor force of 12 million servicemen, and the return home of millions of women workers. The conservative control of Congress blocked liberal legislation, and "[[Operation Dixie]]", the CIO's efforts to expand massively into the [[Southern United States]], failed.<ref name="Ziegler, pp. 212"/>

The [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] exploited public anger at the unions in 1946, winning a smashing landslide. Labor responded afterwards by taking strong actions. The CIO systematically purged communists and far-left sympathizers from leadership roles in its unions.<ref>Harvey A. Levenstein, ''Communism, Anti-communism, and the CIO'' (Praeger, 1981).</ref> The CIO expelled some unions that resisted the purge, notably its third-largest affiliate the [[United Electrical, Radio and Machine Workers of America]] (UE), and set up a new rival [[International Union of Electrical Workers|IUE]] to take away the UE membership.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Ronald L. Filippelli|author2=Mark D. McColloch|title=Cold War in the Working Class: The Rise and Decline of the United Electrical Workers|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XkNmcyA9EfsC&pg=PA10|year=1995|publisher=SUNY Press|pages=10–11|isbn=9780791421826}}</ref>

Meanwhile, the AFL in 1947 set up its first explicitly political unit, Labor's League for Political Education. The AFL increasingly abandoned its historic tradition of nonpartisanship, since neutrality between the major parties was impossible. By 1952, the AFL had given up on decentralization, local autonomy, and non-partisanship, and had developed instead a new political approach marked by the same style of centralization, national coordination, and partisan alliances that characterized the CIO.<ref>Joseph E. Hower,  "'Our conception of non-partisanship means a partisan non-partisanship': the search for political identity in the American Federation of Labor, 1947–1955." ''Labor History'' 51.3 (2010): 455-478.</ref> After these moves, the CIO and AFL were in a good position to fight off [[Henry A. Wallace|Henry Wallace]] in the [[1948 United States presidential election|1948 presidential election]] and work enthusiastically for [[Harry S. Truman]]'s reelection. The CIO and AFL no longer had major points of conflict, so they merged amicably in 1955 as the [[AFL–CIO]].<ref>Daniel B. Cornfield and Holly J. McCammon, "Approaching merger: The converging public policy agendas of the AFL and CIO, 1938–1955." in Nella Van Dyke and Holly J. McCammon, eds., ''Strategic Alliances: Coalition Building and Social Movements ''(2010): 79-98.</ref>

===Taft-Hartley Act===
{{further|Taft–Hartley Act}}

The [[Taft–Hartley Act|Labor Management Relations Act of 1947]], also known as the ''Taft–Hartley Act'', revised the [[National Labor Relations Act of 1935|Wagner Act]] to include restrictions on unions as well as management. It was a response to public demands for action after the wartime coal strikes and the postwar strikes in steel, autos and other industries that were perceived to have damaged the economy, as well as a threatened 1946 railroad strike that was called off at the last minute before it shut down the national economy. The Act was bitterly fought by unions, vetoed by President [[Harry S. Truman]], and passed over his veto. Repeated union efforts to repeal or modify it always failed, and it remains in effect today.<ref>Adam Dean, and Jonathan Obert, "Rewarded by Friends and Punished by Enemies: The CIO and the Taft-Hartley Act." ''Labor'' 18.3 (2021): 78-113.</ref>

The Act was sponsored by Senator [[Robert A. Taft]] and Representative [[Fred A. Hartley Jr.|Fred Hartley]], both Republicans. Congress overrode the veto on June 23, 1947, establishing the act as a law. Truman described the act as a "slave-labor bill" in his veto, but after it was enacted over his veto, he used its emergency provisions a number of times to halt strikes and lockouts. The new law required all union officials to sign an affidavit that they were not Communists or else the union would lose its federal bargaining powers guaranteed by the [[National Labor Relations Board]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Judith Stepan-Norris and Maurice Zeitlin|title=Left Out: Reds and America's Industrial Unions|title-link=Left Out: Reds and America's Industrial Unions|year=2003|page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=sgs38cHpp_EC&pg=PA9 9]|publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9780521798402}}</ref> (That provision was declared to be an [[Constitutionality|unconstitutional]] [[bill of attainder]] by a 1965 Supreme Court decision, [[United States v. Brown (1965)|United States v. Brown]].)<ref>{{cite court |litigants=United States v. Brown (1965) |vol=381|reporter=U.S. |opinion=437 |court=[[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] |date=June 7, 1965|url=https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/381/437 |access-date=November 24, 2015 |quote=Held: Section 504 constitutes a bill of attainder and is therefore unconstitutional.}}</ref>

The Taft-Hartley Act amended the Wagner Act, officially known as the [[National Labor Relations Act of 1935|National Labor Relations Act]], of 1935. The amendments added to the NLRA a list of prohibited actions, or "unfair labor practices", on the part of unions. The NLRA had previously prohibited only unfair labor practices committed by employers. It prohibited [[jurisdictional strike]]s, in which a union strikes in order to pressure an employer to assign particular work to the employees that union represents, and [[Solidarity action|secondary boycotts]] and "common situs" [[picketing]], in which unions picket, strike, or refuse to handle the goods of a business with which they have no primary dispute but which is associated with a targeted business. A later statute, the [[Labor Management Reporting and Disclosure Act of 1959|Labor Management Reporting and Disclosure Act]], passed in 1959, tightened these restrictions on secondary boycotts still further.

The Act outlawed [[closed shop]]s, which were contractual agreements that required an employer to hire only union members. [[Union shop]]s, in which new recruits must join the union within a certain amount of time, are permitted, but only as part of a [[Collective agreement|collective bargaining agreement]] and only if the contract allows the worker at least thirty days after the date of hire or the effective date of the contract to join the union. The [[National Labor Relations Board]] and the courts have added other restrictions on the power of unions to enforce [[Union security agreement|union security]] clauses and have required them to make extensive financial disclosures to all members as part of their [[duty of fair representation]]. On the other hand, a few years after the passage of the Act Congress repealed the provisions requiring a vote by workers to authorize a union shop, when it became apparent that workers were approving them in virtually every case. The amendments also authorized individual states to outlaw union security clauses entirely in their jurisdictions by passing [[Right-to-work law|"right-to-work" laws]]. Currently all of the states in the [[Deep South]] and a number of traditionally Republican states in the [[Midwestern United States|Midwest]], [[Great Plains|Plains]] and [[Rocky Mountains]] regions have right-to-work laws. The amendments required unions and employers to give sixty days' notice before they may undertake strikes or other forms of economic action in pursuit of a new collective bargaining agreement; it did not, on the other hand, impose any "cooling-off period" after a contract expired. Although the Act also authorized the president to intervene in strikes or potential strikes that create a national emergency, the president has used that power less and less frequently in each succeeding decade.

Historian [[James T. Patterson (historian)|James T. Patterson]] concludes that:
:: By the 1950s most observers agreed that Taft-Hartley was no more disastrous for workers than the Wagner Act had been for employers. What ordinarily mattered most in labor relations was not government laws such as Taft-Hartley, but the relative power of unions and management in the economic marketplace. Where unions were strong they usually managed all right; when they were weak, new laws did them little additional harm.<ref>{{cite book|author=James T. Patterson|title=Grand Expectations: The United States, 1945-1974|publisher=Oxford University Press|url=https://archive.org/details/grandexpectation00patt|url-access=registration|year=1996|page=[https://archive.org/details/grandexpectation00patt/page/52 52]|isbn=9780195076806}}</ref>

===Anti-communism===
{{Main|Anti-communism#United States|History of the socialist movement in the United States#20th_century|l2 = Socialist movement in the United States, 20th Century}}

The AFL had always opposed communists inside the labor movement. After 1945 they took their crusade worldwide. The CIO had major communist elements who played a key role in organizational work in the late 1930s and war years. By 1949 they were purged. The AFL and CIO strongly supported the [[Cold War]] policies of the Truman administration, including the [[Truman Doctrine]], the [[Marshall Plan]] and [[NATO]].<ref>Jennifer Luff,  "Labor Anticommunism in the United States of America and the United Kingdom, 1920–49." ''Journal of Contemporary History'' 53.1 (2018): 109-133. [https://www.academia.edu/download/51077440/0022009416658701.pdf online]</ref>

Left-wing elements in the CIO protested and were forced out of the main unions. [[Walter Reuther]] of the [[United Auto Workers|United Automobile Workers]] purged the UAW of communist members. He was active in the CIO umbrella as well, taking the lead in expelling eleven communist-dominated unions from the CIO in 1949.<ref>Harvey A. Levenstein, ''Communism, Anticommunism, and the CIO'' (1981)</ref> As a leader of the anti-communist center-left, Reuther was a founder of the liberal umbrella group [[Americans for Democratic Action]] in 1947. In 1949 he led the CIO delegation to the London conference that set up the [[International Confederation of Free Trade Unions]] in opposition to the communist-dominated [[World Federation of Trade Unions]]. He had left the Socialist Party in 1939, and throughout the 1950s and 1960s was a leading spokesman for liberal interests in the CIO and in the Democratic Party.<ref name=nelson>{{cite book|last=Lichtenstein|first=Nelson|title=Walter Reuther: The Most Dangerous Man in Detroit|year=1995|publisher=BasicBooks|location=New York|isbn=978-0465090808|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m2TIwqhOHRwC}}</ref> [[James B. Carey]] also helped influence the CIO's pullout from the WFTU and the formation of the [[International Confederation of Free Trade Unions]] dedicated to promoting free trade and democratic unionism worldwide. Carey in 1949 had formed the [[International Union of Electrical Workers]], a new CIO union for electrical workers, because the old one, the [[United Electrical, Radio and Machine Workers of America]], was tightly held by the left.<ref>Ronald Lee Filippelli, " The United Electrical Radio and Machine Workers of America, 1933–1949 the struggle for control" (PhD Dissertation, Pennsylvania State University;' ProQuest Dissertations & Theses, 1970. 7024156).</ref>

Marxian economist [[Richard D. Wolff]] argues that anti-communism was part of a strategy by big business, Republicans and conservatives to single out and destroy the members of the coalition that forced through the [[New Deal]], namely organized labor, socialist and communist parties.<ref>[[Richard D. Wolff]] (September 2, 2013). [https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2013/sep/02/labor-unions-decline-can-turnaround Organized labor's decline in the US is well-known. But what drove it?] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201132136/https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2013/sep/02/labor-unions-decline-can-turnaround |date=December 1, 2017 }} ''[[The Guardian]].'' Retrieved January 4, 2014.</ref>

==Union decline, 1955–2016==
[[File:1907- Income inequality and union participation.svg|thumb|Income inequality and union participation have had a distinctly inverse relationship, with the disparity increasing since the 1980s.<ref name=NYTimes_20230707>{{cite news |last1=Leonhardt |first1=David |title=How Elba Makes a Living Wage |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/07/07/briefing/unions-living-wage-working-documentary.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=July 7, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230708002328/https://www.nytimes.com/2023/07/07/briefing/unions-living-wage-working-documentary.html |archive-date=July 8, 2023 |url-status=live }}</ref>]]
[[File:U.S. Compensation as Percent of GDP - v1.png|right|thumb|400px|Labor income as a share of GDP (vs. income from capital) has declined 1970 to 2016, measured based on total compensation as well as salaries & wages. All employment is included, not just union members.]]
Since its peak in the mid-20th century, the American labor movement has been in steady decline, with losses in the private sector larger than gains in the public sector. In the early 1950s, as the AFL and CIO merged, around a third of the American [[Labor force in the United States|labor force]] was unionized; by 2012, the proportion was 11 percent, constituting roughly 5 percent in the private sector and 40 percent in the public sector. Organized labor's influence steadily waned and workers' collective voice in the political process has weakened. Partly as a result, wages have stagnated and [[Income inequality in the United States|income inequality]] has increased.<ref name="Workerswrl">{{cite journal |url= http://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/137522/bruce-western-and-jake-rosenfeld/workers-of-the-world-divide |last1= Western |first1= Bruce |last2= Rosenfeld |first2= Jake |year= 2012 |title= Workers of the World Divide |journal= [[Foreign Affairs]] |volume= 91 |issue= 3 |access-date= June 10, 2012 |url-status= live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120610020158/http://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/137522/bruce-western-and-jake-rosenfeld/workers-of-the-world-divide |archive-date= June 10, 2012 }}</ref> "Although the [[National Labor Relations Act of 1935|National Labor Relations Act]] was initially a boon for unions, it also sowed the seeds of the labor movement's decline. The act enshrined the right to unionize, but the system of workplace elections it created meant that unions had to organize each new factory or firm individually rather than organize by industry. In many European countries, collective-bargaining agreements extended automatically to other firms in the same industry, but in the United States, they usually reached no further than a plant's gates. As a result, in the first decades of the postwar period, the organizing effort could not keep pace with the frenetic rate of job growth in the economy as a whole".<ref name="Workerswrl"/> On the political front, the shrinking unions lost influence in the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]], and pro-union [[Rockefeller Republican|liberal Republicans]] faded away.<ref name="Nicol C. Rae 1989"/> Intellectuals lost interest in unions, focusing their attention more on the [[Vietnam War]], [[Minorities in the United States|minorities]], [[Feminism in the United States|women]] and [[Environmental issues in the United States|environmental issues]].<ref>Richard Rorty, ''Achieving Our Country: Leftist Thought in Twentieth-Century America'' (1999) p 77</ref>

By the 1970s, a rapidly increasing flow of imports (such as automobiles, steel and electronics from Germany and Japan, and clothing and shoes from Asia) undercut American producers.<ref>{{cite book|author=Susan Margaret Collins|title=Imports, Exports, and the American Worker|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ODj2YKiWNyAC&pg=PA288|year=1998|publisher=Brookings Institution Press|pages=288–90|isbn=978-0815714996}}</ref> By the 1980s there was a large-scale shift in employment with fewer workers in high-wage sectors and more in the low-wage sectors.<ref>{{cite book|author=Frank Levy, Larry Mishel and Jared Bernstein|title=Running in Place: Recent Trends in U.S. Living Standards|url=https://archive.org/details/runninginplacere00levy|url-access=registration|year=1996|publisher=DIANE Publishing|pages=[https://archive.org/details/runninginplacere00levy/page/53 53]–56|isbn=9780788145735}}</ref> Many companies closed or moved factories to Southern states (where unions were weak).<ref>{{cite book|author=James Charles Cobb and William Whitney Stueck|title=Globalization and the American South|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CyXZHE3jlBkC&pg=PA41|year=2005|publisher=University of Georgia Press|page=41|isbn=9780820326474}}</ref> The effectiveness of strikes declined sharply, as companies after the 1970s threatened to close down factories or move them to low-wage states or to foreign countries.<ref name="Carter A. Wilson 2013 256–57">{{cite book|author=Carter A. Wilson|title=Public Policy: Continuity and Change, Second Edition|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WewkAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA257|year=2013|publisher=Waveland Press|pages=256–57|isbn=9781478610625}}</ref> The number of major work stoppages fell by 97 percent from 381 in 1970 to 187 in 1980 to only 11 in 2010.<ref>See [https://www.census.gov/compendia/statab/2012/tables/12s0663.pdf US Census Bureau, ''Statistical Abstract of the United States: 2012'' (2011) p 428 table 663] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111020114556/http://www.census.gov/compendia/statab/2012/tables/12s0663.pdf |date=October 20, 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Aaron Brenner|title=The Encyclopedia of Strikes in American History|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EHzk54IjNpEC&pg=PA234|year=2011|publisher=M.E. Sharpe|pages=234–35|display-authors=etal|isbn=9780765626455}}</ref> The accumulating weaknesses were exposed when President [[Ronald Reagan]]—a former union president—broke the [[Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization (1968)|Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization (PATCO)]] strike in 1981, dealing a major blow to unions.<ref name=round>{{cite book|last=Round|first=Michael A.|title=Grounded: Reagan and the PATCO Crash|year=1999|publisher=Taylor & Francis|location=New York, NY|isbn=9780815335061|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LuM4dyYolK4C}}</ref>

Union membership among workers in private industry shrank dramatically, though after 1970 there was growth in employees unions of federal, state and local governments.<ref>{{cite book|author=James T. Bennett and Bruce E. Kaufman|title=The Future of Private Sector Unionism in the United States|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v0sqo-9KOPcC&pg=PA373|year=2002|publisher=M.E. Sharpe|pages=373–78|isbn=9780765608529}}</ref><ref>Robert H. Zieger, and Gilbert J. Gall, ''American Workers, American Unions: The Twentieth Century'' (3rd ed. 2002); Lawrence Richards, ''Union-Free America: Workers and Antiunion Culture'' (2010)</ref> The intellectual mood in the 1970s and 1980s favored [[deregulation]] and free competition.<ref name=Derthick218>Martha Derthick and Paul J. Quirk, ''The Politics of Deregulation'' (1985) p. 218</ref> Numerous industries were deregulated, including airlines, trucking, railroads and telephones, over the objections of the unions involved.<ref>Derthick and Quirk, ''The Politics of Deregulation'' (1985) pp. vii, 11, 104, 137</ref>

Republicans, using conservative [[think tank]]s as idea farms, began to push through legislative blueprints to curb the power of public employee unions as well as eliminate business regulations.<ref name="Carter A. Wilson 2013 256–57"/>

Union weakness in the South undermined unionization and social reform throughout the nation, and such weakness is largely responsible for the anaemic US [[welfare state]].<ref>Friedman, Gerald (June 2000). [https://www.jstor.org/stable/2566376 The Political Economy of Early Southern Unionism: Race, Politics, and Labor in the South, 1880-1953] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160306112958/http://www.jstor.org/stable/2566376 |date=March 6, 2016 }}. ''[[The Journal of Economic History]]'' Vol. 60, No. 2, pp. 384-413.</ref>

===AFL and CIO merger 1955===
The friendly merger of the AFL and CIO marked an end not only to the acrimony and jurisdictional conflicts between the coalitions, it also signaled the end of the era of experimentation and expansion that began in the mid-1930s. Merger became politically possible because of the deaths of Green of the AFL and Murray of the CIO in late 1952, replaced by [[George Meany]] and Reuther. The CIO was no longer the radical dynamo, and was no longer a threat in terms of membership for the AFL had twice as many members.<ref name="Zieger, CIO p. 357–69">Zieger, ''CIO'' p. 357–69</ref>

Furthermore, the AFL was doing a better job of expanding into the fast-growing white collar sector, with its organizations of clerks, public employees, teachers, and service workers. Although the AFL building trades maintained all-white policies, the AFL had more black members in all as the CIO. The problem of union corruption was growing in public awareness, and CIO's industrial unions were less vulnerable to penetration by criminal elements than were the AFL's trucking, longshoring, building, and entertainment unions. But Meany had a strong record in fighting corruption in New York unions, and was highly critical of the notoriously corrupt Teamsters.<ref name="Zieger, CIO p. 357–69"/>

Unification would help the central organization fight corruption, yet would not contaminate the CIO unions. The defeat of the New Deal in the 1952 election further emphasized the need for unity to maximize political effectiveness. From the CIO side the merger was promoted by [[David J. McDonald|David McDonald]] of the Steelworkers and his top aide [[Arthur Goldberg|Arthur J. Goldberg]]. To achieve the successful merger, they jettisoned the more liberal policies of the CIO regarding civil rights and membership rights for blacks, jurisdictional disputes, and industrial unionism. Reuther went along with the compromises and did not contest the selection of Meany to head the AFL-CIO.<ref name="Zieger, CIO p. 357–69"/>

Fearing the fallout of a drawn-out negotiation process, the AFL and CIO leadership decided on a "short route" to reconciliation. This meant all AFL and CIO unions would be accepted into the new organization "as is," with all conflicts and overlaps to be sorted out after the merger.<ref>Goldberg, Arthur (1956). ''AFL-CIO Labor United''. New York, New York: McGraw Hill. pp. 85–86.</ref> Negotiations were conducted by a small, select group of advisors. The draft constitution was primarily written by AFL Vice President [[Matthew Woll]] and CIO General Counsel [[Arthur Goldberg]], while the joint policy statements were written by Woll, CIO Secretary-Treasurer [[James B. Carey|James Carey]], CIO vice presidents [[David J. McDonald|David McDonald]] and [[Joseph Curran]], Brotherhood of Railway Clerks President [[George McGregor Harrison|George Harrison]], and Illinois AFL-CIO President [[Reuben G. Soderstrom|Reuben Soderstrom]].<ref>Soderstrom, Carl; Soderstrom, Robert; Stevens, Chris; Burt, Andrew (2018). [https://www.fortygavels.com/ ''Forty Gavels: The Life of Reuben Soderstrom and the Illinois AFL-CIO''.] '''3'''. Peoria, IL: CWS Publishing. pp. 95-96. {{ISBN|978-0998257532}}</ref>

===Conservative attacks===

Labor unions were a whole high-profile target of Republican activists throughout the 1940s and 1950s, especially the [[Taft–Hartley Act|Taft-Hartley Act]] of 1947. Both the business community and local Republicans wanted to weaken unions, which played a major role in funding and campaigning for Democratic candidates.<ref>Elizabeth A. Fones-Wolf, ''Selling free enterprise: The business assault on labor and liberalism, 1945-60'' (U of Illinois Press, 1994).</ref> The strategy of the Eisenhower administration was to consolidate the anti-union potential inherent in Taft-Hartley.<ref>M. Stephen Weatherford, "The Eisenhower Transition: Labor Policy in the New Political Economy." ''Studies in American Political Development'' 28#2 (2014): 201-223.</ref> Pressure from the Justice Department, the Labor Department, and especially from congressional investigations focused on criminal activity and racketeering in high-profile labor unions, especially the [[International Brotherhood of Teamsters|Teamsters Union]]. Republicans wanted to delegitimize unions by focusing on their shady activities. The [[United States Senate Select Committee on Improper Activities in Labor and Management|McClellan Committee]] hearings targeted Teamsters president [[Jimmy Hoffa|James R. Hoffa]] as a public enemy. Young [[Robert F. Kennedy]] played a major role working for the committee.<ref>Ronald L. Goldfarb, ''Perfect Villains, Imperfect Heroes: Robert F. Kennedy's War Against Organized Crime'' (2002).</ref> Public opinion polls showed growing distrust toward unions, and especially union leaders — or "labor bosses," as Republicans called them. The bipartisan [[Conservative coalition|Conservative Coalition]], with the aid of liberals such as the Kennedy brothers, won new Congressional restrictions on organized labor in the form of the [[Labor Management Reporting and Disclosure Act of 1959|Landrum-Griffin Act]] (1959). The main impact was to force more democracy on the previously authoritarian union hierarchies.<ref>David Witwer,  "The Racketeer Menace and Antiunionism in the Mid-Twentieth Century US." ''International Labor and Working-Class History'' 74#1 (2008): 124-147.</ref><ref>Alton R. Lee, ''Eisenhower and Landrum-Griffin: A study in labor-management politics'' (UP of Kentucky, 1990).</ref> However, in [[1958 United States elections|the 1958 elections]], taking place during a sharp economic recession, the unions fought back especially against state [[Right-to-work law|Right to Work laws]] and defeated many conservative Republicans.<ref>John H. Fenton, "The right-to-work vote in Ohio." ''Midwest Journal of Political Science'' 3#3 (1959): 241-253. {{JSTOR|2109251}}</ref><ref>Elizabeth Tandy Shermer,  "Counter-Organizing the Sunbelt: Right-to-Work Campaigns and Anti-Union Conservatism, 1943–1958." ''Pacific Historical Review'' 78.1 (2009): 81-118. {{JSTOR|10.1525/phr.2009.78.1.81}}</ref>

The Teamsters union was expelled from the AFL for its notorious corruption under president [[Dave Beck]]. Its troubles gained national attention from highly visible Senate hearings.<ref name=witwer>{{cite book|last=Witwer|first=David Scott|title=Corruption and Reform in the Teamsters Union|year=2003|publisher=University of Illinois Press|isbn=9780252028250|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pJPqoncrFZAC}}</ref> The target was [[Jimmy Hoffa]] (1913–1975), who replaced Beck and held total power until he was imprisoned in 1964.

===1960s: Liberal achievement in Civil Rights and backlash===
{{Main|1964 United States elections|1966 United States elections|1968 United States elections}}
The UAW under Reuther played a major role in funding and supporting the [[Civil rights movement|Civil Rights Movement]] in the 1950s and 1960s.<ref>Kevin Boyle, ''The UAW and the Heyday of American Liberalism, 1945–1968'', (1995), ch. 7.</ref> More traditional unions favored their white members and encountered federal court intervention.<ref>Paul Frymer, "Acting when elected officials won't: federal courts and civil rights enforcement in US labor unions, 1935–85." ''American Political Science Review'' 97.3 (2003): 483-499. [https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Paul-Frymer/publication/228207803_Acting_When_Elected_Officials_Won't_Federal_Courts_and_Civil_Rights_Enforcement_in_US_Labor_Unions_1935-1985/links/544871c20cf2f14fb8142647/Acting-When-Elected-Officials-Wont-Federal-Courts-and-Civil-Rights-Enforcement-in-US-Labor-Unions-1935-1985.pdf online]</ref>

After the smashing reelection victory of [[Presidency of Lyndon B. Johnson|President Lyndon B. Johnson in 1964]], the heavily Democratic Congress passed a raft of liberal legislation. Labor union leaders claimed credit for the widest range of liberal laws since the New Deal era, including the Civil Rights Act of 1964; the Voting Rights Act of 1965; the War on Poverty; aid to cities and education; increased Social Security benefits; and Medicare for the elderly. The 1966 elections were an unexpected disaster, with defeats for many of the more liberal Democrats. According to Alan Draper, the AFL-CIO Committee on Political Action (COPE) was the main electioneering unit of the labor movement. It ignored the white backlash against civil rights, which had become a main Republican attack point. The COPE assumed falsely that union members were interested in issues of greatest salience to union leadership, but polls showed this was not true. The members were much more conservative. The younger ones were much more concerned about taxes and crime, and the older ones had not overcome racial biases. Furthermore, a new issue—the War in Vietnam—was bitterly splitting the [[New Deal coalition]] into hawks (led by Johnson and Vice-president [[Hubert Humphrey]]) and doves (led by Senators [[Eugene McCarthy]] and [[Robert Kennedy]]).<ref>Alan Draper, "Labor and the 1966 Elections." ''Labor History'' 30.1 (1989): 76-92.</ref><ref>Maurice Isserman, and Michael Kazin.  ''America divided: The civil war of the 1960s'' (6th ed. Oxford UP, 2020) pp 187-203.</ref>

===Hispanics===
====Chavez and the United Farm Workers====
{{Main|United Farm Workers|Cesar Chavez}}
Hispanics form a large fraction of the farm labor force, but due to the fact that agricultural workers were not protected under the [[National Labor Relations Act of 1935|National Labor Relations Act (NLRA)]] of 1935,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/ssb/v70n4/v70n4p49.html|title=The Decision to Exclude Agricultural and Domestic Workers from the 1935 Social Security Act|last=DeWitt|first=Larry|website=Social Security Administration}}</ref> there was little successful unionization before the arrival in the 1960s of [[Cesar Chavez]] (1927–1993) and [[Dolores Huerta|Dolores Huerta (1930)]], who mobilized California workers into the [[United Farm Workers]] (UFW) organization.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gordon|first=Robert|date=1999|title=Poisons in the Fields: The United Farm Workers, Pesticides, and Environmental Politics|journal=Pacific Historical Review|volume=68|issue=1|pages=51–77|doi=10.2307/3641869|jstor=3641869}}</ref>

Chavez's use of non-violent methods combined with Huerta's organizational skills allowed for many of the bigger successes of the organization.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Rose|first=Margaret|date=1990|title=Traditional and Nontraditional Patterns of Female Activism in the United Farm Workers of America, 1962 to 1980|journal=Frontiers: A Journal of Women Studies|volume=11|issue=1|pages=26–32|doi=10.2307/3346700|jstor=3346700}}</ref>

A key success for the UFW was in partnering with the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee (AWOC), which primarily worked with Filipino farm workers, and creating the eventual United Farmworkers Union in 1972.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ufw.org/the-rise-of-the-ufw/|title=The Rise of the UFW|website=UFW|language=en-US|access-date=September 27, 2018|date=April 3, 2017}}</ref> Together, they organized a worker strike and consumer boycott of the grape growers in California that lasted for over five years. Through collaboration with consumers and student protesters, the UFW was able to secure a three-year contract with the state's top grape growers to increase the safety and pay of farm workers.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Dark Sweat, White Gold: California Farm Workers, Cotton, and the New Deal|last=Weber|first=Devra|publisher=New York: Houghton Mifflin Courtyard|year=1998|isbn=978-0-15-600598-2|url=https://archive.org/details/fightinfieldsces00susa}}</ref>

Chavez had a significant political impact; as Jenkins points out, "state and national elites no longer automatically sided with the growers." Thus, the political insurgency of the UFW was successful because of effective strategizing in the right kind of political environment.<ref>{{Cite book|title=The Politics Of Insurgency: The Farm worker Movement In The 1960s|last=Jenkins|first=J. Craig|year=1985|pages=209, 228}}</ref> In the decades following its early success, the UFW experienced a steep decline in membership due to purges of key organizational leaders by Chavez.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Majka|first1=Theo J.|last2=Majka|first2=Linda C.|date=October 1, 1992|title=Decline of the Farm Labor Movement in California: Organizational Crisis and Political Change|journal=Critical Sociology|language=en|volume=19|issue=3|pages=3–36|doi=10.1177/089692059201900301|s2cid=153772108|issn=0896-9205}}</ref> With Chavez unable to lead effectively, the Teamsters Union moved in and replaced the UFW.<ref>Miriam Pawel, ''The Union of Their Dreams: Power, Hope, and Struggle in Cesar Chavez's Farm Worker Movement'' (Bloomsbury, 2009).</ref><ref>Randy Shaw, ''Beyond the Fields: Cesar Chavez, the UFW, and the Struggle for Justice in the 21st Century'' (University of California Press, 2008).</ref> In 2015 José-Antonio Orosco pointed out that the UFW, "devolved from a powerful labor union for farmworkers to a fragile organization that today draws most of its support from mailed donations and represents fewer than five thousand workers in an industry that employs tens of thousands." In her biography of Chavez, Miriam Powell blames one person for the collapse: Chavez himself.<ref>José-Antonio Orosco, Review, ''Journal of American History'' (2015) 102#2 pp. 624-625.</ref><ref>Miriam Powell, ''The Crusades of Cesar Chavez: A Biography'' (Bloomsbury, 2014) pp. 473–476.</ref>

====Hotels====
Nationwide unions have been seeking opportunities to enroll Hispanic members. Much of their limited success has been in the hotel industry, especially in Nevada.<ref>Jake Rosenfeld and Meredith Kleykamp, "Hispanics and Organized Labor in the United States, 1973 to 2007," ''American Sociological Review'' 74 (December 2009) 916-37</ref>

===Reagan era, 1980s===
{{Further|Presidency of Ronald Reagan#Labor}}
Dana Cloud argues, "the emblematic moment of the period from 1955 through the 1980s in American labor was the tragic PATCO strike in 1981."<ref>{{cite book|last=Dana L. Cloud|title=We Are the Union: Democratic Unionism and Dissent at Boeing|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FO14eZc9uyEC&pg=PA23|year=2011|publisher=U of Illinois Press|page=23|isbn=9780252093418}}</ref> Most unions were strongly opposed to Reagan in the [[1980 United States presidential election|1980 presidential election]], despite the fact that Reagan remains the only union leader (or even member) to become president. On August 3, 1981, the [[Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization (1968)|Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization (PATCO) union]] — which had supported Reagan — rejected the government's pay raise offer and sent its 16,000 members out on strike to shut down the nation's commercial airlines. They demanded a reduction in the workweek to 32 from 40 hours, a $10,000 bonus, pay raises up to 40 percent, and early retirement.<ref name="ReferenceA">Herbert R. Northrup, "The Rise and Demise of PATCO", ''Industrial and Labor Relations Review''; 1984 37(2): 167–184</ref>

Federal law forbade such a strike, and the [[United States Department of Transportation]] implemented a backup plan (of supervisors and military air controllers) to keep the system running. The strikers were given 48 hours to return to work, else they would be fired and banned from ever again working in a federal capacity. A fourth of the strikers came back to work, but 13,000 did not. The strike collapsed, PATCO vanished, and the union movement as a whole suffered a major reversal, which accelerated the decline of membership across the board in the private sector.<ref name="ReferenceA" />

Schulman and Zelizer argue that the breaking of PATCO, "sent shock waves through the entire U.S. labor relations regime.&nbsp;... strike rates plummeted, and union power sharply declined."<ref>{{cite book|author1=Bruce J. Schulman|author2=Julian E. Zelizer|title=Rightward Bound: Making America Conservative in the 1970s|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3A9irCCJR48C&pg=PA225|year=2008|publisher=Harvard UP|page=225|isbn=9780674027572}}</ref> Unions suffered a continual decline of power during the Reagan
administration, with a concomitant effect on wages. The average first-year raise (for 1000-plus–worker contracts) fell from 9.8 percent to 1.2 percent; in manufacturing, raises fell from 7.2 percent to negative 1.2 percent. Salaries of unionized workers also fell relative to non-union workers. Women and Black people suffered more from these trends.<ref name=Moody1998>{{cite book|last=Moody|first=Kim|author-link=Kim Moody|title=An injury to all : the decline of American Unionism|year=1988|publisher=Verso|location=London|isbn=978-0860919292}}</ref><ref>Ruth Milkman, and Joseph A. McCartin, "The legacy and lessons of the PATCO strike after 30 years: A dialogue." Labor History 54.2 (2013): 123-137.</ref>

[[File:Weekly earnings American workers 2014 by union affiliation.jpg|thumb|400px|Union cash advantage 2014<ref>see [https://www.bls.gov/opub/mlr/2015/article/pdf/labor-law-highlights-1915-2015.pdf "Labor law highlights, 1915–2015" ''Monthly Labor Review'' (Oct 2015)] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161226154652/https://www.bls.gov/opub/mlr/2015/article/pdf/labor-law-highlights-1915-2015.pdf |date=December 26, 2016 }}</ref>]]

===Decline of private sector unions===
By 2011 fewer than seven percent of employees in the private sector belonged to unions. The UAW's numbers of automobile union members are representative of the manufacturing sector: 1,619,000 active members in 1970, 1,446,000 in 1980, 952,000 in 1990, 623,000 in 2004, and 377,000 in 2010 (with far more retired than active members).<ref>David Shepardson, [http://detnews.com/article/20110401/AUTO01/104010342/UAW-membership-up-6-percent#ixzz1JEej5tcG "UAW membership up 6 percent", ''Detroit News '' April 1, 2011]</ref>

By 2014, [[coal mining in the United States]] had largely shifted to [[Open-pit mining|open-pit mines]] in [[Wyoming]], and there were only 60,000 active coal miners. The UMW has 35,000 members, of whom 20,000 were coal miners, chiefly in underground mines in [[Kentucky]] and [[West Virginia]]. By contrast it had 800,000 members in the late 1930s. However it remains responsible for pensions and medical benefits for 40,000 retired miners, and for 50,000 spouses and dependents.<ref>Kris Maher, "Mine Workers Union Shrinks but Boss Fights On," ''Wall Street Journal,'' January 9, 2014, p B1</ref>
{{clear}}

== Rise in union activity (2016–present) ==
{{See also|Striketober|Hot labor summer}}

The number of union members nationwide increased from 2016 to 2017, and some states saw union growth for the first time in several years or decades.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Thomas|first1=Arthur|title=Wisconsin union membership grew by 11,000 in 2017|url=https://www.biztimes.com/2018/industries/construction/wisconsin-union-membership-grew-by-11000-in-2017/|website=biztimes.com|publisher=Milwaukee BizTimes|access-date=May 13, 2018|date=January 19, 2018}}</ref> Nearly half a million workers went on strike in 2018 and 2019, the largest numbers in three decades.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Raimonde |first1=Olivia |title=The number of workers on strike hits the highest since the 1980s |date=October 21, 2019 |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2019/10/21/the-number-of-workers-on-strike-hits-the-highest-since-the-1980s.html |publisher=CNBC |access-date=30 April 2020}}</ref> Union growth in 2017 was primarily [[Millennials|millennial]] workers. For instance, about 76 percent of new UAW union members during their increase came from workers under the age of 35.<ref>{{cite web|title=Young Workers Lead Union Growth in 2017|url=https://uaw.org/young-workers-lead-union-growth-2017/|website=uaw.org|access-date=May 13, 2018|date=February 15, 2018|archive-date=May 31, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200531111952/https://uaw.org/young-workers-lead-union-growth-2017/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Although the total number of union members increased 1.7 percent in 2017, the Economic Policy Institute noted that year-to-year union membership often fluctuates due to hiring or layoffs in particular sectors, and cautioned against interpreting one-year changes as trends.<ref name="epi 2018">{{cite web|last1=Mishel|first1=Lawrence|title=Overall union membership rises in 2017, union density holds steady|url=https://www.epi.org/blog/union-membership-density-2017/|website=epi.org|publisher=[[Economic Policy Institute]]|access-date=May 13, 2018|date=January 19, 2018}}</ref> The percentage of the workforce belonging to unions was 10.7 percent in 2017, unchanged over the previous year, but down from 11.1 percent in 2015, and 12.1 percent in 2007.<ref>US Bureau of Labor Statistics, [https://data.bls.gov/pdq/SurveyOutputServlet Databases, Tables & Calculators by Subject], accessed May 19, 2018.</ref>

In recent years, efforts have also been made to extend the protections of the National Labor Relations Act of 1935, which excluded [[domestic worker]]s and [[Farmworker|farm workers]], to those groups on the state level. The [[National Domestic Workers Alliance|National Domestic Workers' Alliance]] has successfully advocated for a [[Domestic Worker's Bill of Rights|Domestic Workers' Bill of Rights]] in New York, California, and Hawaii,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2019/02/21/magazine/national-domestic-workers-alliance.html,%20https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2019/02/21/magazine/national-domestic-workers-alliance.html|title=The New Labor Movement Fighting for Domestic Workers' Rights|last=Hilgers|first=Lauren|date=February 21, 2019|work=The New York Times|access-date=March 10, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> while several states have passed legislation expanding the rights of farm workers.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/labor-laws-left-farm-workers-behind-vulnerable-abuse|title=When labor laws left farm workers behind -- and vulnerable to abuse|date=September 18, 2016|website=PBS NewsHour|language=en-us|access-date=March 10, 2019}}</ref>

On July 15, 2022, the [[National Labor Relations Board]] (NLRB) reported that the amount of union representation petitions filed with the board increased by 58% in the first three quarters of the 2022 fiscal year. This was more than the total amount of petitions filed in the entire 2021 fiscal year.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Correction: First Three Quarters' Union Election Petitions Up 58%, Exceeding All FY21 Petitions Filed |url=https://www.nlrb.gov/news-outreach/news-story/correction-first-three-quarters-union-election-petitions-up-58-exceeding |access-date=2022-10-02 |website=National Labor Relations Board |language=en}}</ref>

=== Teacher strikes ===
{{main|2018–19 education workers' strikes in the United States}}

In 2018, a series of [[2018–19 education workers' strikes in the United States|statewide teacher strikes and protests]] happened garnering nationwide attention due to their success,<ref>{{cite web|last1=Whaley|first1=Monte|title=Pueblo teachers reach tentative agreement with district for 2 percent pay hike|url=https://www.denverpost.com/2018/05/12/pueblo-teacher-strike-is-over/|website=[[The Denver Post]]|access-date=May 13, 2018|date=May 12, 2018}}</ref> as well as the fact that several of them were in states where public-employee strikes are illegal. Many of the major strikes were in [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] majority state legislatures, leading to the name "Red State Revolt".<ref>{{cite web|last1=Carlson|first1=Deven|title=Not just a 'red-state revolt': The story behind the Oklahoma teacher walkout|url=https://www.brookings.edu/blog/brown-center-chalkboard/2018/04/12/oklahoma-teacher-walkouts-backstory/|website=brookings.edu|publisher=[[Brookings Institution]]|access-date=May 2, 2018|date=April 12, 2018}}</ref> Protests were held in [[2018 Arizona teachers' strike|Arizona]], [[2018 Colorado teachers' strike|Colorado]],<ref>{{cite web|last1=Eason|first1=Brian|title=What's driving the latest wave of teacher strikes? Pension problems, some say|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/education/whats-driving-the-latest-wave-of-teacher-strikes-pension-problems-some-say|website=pbs.org|publisher=[[PBS]]|access-date=May 2, 2018|date=May 1, 2018}}</ref> [[2018 North Carolina teachers' walkout|North Carolina]], [[2018 Oklahoma teachers' strike|Oklahoma]],<ref>{{cite web|last1=Weir|first1=Bill|title=Arizona teachers walk out of their poorly equipped classrooms|url=https://www.cnn.com/2018/04/26/us/arizona-teacher-walkout-weir/index.html|website=[[CNN]]|access-date=May 2, 2018|date=April 26, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Jamieson|first1=Dave|last2=Waldron|first2=Travis|title=The Red-State Teacher Revolt Has Been Brewing For Decades|url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/entry/americas-growing-teacher-strikes-were-decades-in-the-making_us_5ac8f468e4b0337ad1e8979c|website=[[HuffPost]]|publisher=[[Oath Inc.]]|access-date=May 2, 2018|date=April 7, 2018}}</ref> and [[2018 West Virginia teachers' strike|West Virginia]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Pearce|first1=Matt|title=Red-state revolt continues: Teachers strike in Oklahoma and protest in Kentucky|url=https://www.latimes.com/nation/la-na-teachers-spending-20180402-story.html|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|access-date=May 2, 2018|date=April 2, 2018}}</ref> Additional smaller protests were held in Kentucky and North Carolina. The protests spread to a [[2018 DeKalb County School District bus drivers' strike|bus driver strike]] in the suburbs of [[Atlanta|Atlanta, Georgia]], where nearly 250 bus drivers participated.<ref>{{cite web|title=More school buses on roads on day 2 of sickout|url=https://www.fox5atlanta.com/news/planned-bus-driver-sickout-slated-to-begin-thursday-in-dekalb-county|website=[[WAGA-TV]]|date=April 20, 2018 |publisher=[[Fox Television Stations]]|access-date=May 2, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Terrell|first1=Ross|title=DeKalb County School Bus Drivers Protest In Sickout|url=https://www.wabe.org/dekalb-county-school-bus-drivers-protest-sickout/|website=WABE|publisher=[[National Public Radio]]|access-date=May 2, 2018|date=April 19, 2018}}</ref> The strikes included an [[VCUarts adjunct workers' protests|adjunct faculty strike]] at [[Virginia Commonwealth University]]<ref>{{cite web|last1=Wilder|first1=Drew|title=VCUarts teachers protest for higher pay|url=https://www.nbc12.com/story/37618535/vcuarts-teachers-protest-for-higher-pay|website=[[WWBT]]|publisher=[[Raycom Media]]|access-date=May 7, 2018|date=February 28, 2018}}</ref> in [[Richmond, Virginia]], leading to an increase in adjunct wages.<ref name="Mattingly May 11">{{cite web|last1=Mattingly|first1=Justin|title=VCU raises tuition 6.4 percent for 2018-19|url=http://www.richmond.com/news/local/education/vcu-raises-tuition-percent-for/article_82ccbd62-c828-5fa5-99f8-d52ae50ed6c3.html|website=[[The Richmond Times-Dispatch]]|access-date=May 13, 2018|date=May 11, 2018}}</ref>

===Unionization in the high tech sector===
{{Main|Unionization in the tech sector#United States}}
The relatively new [[high tech]] sector, typically dealing with the creation, design, development, and engineering of computer hardware and software products, has typically not been unionized as it is considered white-collar jobs, often with high pay rates and benefits. There has been worker activism to try to get the employer to change their practices related to labor, such as a [[2018 Google walkouts|November 2018 walkout at Google]] by 20,000 employees to make the company change its policy on sexual harassment.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.nytimes.com/2018/11/01/technology/google-walkout-sexual-harassment.html | title = Google Walkout: Employees Stage Protest Over Handling of Sexual Harassment | first1 = Daisuke | last1= Wakabayashi |first2= Erin | last2= Griffith | first3= Amie | last3 = Tsang | first4=  Kate | last4 = Conger | date = November 1, 2018 | access-date=  February 18, 2020 | work = [[The New York Times]] }}</ref> However, these efforts have traditionally stopped short of the need for unionization, and achieving the scale of employee involvement to bring a union to their workplace can be difficult due to the numerous benefits these employees may already have and the blue-collar nature that union association may bring.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.nytimes.com/2019/07/08/technology/tech-companies-union-organizing.html | title=  Employee Activism Is Alive in Tech. It Stops Short of Organizing Unions. | first1 = Kate | last1 = Conger | first2= Noam | last2= Scheiber | date = July 8, 2019 | access-date = February 18, 2020 | work = [[The New York Times]] }}</ref>

One area where unionization efforts have become more intense is in the [[video game industry]]. Numerous publicized events since 2004 have revealed the excessive use of "[[Crunch (video games)|crunch time]]" at some companies; where there is a reasonable expectation in the industry that employees may be needed to put in more time near the release of a game product, some companies were noted for using a "crunch time" approach through much longer periods or as a constant expectation of their employees; further, most of those employed in the video game market are exempt from overtime, compounding the issue. Major grassroots efforts through the game industry since 2018 have promoted the creation of a new union or working with an existing union to cover the industry.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.theverge.com/2020/1/7/21055445/game-workers-union-cwa-union-partnership-tech-video-games-organizing | title = A massive telecom union just launched a new campaign to unionize game developers | first = Nick | last = Statt | date = January 7, 2020 | access-date = February 18, 2020 | work = [[The Verge]] }}</ref> One of the first high tech companies to establish a union was [[Kickstarter]], whose employees voted in favor of unionizing in February 2020.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.polygon.com/2020/2/18/21142349/kickstarter-union-board-games-video-games |title=Kickstarter employees vote to unionize, relieving tension among game developers |first=Charlie |last=Hall |date=18 February 2020 |access-date=18 February 2020 |website=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]}}</ref>

On April 1, 2022, [[Amazon (company)|Amazon]] workers at the JFK8 warehouse in [[Staten Island]], [[New York City]] voted in favor of a union, becoming [[Amazon worker organization|Amazon's first unionized workplace]] in the United States.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=O'Brien |first=Sara Ashley |date=April 1, 2022 |title=Amazon workers at New York warehouse vote to form company's first US union |url=https://www.cnn.com/2022/04/01/tech/amazon-union-election-staten-island/index.html |access-date=April 1, 2022 |website=[[CNN]] |language=en}}</ref>

=== Hollywood labor disputes, 2023 ===
{{Main|2023 Hollywood labor disputes}}
From May 2 to November 9, 2023, a series of long [[labor dispute]]s within the [[Cinema of the United States|film]] and [[Television in the United States|television]] industries of the United States took place, mainly focused on the strikes of the [[2023 Writers Guild of America strike|Writers Guild of America]] and [[2023 SAG-AFTRA strike|SAG-AFTRA]].<ref>Jerry Nickelsburg, "Hollywood Restructuring and the Writers and Actors Strikes of 2023" (UCLA Anderson School of Management, March 12, 2024) [https://www.anderson.ucla.edu/news-and-events/hollywood-restructuring-and-writers-and-actors-strikes-2023 online]</ref>

=== Unionization in the food service and grocery industries ===
The food service industry has one of the lowest unionization rates in the United States, with just 1.2% of workers belonging to a union in 2020 and 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |last=U.S. Department of Labor |first=Bureau of Labor Statistics |date=January 20, 2022 |title=Union Members — 2021 |url=https://www.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/union2.pdf }}</ref>

==== Starbucks ====
{{Further|Starbucks unions|List of Starbucks union petitions in the United States}}
In late 2021, a [[Starbucks]] store located in [[Buffalo, New York]], became Starbucks' only unionized location among 9,000 stores in the United States, joining Workers United of the [[Service Employees International Union]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Scheiber |first=Noam |date=2021-12-09 |title=Starbucks workers at a Buffalo store unionize in a big symbolic win for labor. |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/12/09/business/economy/buffalo-starbucks-union.html |access-date=2022-10-02 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> A second location in Buffalo followed, winning an election certified by the NLRB in January 2022. During this time, the number of stores filing petitions to the NLRB grew to over ten locations, seven of them being outside of the Buffalo area.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Scheiber |first=Noam |date=2022-01-10 |title=Union wins election at a second Buffalo-area Starbucks. |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/01/10/business/starbucks-union-election-buffalo.html |access-date=2022-10-02 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

The number of Starbucks stores that have decided to vote on unionization has since grown significantly. As of August 2022, 209 Starbucks locations have voted for unionization, with another 45 locations voting against unionization.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Schoolov |first=Katie |title=Unions are forming at Starbucks, Apple and Google. Here's why workers are organizing now |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/08/05/why-starbucks-apple-and-google-are-unionizing-now-for-the-first-time.html |access-date=2022-10-02 |website=CNBC |date=August 5, 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

==== Trader Joe's ====
{{Further|Trader Joe's unions}}
In late July 2022, workers at a [[Trader Joe's]] in [[Hadley, Massachusetts]], voted to become the first unionized location in the grocery store chain''.''<ref name=":03">{{Cite news |title=Trader Joe's workers vote to unionize for the first time |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2022/07/28/trader-joes-union/ |access-date=2022-10-02 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> Workers at this location chose to create an independent union called [[Trader Joe's unions|Trader Joe's United]], and received administrative and legal support from already existing unions, but decided not to become a part of any larger established union.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1st Trader Joe's union approved at Massachusetts store |url=https://www.boston.com/news/local-news/2022/07/28/trader-joes-workers-in-hadley-approve-union-drive/ |access-date=2022-10-06 |website=www.boston.com |date=July 28, 2022 |language=en-US}}</ref> Two locations, one in [[Boulder, Colorado]], and one in [[Minneapolis]], also filed for unionization around this time.<ref name=":03" /> On August 12, 2022, the Minneapolis location went on to become the second store to unionize, joining Trader Joe's United.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Scheiber |first=Noam |date=2022-08-12 |title=Trader Joe's Workers Vote to Unionize at a Second Store |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/08/12/business/economy/union-vote-trader-joes.html |access-date=2022-10-06 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Comparisons to the unionization efforts of Starbucks locations were made following the success of the Minneapolis vote, with workers of the two respective unions both publicly supporting one another.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Molla |first=Rani |date=2022-08-13 |title=Trader Joe's could be the next Starbucks |url=https://www.vox.com/recode/2022/8/13/23299622/trader-joes-starbucks-union-movement |access-date=2022-10-06 |website=Vox |language=en}}</ref>

As of September 23, 2022, workers in [[Brooklyn|Brooklyn, New York]], have petitioned for unionization with the NLRB, and would potentially become the third unionized location out of over 500 Trader Joe's stores.

==== Chipotle ====
In late June 2022, a [[Chipotle Mexican Grill]] restaurant in [[Augusta, Maine]], became the chain's first location to petition for a union election, looking to organize independently as Chipotle United, citing issues regarding understaffing as well as crew and food safety.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lucas |first=Amelia |title=Chipotle restaurant in Maine becomes chain's first to file for union election |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/06/23/chipotle-restaurant-in-maine-files-petition-for-union-election-.html |access-date=2022-10-11 |website=CNBC |date=June 23, 2022 |language=en}}</ref> In that same month, Chipotle decided to permanently close the location, leading to workers filing a complaint with the NLRB and accusing Chipotle of union-busting. Chipotle has denied such claims, and have stated that the company was unable to provide enough staffing for the location.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rogers |first=Amelia Lucas, Kate |title=Chipotle union files complaint with labor board after chain shutters Maine restaurant seeking to organize |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/07/20/chipotle-union-files-complaint-with-labor-board-after-unionizing-restaurant-shut-down.html |access-date=2022-10-11 |website=CNBC |date=July 20, 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

In late August 2022, workers at a Chipotle in [[Lansing, Michigan]], voted to unionize, becoming the fast food chain's first union in the United States.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Michigan Chipotle outlet the chain's first to unionize |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2022/08/25/chipotle-union-victory-fastfood-michigan/ |access-date=2022-10-02 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> Workers at this location voted 11 to three, opting to unionize with the [[International Brotherhood of Teamsters]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lucas |first=Amelia |title=Chipotle restaurant in Michigan votes to unionize, in a first for the chain |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/08/25/chipotle-restaurant-in-michigan-votes-to-unionize-in-a-first-for-the-chain.html |access-date=2022-10-11 |website=CNBC |date=August 25, 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

==Public-sector unions==
{{main|Public-sector trade unions in the United States}}
Labor unions generally ignored government employees because they were controlled mostly by the patronage system used by the political parties before the arrival of civil service.
Post Office workers did form unions. The [[National Association of Letter Carriers]] started in 1889 and grew quickly. By the mid-1960s it had 175,000 members in 6,400 local branches.<ref>{{cite book|author=Morris S. Ogul|title=Congress Oversees the Bureaucracy|url=https://archive.org/details/congressoversees00morr|url-access=registration|date=May 15, 1976|publisher=U. of Pittsburgh Press|page=[https://archive.org/details/congressoversees00morr/page/65 65]|isbn=9780822976097}}</ref>

Several competing organizations of postal clerks emerged starting in the 1890s. Merger discussions dragged on for years, until finally the NFPOC, UNMAPOC and others merged in 1961 as the [[United Federation of Postal Clerks]]. Another round of mergers in 1971 produced the [[American Postal Workers Union]] (APWU). In 2012 the APWU had 330,000 members.<ref>Gary M Fink, ed., ''Labor Unions'' (1977)  pp 291-94</ref> The various postal unions did not engage in strikes.

{{main|Boston Police Strike}}
Historian Joseph Slater, says, "Unfortunately for public sector unions, the most searing and enduring image of their history in the first half of the twentieth century was the Boston police strike. The strike was routinely cited by courts and officials through the end of the 1940s."<ref>Joseph Slater, "The Boston Police Strike'' in Aaron Brenner et al. eds. ''The Encyclopedia of Strikes in American History'' (2011) [https://books.google.com/books?id=EHzk54IjNpEC&pg=PA241]''</ref> Governor [[Calvin Coolidge]] broke the strike and the legislature took control of the police away from city officials.<ref>Francis Russell, ''A city in terror: Calvin Coolidge and the 1919 Boston police strike'' (Beacon Press, 1975)</ref>

The police strike chilled union interest in the public sector in the 1920s. The major exception was the emergence of unions of public school teachers in the largest cities; they formed the [[American Federation of Teachers]] (AFT), affiliated with the AFL. In suburbs and small cities, the [[National Education Association]] (NEA) became active, but it insisted it was not a labor union but a professional organization.<ref>Marjorie Murphy, ''Blackboard Unions: The AFT and the NEA, 1900-1980'' (1992)</ref>

===New Deal era===

In the mid-1930s efforts were made to unionize [[Works Progress Administration]] workers, but were opposed by President [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]].<ref>Chad Alan Goldberg, "Contesting the Status of Relief Workers during the New Deal The Workers Alliance of America and the Works Progress Administration, 1935-1941." ''Social Science History'' (2005) 29#3 pp: 337-371.</ref> Moe points out that Roosevelt, "an ardent supporter of collective bargaining in the private sector, was opposed to it in the public sector."<ref>{{cite book|author=Moe|title=Special Interest: Teachers Unions and America's Public Schools|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lDFz6oYRtuIC&pg=PA33|year=2011|page=33|publisher=Brookings Institution Press |isbn=978-0815721307}}</ref> Roosevelt in 1937 told the nation what the position of his government was: "All Government employees should realize that the process of collective bargaining, as usually understood, cannot be transplanted into the public service.... The very nature and purposes of government make it impossible for administrative officials to represent fully or to bind the employer in mutual discussions with government employee organizations.<ref>see [https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/ws/index.php?pid=15445#axzz1Jy35UQb9 "Letter on the Resolution of Federation of Federal Employees Against Strikes in Federal Service August 16, 1937"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151116002831/http://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/ws/index.php?pid=15445 |date=November 16, 2015 }}</ref>

==="Little New Deal" era===
Change came in the 1950s. In 1958 New York mayor [[Robert F. Wagner Jr.|Robert Wagner, Jr.]] issued an executive order, called "the little Wagner Act," giving city employees certain bargaining rights, and gave their unions with exclusive representation (that is, the unions alone were legally authorized to speak for all city workers, regardless of whether or not some workers were members.) Management complained but the unions had power in city politics.<ref>Anthony C. Russo, "Management's View of the New York City Experience," ''Proceedings of the Academy of Political Science'' Vol. 30, No. 2, "Unionization of Municipal Employees" (Dec. 1970), pp. 81-93 {{JSTOR|1173366}}</ref>

By the 1960s and 1970s public-sector unions expanded rapidly to cover teachers, clerks, firemen, police, prison guards and others. In 1962, President [[John F. Kennedy]] issued [[Executive Order 10988]], upgrading the status of unions of federal workers.<ref>David Schultz, ''Encyclopedia of public administration and public policy'' (2004) p. 143</ref>

===Recent years===
After 1960, public sector unions grew rapidly and secured good wages and high pensions for their members. While manufacturing and farming steadily declined, state- and local-government employment quadrupled from 4 million workers in 1950 to 12 million in 1976 and 16.6 million in 2009.<ref>US Census Bureau,  [https://www.census.gov/newsroom/releases/archives/governments/cb10-132.html "Census Bureau Reports State and Local Government Employment Remains at 16.6 Million" (press release Aug. 10, 2010)] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140811071727/http://www.census.gov/newsroom/releases/archives/governments/cb10-132.html |date=August 11, 2014 }}</ref>

In 2009, the US membership of public sector unions surpassed membership of private sector unions for the first time, at 7.9 million and 7.4 million respectively.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationalaffairs.com/publications/detail/the-trouble-with-public-sector-unions|title=The Trouble with Public Sector Unions|website=nationalaffairs.com|access-date=May 4, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180211145439/http://www.nationalaffairs.com/publications/detail/the-trouble-with-public-sector-unions|archive-date=February 11, 2018}}</ref>

In 2011, states faced a growing fiscal crisis and the Republicans had made major gains in the [[2010 United States elections|2010 elections]]. Public sector unions came under heavy attack [[2011 Wisconsin protests|especially in Wisconsin]], as well as Indiana, New Jersey and Ohio from conservative Republican legislatures.<ref>John Logan, "Is this the end for organised labour in the US?," [https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/cifamerica/2011/mar/11/us-unions-wisconsin guardian.co.uk, March 11, 2011] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151122100620/http://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/cifamerica/2011/mar/11/us-unions-wisconsin |date=November 22, 2015 }}</ref><ref>see [https://www.nytimes.com/roomfordebate/2011/02/18/the-first-blow-against-public-employees ''New York Times'' "Public employees"]</ref><ref>see [https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/special/politics/state-budget-crisis/index.html ''Washington Post,'' "Budget crisis"]</ref> Conservative [[State legislature (United States)|state legislatures]] tried to drastically reduce the abilities of unions to collectively bargain. Conservatives argued that public unions were too powerful since they helped elect their bosses, and that overly generous pension systems were too heavy a drain on state budgets.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Theda Skocpol|author2=Vanessa Williamson|title=The Tea Party and the Remaking of Republican Conservatism|url=https://archive.org/details/teapartyremaking0000skoc|url-access=registration|year=2012|publisher=Oxford UP|page=[https://archive.org/details/teapartyremaking0000skoc/page/192 192]|isbn=9780199912834}}</ref><ref>Richard B. Freeman and Eunice Han. "The war against public sector collective bargaining in the US." ''Journal of Industrial Relations'' (2012) 54#3 pp: 386-408.</ref>

A 2023 study published by [[Oxfam]] found that the United States ranks among the worst among developed countries for [[labour protection|labor protection]]s, including the right to organize, ranking 32 out of 38 among [[OECD]] countries.<ref>{{cite news |last=Ghilarducci|first=Teresa |date=June 14, 2023 |title=New Study: U.S. Tops Rich Nations As Worst Place To Work|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/teresaghilarducci/2023/06/14/new-study-us-tops-rich-nations-in-worst-place-to-work/?sh=403bcced3be6|work=Forbes |location= |access-date=July 27, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.oxfamamerica.org/explore/research-publications/where-hard-work-doesnt-pay-off/|title=Where hard work doesn't pay off: An index of US labor policies compared to peer nations|last=Henderson|first= Kaitlyn |date=May 3, 2023 |website= |publisher=Oxfam |access-date=July 27, 2023 |quote=}}</ref>

In March 2025 President [[Donald Trump]] signed an executive order that instructed many federal agencies to end collective bargaining with many federal unions.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Pager |first=Tyler |date=2025-03-28 |title=Trump Moves to End Federal Union Protections Across Government |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/28/us/politics/trump-unions-executive-order.html |access-date=2025-03-29 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The [[Second presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]] also launched a lawsuit against the [[American Federation of Government Employees]] seeking to invalidate existing federal collective bargaining agreements between federal agencies and federal unions arguing it constrains the executive branch.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kanu |first=Hassan Ali |date=2025-03-28 |title=Trump administration sues to end some federal workers' union contracts |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/03/28/federal-workers-unions-lawsuit-donald-trump-00257991 |access-date=2025-03-29 |website=POLITICO |language=en}}</ref>

==Analysis==
[[File:Number of workers involved in strikes, US Bureau of Labor Statistics.svg|thumb|[[List of striking US workers by year|Number of striking workers by year]], ''Bureau of Labor Statistics''|right|301x301px]]
According to labor historians, the US has the most violent labor history of any industrialized nation.<ref>Philip Taft and Philip Ross, "[https://books.google.com/books?id=9NQDAQAAIAAJ&pg=PA221 American Labor Violence: Its Causes, Character, and Outcome]," The History of Violence in America: A Report to the National Commission on the Causes and Prevention of Violence, ed. Hugh Davis Graham and Ted Robert Gurr, 1969. p. 221</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Goldstein |first=Robert Justin |date=2001 |title=Political Repression in Modern America |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2Za8lifq1mYC&pg=PA3 |location= |publisher=[[University of Illinois Press]] |page=3 |isbn=978-0252069642}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Lipold |first=Paul F. |date=2015 |title="Striking Deaths" at their Roots: Assaying the Social Determinants of Extreme Labor-Management Violence in US Labor History—1877–1947 |journal=[[Social Science History]] |volume=38 |issue=3–4 |pages=541–575 |doi=10.1017/ssh.2015.24 |s2cid=142526387 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Some historians have attempted to explain why a labor party did not emerge in the United States, in contrast to Western Europe.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691149349/why-is-there-no-labor-party-in-the-united-states |author1=Robin Archer |title=Why Is There No Labor Party in the United States? |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2007 |isbn=9780691149349 |access-date=2025-04-26}}</ref> Historian [[Gary Gerstle]] asserts that organized labor in the US was strongest when the fear of [[communism]] reached its peak, and the former's decline coincided with the collapse of the latter. Gerstle argues that capitalist elites were much less willing to compromise with the [[Working class in the United States|working class]] once the threat of communism disappeared and [[neoliberal]] [[capitalism]] became the dominant global system. He emphasizes that this analysis is not meant to rehabilitate communist governments, which he describes as tyrannies.<ref>{{cite book |last=Gerstle|first=Gary|author-link=Gary Gerstle|date=2022 |title=The Rise and Fall of the Neoliberal Order: America and the World in the Free Market Era|url=https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-rise-and-fall-of-the-neoliberal-order-9780197519646?cc=us&lang=en&|location= |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|page=12|isbn=978-0197519646}}</ref>  [[Elizabeth S. Anderson]] posits that with the end of the [[Cold War]] and the victory of "ostensibly" [[free markets]], there was a sharp decline of organized labor in the United States along with a collapse in academic and public discourse about the pervasiveness of "authoritarian private governments" in the form of large, hierarchal corporations birthed during the [[Industrial Revolution]], which was something that "organized workers of the nineteenth century saw clearly."<ref>{{cite book |last= Anderson|first=Elizabeth S.|date=2017 |title=Private Government: How Employers Rule Our Lives (and Why We Don't Talk about It)|publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |location= |isbn=978-0691192246|pages=33-41, 62 |url=https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691176512/private-government?srsltid=AU7gw4WyV1oESxuaIAB1enY-tpgwaehLgxAmVEPkM7jLxPCO5yQ1HFbI|access-date=}}</ref>

Labor historian [[Julie Greene (historian)|Julie Greene]] writes that the [[Second Gilded Age]] has seen the entrenchment of corporate power and the dismantling of labor movements, which has resulted in falling real wages and increased working class acquiescence to [[Exploitation of labour|exploitation]]. She argues that this is a key difference from the original [[Gilded Age]] when there was violent capital-labor conflict as working class people created powerful labor movements to improve wages and working conditions, which helped pave the way to what she describes as a "gentler capitalism" in the mid 20th century. According to Greene, the disappearance of any alternatives to capitalism globally, in particular the [[dissolution of the Soviet Union]] and China's [[Reform and opening up|economic liberalization]], has made the process of expanding corporate power and dismantling labor movements easier.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Greene|first1=Julie|author-link1= Julie Greene (historian)|date=April 2020|title=Bookends to a Gentler Capitalism: Complicating the Notion of First and Second Gilded Ages|url=|journal=[[The Journal of the Gilded Age and Progressive Era]] |volume=19 |issue=2 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|pages=197–205|doi=10.1017/S1537781419000628|pmc= |pmid= }}</ref>

==Labor Statistics==
The [[Bureau of Labor Statistics]], and the predecessor organizations it cites, have kept track of the number of striking workers per year since 1881.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dubofsky |first=Melvyn |year=1995 |title=Labor Unrest in the United States, 1906-90 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40241326 |journal=Review (Fernand Braudel Center) |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=125–135 |jstor=40241326 |issn=0147-9032}}</ref><ref name=":1a" /><ref name=":0a">{{Cite journal |title=Strikes in the United States, 1880-1936 : Bulletin of the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics, No. 651 |url=https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/files/docs/publications/bls/bls_0651_1938.pdf |journal=Bureau of Labor Statistics}}</ref><ref name=":02a">{{Cite web |title=Major Work Stoppages: 1947 - Present |url=https://www.bls.gov/web/wkstp/annual-listing.htm |access-date=2023-07-27 |website=bls.gov |language=en-us}}</ref><ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last= |first= |date=1976-01-01 |title=BLS Handbook of Methods for Surveys and Studies : Bulletin of the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics, No. 1910 |url=https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/title/bls-handbook-methods-surveys-studies-4661 |journal= |language=en |volume=Bureau of Labor}}</ref>

For data from 1881 to 1905 the Commissioner of Labor, then within the [[United States Department of the Interior|Department of Interior]] conducted four periodic surveys{{Efn|In 1887, 1894, 1901 & 1906}} covering that period. The data is considered likely un-comprehensive but still used the same definition of strikes as later periods. For this era, all strikes with more than six workers or less than one day were excluded.<ref name=":0a" />{{Rp|pages=2–3, 36}} No concrete data was collected for the amount of strikes from 1906 to 1913 federally.<ref name=":0a" />{{Rp|page=2–3|location=(8-9 in pdf)}} Data from 1915 to 1926 is more comprehensive.
