including [[utilities]], [[mail]], [[rail transport]], [[airline]]s, [[electrical power industry]], [[fossil fuels]], the [[chemical industry]], [[steel mill|steel mills]], [[electronics industry|electronics]], [[machine industry|machine]], [[aerospace manufacturer|aerospace manufacturing]], [[shipbuilding]], and the [[arms industry]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Bruening|first=Matt|date=5 August 2017|url=https://www.peoplespolicyproject.org/2017/08/05/nordic-socialism-is-realer-than-you-think/|title=Nordic Socialism Is Realer Than You Think|publisher=People's Policy Project|access-date=31 August 2021|archive-date=26 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210826105954/https://www.peoplespolicyproject.org/2017/08/05/nordic-socialism-is-realer-than-you-think/|url-status=live}}</ref> 

In 2013, ''[[The Economist]]'' described these countries as "stout free-traders who resist the temptation to intervene even to protect iconic companies", while also looking for ways to temper capitalism's harsher effects. It declared that the Nordic countries "are probably the best-governed in the world".<ref name="Economist leaders"/><ref name="Economist">{{cite news |url=https://www.economist.com/news/special-report/21570835-nordic-countries-are-probably-best-governed-world-secret-their |title=The secret of their success |newspaper=[[The Economist]] |date=2 February 2013 |access-date=21 December 2019 |archive-date=10 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171010033845/https://www.economist.com/news/special-report/21570835-nordic-countries-are-probably-best-governed-world-secret-their |url-status=live }}</ref> Some economists have referred to the Nordic economic model as "cuddly capitalism", with low levels of inequality, generous welfare states, and fewer top incomes, contrasting it with the US' more "cut-throat capitalism", which has high levels of [[Income inequality in the United States|inequality]].<ref name="nordicmodel" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://blogs.lse.ac.uk/europpblog/2014/01/29/lower-levels-of-inequality-are-linked-with-greater-innovation-in-economies/|title=Lower levels of inequality are linked with greater innovation in economies|first1=Jonathan|last1=Hopkin|author-link1=Jonathan Hopkin|first2=Victor|last2=Lapuente|first3=Lovisa|last3=Moller|date=29 January 2014|publisher=[[London School of Economics]]|access-date=27 June 2016|archive-date=19 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160219180907/http://blogs.lse.ac.uk/europpblog/2014/01/29/lower-levels-of-inequality-are-linked-with-greater-innovation-in-economies/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title = Social Democratic America|first=Kenworthy|last=Lane|author-link=Lane Kenworthy|year=2013|isbn=978-0-19-932252-7|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=eVTSAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA88 88]–93|location=New York City}}</ref>

In the early 21st century, the Nordic model was a market economic system that featured private ownership,<ref>{{cite book|chapter=Revisiting the Nordic Model: Evidence on Recent Macroeconomic Performance|last=Sachs|first=Jeffrey|year=2006|publisher=Center for Capitalism & Society, Venice Summer Institute|quote=First, like the Anglo-Saxon economies, the Nordic economies are overwhelmingly private-sector owned, open to trade, and oriented to international markets. Financial, labor, and product market forces operate powerfully throughout non-state sector. In short, these are capitalist economies. ... Second, there is no single Nordic model, and still less, an unchanging Nordic model. What has been consistently true for decades is a high level of public social outlays as a share of national income, and a sustained commitment to social insurance and redistributive social support for the poor, disabled, and otherwise vulnerable parts of the population.|doi=10.7551/mitpress/9780262015318.003.0012|title=Perspectives on the Performance of the Continental Economies|pages=387–412|isbn=978-0-262-01531-8}}</ref> with the exception of Norway, which included many [[state-owned]] enterprises and state ownership in public firms.<ref name="Norway: The rich cousin" />

As a result of the [[Sweden financial crisis of 1990–1994|Swedish financial crisis of 1990–1994]], Sweden [[deregulation|deregulated]] its economy and strengthened [[competition law]]s. Despite this, Sweden still has the highest government spending-to-GDP ratio among the Nordics. It retains national-level sectoral bargaining unlike [[Denmark]] and [[Iceland]], with over 650 national-level bargaining agreements.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://lo.se/english/the_collective_agreement | title=The Collective Agreement | date=6 May 2013 | access-date=21 December 2023 | archive-date=21 December 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231221130138/https://lo.se/english/the_collective_agreement | url-status=live }}</ref> It retains the [[Ghent system]], unlike [[Norway]] and Iceland and consequently has the world's second-highest unionization rate.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://nordics.info/show/artikel/solidaristic-wage-policy#:~:text=While%20wage%20solidarity%20remains%20a,greater%20range%20for%20wage%20dispersion | title=Solidaristic wage policy | date=18 February 2019 | access-date=20 December 2023 | archive-date=20 December 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231220022515/https://nordics.info/show/artikel/solidaristic-wage-policy#:~:text=While%20wage%20solidarity%20remains%20a,greater%20range%20for%20wage%20dispersion | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="auto">{{cite journal |series=[[Transfer (journal)|Transfer: European Review of Labour and Research]] |url=http://lup.lub.lu.se/luur/download?func=downloadFile&recordOId=155589&fileOId=625408 |format=pdf |via=Lund University |date=4 April 2006 |first=Anders |last=Kjellberg |title=The Swedish unemployment insurance – will the Ghent system survive? |journal=Transfer: European Review of Labour and Research |volume=12 |pages=87–98 |issn=1024-2589 |doi=10.1177/102425890601200109 |s2cid=153819218 |access-date=26 July 2016 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304062553/http://lup.lub.lu.se/luur/download?func=downloadFile&recordOId=155589&fileOId=625408 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Erlandsen|first1=Espen|last2=Lundsgaard|first2=Jens|year=2007|title=How Regulatory Reforms in Sweden Have Boosted Productivity|journal=OECD Economics Department Working Paper|series=OECD Economics Department Working Papers |location=Paris|publisher=OECD Publishing|issue=577|doi=10.1787/084244078600|doi-access=free}}</ref> As one of the most equal OECD nations, from 1985 to the 2010s Sweden saw the largest growth in income inequality among OECD economies.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://www.oecd.org/els/soc/dividedwestandwhyinequalitykeepsrising.htm|title=Divided We Stand: Why Inequality Keeps Rising|edition=paperback|location=Paris|publisher=OECD Publishing|date=2011|isbn=978-92-64-11163-9|access-date=30 June 2021|archive-date=9 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210709182745/https://www.oecd.org/els/soc/dividedwestandwhyinequalitykeepsrising.htm|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Nilsson|first=Patricia|date=29 August 2018|url=https://www.ft.com/content/3b9566e4-941a-11e8-b747-fb1e803ee64e|title=Swedish society's big divisions – in 6 charts|work=Financial Times|access-date=31 August 2021|archive-date=19 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211019034218/https://www.ft.com/content/3b9566e4-941a-11e8-b747-fb1e803ee64e|url-status=live}}</ref> Other effects of the 1990s reforms were the growth of [[mutual fund]] savings, which largely began with the Allemansfonder program in the 1980s in which the government subsidized savings;<ref>{{cite news|last=Hoikkala|first=Hanna|date=22 May 2019|url=https://www.bloombergquint.com/business/swedes-become-world-champions-with-100-stashing-cash-in-funds|title=Swedes Become World Champions With 100% Stashing Cash in Funds|website=BloombergQuint|agency=Bloomberg News|access-date=31 August 2021|archive-date=19 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211019034218/https://www.bloombergquint.com/business/swedes-become-world-champions-with-100-stashing-cash-in-funds|url-status=live}}</ref> As of 2019 4 out of 5 Swedes aged 18–74 have fund savings.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Heyman|first1=Fredrik|last2=Norbäck|first2=Pehr-Johan|last3=Persson|first3=Lars|date=24 June 2019|title=The Turnaround of the Swedish Economy: Lessons from Large Business Sector Reforms|journal=The World Bank Research Observer|volume=34|issue=2|pages=274–308|doi=10.1093/wbro/lky007|issn=0257-3032|hdl=10986/35085|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

==== Norway ====
Norway has ownership stakes in many of the country's largest listed companies, including 37% of the Oslo stock market.<ref name="Norway: The rich cousin"/> It operates some of the country's largest non-listed companies, including [[Equinor]] and [[Statkraft]]. In January 2013, ''[[The Economist]]'' reported, "after the Second World War the government nationalised all German business interests in Norway and ended up owning 44% of [[Norsk Hydro]]'s shares. The formula of controlling business through shares rather than regulation seemed to work well, so the government used it wherever possible. 'We invented the [[Socialist market economy|Chinese way of doing things]] before the Chinese', says Torger Reve of the Norwegian Business School."<ref name="Norway: The rich cousin"/> 

The government operates a sovereign wealth fund, the [[Government Pension Fund of Norway]], largely funded by oil revenues, whose partial objective is to prepare Norway for a post-oil future. However, "unusually among oil-producing nations, it is also a big advocate of human rights{{snd}}and a powerful one, thanks to its control of the Nobel Peace Prize."<ref name="Economist" />

Norway is the only major economy in Northern Europe where younger generations are getting richer, with a 13% increase in [[Disposable and discretionary income|disposable income]] for 2018, bucking the trend seen in other Northern European nations of [[millennials]] becoming poorer than the generations which came before.<ref>{{cite news|last=Savage|first=Maddy|date=10 July 2018|title=Unlike most millennials, Norway's are rich|url=http://www.bbc.com/capital/story/20180709-unlike-most-millennials-norways-are-rich|agency=BBC News|access-date=11 July 2018|archive-date=11 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180711013838/http://www.bbc.com/capital/story/20180709-unlike-most-millennials-norways-are-rich|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Social democracy ===
[[File:Social democratic parties in Nordic countries - percentage.svg|thumb|300px|Vote percentage over time of the main social democratic parties in Denmark, Finland, Sweden, and Norway:<ref name="BrandalEtAl2013">{{cite book |last1=Brandal |first1=Nik |title=The Nordic model of social democracy |last2=Bratberg |first2=Øivind |last3=Thorsen |first3=Dag |date=2013 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-1-349-43669-9 |page=2 |doi=10.1057/9781137013279}}</ref>{{rp|p=2}}
{{legend|#fd0100|[[Swedish Social Democratic Party]]}}
{{legend|#c10001|[[Labour Party (Norway)]]}}
{{legend|#fcc0bf|[[Social Democrats (Denmark)]]}}
{{legend|#ff7266|[[Social Democratic Party of Finland]]}}]]
''[[Social democracy]]'' is a centre-left, social, economic, predominantly capitalist political ideology. Social democrat parties long governed in Sweden and Norway, while in the others social democrat parties and others at times formed coalition governments.<ref name="Ferragini & Seeleib-Kaiser 2011">{{cite journal |last1=Ferragina |first1=Emanuele |last2=Seeleib-Kaiser |first2=Martin |date=October 2011 |title=Welfare Regime Debate: Past, Present, Futures? |url=https://halshs.archives-ouvertes.fr/halshs-01347336/file/Welfare_regime_debate.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Policy and Politics |publisher=Policy Press |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=583–611 |doi=10.1332/030557311X603592 |s2cid=146986126 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210729152045/https://halshs.archives-ouvertes.fr/halshs-01347336/file/Welfare_regime_debate.pdf |archive-date=29 July 2021 |access-date=29 July 2021}}</ref> Policies enacted by social democrats helped foster [[social cohesion]].<ref name="BrandalEtAl2013" />{{rp|pp=vi, 159}} 

While many countries have at times adopted social democracy, only the Nordic countries did so consistently.  

Since the 1990s politicians, researchers and the media have increasingly explained the Nordic model in cultural rather than political terms. Earlier interpretations of the welfare state were attributed to political developments. However, in later years political factors increased in importance.<ref name="Liukas 2019" />

=== Lutheran influence ===
[[Lutheranism]] is the [[religious tradition]] of the Nordic countries. It promoted the idea of a nationwide community of believers and led to increased state involvement in economic and social life.<ref>{{cite book|last=Schröder|first=Martin|year=2013|title=Integrating Varieties of Capitalism and Welfare State Research|location=London|publisher=Palgrave Macmillan|pages=96, 144–145, 149, 155, 157}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Markkola|first=Pirjo|editor1-last=Kettunen|editor1-first=Pauli|editor2-last=Petersen|editor2-first=Klaus|year=2011|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4ChHcCoq7f0C&pg=PA102|title=The Lutheran Nordic Welfare States|journal=Beyond Welfare State Models. Transnational Historical Perspectives on Social Policy|location=Cheltenham|publisher=Edward Elgar Publishing|pages=102–118|isbn=978-1-84980-960-3|via=Google Books|access-date=27 August 2020|archive-date=3 November 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231103161406/https://books.google.com/books?id=4ChHcCoq7f0C&pg=PA102#v=onepage&q&f=false|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=Kettunen>{{cite journal|last=Kettunen|first=Pauli|year=2010|url=https://helda.helsinki.fi/bitstream/handle/10138/41875/nordwel1.pdf?sequence=1#page=18|title=The Sellers of Labour Power as Social Citizens: A Utopian Wage Work Society in the Nordic Visions of Welfare|journal=NordWel Studies in Historical Welfare State Research|pages=16–45|access-date=11 January 2020|archive-date=5 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200805170126/https://helda.helsinki.fi/bitstream/handle/10138/41875/nordwel1.pdf?sequence=1#page=18|url-status=live}}</ref> 

Lutheran revival movements increased support for the modern welfare state, leading important social responsibilities (health care, education, and social work) to be absorbed by the state.<ref>{{Cite book|url = https://oa.finlit.fi/site/books/10.21435/sfh.25/read/?loc=On_the_Legacy_of_Lutheranism_in_Finland-19.xhtml|doi = 10.21435/sfh.25|title = On the Legacy of Lutheranism in Finland: Societal Perspectives|year = 2019|isbn = 978-951-858-135-5|editor1-last = Sinnemäki|editor1-first = Kaius|editor2-last = Portman|editor2-first = Anneli|editor3-last = Tilli|editor3-first = Jouni|editor4-last = Nelson|editor4-first = Robert H|access-date = 11 September 2020|archive-date = 23 October 2020|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20201023150219/https://oa.finlit.fi/site/books/10.21435/sfh.25/read/?loc=On_the_Legacy_of_Lutheranism_in_Finland-19.xhtml|url-status = live}}</ref><ref name="Kettunen" /><ref>{{cite book|last=Nelson|first=Robert H.|year=2017|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=j4FaDwAAQBAJ|title=Lutheranism and the Nordic Spirit of Social Democracy: A Different Protestant Ethic|location=Bristol|publisher=ISD|pages=21, 121|isbn=978-87-7184-416-0|via=Google Books|access-date=11 January 2020|archive-date=3 November 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231103161358/https://books.google.com/books?id=j4FaDwAAQBAJ|url-status=live}}</ref> This was made easier by the church's centralized structure, which made the transition less disruptive.<ref>{{cite book|last=Hilson|first=Mary|year=2008|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m_xi60bdHXoC&pg=PA112|title=The Nordic Model: Scandinavia since 1945|location=London|publisher=Reaktion Books|pages=112–133|isbn=978-1-86189-461-8|via=Google Books|access-date=28 February 2020|archive-date=3 November 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231103161358/https://books.google.com/books?id=m_xi60bdHXoC&pg=PA112#v=onepage&q&f=false|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Labour markets ===
The Nordic countries have similar labour market policies intended to reduce conflict between labour and business. This system is most extensive in Norway and Sweden, where employer federations and labour representatives bargain at the national level, mediated by the government. Labour market interventions emphasize job retraining and relocation.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Rosser|first1=Mariana V.|last2=Rosser Jr.|first2=J. Barkley|title=Comparative Economics in a Transforming World Economy|publisher=MIT Press|date= 2003|isbn=978-0-262-18234-8|page=226|quote=Liberal corporatism is largely self-organized between labor and management, with only a supporting role for government. Leading examples of such systems are found in small, ethnically homogeneous countries with strong traditions of social democratic or labor party rule, such as Sweden's Nordic neighbors. Using a scale of 0.0 to 2.0 and subjectively assigning values based on six previous studies, Frederic Pryor in 1988 found Norway and Sweden the most corporatist at 2.0 each, followed by Austria at 1.8, the Netherlands at 1.5, Finland, Denmark, and Belgium at 1.3 each, and Switzerland and West Germany at 1.0 each. ... [W]ith the exception of Iceland, all the Nordic countries have higher taxes, larger welfare states, and greater corporatist tendencies than most social market economies.}}</ref>

The Nordic labour market is flexible, with laws making it easy for employers to hire and shed workers or introduce technology. Labour market policies rely on generous social welfare, job retraining and relocation services to mitigate potential conflicts.{{cn|date=July 2026}}

In Sweden [[Trade union|trade unions]] and [[Employers' organization|employer organisations]] negotiate working conditions and [[Wage|pay]] without government involvement.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Den svenska arbetsmarknadsmodellen |url=https://www.svensktnaringsliv.se/medlem/den-svenska-arbetsmarknadsmodellen_1196133.html |access-date=6 March 2026 |website=Svenskt Näringsliv |language=sv}}</ref> Workers agree not to [[Strike action|strike]] while employers agree not to [[Lockout (industry)|lock them out]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=20 May 2015 |title=Den svenska modellen |url=https://www.kommunal.se/den-svenska-modellen |access-date=6 March 2026 |website=Kommunal |language=sv}}</ref> While some laws regulate basic labour rights, Sweden has no statutory [[minimum wage]]. Instead, pay is regulated through agreements. Should workers strike, the employer can claim [[Refusal of work|refusal to work]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ny lag om minimilöner i EU – varför är det ett hot mot löner i Sverige? |url=https://www.unionen.se/opinion/ny-lag-om-minimiloner-i-eu-varfor-ar-det-ett-hot-mot-loner-i-sverige |access-date=6 March 2026 |website=Unionen |language=sv}}</ref>Under a collective agreement, neither the trade union nor the employer is allowed to take any labour action such as strikes or lockouts until the agreement expires.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arbetsfred |url=https://www.saco.se/fortroendevald/material/ordlista-for-fortroendevalda/arbetsfred/ |access-date=6 March 2026 |website=www.saco.se |language=sv}}</ref> The two largest trade unions are [[Swedish Trade Union Confederation|Landsorganisationen]] (LO) and [[Swedish Confederation of Professional Associations|SACO]]. Both are [[Umbrella organization|umbrella organisations]] comprising 34 trade unions, representing occupations such as [[Bus driver|bus]] and [[Train driver|train drivers]], [[Construction worker|constructions workers]], [[Teacher|teachers]], [[industrial workers]], and [[Engineer|engineers]]. The main employer organisations are Sveriges Kommuner och Regioner (SKR) and [[Svenskt Näringsliv]], which represent companies in the [[public sector]] and the [[Private sector|private]]  and [[business sector|business sectors]], respectively.

=== Welfare model ===
The Nordic model is distinguished from others by its emphasis on maximising [[labour force participation]], promoting [[gender equality]], [[egalitarian|egalitarianism]], extensive benefits, income redistribution, and liberal use of expansionary fiscal policy.<ref name="Esping-Andersen">{{cite book |last=Esping-Andersen |first=G. |year=1991 |title=The three worlds of welfare capitalism |location=Princeton, New Jersey |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]]}}</ref>

The Nordic countries all share a broad commitment to [[social cohesion]], universal welfare provision, and maximising public participation in social decision-making. It is characterized by flexibility and innovation. Nordic welfare systems are mainly funded through government spending.<ref name="The Nordic Council">{{cite web |url=http://www.norden.org/en/about-nordic-co-operation/areas-of-co-operation/the-nordic-welfare-model/about-the-nordic-welfare-model |title=About the Nordic welfare model |author=The Nordic Council |publisher=Norden |access-date=2 April 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140407084537/http://www.norden.org/en/about-nordic-co-operation/areas-of-co-operation/the-nordic-welfare-model/about-the-nordic-welfare-model |archive-date=7 April 2014 }}</ref>

Nordic countries take different approaches to the administration of the welfare state. Denmark adopted [[private sector]] provision of public services and welfare, alongside an assimilation immigration policy. Iceland's welfare model is based on a "welfare-to-work" ([[workfare]]) model, while Finland relies on non-profits to play a significant role in [[elder care]]. Norway relies most extensively on public provision of welfare.<ref name="The Nordic Council"/>

==== Gender equality ====
Nordic countries maintain one of the smallest gaps in gender employment inequality of all OECD countries,<ref name=":0">{{cite journal|date=May 2018|title=Is the Last Mile the Longest?|url=https://www.oecd.org/els/emp/last-mile-longest-gender-nordic-countries-brief.pdf|journal=Nordic Council of Ministers|via=OECD|access-date=21 April 2019|archive-date=30 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190630135346/https://www.oecd.org/els/emp/last-mile-longest-gender-nordic-countries-brief.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> according to [[International Labour Organization]] standards.<ref name=":1">{{cite web|url=https://www.ilo.org/global/about-the-ilo/multimedia/maps-and-charts/enhanced/WCMS_556528/lang--en/index.htm|title=Which countries have the highest gender gap in the workplace?|website=International Labor Organization|date=6 June 2017|access-date=12 January 2020|archive-date=5 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200205224707/http://www.ilo.org/global/about-the-ilo/multimedia/maps-and-charts/enhanced/WCMS_556528/lang--en/index.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> They implemented many policies to promote gender equality; they were some of the first to forbade companies to dismiss women on grounds of marriage or motherhood. Mothers in Nordic countries are more likely to work than in any other region. Families enjoy supportive parental leave policies that compensate mothers and fathers for moving from work to home to care for their children.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nikk.no/en/about-nikk/background/family-policy-2009-2011/nordic-family-policies-between-quotas-and-freedom-of-choice/|title=Nordic family policies – between quotas and freedom of choice|last=Moustgaard|first=Ulrikke|date=19 October 2017|website=Nordic Information on Gender|access-date=1 April 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190523172621/https://www.nikk.no/en/about-nikk/background/family-policy-2009-2011/nordic-family-policies-between-quotas-and-freedom-of-choice/|archive-date=23 May 2019}}</ref> Work place policies vary from country to country, but Nordic countries support "continuous full-time employment"&nbsp;for both men and women, including single parents. Aside from support for parental leave, families benefit from subsidized [[early childhood education]] and care and activities for out-of-school hours for schoolchildren.<ref name=":0"/>

Nordic countries champion gender equality and corresponding women's employment. Between 1965 and 1990, Sweden's employment rate for working-age women (15–64) went from 52.8% to 81.0%.<ref name=":1"/> In 2016, nearly three out of every four women of working-age were in paid work. Women are the main users of parental leave (fathers use less than 30% of their allotment), while foreign women are under-represented.<ref name=":0"/>

==== Poverty reduction ====
The Nordic model has significantly reduced poverty.<ref>{{cite magazine |first=Kevin |last=Drum |date=26 September 2013 |url=https://www.motherjones.com/kevin-drum/2013/09/we-can-reduce-poverty-if-we-want-we-just-have-want |title=We Can Reduce Poverty If We Want To. We Just Have To Want To. |magazine=[[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]] |access-date=5 October 2013 |archive-date=16 November 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191116064014/https://www.motherjones.com/kevin-drum/2013/09/we-can-reduce-poverty-if-we-want-we-just-have-want/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2011, poverty rates before tax and transfers ranged from Finland (31.9%) to Iceland (21.6%), with Denmark ( 24.7%), Norway (25.6%), and Sweden (26.5%) in between. After tax and transfers, the poverty rates for the same year shrank to 7.5%, 5.7%, 6%, 7.7%,  and 9.7% respectively, averaging a reduction of 18.7 p.p.<ref name="compareyourcountry.org">{{cite web|url=http://www.compareyourcountry.org/inequality?cr=usa&lg=en|title=Compare your country – Income distribution and poverty|publisher=[[OECD]]|access-date=12 May 2015|archive-date=3 November 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231103161405/http://www.compareyourcountry.org/inequality?cr=usa&lg=en|url-status=live}}</ref> Compared to the United States, which has a pre-tax/transfer poverty level of 28.3% and post-tax/transer of 17.4% for a reduction of 10.9%, the effects of tax and transfers on poverty in all the Nordic countries are substantially bigger.<ref name="compareyourcountry.org"/> In comparison to France (27 percentage point reduction) and Germany (24.2% p.p reduction), taxes and transfers in the Nordic countries are smaller.<ref name="compareyourcountry.org"/>

== History ==
{{Scandinavia|Economy}}
During the [[Viking Age]] and [[High Middle Ages]], especially in [[Sweden]], royal power was initially weak.<ref>Peter Sawyer: ''The Making of Sweden''. 1988, pp. 3–4</ref> In areas outside the rule of the Swedish king, as well as in Iceland where the [[Icelandic Commonwealth]] was an unusually large and sophisticated peasant republic building on the same democratic traditions.<ref>Arnulf Krause: ''Die Welt der Wikinger''. Campus, Frankfurt/Main 2006, pp. 155–158</ref> Some historians argued that [[Gotland]] was a peasant republic before it was [[Battle of Visby|attacked by the Danes in 1361]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Staecker |first=Jörn |title=Prozesse der Normbildung und Normveränderung im mittelalterlichen Europa |date=2000 |publisher=Steiner |editor1-last=Ruhe |editor1-first=Doris |location=Stuttgart |page=149f |language=de |trans-title=Processes of norm formation and norm change in medieval Europe |chapter=Die normierte Bestattung – Gotlands Kirchfriedhöfe im Spiegel mittelalterlicher Normen und Gesetze |trans-chapter=The standardized burial – Gotland's church cemeteries as reflected in medieval norms and laws |editor2-last=Spieß |editor2-first=Karl-Heinz}}</ref> Central for the original Scandinavian democratic traditions was assemblies called the [[Thing (assembly)|Thing or Moot]].

The Nordic model began with a "grand compromise" between workers and employers spearheaded by farmer and worker parties in the 1930s. Following a period of economic crisis and class struggle, the grand compromise served as the foundation for the post-World War II Nordic model of welfare and labour market organization.<ref name="ThePoliticalOriginsofInequality1">{{cite book|last=Simon Reid|first=Henry|date=2015|title=The Political Origins of Inequality: Why a More Equal World Is Better for Us All|publisher=University of Chicago Press|page=132|isbn=978-0-226-23679-7|quote=The dynamics were slightly different in each country. The social welfare reforms that emerged out of the Kanslergae Agreement in Denmark in 1933 came at the height of the interwar economic crisis and was part of a wider compromise package to save the Danish economy. It was a coincidence, but a telling one, that on the same day that the agreement was ratified, Hitler was appointed Chancellor of the Reich in Berlin, convinced that he had a better way of saving the economy. In Sweden, the politics of grand compromise were pushed forward with the so-called Basic Agreement – essentially a commitment to the spirit of give-and-take in labour disputes – signed by the employer and labour union associations at the unprepossessing seaside retreat of Saltsjobaden in 1938 ... But in truth the Agreement was the foundation for the relative industrial harmony that would mark Scandinavian industrial relations throughout Europe's Golden Age. In Norway, the empowerment of women as well as workers was key. Women workers marched in 1905 and achieved limited suffrage in 1907, with full suffrage coming in 1913, some five years before it came to Sweden.}}</ref> Contrarily, a 2022 study reported that farmer Members of Parliaments consistently opposed generous welfare policies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rasmussen |first=Magnus Bergli |date=2022 |title=Farmers and the Origin of the Welfare State: Evidence from 308 Roll Call Votes between 1882 and 1940 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1467-9477.12222 |journal=Scandinavian Political Studies |volume=45 |issue=2 |pages=202–226 |doi=10.1111/1467-9477.12222 |issn=0080-6757 |access-date=11 March 2022 |archive-date=11 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220311035056/https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1467-9477.12222 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Another key element was a varying mixture of mainly social democratic, [[centrist]], and [[right-wing]] political parties. Social democratic parties played a larger role in Sweden and Norway, whereas in Iceland and Finland, right-wing political parties were more significant. Strong labour unions were important in all four countries.<ref name=":3">{{cite book|last1=Dolvik|first1=Jon Erick|last2=Flotten|first2=Tone|last3=Hippe|first3=Jon M.|last4= Jordfald|first4=Bard|title=The Nordic Model towards 2030: A New Chapter? NordMod2030|date=2015|isbn=978-82-324-0185-7|page=23|quote=The Nordic model therefore cannot exclusively be tied to social democratic party support and political dominance. In Sweden, Denmark and Norway, where the social democrats held power for large periods from the 1930s onwards, that description fits better than it does for Finland and Iceland, where centrist and right-leaning parties have set the terms of debate. But in these countries, too, the building of strong labour unions – in line with Walter Korpi's power resource mobilization thesis (Korpi 1981) – was crucial to the central role of labour and employer organizations in developing universal welfare schemes. A variety of modern social security programmes, whether sickness benefits or pensions, first appeared in negotiated collective agreements. It is moreover likely that inspirational ideas and learning experiences that passed between Nordic countries also transcended party lines within these countries. The political underpinnings of the Nordic model have thus been built on broadbased power mobilization and a higher degree of balance between the core interests in society than is evident in most other countries.}}</ref>

Social security and collective wage bargaining policies were rolled back following economic imbalances in the 1980s and financial crises in the 1990s which led to leaner budgetary policies, most pronounced in Sweden and Iceland. Nonetheless, welfare expenditure remained high compared to the European average.<ref name="NordicModelArrivalandDecline1">{{cite journal |last=Veggel |first=Noralv |year=2014 |title=The Nordic Model – Its Arrival and Decline |url=https://journalofbusiness.org/index.php/GJMBR/article/view/1472/1379 |journal=Global Journal of Management and Business Research: Administration and Management |volume=14 |issue=9 |pages=60–94 |issn=2249-4588 |access-date=30 March 2020 |archive-date=9 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201009194712/https://journalofbusiness.org/index.php/GJMBR/article/view/1472/1379 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Denmark ===
Social welfare reforms emerged from the [[Kanslergade Agreement]] of 1933 as part of a compromise package to save the Danish economy.<ref name=ThePoliticalOriginsofInequality1/> 

=== Finland ===
The [[early 1990s recession]] caused a deep crisis in Finland, and came amid the context of the [[dissolution of the Soviet Union|collapse of the Soviet Union]] and trade with the [[Eastern Bloc]]. Worse than Sweden, Finland's welfare state was weakened and no longer took the social-democratic middle ground, as several social welfare policies were dismantled.<ref name="Liukas 2019"/><ref name="Economy and Finance 1999 d937">{{cite web | title=Finland and the euro | website=Economy and Finance | date=1 January 1999 | url=https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/euro/eu-countries-and-euro/finland-and-euro_en | access-date=29 August 2023 | archive-date=12 September 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230912134254/https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/euro/eu-countries-and-euro/finland-and-euro_en | url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Iceland ===
Iceland in the late 2010s moved away from the Nordic model towards the [[economic liberal|liberal economic]] model of [[workfare]]. At the time, critics claimed that "70% of elderly people now live well below national subsistence criteria, while about 70% of those who live alone and in bad conditions are women."<ref>{{cite news|last=Demurtas|first=Alice|date=9 May 2018|url=https://grapevine.is/news/2018/05/09/iceland-no-longer-following-nordic-welfare-model/|title=Iceland No Longer Following Nordic Welfare Model|work=The Reykjavík Grapevine|access-date=31 August 2021|archive-date=31 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210831013308/https://grapevine.is/news/2018/05/09/iceland-no-longer-following-nordic-welfare-model/|url-status=live}}</ref> However, as of 2021, Iceland had the [[OECD]]'s lowest poverty rate, 4.9%.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021 |title=Government at a Glance 2021: Country Fact Sheet |url=https://www.oecd.org/gov/gov-at-a-glance-2021-iceland.pdf |website=[[OECD]] |access-date=24 June 2023 |archive-date=24 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230624235128/https://www.oecd.org/gov/gov-at-a-glance-2021-iceland.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Norway ===
For a period in the 1980s and the 1990s, Norway underwent more neoliberal reforms and [[marketization]] than Sweden, while still holding to the traditional foundations of the Nordic model.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Fagerberg|first1=Jan|last2=Cappelen|first2= Adne|last3= Mjøset|first3= Lars|last4=Skarstein|first4=Rune|date=May 1990|title= The Decline of Social-Democratic State Capitalism in Norway|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/271521097|journal=New Left Review|pages=60–94|access-date= 30 March 2020|quote=Norway has, together with Sweden, often been idealized as the most successful case of postwar social democracy...the neo-liberal 'blue wave' which rolled over Western Europe in the 1980s has had considerably greater impact in Norway than in Sweden, combining with the pressures of a destabilized international economy to threaten many of the postwar structures. This makes it easier to appreciate the earlier accomplishments of social democracy, but it also shows that the Nordic innovations often depended upon the convergence of specific national conditions with the dynamic phase of Western capitalism that lasted from 1945 to 1973.}}</ref>

Norway earned billions from its portion of [[North Sea oil]], which it used to fund the country's  [[sovereign wealth fund]].<ref name="Liukas 2019"/> As of 2007, the Norwegian state maintained ownership positions in key industrial sectors, including petroleum, natural gas, minerals, lumber, seafood and fresh water. The petroleum industry accounts for around a quarter of the country's [[gross domestic product]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Acher|first=John|url=https://uk.reuters.com/article/norway-economy-forecasts/update-1-statistics-norway-raises-07-gdp-outlook-cuts-08-idUKL0674675920070906|title=Update 1-Statistics Norway raises '07 GDP outlook, cuts '08|work=Reuters|date=6 September 2007|access-date=21 May 2020|archive-date=8 May 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200508062116/https://uk.reuters.com/article/norway-economy-forecasts/update-1-statistics-norway-raises-07-gdp-outlook-cuts-08-idUKL0674675920070906}}</ref>

=== Sweden ===
In Sweden, the Nordic model started with the [[Saltsjöbaden Agreement]] signed by employer and trade union associations in 1938. It was advanced by the [[Swedish Social Democratic Party]], which led the nation from 1932 until 1976. Initially differing little from other capitalist countries, the state's role in providing welfare and infrastructure expanded after WWII, reaching a broadly [[social democratic]] consensus in the 1950s which became known as [[social liberal]]<nowiki/>ism,<ref name=ThePoliticalOriginsofInequality1/> followed by the [[neoliberal]] paradigm by the 1980s and 1990s.<ref>{{cite book|last=Carson|first=Marcus|year=2004|title=From Common Market to Social Europe?: Paradigm Shift & Institutional Change in European Union Policy on Food, Asbestos & Chemicals, & Gender Equality|location=Stockholm|publisher=Stockholm University|page=231|isbn=978-91-22-02088-2}}</ref> 

In the 1950s, [[Olof Palme]] and prime minister [[Tage Erlander]] formulated the basis of Swedish social democracy, the "Swedish model". The party wanted to help workers, and adopted the [[Fabian Society|Fabian]] argument that the country could move to socialism. This would come about through [[welfare capitalism|welfare funded by capitalism]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Berman|first=Sheri|year=2006|title=The Primacy of Politics: Social Democracy and the Making of Europe's Twentieth Century|location=Cambridge|publisher=Cambridge University Press|page=156|isbn=978-1-139-45759-0}}</ref> It supported a strong labour movement as well as publicly funded and often publicly administered welfare institutions.<ref name=ThePoliticalOriginsofInequality1/>

By the early 1980s, the Swedish model began to suffer from trade imbalances, declining competitiveness, and capital flight. Two solutions emerged. The country could transition to socialism, [[Socialization as a process|socializing]] (taking ownership of) industry or commit capitalism and markets by embracing [[neoliberalism]]. The Swedish model was first challenged in 1976 by the [[Meidner Plan]] promoted by the [[Swedish Trade Union Confederation]] that aimed at the socialization of Swedish companies through wage earner funds. The Meidner Plan aimed to collectivize capital formation over two generations by having wage earner funds buy dominant stakes in Swedish corporations.<ref>{{cite book|last=O'Hara|first=Phillip|title=Encyclopedia of Political Economy: L–Z|publisher=Routledge|year=1999|isbn=978-0-415-15426-0|page=1248|quote=The critical issues were perhaps revealed most clearly in the Swedish case. Among the most advanced of the social welfare states, Sweden in the early 1980s faced a pivotal choice between capitalism and the transition to socialism. In the discourse focused upon its nagging problems of international imbalances, declining competitiveness, and capital flight, two polar solutions emerged. Olof Palme supported an aggressive use of workers' funds, by which capital formation would have been largely collectivized in two generations. The funds would have come to own predominant stakes in Swedish corporations on behalf of workers. The other alternative was to retrench the welfare state and provide conditions favorable to private capitals formation. Palme's proposal appears never to have garnered widespread support and was left with no champion in the wake of his assassination.}}</ref> A different type of wage earner fund was implemented following the success of the Social Democrats in the [[1982 Swedish general election|1982 election]]. They were disbanded after the [[1991 Swedish general election|1991 election]] when conservatives came to power.<ref>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120503162218/http://www.foretagsamheten.se/Naringslivets-utveckling/Historisk-oversikt/1980-talet/4-oktober-manifestationen/|url=http://www.foretagsamheten.se/Naringslivets-utveckling/Historisk-oversikt/1980-talet/4-oktober-manifestationen/ |archive-date=3 May 2012 |title=4 oktober-manifestationen |language=sv |trans-title=The Demonstration of October 4 |first=Bo |last=Ekegren}}</ref>

Upon returning to power in 1982, the Social Democratic party inherited a slowing economy following the post-war boom. The Social Democrats adopted [[monetarist]] and neoliberal policies, [[deregulating|deregulated]] the banking industry, and [[Economic liberalization|liberalized]] currency in the 1980s. The 1990s economic crisis brought greater [[austerity]] measures, deregulation, and [[privatization]] of public services.<ref name=ThePoliticalOriginsofInequality1/> In the 21st century, it affected Sweden's welfare state. Sweden remained more [[Eurosceptic]] than Finland, and its struggles affected other Nordics, as "the guiding star of the north". Other Nordic countries felt they were losing their political identities.<ref name="Liukas 2019"/> The Nordic model was gradually rediscovered, and cultural explanations were sought for the Nordic model.<ref name="Liukas 2019"/>

== Reception ==

=== Proponents ===
The Nordic model was positively received by some American politicians and political commentators. [[Jerry Mander]] likened the Nordic model to a kind of "hybrid" system that blends [[capitalist]] economics with [[socialist]] values, an alternative to [[Anglo-Saxon model|American-style capitalism]].<ref>{{cite magazine |author-link=Jerry Mander |first=Jerry |last=Mander |date=24 July 2013 |url=http://www.alternet.org/books/there-are-good-alternatives-us-capitalism-no-way-get-there?page=0%2C2 |title=There Are Good Alternatives to US Capitalism, But No Way to Get There |magazine=[[Alternet]] |access-date=27 July 2013 |archive-date=20 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171020041538/https://www.alternet.org/books/there-are-good-alternatives-us-capitalism-no-way-get-there?page=0%2C2 |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Vermont]] Senator [[Bernie Sanders]] claimed that the US could learn from the Nordic model, particularly worker benefits and social protections and its universal healthcare.<ref>{{cite news |last=Sanders |first=Bernie |date=26 May 2013 |url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/rep-bernie-sanders/what-can-we-learn-from-de_b_3339736.html |title=What Can We Learn From Denmark? |work=[[The Huffington Post]] |access-date=11 March 2014 |archive-date=10 December 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151210152900/http://www.huffingtonpost.com/rep-bernie-sanders/what-can-we-learn-from-de_b_3339736.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|first=Sasha|last=Issenberg|date=9 January 2010|url=http://archive.boston.com/news/local/vermont/articles/2010/01/09/sanders_a_growing_force_on_the_far_far_left/|title=Sanders a growing force on the far, far left|newspaper=[[Boston Globe]]|quote=You go to Scandinavia, and you will find that people have a much higher standard of living, in terms of education, health care, and decent paying jobs.|access-date=11 March 2014|archive-date=4 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140404153943/http://www.boston.com/news/nation/washington/articles/2010/01/09/sanders_a_growing_force_on_the_far_far_left/?page=1|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |first=Zeeshan |last=Aleem |date=4 May 2015 |url=http://mic.com/articles/117334/bernie-sanders-says-the-u-s-could-learn-a-lot-from-scandinavia-here-s-why-he-s-right |title=Bernie Sanders Says the U.S. Could Learn a Lot From Scandinavia. Here's Why He's Right |work=[[Mic (media company)|Mic]] |access-date=5 May 2015 |archive-date=5 May 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150505190042/http://mic.com/articles/117334/bernie-sanders-says-the-u-s-could-learn-a-lot-from-scandinavia-here-s-why-he-s-right |url-status=live }}</ref> Scandinavian political scientist Daniel Schatz argued that Sanders is wrong, saying that "the success of Nordic countries....has its roots in cultural rather than economic factors", particularly its "high levels of social trust, robust work ethic, and social cohesion".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Schatz |first=Daniel |date=15 March 2020 |title=I'm a Scandinavian political scientist. Bernie's wrong about democratic socialism. |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/think/opinion/bernie-sanders-wrong-democratic-socialism-sweden-everywhere-else-ncna1158636 |access-date=6 July 2023 |website=NBC News |language=en |archive-date=7 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230707162310/https://www.nbcnews.com/think/opinion/bernie-sanders-wrong-democratic-socialism-sweden-everywhere-else-ncna1158636 |url-status=live }}</ref>

According to [[Luciano Pellicani]], Nordic social and political measures are the same that some other European left-wing politicians theorised to combine ''justice and freedom'', referring to [[liberal socialism]] and movements like ''[[Giustizia e Libertà]]'' and ''[[Fabian Society]]''.<ref>{{cite news|last=Petti|first=Edoardo|url=https://formiche.net/2014/12/renzi-blair-parla-pellicani/|title=Le critiche di D'Alema alla Terza Via? Frutto della presunzione storica del Pci. Parla Pellicani|newspaper=Formiche.net|language=it|date=1 December 2014|access-date=28 February 2022|archive-date=21 February 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220221124810/https://formiche.net/2014/12/renzi-blair-parla-pellicani/|url-status=live}}</ref> According to Naomi Klein, former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev sought to move the Soviet Union in a similar direction to the Nordic system, combining free markets with a social safety net, but still retaining public ownership of key sectors of the economy – ingredients that he believed would transform the Soviet Union into "a socialist beacon for all mankind."<ref>{{cite book |author-link=Naomi Klein |last=Klein |first=Naomi |year=2008 |title=The Shock Doctrine: The Rise of Disaster Capitalism |publisher=[[Picador (imprint)|Picador]] |isbn=978-0-312-42799-3 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PwHUAq5LPOQC&pg=PA276 |page=276 |access-date=28 February 2020 |archive-date=3 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231103161401/https://books.google.com/books?id=PwHUAq5LPOQC&pg=PA276#v=onepage&q&f=false |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first1=Philip |last1=Whyman |first2=Mark |last2=Baimbridge |first3=Andrew |last3=Mullen |year=2012 |title=The Political Economy of the European Social Model (Routledge Studies in the European Economy) |publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=978-0-415-47629-4 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e-M_cdwdgoMC&pg=PA108 |page=108 |quote=In short, Gorbachev aimed to lead the Soviet Union towards the Scandinavian social democratic model. |access-date=28 February 2020 |archive-date=3 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231103161402/https://books.google.com/books?id=e-M_cdwdgoMC&pg=PA108#v=onepage&q&f=false |url-status=live }}</ref>

The Nordic model was positively received by left-wing social scientists and economists. American professor of sociology and political science [[Lane Kenworthy]] advocated for the US to follow the Nordic model.<ref>{{cite news |last=Matthews |first=Dylan |date=9 January 2014 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/wonkblog/wp/2014/01/09/this-sociologist-has-a-plan-to-make-america-more-like-sweden/ |title=This sociologist has a plan to make America more like Sweden |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |access-date=11 March 2014 |archive-date=14 January 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140114091917/http://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/wonkblog/wp/2014/01/09/this-sociologist-has-a-plan-to-make-america-more-like-sweden/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

American author [[Ann Jones (author)|Ann Jones]], who lived in Norway for four years, posits that "the Nordic countries give their populations freedom ''from'' the market by using capitalism as a tool to benefit everyone" whereas in the United States "[[neoliberal]] politics puts the foxes in charge of the henhouse, and capitalists have used the wealth generated by their enterprises (as well as financial and political manipulations) to capture the state and pluck the chickens."<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.thenation.com/article/archive/after-i-lived-in-norway-america-felt-backward-heres-why/ |title=After I Lived in Norway, America Felt Backward. Here's Why |journal=[[The Nation]] |date=28 January 2016 |access-date=21 December 2019 |archive-date=30 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200130013750/https://www.thenation.com/article/archive/after-i-lived-in-norway-america-felt-backward-heres-why/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences|Nobel Prize]]-winning economist [[Joseph Stiglitz]] stated that social mobility is higher in Scandinavian countries than in the United States and that Scandinavia had become the land of opportunity that the United States once was.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://money.cnn.com/2015/06/03/news/economy/stiglitz-income-inequality/index.html |title='Scandinavian Dream' is true fix for America's income inequality |work=CNN Money |date=3 June 2015 |access-date=21 December 2019 |archive-date=8 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200608125534/https://money.cnn.com/2015/06/03/news/economy/stiglitz-income-inequality/index.html }}</ref> 

Economist [[Jeffrey Sachs]] is a proponent, saying that the Nordic model is "the proof that modern capitalism can be combined with decency, fairness, trust, honesty, and environmental sustainability".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.globalhealthminders.dk/prof-jeffrey-sachs-plea-to-the-nordic-countries/ |title=Prof Jeffrey Sachs' plea to the Nordic countries |work=Global Health Minders |date=18 November 2015 |access-date=21 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190901042717/http://www.globalhealthminders.dk/prof-jeffrey-sachs-plea-to-the-nordic-countries/ |archive-date=1 September 2019 }}</ref> A 2016 survey by [[Israel Democracy Institute]] reported that nearly 60 percent of [[Israeli Jews]] preferred a "Scandinavian model" economy, with high taxes and a robust welfare state.<ref>{{cite news|last=Sales|first=Ben|title=Survey: Israeli Jews Want Broader Welfare State, Israeli Arabs Prefer 'American Model'|url=https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/1.721012|work=[[Haaretz]]|date=23 May 2016|access-date=21 December 2019|archive-date=20 October 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171020075457/https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/1.721012}}</ref>

=== Criticism ===
Socialist economists [[Pranab Bardhan]] and [[John Roemer]] stated that Nordic-style social democracy required a strong [[labour movement]] to sustain it and was not applicable to countries with weaker labour movements. They further questioned its sustainability given its decline in Scandinavia since the 1990s. They advocated that market-based government ownership would beat social democratic redistribution for promoting egalitarian outcomes.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Market socialism, a case for rejuvenation|first1=Pranab|last1=Bardhan|first2=Johen E.|last2=Roemer|year=1992|journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives|volume=6|number=3|page=104|quote=[W]e believe that social democracy requires rather special political circumstances that are absent in many countries for which our market socialism proposal may be feasible. Since it (social democracy) permits a powerful capitalist class to exist (90 percent of productive assets are privately owned in Sweden), only a strong and unified labor movement can win the redistribution through taxes that is characteristic of social democracy. It is idealistic to believe that tax concessions of this magnitude can be effected simply through electoral democracy without an organized labor movement, when capitalists organize and finance influential political parties. Even in the Scandinavian countries, strong apex labor organizations have been difficult to sustain and social democracy is somewhat on the decline now.|doi=10.1257/jep.6.3.101|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In a 2017 study, economists [[James Heckman]] and Rasmus Landersøn compared American and Danish social mobility, and found that Denmark ranked higher in income mobility, although Danish social mobility was lower than typically reported. Before taxes and transfers, Danish and American social mobility were similar, although after taxes and transfers Danish social mobility relatively improved, indicating that Danish economic redistribution was beneficial. However, Denmark's investment in public education did not improve the likelihood that children of non-college educated parents would attend college, although cognitive skills improved among poor Danish children compared to their American peers. Instead, generous welfare policies appeared to discourage higher-level education due to the reduced relative economic benefits from college education.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=James |last1=Heckman |first2=Rasmus |last2=Landersøn |title=The Scandinavian Fantasy: The Sources of Intergenerational Mobility in Denmark and the US |journal=[[Scandinavian Journal of Economics]] |volume=119 |issue=1 |year=2017 |pages=178–230 |doi=10.1111/sjoe.12219 |pmid=28649168 |pmc=5476927 |url=http://www.nber.org/papers/w22465.pdf |access-date=7 June 2017 |archive-date=22 July 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170722081621/http://www.nber.org/papers/w22465.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref>

Some welfare and gender researchers suggest that social issues associated with bodily integrity or bodily citizenship,<ref>{{cite book |last=Pringle |first=Keith |year=2016 |chapter=Doing (Oppressive) Gender via Men's Relations with Children |editor-last1=Häyrén |editor-first1=Anneli |editor-last2=Wahlström Henriksson |editor-first2=Helena |title=Critical Perspectives on Masculinities and Relationalities: In Relation to What? |location=New York |publisher=Springer |pages=23–34 |isbn=978-3-319-29011-9}}</ref> such as some forms of male domination continue in the Nordic countries, in areas of business, violence to women, sexual violence to children, the military, academia, and religion.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hearn|first1=Jeff|last2=Pringle|first2=Keith|year=2006|title=European Perspectives on Men and Masculinities: National and Transnational Approaches|location=Houndmills|publisher=Palgrave Macmillan|isbn=978-0-230-59447-0}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Pringle|first=Keith|year=2011|chapter=Comparative Studies of Well-Being in Terms of Gender, Ethnicity and the Concept of Bodily Citizenship: Turning Esping-Andersen on His Head?|editor-last1=Golańska|editor-first1=Dorota|editor-last2=Hearn|editor-first2=Jeff|editor-last3=Olesky|editor-first3=Elżbieta H.|title=The Limits of Gendered Citizenship: Contexts and Complexities|location=London|publisher=Routledge|pages=137–156|isbn=978-0-415-85126-8}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Balkamar|first1=Dag|last2=Hearn|first2=Jeff|last3=Pringle|first3=Keith|year=2018|chapter=Men, Masculinities and Social Policy|editor-last=Shaver|editor-first=Sheila|title=Handbook of Gender and Social Policy|location=Oxford|publisher=Edward Elgar|pages=55–73|isbn=978-1-78536-712-0}}</ref>

While praising the Nordic model as a "clear and compelling contrast to the neoliberal ideology that has strafed the rest of the world with inequality, ill-health and needless poverty," economic anthropologist [[Jason Hickel]] sharply criticizes the "ecological disaster" that accompanies it, noting that data shows the Nordic countries "have some of the highest levels of resource use and CO2 emissions in the world, in consumption based terms, drastically overshooting safe planetary boundaries," and rank towards the bottom of the Sustainable Development Index. He argues that the model needs to be updated for the [[Anthropocene]], and reduce [[overconsumption]] while retaining the positive elements of progressive social democracy including universal healthcare and education, paid vacations and reasonable working hours, which have resulted in much better health outcomes and poverty reduction compared to overtly neoliberal countries like the United States, in order to "stand as a beacon for the rest of the world in the 21st century."<ref>{{cite news|last=Hickel|first=Jason|date=6 December 2019|title=The dark side of the Nordic model|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2019/12/6/the-dark-side-of-the-nordic-model|work=Al Jazeera|location=|access-date=29 June 2022|archive-date=29 June 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220629180110/https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2019/12/6/the-dark-side-of-the-nordic-model|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sullivan |first1=Dylan |last2=Hickel|first2=Jason|date=2023 |title=Capitalism and extreme poverty: A global analysis of real wages, human height, and mortality since the long 16th century|url= |journal=[[World Development (journal)|World Development]]|volume=161 |issue= |article-number=106026 |doi=10.1016/j.worlddev.2022.106026|s2cid=252315733 |quote=...amongst the developed capitalist countries, the social democracies with generous welfare states (i.e., Scandinavia) have superior health outcomes to neo-liberal states like the US. Poverty alleviation and gains in human health have historically been linked to socialist political movements and public action, not to capitalism.|doi-access=free |bibcode=2023WoDev.16106026S }}</ref>

Swedish economist John Gustavsson criticized the Nordic model for its high taxation rates, including on the middle and lower classes.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gustavsson |first=John |date=12 October 2021 |title=Why the Nordic Model Wouldn't Work in the U.S. |url=https://thedispatch.com/article/why-the-nordic-model-wouldnt-work/ |access-date=18 June 2023 |website=The Dispatch |language=en-US |archive-date=18 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230618204400/https://thedispatch.com/article/why-the-nordic-model-wouldnt-work/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Misconceptions ===
[[George Lakey]] claimed that Americans misunderstand the Nordic model: "Americans imagine that 'welfare state' means the U.S. welfare system on steroids....Nordics provide...universal services, which means everyone{{snd}}rich and poor{{snd}}gets free higher education, free medical services, free eldercare, etc".<ref>{{cite news|url=http://americamagazine.org/content/all-things/continuing-revelation-scandinavian-economies|title=The "Continuing Revelation" of Scandinavian Economies|work=America|date=22 July 2016|access-date=21 December 2019|archive-date=1 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190901042717/https://www.americamagazine.org/content/all-things/continuing-revelation-scandinavian-economies|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Lars Løkke Rasmussen]], the Danish prime minister from the conservative-liberal [[Venstre (Denmark)|Venstre]] party, stated: "I know that some people in the US associate the Nordic model with some sort of socialism. Therefore, I would like to make one thing clear. Denmark is far from a socialist planned economy. Denmark is a market economy."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.vox.com/2015/10/31/9650030/denmark-prime-minister-bernie-sanders|title=Denmark's prime minister says Bernie Sanders is wrong to call his country socialist|website=Vox|date=31 October 2015|access-date=21 December 2019|archive-date=4 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200204164216/https://www.vox.com/2015/10/31/9650030/denmark-prime-minister-bernie-sanders|url-status=live}}</ref>
