======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Economic policy of the Biden administration
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=September 2024}}
{{Joe Biden series|expanded=Policies}}

The '''economic policy of the Joe Biden administration''', colloquially known as '''Bidenomics''' (a [[portmanteau]] of ''Biden'' and ''economics''), is characterized by relief measures and vaccination efforts to address the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], investments in infrastructure, and strengthening the social safety net, funded by tax increases on higher-income individuals and corporations. Other goals include increasing the [[minimum wage in the United States|national minimum wage]] and expanding worker training, narrowing [[income inequality]], expanding access to affordable healthcare, and forgiveness of student loan debt.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Tankersley |first1=Jim |title=Biden Team Prepares $3 Trillion in New Spending for the Economy |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/03/22/business/biden-infrastructure-spending.html |work=The New York Times |date=March 22, 2021}}</ref> The March 2021 enactment of the [[American Rescue Plan Act of 2021|American Rescue Plan]] to provide relief from the [[Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States|economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic]] was the first major element of the policy. Biden's [[Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act]] was signed into law in November 2021 and contains about $550 billion in additional investment, to repair infrastructure like roads, bridges and water pipes and expand passenger rail and broadband. Biden signed two additional major pieces of longer-term economic legislation to boost [[semiconductor]] investments and public basic research, and expand green energy and health insurance subsidies.<ref name="Baker-2024">{{Cite magazine |last=Baker |first=Dean |date=July 29, 2024 |title=The Biggest Success Story the Country Doesn't Know About |url=https://newrepublic.com/article/184223/biden-administration-success-story-country-doesnt-know |access-date=July 31, 2024 |magazine=The New Republic |issn=0028-6583}}</ref>

The first year of the [[Presidency of Joe Biden|Biden presidency]] (2021) saw strong growth in real GDP, wages, employment, stock market returns, and household net worth, coupled with an increase in inflation, as the economy recovered from the [[COVID-19 recession|pandemic recession]] of 2020. During 2022–2023, the unemployment rate averaged 3.6%. By April 2024, the unemployment rate had remained below 4.0% for the longest sustained period since 1953.<ref name="U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics">{{cite web|url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/UNRATE|title=Civilian Unemployment Rate|last=U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics|date=January 1, 1948|website=FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis|access-date=June 4, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Sainato |first1=Michael |title=US adds 175,000 April jobs as hiring slows and unemployment stays steady |url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/article/2024/may/03/us-april-jobs-report |work=The Guardian |date=May 3, 2024|quote=It was the 40th straight month of job gains in the US and the 27th consecutive month with the unemployment rate below 4% – the longest such streak since 1953.}}</ref> Monthly job creation averaged a robust 402,000 from inauguration through February 2024, or 273,000 from June 2022, when the pre-pandemic jobs level was regained.<ref name="Jobs_Payems">{{cite web|url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PAYEMS|title=All Employees, Total Nonfarm|last=FRED|date=December 28, 2021|website=FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis|access-date=December 28, 2021}}</ref> However, past this point unemployment continued to increase to 4.3% in July 2024.<ref name="U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics"/> [[2021-2022 inflation surge|Inflation]] increased up to 9.0% (measured vs. a year earlier) in June 2022, then began falling. By June 2023 inflation was 3.1% and remained around that level through June 2024. As of November 2024, the inflation rate was 2.7%, with rent price increases contributing roughly half.<ref name="Baker-2024" /> While inflation was similar to peer countries, the U.S. has outgrown its peers.<ref name="Baker-2024" /> The Federal Reserve rapidly raised a [[Federal funds rate|key interest rate]] from March 2022 until August 2023, and is expected to lower interest rates in the second half of 2024.<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://apnews.com/video/federal-reserve-system-inflation-government-policy-financial-services-national-35c30ca18ab84c64b4177224340907b1 |title=The Federal Reserve sees cooler inflation and slower job market, suggesting a rate cut is nearing |language=en |access-date=August 3, 2024 |via=apnews.com}}</ref> The stock market repeatedly broke record highs in 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Choe |first=Stan |date=May 24, 2024 |title=Stock market today: Nasdaq sets another record as Wall Street wins back earlier losses |url=https://apnews.com/article/stock-market-inflation-rates-aa1af5469c3b931245bfc4bdc1b4e9ee |access-date=August 3, 2024 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref>

''[[The New Republic]]'' praised Biden's economic record in July 2024, highlighting how record low unemployment led to wage growth at the lower half of the distribution. In October 2024, 35% of households with incomes below $50,000 a year were living paycheck to paycheck, up from 32% in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-24 |title=A quarter of U.S. households live paycheck to paycheck, analysis finds - CBS News |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/paycheck-to-paycheck-definition/ |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}}</ref> The expansion of the [[Affordable Care Act]], the [[Child tax credit (United States)|child tax credit]], $1400 [[Stimulus (economics)|stimulus]] checks, and the expansion of [[Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program|SNAP]] benefits also boosted balance sheets for low and middle-income Americans.<ref name="Baker-2024" /> New business formation rose 30% from pre-pandemic levels, with a disproportionate rise among women, including women of color.<ref name="Baker-2024" /> Biden appointed [[Lina Khan]] as chair of the [[Federal Trade Commission|FTC]]; her initiatives involved an [[New Brandeis movement|expansion of antitrust enforcement]].<ref name="Baker-2024" /> The administration also pursued lower drug prices by allowing Medicare to negotiate the prices it pays and capping the price of [[Insulin (medication)|insulin]].<ref name="Baker-2024" />

Surveys have also found most Americans view their own economic situation positively and rate their local and state economies as doing better than the national economy,<ref name="Ip-2024" /> hinting at a disconnect fueled more by media narrative.<ref name="Baker-2024" /> For example, a March 2024 CBS News poll found that 65% of Americans viewed the economy under Biden's predecessor (and eventual successor), [[Donald Trump]], as good, whereas only 38% expressed a similar positive opinion of the current economy under Biden.<ref name="Anne Marie Lee-2024" /> However, [[Exit poll|exit polls]] of voters in the 2024 presidential election found that 45% of voters stated their personal financial situation was worse than in 2020, which exceeded the 42% number in the 2008 election and was the highest since the question was asked. Only 24% of voters said their personal economic situation was better. This negative perception was credited for Trump's reelection.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Exit polls 2024: Deep economic discontent with Biden drove voters to Trump|url=https://abc7ny.com/post/2024-exit-polls-abc-poll-shows-fears-american-democracy-economic-discontent-drive-voters/15514059/|website=ABC7 New York|date=2024-11-05|access-date=2025-12-01|language=en}}</ref>

==Overview==
President Biden described his economic philosophy via Twitter in June 2023: "Bidenomics is about growing the economy from the middle out and the bottom up, not the top down. It's an economic vision where we make smart investments in America, educate and empower American workers, and promote competition to lower costs and help small businesses."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://twitter.com/POTUS/status/1674076443607719943|title=Bidenomics|publisher=Twitter.com|access-date=June 28, 2023}}</ref>

===2021===
President Biden inherited a challenging economic and budgetary situation from President [[Donald Trump]], due significantly to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United States|COVID-19 pandemic]]. As of December 2020, the jobs level was nearly 10 million (6%) below the early 2020 peak, and the [[Unemployment in the United States|unemployment rate]] was an elevated 6.7%.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/empsit.pdf|title=The Employment Situation – December 2020|publisher=[[United States Department of Labor]]|date=January 8, 2021|access-date=January 20, 2021}}</ref> There was a record budget deficit in fiscal year 2020 of $3.1 trillion, or 14.9% GDP.<ref name="MBR_FY2020">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/56661|title=Monthly Budget Review for September 2020|publisher=cbo.gov|date=September 2020|access-date=January 22, 2021}}</ref>

Biden's first major legislative response was the [[American Rescue Plan Act of 2021|American Rescue Plan Act]] enacted in March 2021, a $1.9 trillion package that included $1,400 checks per adult, an expanded child tax credit for a year with $250–300 monthly checks per child expected to drastically reduce [[child poverty]], extended unemployment benefits, and expanded eligibility for healthcare benefits, among others. The primary impact was in fiscal year (FY) 2021, with a smaller impact in FY 2022. No Republicans in the House of Representatives or the Senate voted for the Rescue Act.

Biden followed-up with the [[Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act]], signed into law in November 2021. It authorized infrastructure investment of $1 trillion total over a decade for roads, bridges, airports, sea ports, rail, broadband, water, and public transit, among others. CBO estimated the deficit impact at $250 billion total, as they considered prior infrastructure investment trends as a baseline for comparison. The law passed the Senate in bi-partisan fashion, 69–30.<ref name="NPR_Infra1"/>

Real GDP grew 5.9% during Biden's first year, the fastest rate since 1984.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Mutikani |first1=Lucia |title=U.S. economic growth revised up; gap between GDP and GDI narrows sharply |url=https://www.reuters.com/markets/us/us-economic-growth-revised-up-gap-between-gdp-gdi-narrows-sharply-2022-09-29/ |publisher=Reuters |date=September 29, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Tappe |first1=Anneken |title=The US economy grew at the fastest rate in 2021 since the Reagan administration |url=https://www.cnn.com/2022/01/27/economy/us-fourth-quarter-2021-gdp/index.html |publisher=CNN |date=January 27, 2022}}</ref> Amid record job creation, the unemployment rate fell at the fastest pace on record during Biden's first year, from 6.4% in January 2021 to 3.9% by December 2021.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Mutikani |first1=Lucia |title=U.S. labor market eyes maximum employment despite underwhelming December payrolls |url=https://www.reuters.com/markets/us/us-employment-growth-misses-expectations-unemployment-rate-falls-39-2022-01-07/ |publisher=Reuters |date=January 7, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Pickert |first1=Reade |title=U.S. Sees Record Job Growth in 2021 After Millions Lost in 2020 |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-01-07/u-s-sees-record-job-growth-in-2021-after-millions-lost-in-2020 |publisher=Bloomberg News |date=January 7, 2022}}</ref> However, [[2021–2023 inflation surge|inflation significantly increased in 2021]] relative to 2020 in the U.S. and Europe, attributed to factors such as strong consumer demand for goods (empowered by government relief programs), supply restrictions in port capacity and microchips, and lower 2020 prices.<ref>{{cite news |title=2022 Economic Outlook|url=https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/pages/outlook-2022-the-long-road-to-higher-rates.html|work=Goldman-Sachs|date=November 10, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Fastest inflation in 31 years puts more heat on Washington|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/10/business/economy/consumer-price-inflation-october.html|work=New York Times|date=November 12, 2021|author=Jeanna Smialek}}</ref>

Inflation was partially offset by strong wage growth; by [[Employment cost index|one measure]], worker wages and benefits increased at the fastest rate in at least 20 years.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Tan |first1=Weizhen |title=Goldman economist says it's tough to sustain wage gains of 5% to 6% without 'meaningfully high' inflation |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/01/25/goldman-sachs-chief-economist-on-wage-gains-inflation-in-the-us.html |publisher=CNBC |date=January 25, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Rubin |first1=Gabriel T. |title=U.S. Wages, Benefits Rose at Two-Decade High as Inflation Picked Up |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/us-employers-labor-costs-inflation-11643331612 |work=The Wall Street Journal |date=January 28, 2022}}</ref> The administration noted that high inflation was also present in the [[Eurozone]], Canada and the United Kingdom, though economists said the $5 trillion in government stimulus spending in the United States during 2020 and 2021 was disproportionately large compared to that of other countries and was a significant contributor to domestic inflation.<ref>{{cite news |title=Rapid Inflation Fuels Debate Over What's to Blame: Pandemic or Policy |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/01/22/business/economy/inflation-biden-pandemic.html |work=The New York Times |date=January 22, 2022|author1=Jeanna Smialek|author2=Ana Swanson}}</ref>

Despite the pandemic and inflation challenges, ''[[Bloomberg News]]'' reported in November 2021 that the S&P 500 stock market return of 37.4% in Biden's first year (measured from election day) was the highest of any modern president.<ref>{{cite news |title=S&P 500 Is Up 37% Since Biden's Election One Year Ago, Setting Presidential Record |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-11-03/s-p-500-notches-best-one-year-run-after-a-presidential-election |work=Bloomberg News |date=November 3, 2021|author1=Emily Graffeo |author2=Lu Wang}}</ref> The stock market gains and significant housing price increases contributed to record household net worth of $142 trillion by Q4 2021.<ref name="Households; Net Worth, Level">{{Cite web|url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BOGZ1FL192090005Q|title=Households; Net Worth, Level|publisher=fred.stlouisfed.org|access-date=June 11, 2023}}</ref>

The budget deficit in fiscal year (FY) 2021, the last year budgeted by President Trump, was $2.8 trillion, down from $3.1 trillion in FY 2020.<ref name="Households; Net Worth, Level"/>

===2022===
[[File:Inflation rate, United States and eurozone, January 2018 through June 2023.png|thumb|330px|Inflation rate, United States and eurozone, January 2018 through June 2023]]

A global [[2021–2023 inflation surge|inflation surge]] that began in 2021 and peaked in June 2022 before declining through 2023 and into 2024.

The unemployment rate averaged 3.6% in 2022, the lowest since 1969.<ref name="Unemployment Rate">{{Cite web|url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/Unrate|title=Unemployment Rate|publisher=fred.stlouisfed.org|access-date=June 11, 2023}}</ref> The number of persons working regained the pre-pandemic peak in June 2022 after revisions, and continued to set records monthly thereafter, reaching 154.5 million by December 2022, with monthly job creation averaging a robust 400,000.<ref name="All Employees, Total Nonfarm">{{Cite web|url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PAYEMS|title=All Employees, Total Nonfarm|publisher=fred.stlouisfed.org|access-date=July 29, 2022}}</ref>

In July 2022, ''The Wall Street Journal'' reported that "Household finances are as strong as they've been in decades, thanks to money saved during the pandemic, debt paid off over the past decade and a strong job market." As of Q1 2022, households had also accumulated $5 trillion more in deposit, savings and money market accounts than pre-pandemic. However, some measures of consumer sentiment indicated near record low satisfaction with the economy, mainly due to inflation.<ref>{{cite news |title=People have money but feel glum|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/people-have-money-but-feel-glumwhat-does-that-mean-for-economy-11657808195 |work=Wall Street Journal |date=July 14, 2022|author1=Jon Hilsenrath|author2=Rachel Wolfe}}</ref>

Biden said in May 2022 that "Bringing down the deficit is one way to ease inflationary pressures in an economy." The budget deficit fell by $350 billion in FY 2021. It fell by $1.4 trillion in FY 2022, about 50%, or $1.8 trillion (66%) excluding student loan forgiveness of $425 billion, which CBO had scored as spending but later was blocked by court rulings.<ref name="CBO_Nov22">{{cite web|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/58592|title=CBO Monthly Budget Review: Summary for Fiscal Year 2022|date=November 2022|website=cbo.gov|access-date=December 10, 2022}}</ref>

During July 2022, there was much media discussion regarding whether the U.S. had entered a recession, despite a strong labor market with low unemployment and robust job creation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/07/28/business/economy/gdp-q2-economy.html|title=U.S. Economy Shows Another Decline, Fanning Recession Fears|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=July 28, 2022|access-date=July 29, 2022}}</ref> The real (inflation-adjusted) GDP level fell slightly during Q1 and Q2 2022, but then rebounded in Q3 2022 to surpass the previous record level set in Q4 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPC1|title=Real Gross Domestic Product|publisher=[[US Bureau of Economic Analysis]]|access-date=July 29, 2022}}</ref> Some countries use two negative quarters as the definition of a recession. However, the [[National Bureau of Economic Research]] (NBER) is the organization that declares an economic peak and starting point of recessions in the U.S.{{clarify|date=May 2025}}{{citation needed|date=May 2025}} They reference six key measures in their analyses.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nber.org/business-cycle-dating-procedure-frequently-asked-questions|title=Business Cycle Dating Procedure: Frequently Asked Questions|publisher=[[National Bureau of Economic Research]]|access-date=July 29, 2022}}</ref> All six measures increased from December 2021 to November 2022, signs of growth rather than recession.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/?graph_id=1071332|title=Custom FRED Graph|publisher=fred.stlouisfed.org|access-date=July 29, 2022}}</ref> Predictions of an imminent recession continued through 2023, but by October indicators showed economic acceleration and analysts revised their economic forecasts upward; a ''Wall Street Journal'' survey of economists that month found a recession was not foreseen in the coming twelve months.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Harrison |first1=David |title=The Economy Was Supposed to Slow by Now. Instead It's Revving Up. |url=https://www.wsj.com/economy/the-economy-was-supposed-to-slow-by-now-instead-its-revving-up-3c0f7a2e |work=The Wall Street Journal |date=October 23, 2023|quote=Recent economic data suggest the economy is accelerating despite higher borrowing costs, the resumption of student-loan payments, and wars in Ukraine and the Middle East ... Analysts, many of whom had expected a recession this year, are pushing up their forecasts ... After predicting a recession for the past year, economists surveyed by The Wall Street Journal this month said they now believe that the economy will avoid a downturn in the next 12 months.}}</ref>

During August 2022, Biden signed into law the [[CHIPS and Science Act]] and [[Inflation Reduction Act of 2022|Inflation Reduction Act]].

Concerns regarding inflation resulted in the Federal Reserve raising interest rates significantly during 2022, to slow the economy, specifically the "very strong" labor market. Strong household financial positions, rapid wage growth, low unemployment, and a record ratio of open jobs to unemployed were cited by Fed officials as key inflationary concerns. The December 2022 Fed forecast projected an increase in unemployment from 3.7% in November 2022 to 4.6% by the end of 2023, with the Fed driving unemployment higher through raising interest rates and other measures.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcpresconf20221214.htm|title=December 13–14, 2022 FOMC Meeting|publisher=Federal Reserve|access-date=December 28, 2022}}</ref>

The number of persons without health insurance under age 65 fell from 31.2 million in 2020 under President Trump, to 27.0 million during the first half of 2022 under President Biden, a reduction of 3.2 million or 13%. The percentage of uninsured fell from 11.5% to 9.9% during that time. Both the number and % were record lows for data back to 1997.<ref name="NCHS_H122"/>

===2023===
[[File:Prosperity Matrix - August 2024.png|thumb|400px|Average unemployment rate and real (inflation-adjusted) hourly wages by U.S. president, LBJ to Biden. As of August 2024, Biden had the best average readings for both measures among these presidents.]]
Widespread predictions of the economy entering a recession in 2023 proved unfounded.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Peck |first1=Emily |title=Why everyone was so wrong about the 2023 economy |url=https://www.axios.com/2023/12/22/2023-economy-predictions-wrong-recession |work=Axios |date=December 22, 2023}}</ref> Real gross domestic product grew 2.5% in 2023, significantly outpacing growth in all other [[G7]] nations.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Cox |first1=Jeff |title=The U.S. economy grew at blistering 3.3% pace in Q4 while inflation pulled back |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/25/gdp-q4-2023-the-us-economy-grew-at-a-3point3percent-pace-in-the-fourth-quarter.html |publisher=CNBC |date=January 25, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Real Gross Domestic Product |url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/A191RL1A225NBEA |publisher=Bureau of Economic Analysis |date=January 25, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Irwin |first1=Neil |title=U.S. winning world economic war |url=https://www.axios.com/2024/01/31/us-economy-2024-gdp-g7-nations |work=Axios |date=January 31, 2024}}</ref> Real GDP growth averaged a robust 3.4% during the first three years of the Biden presidency.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Galston |first1=William |title=Inflation and the gap between economic performance and economic perceptions |url=https://www.brookings.edu/articles/inflation-and-the-gap-between-economic-performance-and-economic-perceptions/ |publisher=Brookings Institution |date=March 25, 2024}}</ref>

The labor market was strong in 2023. The unemployment rate averaged a very low 3.6% in 2023, as it had in 2022; the last year with an average 3.5% unemployment rate was 1969.<ref name="Unemployment Rate"/> The number of persons with jobs continued setting records monthly as it had since June 2022 when the pre-pandemic peak was regained, reaching 157.3 million in December 2023. An average of 251,000 jobs per month were added in 2023, a total of 3.0 million.<ref name="All Employees, Total Nonfarm"/>

Wage gains exceeded inflation in 2023, with real (inflation-adjusted) hourly earnings for all employees increasing 0.8% from December 2022 to December 2023.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/realer_01112024.htm|title=Real Earnings News Release|date=January 11, 2024|publisher=bls.gov|access-date=March 16, 2024}}</ref> The inflation rate measured vs. one year earlier was 6.4% in January 2023 and 3.1% in December as the [[disinflation|inflation rate slowed]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL|title=CPI All Inflation|publisher=fred.stlouisfed.org|access-date=June 11, 2023}}</ref> Census data released in January 2024 showed that record-high new business applications were filed in 2023, the third consecutive annual record high.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gruver |first1=Ed |title=SBA reports new business applications reach record high numbers |url=https://www.cpbj.com/sba-reports-new-business-applications-reach-record-high-numbers/ |work=Central Penn Business Journal |date=January 12, 2024}}</ref>

CBO reported the budget deficit increased from $1,376 billion (5.4% GDP) in fiscal year (FY) 2022 to $1,695 billion (6.3% GDP) in FY 2023, an increase of $319 billion or 23%.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/59710|title=The Budget and Economic Outlook: 2024–2034|date=February 7, 2024|publisher=cbo.gov|access-date=March 11, 2024}}</ref>

During May, Republicans threatened to not raise the U.S. [[United States debt ceiling|debt ceiling]], risking a possible debt default. President Biden signed the [[Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023]] on June 3, 2023, to avert a potential crisis. The law restricts some spending for two years, imposes new work requirements on older Americans receiving food aid, and reduces barriers to some infrastructure and energy projects.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/biden-signs-bipartisan-bill-that-suspends-debt-limit-until-2025-cuts-spending|title=Biden signs bipartisan bill that suspends debt limit until 2025, cuts spending|date=June 3, 2023 |publisher=pbs.org|access-date=June 11, 2023}}</ref>

With Republicans in control of the House of Representatives, no significant economic legislation was passed. Only 27 bills were signed into law during 2023, the least since the Great Depression.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://spectrumnews1.com/oh/columbus/news/2023/12/21/congress-ineffective-2023?|title=Congress only passed 27 bills that were signed into law in 2023, the least since the Great Depression|date=June 3, 2023 |publisher=spectrumnews1.com|access-date=March 11, 2024}}</ref>

In 2023, the administration also pursued lower drug prices by allowing Medicare to negotiate the prices it pays and capping the price of [[Insulin (medication)|insulin]].<ref name="Baker-2024"/>

=== 2024 ===
In 2024, the number of persons with jobs continued setting records monthly, reaching 159.3 million in November, about 7.0 million jobs above the pre-pandemic peak, which had been regained in June 2022.<ref name="Jobs_Payems"/> The unemployment rate increased from 3.7% in January to 4.2% in November.<ref name="U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics"/> The stock market (S&P 500 Index) increased 29% from December 2023 to November 2024, using monthly average levels.<ref name="S&P 500"/> Real (inflation-adjusted) hourly wages increased from $30.29 in January to $30.57 in November, among the highest readings for data back to 1964, indicating robust purchasing power despite inflation in 2021–2022.<ref name="Real Hourly Wages per Hour">{{cite web|url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/?graph_id=590242&rn=461|title=Real Average Hourly Earnings of Production and Non-Supervisory Employees, Total Private|date=March 16, 2024|website=fred.stlouisfed.org|access-date=March 16, 2024}}</ref>

For data through November 2024, President Biden on average had the lowest unemployment rate (4.12%) and highest real hourly wages for production & non-supervisory workers ($30.11) among presidents back to 1964.<ref name="Real Hourly Wages per Hour"/><ref name="U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics"/>

In 2024, Biden pushed to limit [[junk fees]] through the FTC, [[Federal Communications Commission|FCC]] and [[Consumer Financial Protection Bureau|CFPB]].<ref name="Narea-2024">{{Cite web |last=Narea |first=Nicole |date=August 13, 2024 |title=Biden wants to free you from all those subscriptions you meant to cancel but didn't |url=https://www.vox.com/policy/366838/biden-subscription-membership-junk-fees |access-date=August 14, 2024 |website=Vox |language=en-US}}</ref> Biden has taken antitrust more seriously than presidents in recent memory, as seen by the work of [[Lina Khan]] at the [[Federal Trade Commission|FTC]],<ref name="Baker-2024" /> a historic court victory [[United States v. Google LLC (2020)|against Google's search monopoly]], and a [[United States v. Live Nation Entertainment|lawsuit]] to break-up [[Live Nation Entertainment|Live Nation]] and [[Ticketmaster]].<ref name="Narea-2024" />

In February 2024, the total [[National debt of the United States|federal government debt]] grew to $34.4 trillion after having grown by approximately $1 trillion in both of two separate 100-day periods since the previous June.<ref>{{cite news|last=Fox|first=Michelle|date=March 1, 2024|title=The U.S. national debt is rising by $1 trillion about every 100 days|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2024/03/01/the-us-national-debt-is-rising-by-1-trillion-about-every-100-days.html}}</ref> However, the ratio of debt held by the public to GDP fell from 97.1% in Q1 2021 when Biden started to 95.2% in Q2 2024, as growth outpaced debt increases.<ref name="DHBP to GDP">{{cite web|url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FYGFGDQ188S|title=Federal Debt Held by the Public as Percent of Gross Domestic Product|website=fred.stlouisfed.org|access-date=October 16, 2024}}</ref>

In August 2024, the [[United States Department of Justice|DOJ]] filed an [[anti-trust]] lawsuit against [[RealPage]] alleging that it was allowing [[landlord]]s across the United States to engage in [[price fixing]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Vogell |first=Heather |date=August 23, 2024 |title=DOJ Files Antitrust Suit Against Maker of Rent-Setting Algorithm |url=https://www.propublica.org/article/realpage-lawsuit-doj-antitrustdoj-files-antitrust-suit-against-maker-of-rent-setting-algorithm |access-date=August 24, 2024 |website=ProPublica |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Vogell |first1=Heather |last2=Coryne |first2=Haru |last3=Little |first3=Ryan |date=October 15, 2022 |title=Rent Going Up? One Company's Algorithm Could Be Why. |url=https://www.propublica.org/article/yieldstar-rent-increase-realpage-rent |access-date=August 21, 2024 |website=ProPublica |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Sisco |first=Josh |date=March 20, 2024 |title=DOJ escalates price-fixing probe on housing market |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/03/20/rental-housing-market-doj-investigation-00147333 |work=Politico}}</ref>

CBO reported in July 2024 that Biden's immigration surge was forecast to add nearly 9 million immigrants to the economy between 2021 and 2026, above the pre-2020 trend. CBO estimated this would add about $9 trillion to GDP or national income ($65,000 per household) over the 2024-2034 period, with wages 3% cumulatively higher by 2034 than without the surge. The budget deficits would be reduced by nearly $1 trillion, with $1.2 trillion more revenue partially offset by $0.3 trillion more spending.<ref name="CBO_Immigration Surge">{{cite web|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/60165|title=Effects of the Immigration Surge on the Federal Budget and the Economy|website=cbo.gov|access-date=July 14, 2025}}</ref>

The Census Bureau reported that real (inflation-adjusted) median household income was $83,730 in 2024, the highest on record. The 2024 poverty rate of 10.6% was the second lowest on record and one of only two years with a poverty rate below 11.0%. The uninsured rate of 8.0% was tied for 2nd lowest on record.<ref name="Census_2024">{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025/income-poverty-health-insurance-coverage.html|title=Income, Poverty and Health Insurance Coverage in the United States:2024|website=census.gov|access-date=September 21, 2025}}</ref>

==Key legislation==
===American Rescue Plan Act===
{{Main|American Rescue Plan Act of 2021}}

[[File:0 ARPA 2021 Infographic.png|thumb|right|330px|American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 – Infographic]]

Biden's $1.9 trillion relief package, the American Rescue Plan Act, was signed into law in March 2021. Many observers identified it to be the largest social welfare initiative undertaken by the federal government in decades, and economists predict low income households will benefit the most from the plan.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Fowers|first1=Alyssa|last2=Long|first2=Heather|last3=Schaul|first3=Kevin|date=March 10, 2021|title=How big is the Biden stimulus bill? And who gets the most help?|language=en-US|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2021/03/10/how-big-is-biden-stimulus/|access-date=March 11, 2021|issn=0190-8286}}</ref> Analysts also predict that the adult [[Poverty in the United States|poverty rate]] could be cut by a quarter, and the child poverty rate cut by half as a result of its passage.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Tankersley|first=Jim|date=March 6, 2021|title=To Juice the Economy, Biden Bets on the Poor|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/03/06/business/economy/biden-economy.html|access-date=March 11, 2021|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

The key elements of the Rescue Act include:

*$1,400 direct payments to individuals earning up to $75,000 a year;
*Extending expanded unemployment benefits through the end of September 2021;
*Increased the value and expanded eligibility for the [[child tax credit (United States)|child tax credit]]; to $3,600 per child under age 6 and $3,000 per child ages 6–17, up from $2,000. An estimated 39 million families with children will receive the additional benefits. Payments are scheduled monthly for July to December 2021, with the remaining six months of benefits due when the tax return is filed for 2021. The credit was changed from non-refundable to refundable, meaning those with low income who previously didn't have sufficient tax liability to receive the credit, will now receive the payment. This is a one-year program, that the administration hopes to make permanent.<ref>{{Cite news|title=New Monthly Child Tax Credits Are Starting To Go Out. Here's What It Means For Your Family|work=npr.org|url=https://www.npr.org/2021/05/17/997698543/new-monthly-child-tax-checks-will-hit-bank-accounts-july-15-what-you-need-to-kno?|access-date=July 20, 2021}}</ref>
*$130 billion to primary and secondary schools;
*$45 billion in rental, mortgage, and utility assistance;
*Billions for small businesses;
*$14 billion for a national vaccine program, including preparation of community vaccination centers;
*$350 billion to help state, local, and tribal governments bridge budget shortfalls.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Cochrane|first=Emily|date=March 6, 2021|title=Divided Senate Passes Biden's Pandemic Aid Plan|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/03/06/us/politics/biden-stimulus-plan.html|access-date=March 11, 2021|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

The [[Tax Policy Center]] reported that the law would cut taxes by an average of $3,000 per household and raise after-tax incomes by an average of 3.8% in 2021, with 70% of the benefit going to lower- and middle-income households. This is in sharp contrast to the [[Tax Cuts and Jobs Act]], in which half of the benefits went to the top 5% highest income households.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Pandemic Bill Would Cut Taxes by An Average of $3,000, With Most Relief Going to Low- And Middle-Income Households|language=en-US|work=taxpolicycenter.org|url=https://www.taxpolicycenter.org/taxvox/pandemic-bill-would-cut-taxes-average-3000-most-relief-going-low-and-middle-income-households|access-date=April 25, 2021}}</ref>

===Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act===
[[File:Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act Summary.png|thumb|right|400px|Investment categories ($ billion) in the [[Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act]] of 2021, adding to about $550 billion<ref name="NPR_Infra1"/>]]
The [[Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act]] is a key pillar in Biden's American Jobs Plan. It passed the House and Senate and was signed into law on November 15, 2021. While referred to as the $1 trillion infrastructure plan, it includes $550 billion in additional spending beyond previous legislation and was scored by the CBO to add about $250 billion to the deficit over a decade. It includes investments for: Roads and bridges ($110B), power infrastructure ($73B), passenger and freight rail ($66B), broadband ($65B), clean drinking water ($55B), western water storage ($50B), public transit ($39B), Airports ($25B), water & soil purification ($21B), ports ($17B), electric vehicles ($15B) and transportation safety programs ($11B).<ref name="NPR_Infra1">{{Cite news|title=Biden says final passage of $1 trillion infrastructure plan is a big step forward|language=en-US|work=NPR|url=https://www.npr.org/2021/11/05/1050012853/the-house-has-passed-the-1-trillion-infrastructure-plan-sending-it-to-bidens-des|date=November 6, 2021}}</ref> As of September 2024, over 60,000 projects funded by the law were underway across the U.S.<ref name="DOT_Infra1">{{Cite news|title=INVESTING IN AMERICA: At 60K Projects and Counting, USDOT Celebrates Biden-Harris Administration's Progress on Implementing the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law|language=en-US|work=DOT|url=https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/investing-america-60k-projects-and-counting-usdot-celebrates-biden-harris|date=September 18, 2024}}</ref>

===CHIPS and Science Act===
The [[CHIPS and Science Act]] passed the House and Senate with bi-partisan support during July 2022 and was signed into law by Biden on August 9, 2022. Biden said: “America invented the semiconductor. It’s time to bring it home.” ''The New York Times'' reported that it is valued at $280 billion and is designed to help strengthen America's manufacturing and technology capabilities, including "$200 billion for scientific research, especially into artificial intelligence, robotics, quantum computing, and a variety of other technologies."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/07/27/us/politics/senate-chips-china.html |title=Senate Passes $280 Billion Industrial Policy Bill to Counter China|work=[[The New York Times]] |date=July 27, 2022|access-date=July 30, 2022}}</ref>

CNBC reported that it includes $52 billion for U.S. companies producing computer chips, plus additional tax credits to encourage chip manufacturing in the U.S. This was in response to a pandemic-related chip shortage, disrupting auto production and driving up car prices and inflation. Further, most chips are manufactured in Taiwan, which increases the risk of disruption should China intervene there.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/07/28/china-competitiveness-and-chip-bill-passes-house-goes-to-biden.html |title=House passes bill to boost U.S. chip production and China competition, sending it to Biden |publisher=CNBC.com |date=July 30, 2022|access-date=July 30, 2022}}</ref>

The White House issued a press release stating: "The CHIPS and Science Act is exactly what we need to be doing to grow our economy right now. By making more semiconductors in the United States, this bill will increase domestic manufacturing and lower costs for families. And, it will strengthen our national security by making us less dependent on foreign sources of semiconductors. This bill includes important guardrails to ensure that companies receiving tax payer dollars invest in America and that union workers are building new manufacturing plants across the country."<ref>{{Cite web| url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/07/28/statement-from-president-biden-on-house-passage-of-chips-and-science-act-to-lower-costs-create-good-pay-jobs-and-strengthen-our-national-security/|title=House Passage of CHIPS and Science Act to Lower Costs, Create Good-Pay Jobs and Strengthen Our National Security|publisher=[[White House]]|date=July 28, 2022|access-date=July 30, 2022}}</ref>

===Inflation Reduction Act===
[[File:Inflation-reduction-act-50.png|thumb|right|330px|Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) Summary]]

The [[Inflation Reduction Act of 2022|Inflation Reduction Act]] passed the House and Senate using [[Reconciliation (United States Congress)|reconciliation]] along party lines in August 2022. President Biden signed it into law on August 16. [[Vox Media|Vox]] reported that key objectives include:
*Reduce [[Greenhouse gas emissions|carbon emissions]] significantly through climate protection incentives. This includes tax credits and rebates for renewable technologies (e.g., solar, wind and electric vehicles). It uses incentives rather than penalties primarily.
*Improve health insurance coverage and affordability, by extending ACA subsidy enhancements scheduled to expire in 2022 by three years through 2025. These helped an estimate 7 million people get free health insurance.
*Lower healthcare costs by allowing Medicare to negotiate [[Prescription drug prices in the United States|drug prices]] for key drugs and cap insulin costs for Medicare patients at $35 per month. This does not apply to private insurance.
*Enhance tax enforcement, by investing $80B in the IRS over a decade on systems and personnel. CBO estimates an additional $200B in collections over a decade.
*Increase corporate taxes, by implementing a 15% minimum tax applied to accounting income and a 1% tax on [[stock buybacks]]. The Act does not directly increase taxes on individuals.<ref>{{Cite news|title=The Inflation Reduction Act, explained|language=en-US|work=vox.com|url=https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2022/7/28/23282217/climate-bill-health-care-drugs-inflation-reduction-act|date=August 11, 2022}}</ref>

The CBO estimated the Act would reduce the budget deficit by about $100 billion over a decade, or $300 billion if enhanced IRS collections are included. CBO also reported that the Act would have little impact on inflation, as shifting money from corporations to healthcare subsidies would boost the economy approximately as much as the deficit decrease would slow it.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Estimated Budgetary Effects of H.R. 5376, the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022|language=en-US|work=cbo.gov|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/58366|date=August 3, 2022}}</ref>

The [[Tax Policy Center]] estimated that the bottom 80% tax filers by income would receive a net benefit, if ACA premium tax credits (subsidies) are included. The 80th–99th percentile would incur a small cost (0-0.1% increase in average federal tax rate) while the top 1% would incur a 0.2% increase. The costs mainly are imposed indirectly as corporations facing higher taxes may reduce the wage increases or levels for workers; individual tax rates were not changed.<ref>{{Cite news|title=The Inflation Reduction Act Primarily Impacts Top 1 Percent of Taxpayers|language=en-US|work=taxpolicycenter.org|url=https://www.taxpolicycenter.org/taxvox/inflation-reduction-act-primarily-impacts-top-1-percent-taxpayers|date=August 11, 2022}}</ref>

==Plans and legislative strategies==
===American Jobs Plan===
{{Main|American Jobs Plan}}

[[File:Job Growth by U.S. President - v1.png|thumb|right|400px|Job growth by U.S. president, measured as cumulative percentage change from month of inauguration (period 0) to end of term. Measured through the end of his term, President Biden had the second fastest cumulative job creation at month 48 of any president from Carter to present, at +11.3%, behind Carter at +12.8%.]]
In March 2021, Biden proposed a $2.65 trillion infrastructure package known as the American Jobs Plan with investments over 10 years, fully paid for by corporate tax increases over 15 years. A White House fact sheet described the plan: "This is the moment to reimagine and rebuild a new economy. The American Jobs Plan is an investment in America that will create millions of good jobs, rebuild our country's infrastructure, and position the United States to out-compete China." The fact sheet further described the U.S. as ranking 13th in the world in infrastructure, with a vulnerable electrical grid. It expands the concept of infrastructure from physical assets like roads and bridges, to human infrastructure investments like caregiving and training.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Fact Sheet: The American Jobs Plan|language=en-US|work=The White House|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/03/31/fact-sheet-the-american-jobs-plan/|access-date=April 20, 2021}}</ref>

The [[Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget]] (CRFB) summarized the investments as follows ($ in billions):
*Climate $782 
*Transportation $447
*Health & Childcare $443
*Housing & Buildings $258
*Jobs & economic development $196
*Research & Development $159
*Manufacturing $154
*Clean water $111
*Broadband $100

CRFB also summarized the revenue elements over 15 years:
*Increase corporate tax rate from 21% to 28%, generating $1,300 billion in revenue. The rate had been lowered from 35% in 2017 to 21% in 2018 by the [[Tax Cuts and Jobs Act]].
*Implement a [[global minimum tax]], raising $750 billion.
*Several other elements to address corporate tax loopholes and shelters, raising $680 billion.<ref>{{Cite news|title=What's in President Biden's American Jobs Plan?|language=en-US|work=CRFB|url=https://www.crfb.org/blogs/whats-president-bidens-american-jobs-plan|access-date=April 20, 2021}}</ref>

===American Families Plan===
{{Main|American Families Plan}}

In April 2021, Biden proposed "The American Families Plan", which a White House fact sheet described as: "[A]n investment in our children and our families{{snd}}helping families cover the basic expenses that so many struggle with now, lowering health insurance premiums, and continuing the American Rescue Plan's historic reductions in child poverty." The plan elements include: 
*Adding at least four years of free education, including two years of pre-school for 3–4 year-olds, and two years of community college. The Biden administration estimates the pre-school program will benefit 5 million children each year and save the average family $13,000. The community college program will help about 5.5 million students per year pay $0 in fees, about $109 billion over a decade.
*Providing child care subsidies to limit spending of low- and middle-income families to 7% of income.
*Creating national paid family and medical leave program, comparable to other developed nations.
*Expanding food assistance, including in schools to reduce child hunger.
*Extending tax cuts in the American Rescue plan indefinitely, including the [[Child tax credit (United States)|Child Tax Credit]], [[Earned Income Tax Credit]], and the Dependent Care Tax Credit.
*Expanding healthcare subsidies in the American Rescue plan indefinitely, including $50/month subsidies (on average) received by nine million people.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Fact Sheet: The American Families Plan|language=en-US|work=The White House|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/04/28/fact-sheet-the-american-families-plan/|access-date=May 1, 2021}}</ref>

The ''New York Times'' estimated the American Families Plan would invest about $1.8 trillion over 10 years, with about $800 billion in tax credits, $545 billion in child and family support, $511 billion for education, and $80 billion to expand the ability of the [[Internal Revenue Service]] to collect taxes from the wealthy.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Biden's $4 Trillion Economic Plan, in One Chart|language=en-US|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/04/28/upshot/biden-families-plan-american-rescue-infrastructure.html|access-date=April 20, 2021}}</ref>

===Build Back Better Act===
{{Main|Build Back Better Act}}

The Build Back Better Act, a [[Reconciliation (United States Congress)|reconciliation]] package including about $2.2 trillion in spending/investments and $2.0 trillion in additional revenue over a decade, passed the House of Representatives November 19, 2021, and is pending before the Senate. Most of the bill's provisions have finite duration.

''The New York Times'' reported that enacting the bill would fund benefits such as:<ref name="NYT_B^3">{{Cite news|title=Everything in the House Democrats' Budget Bill|language=en-US|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2021/11/18/upshot/whats-in-democrats-reconciliation-bill.html?|date=November 18, 2021}}</ref>
*Child care program for children up to five years of age, capping family expenses at 7% of income ($273 billion).
*Paid family and medical leave of four weeks ($205 billion).
*Child tax credit extension through 2023 ($185 billion).
*Universal preschool for 3- and 4-year-olds ($109 billion).
*Healthcare programs, such as funds for home health care under Medicaid ($150 billion), and expansion to ACA eligibility and subsidies ($74 billion).
*Climate programs with various tax incentives, pollution controls, and financial assistance ($495 billion).
*Housing programs such as public housing, rental assistance, and affordable housing ($166 billion).

The revenue or cost reduction sources include:
*Corporate tax increases of $814 billion, including new methods such as an alternative minimum tax on accounting profits and taxing stock buybacks.
*Individual tax increases of $655 billion, focused on high-income households, including surtaxes for incomes over $10 million or $25 million.
*Allowing government to negotiate prices for Medicare prescriptions (cost reduction of $76 billion).
*Limiting prescription drug price increases (cost reduction of $84 billion).<ref name="NYT_B^3"/>

The CBO estimated the bill would add $350 billion total to the national debt over the 2022–2031 period, excluding about $200 billion in estimated collections from stronger IRS enforcement (bringing the net impact closer to $150 billion), overall a relatively minor net impact on the national debt.<ref name="NYT_B^3"/>

==Biden's first budget FY 2022==
President Biden published his first budget for fiscal year 2022, covering the FY 2022–2031 decade. The [[Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget]] (CRFB) summarized it as follows: "The President's budget proposes about $5 trillion of new spending and tax breaks, reflecting the previously proposed American Jobs Plan, American Families Plan, and nondefense discretionary spending increases. These provisions would be partially offset with nearly $3.6 trillion of new revenue and over $200 billion of budget cuts and savings. The budget would also add $163 billion of interest costs.” CRFB estimated this as a net $1.354 trillion increase in the budget deficit over a decade, or $135 billion/year. This budget is incremental to the $2.0 trillion impact of the American Rescue Plan, which was enacted in March 2021 and already included in the baseline forecast used for the CRFB computations.<ref name="CRFB_Budget22">{{Cite news|title=President Biden's Full FY 2022 Budget|language=en-US|work=crfb.org|url=https://www.crfb.org/papers/president-bidens-full-fy-2022-budget}}</ref> For scale, Trump's [[Tax Cuts and Jobs Act]] represented about $2 trillion in deficit additions over a decade, or $200 billion/year.

CRFB also commented on the economic assumptions in the budget as being comparable to other major forecasts: "The budget's growth assumptions of 2.2 percent per year over the decade and 1.9 percent per year in the second half of the decade are somewhat higher than CBO's projections of 2.0 and 1.6 percent and the Federal Reserve's 2.0 and 1.8 percent estimates. However, they are in line with the Blue Chip consensus, which is also 2.2 percent per year over the next decade and 1.9 percent per year in the longer term." CRFB commented that Biden's budget is somewhat more optimistic on unemployment rates than these other forecasters.<ref name="CRFB_Budget22"/>

==COVID-19==
===January 2021===
In January 2022, President Biden said there's no federal solution to the pandemic as cases were climbing dramatically.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Elving |first=Ron |date=2022-01-01 |title=Week in politics: Biden says there is no federal solution to the pandemic |url=https://www.npr.org/2022/01/01/1069610932/week-in-politics-biden-says-there-is-no-federal-solution-to-the-pandemic |work=NPR}}</ref> He then issued an executive order intended to deliver economic relief to families and businesses. This included:
*Increasing access to food for students missing meals due to school closures and enhancing SNAP (food stamps) benefits;
*Improving delivery of direct stimulus payments;
*Request Department of Labor to clarify that workers can still access unemployment insurance if employment would have jeopardized their health due to COVID-19;
*Develop support network to help families and businesses access government benefits; and
*Require federal contractors to pay $15 minimum wage.<ref name="ExecOrd_Jan22">{{Cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/01/22/fact-sheet-president-bidens-new-executive-actions-deliver-economic-relief-for-american-families-and-businesses-amid-the-covid-19-crises/|title=Fact Sheet: President Biden's New Executive Actions Deliver Economic Relief for American Families and Businesses Amid the COVID-19 Crises|publisher=[[White House]]|date=January 22, 2021|access-date=January 23, 2021}}</ref>

==Minimum wage==
{{See also|Minimum wage in the United States}}
Biden's COVID-19 stimulus package, the [[American Rescue Plan Act of 2021|American Rescue Plan]], originally included raising the minimum wage to $15 per hour, but this was later removed after moderate Senate Democrats and Republicans objected to the proposal. A CBO study in 2019 estimated that raising the minimum wage to $15 by 2025 would increase wages for 17 million directly in that year, although the number of persons with jobs could be reduced in a range of zero to 3.7 million.<ref name="CBO_Minwage2019">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/55410|title=The Effects on Employment and Family Income of Increasing the Federal Minimum Wage|publisher=cbo.gov|date=July 8, 2019|access-date=January 22, 2021}}</ref>

Three months into office, Biden signed an executive order to increase the minimum wage for federal contractors by nearly 37%, to $15 per hour. The order went into effect for 390,000 workers in January 2022.<ref>{{cite news |title=Biden raising minimum wage for federal contractors to $15/hr |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/biden-raises-minimum-wage-federal-contractors-15hr-2021-04-27/ |publisher=Reuters |date=April 27, 2021|author1=Nandita Bose|author2=Jarrett Renshaw}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Nearly 400,000 federal contractors will get paid $15 an hour starting this weekend. Biden's labor secretary says there's 'no question' it'll cut down on labor shortages. |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/federal-contractors-15-hour-minimum-wage-could-end-labor-shortges-2022-1 |work=Business Insider |date=January 28, 2022}}</ref>

==Trade==
[[File:P20231115AS-0524.jpg|thumb|Talks between U.S. delegation headed by Biden and Chinese delegation headed by Xi at the Filoli Estate in [[Woodside, California]], November 2023]]
''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'' reported that instead of negotiating access to Chinese markets for large American financial-service firms and pharmaceutical companies, the Biden administration focused on trade policies that boost exports or domestic jobs. [[U.S. Trade Representative]] [[Katherine Tai]] said the administration wants a "worker-centered trade policy".<ref name="wsj._Biden_Team">{{Cite web |title=Biden Team Promises New Look in Trade Policy |last=Davis |first=Bob |newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |date=January 24, 2021 |access-date=January 26, 2021 |url= https://www.wsj.com/articles/biden-team-promises-new-look-in-trade-policy-11611484201}}</ref><ref name="axio_Biden_sets">{{Cite web |title=Biden set his sights on China |last=Allen-Ebrahimian |first=Bethany |work=[[Axios (website)|Axios]] |date=January 26, 2021 |access-date=January 26, 2021 |url= https://www.axios.com/biden-administration-china-policy-trump-136a1da4-f49d-42df-9fb6-29090a589087.html}}</ref> [[U.S. Secretary of Commerce]] [[Gina Raimondo]] said she planned to aggressively enforce trade rules to combat unfair practices by China.<ref name="nyti_Bidens_Commerce">{{Cite web |last=Swanson |first=Ana |date=January 26, 2021 |title=Biden's Commerce Pick Vows to Combat China and Climate Change |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2021/01/26/business/economy/gina-raimondo-commerce.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=January 26, 2021}}</ref>

In March 2021, Katherine Tai said that the U.S. would not lift tariffs on Chinese imports in the near future, despite lobbying efforts from "free traders," including former Secretary of Treasury [[Hank Paulson]] and the [[Business Roundtable]], that pressed for tariff repeal.<ref name="wsj._New_Trade">{{Cite web |title=New Trade Representative Says U.S. Isn't Ready to Lift China Tariffs |last1=Davis |first1=Bob |last2=Hayashi |first2=Yuka |newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |date=March 28, 2021 |access-date=March 29, 2021 |url= https://www.wsj.com/articles/new-trade-representative-says-u-s-isnt-ready-to-lift-china-tariffs-11616929200}}</ref>

At the [[2021 G20 Rome summit|October 2021 G20 Rome summit]], the Biden administration and the European Union reached agreement to roll back the steel and aluminum tariff regime that had been [[First Trump tariffs|imposed by the Trump administration in 2018]]. The agreement retained some protection for American steel and aluminum producers by adopting a [[tariff-rate quota]] regime. It also ended retaliatory tariffs on American goods the EU had imposed and canceled a scheduled tariff increase by the EU.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/10/30/business/economy/biden-steel-tariffs-europe.html|title=U.S. Agrees to Roll Back European Steel and Aluminum Tariffs|first1=Ana|last1=Swanson|first2=Katie|last2=Rogers|work=The New York Times |date=October 30, 2021|via=NYTimes.com}}</ref>

China failed by a wide margin to purchase American goods and services as agreed under the January 2020 Phase One trade deal, which expired on December 31, 2021. The Biden administration continued to formulate its China trade policy and faced a decision as to whether to reinstate some tariffs and risk retaliation, or to ignore China's breach amid elevated inflation that might be exacerbated by additional tariffs.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Zumbrun |first1=Josh |title=Beijing Fell Short on Trade Deal Promises, Creating Dilemma for Biden |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/beijing-fell-short-on-trade-deal-promises-creating-dilemma-for-biden-11640946782 |work=The Wall Street Journal |date=December 31, 2021}}</ref>

As of December 2023, Biden has largely maintained Trump's protectionist trade policies, and has not negotiated any new [[United States free trade agreements|free trade agreements]]. Labor unions, an important constituency for Biden's re-election, opposed removing Trump's tariffs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/biden-struggles-to-push-trade-deals-with-allies-as-election-approaches-fc512595?mod=RSSMSN|title=Biden Struggles to Push Trade Deals with Allies as Election Approaches|website=The Wall Street Journal|first=Yuka|last=Hayashi|date=December 28, 2023}}</ref> In May 2024, the Biden administration doubled [[tariff]]s on [[solar cell]]s imported from China and more than tripled tariffs on [[Lithium-ion battery|lithium-ion electric vehicle batteries]] imported from China.<ref name="Boak-2024">{{Cite web |last1=Boak |first1=Josh |last2=Hussein |first2=Fatima |last3=Wiseman |first3=Paul |last4=Tang |first4=Didi |date=May 14, 2024 |title=Biden hikes tariffs on Chinese EVs, solar cells, steel, aluminum — and snipes at Trump |url=https://apnews.com/article/biden-china-tariffs-electric-vehicles-evs-solar-2024ba735c47e04a50898a88425c5e2c |access-date=May 16, 2024 |website=[[AP News]] |language=en}}</ref> It also raised tariffs on imports of Chinese steel, aluminum, and medical equipment.<ref name="Boak-2024" /> The tariff increases will be phased in over a period of three years.<ref name="Boak-2024" />

==Clean energy==
{{Main|Environmental policy of the Biden administration}}

Despite Biden's promotion of clean energy, and Republican assertions he was waging "war on American energy," by the end of his third year the United States was producing more crude oil than any country in history.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Egan |first1=Matt |title=The United States is producing more oil than any country in history |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2023/12/19/business/us-production-oil-reserves-crude/index.html |publisher=CNN |date=December 19, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Narea |first1=Nicole |title=Biden isn't advertising America's record oil boom |url=https://www.vox.com/climate/24098983/biden-oil-production-climate-fossil-fuel-renewables |work=Vox |date=March 13, 2024}}</ref>

==Education==
{{See also|Education in the United States}}

Biden has proposed paying for college tuition and pre-K for middle-class families. He also attempted to forgive some student loans, with mixed success.<ref name="Biden_Wants">{{Cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/21340746/joe-biden-covid-19-coronavirus-recession-harris|title=This is the future Joe Biden wants|publisher=Vox|date=August 17, 2020|access-date=January 22, 2021}}</ref>

===Student loan forgiveness===
{{See also|Student loans in the United States|Issues in higher education in the United States|Higher education financing issues in the United States}}
Biden supported canceling student loan debt up to $10,000 during 2020, for some borrowers. Other prominent Democrats (Senators Warren and Schumer) co-authored a resolution including cancelations up to $50,000 for all borrowers. There is an active debate about whether legislation or executive order is sufficient to cancel student loans. Critics argued that canceling student loans is regressive rather than progressive, as most with student loans are college educated and earn more. Further, the impact on college tuition pricing and access is unclear.<ref name="NPR_StudentLoans1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/biden-transition-updates/2020/11/17/935743741/biden-wants-to-help-pay-some-student-loans-but-theres-pressure-to-go-further|title=Biden Wants To Help Pay Some Student Loans, But There's Pressure To Go Further|publisher=npr.org|date=November 17, 2020|access-date=January 23, 2021}}</ref>

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported that student loans totaled $1.5 trillion in 2019, with 43 million borrowers. The average balance was $33,500. About 14 million borrowers (33%) had balances below $10,000; 20 million (47%) had balances $10,000–50,000, and 9 million (20%) had balances over $50,000.<ref name="FRBNY_College1">{{Cite web|url=https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2019/10/who-borrows-for-collegeand-who-repays.html|title=Who Borrows for College – and Who Repays?|publisher=newyorkfed.org|date=October 9, 2019|access-date=January 23, 2021}}</ref>

The [[Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget]] reported in November 2020 that canceling student loans had several pros and cons, but was a relatively ineffective economic stimulus. While household net worth would rise by $1.5 trillion if all loans were canceled, in terms of monthly spending the typical household with student loan debt would be avoiding a $200–300 monthly payment. Re-directing this savings to other spending would have limited economic impact of about $100 billion/year. One important consideration is the tax treatment of the forgiven debt; if treated as a gain (income), it would likely be taxable in the absence of legislation negating the gain, offsetting the small positive economic impact.<ref name="CRFB_StudentLoans1">{{Cite web|url=http://www.crfb.org/blogs/canceling-student-loan-debt-poor-economic-stimulus|title=Canceling Student Loan Debt Is Poor Economic Stimulus|publisher=crfb.org|date=November 2020|access-date=January 23, 2021}}</ref>

CNBC reported that forgiving $10,000 in student debt for all borrowers would cost the government $377 billion, but forgiving $10,000 just for those with debt below $10,000 (about a third of borrowers) would cost $75 billion. Debtors in the latter category tend to be those struggling to pay off their debt.<ref name="CNBC_SL1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/01/22/experts-weigh-in-on-10000-in-student-debt-forgiveness.html|title=Experts weigh in on Biden's support of $10,000 in student debt forgiveness|publisher=cnbc.com|date=January 22, 2021|access-date=January 24, 2021}}</ref>

By the end of Biden's first year in office, the [[Department of Education]] had forgiven $15 billion in debt for 675,000 borrowers.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Quintana |first1=Chris |title=Student loan forgiveness has arrived for 70,000 borrowers working public service jobs |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/education/2022/01/20/student-loan-forgiveness-public-service-loans/6584434001/ |work=USA Today |date=January 20, 2022}}</ref>

In August 2022, Biden announced a [[United States Department of Education|U.S. Department of Education]] program to [[Debt relief|cancel]] certain federally owned [[Student loans in the United States|student loan debt]] under the [[Higher Education Relief Opportunities For Students Act|HEROES Act]]. Borrowers earning under $125,000 per year, or under $250,000 for married couples who file jointly, would have been eligible for up to $10,000 in loan forgiveness. Borrowers who received a [[Pell Grant]] while attending college would have qualified for up to an additional $10,000 in loan forgiveness, for a total of $20,000.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Turner |first1=Cory |last2=Carrillo |first2=Sequoia |title=Biden is canceling up to $10K in student loans, $20K for Pell Grant recipients |url=https://www.npr.org/2022/08/24/1118879917/student-loan-forgiveness-biden |work=NPR |date=August 24, 2022}}</ref> The administration estimated that about 43 million borrowers would have been covered by the plan, including about 20 million individuals whose student debt would be completely forgiven.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Douglas-Gabriel |first1=Danielle |last2=Stein |first2=Jeff |title=Who qualifies for Biden's plan to cancel $10,000 in student debt? |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/education/2022/08/24/student-loan-forgiveness-plan-explained/ |access-date=August 26, 2022 |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=August 24, 2022}}</ref> Estimates had stated that the plan would cost as much as $519 billion for the "debt cancellation alone",<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-08-26 |title=The Biden Student Loan Forgiveness Plan: Budgetary Costs and Distributional Impact |url=https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/issues/2022/8/26/biden-student-loan-forgiveness#:~:text=We%20estimate%20that%20debt%20cancellation,will%20cost%20another%20$16%20billion. |access-date=2024-12-23 |website=Penn Wharton Budget Model |language=en-US}}</ref> and critics characterized Biden's plans to cancel hundreds of billions of dollars in debt as a "disaster".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Camp |first=Emma |date=2024-12-14 |title=Biden's attempts to forgive student debt were a disaster |url=https://reason.com/2024/12/14/student-debt-disaster/?utm_medium=reason_email&utm_source=new_at_reason&utm_campaign=reason_brand&utm_content=Senate%20Tees%20Up%20$200%20Billion%20Social%20Security%20Giveaway%20to%20Public%20Sector%20Workers&utm_term=&time=December%2016th,%202024&mpid=38717&mpweb=2534-5255-38717 |access-date=2024-12-23 |website=Reason.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

After 6 state governments filed lawsuits challenging the program,<ref>{{cite news|title=Six states urge U.S. Supreme Court to keep block on Biden student debt relief|date=November 23, 2022|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/11/23/six-states-urge-us-supreme-court-to-keep-block-on-biden-student-debt-relief.html|access-date=May 15, 2024}}</ref> the Supreme Court held in ''[[Biden v. Nebraska]]'' (2023) that the program exceeded the authority delegated to the Department of Education under the HEROES Act.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Student Loan Forgiveness: Supreme Court Rejects Biden's Debt Forgiveness Plan |url=https://www.nytimes.com/live/2023/06/30/us/student-loans-supreme-court-biden |date = June 30, 2023 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{ussc|name=Biden v. Nebraska|volume=600|year=2023|docket=22-506}}</ref> In April 2024, Biden announced a revised student loan forgiveness program citing statutory authority under the [[Higher Education Act of 1965]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Nova|first=Annie|date=April 8, 2024|title=Biden announces new student loan forgiveness plan affecting tens of millions of Americans|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2024/04/08/biden-will-announce-details-of-new-student-loan-forgiveness-plan.html|access-date=May 15, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Nova|first=Annie|date=April 17, 2024|title=Biden administration releases formal proposal for new student loan forgiveness plan|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2024/04/17/biden-administration-releases-new-student-loan-forgiveness-proposal.html|access-date=May 15, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Nova|first=Annie|date=April 23, 2024|title=Here's why Biden administration believes new student loan forgiveness plan will survive legal challenges|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2024/04/23/biden-administration-believes-student-loan-forgiveness-plan-will-survive.html|access-date=May 15, 2024}}</ref>

Under the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021, student loan forgiveness was designated as [[Tax exemption|tax-exempt income]] through the end of 2025,<ref>{{cite news|last=Nova|first=Annie|date=March 11, 2021|title=Student loan forgiveness is now tax-free. What that means for borrowers if Biden cancels the debt|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/03/11/student-loan-forgiveness-is-now-tax-free-is-cancellation-coming-.html|access-date=May 15, 2024}}</ref> and Biden proposed making the tax exemption permanent in March 2024.<ref>{{cite news|last=Nova|first=Annie|date=March 18, 2024|title=Biden wants to make student loan forgiveness tax-free permanently|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2024/03/18/student-loan-forgiveness-would-remain-tax-free-under-bidens-budget.html|access-date=May 15, 2024}}</ref> In June 2022, the Department of Education agreed to forgive the student loans of approximately 200,000 borrowers (amounting to approximately $6 billion) to settle a class-action lawsuit the students filed against the Department in June 2019 for refusing to process their [[loan waiver|waiver]]s under [[Borrower Defense to Repayment]] from debt owed to [[For-profit colleges in the United States|for-profit institutions]] that [[Misrepresentation|misled]] the students about the financial remuneration, the quality of vocational training, and the career advancement they would receive by attending the institutions.<ref>{{cite news|last=Nova|first=Annie|date=June 23, 2022|title=Education Department agrees to cancel $6 billion in debt for some 200,000 student loan borrowers|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/06/23/education-department-to-cancel-200000-student-loan-borrowers-debt.html|access-date=June 23, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Sweet v. Cardona|website=Project on Predatory Student Lending|publisher=[[Harvard Law School]]|url=https://predatorystudentlending.org/cases/sweet-v-devos/|access-date=June 23, 2022|archive-date=June 23, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220623141718/https://predatorystudentlending.org/cases/sweet-v-devos/|url-status=dead}}</ref> In August 2022, the Department of Education announced that it would cancel the student loans of 208,000 borrowers who attended [[ITT Technical Institute]] (amounting to $3.9 billion).<ref>{{cite news|last=Nova|first=Annie|date=August 16, 2022|title=Biden administration cancels $3.9 billion in student debt for 208,000 borrowers defrauded by ITT Tech|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/08/16/education-dept-cancels-3point9-billion-in-student-loans-for-itt-tech.html|access-date=December 6, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Smith|first=Morgan|date=August 16, 2022|title=Education Department cancels $3.9 billion in student debt for more than 200,000 borrowers—here's who qualifies|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/08/16/ed-dept-cancels-3point9-billion-in-student-debt-for-over-200k-borrowers.html|access-date=December 6, 2022}}</ref> In October 2022, the department released final regulations to expand and streamline targeted debt relief programs for students that were [[Fraud|defrauded]] by the institutions they attended,<ref>{{cite news|last=Nova|first=Annie|date=October 31, 2022|title=Education Department overhauls federal student loan system, aiming to make it 'simpler, fairer and more ==Healthcare==
[[File:US Uninsured Under Age 65.png|thumb|right|400px|U.S. Uninsured under age 65, number (left axis in millions) and % (right axis) from 2010 to 2022 first half (H1). Blue shows Democratic party president, red a Republican party president. The number and % uninsured under Biden fell to lowest levels since 1997.<ref name="NCHS_H122">{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/releases.htm|title=Health Insurance Coverage: Early Release of Estimates from the NHIS, January – June 2022|publisher=CDC.gov|date=January 27, 2023}}</ref>]]

Biden has proposed lowering the Medicare age from 65 to 60, and expanding the [[Affordable Care Act]] subsidies and eligibility.<ref name="Biden_Wants"/> Some 23 million persons age 60–64 who could directly benefit, either by paying lower insurance premiums or no longer needing to obtain their insurance through an employer. There are about 1.7 million in the 60–64 age range who are uninsured, and 3.2 million who buy coverage because they are not covered by an employer. Hospitals would receive lower reimbursement rates for age 60–64 patients that enroll in Medicare. This plan would also increase the budget deficit, although the CBO has not officially scored the proposal as of January 2021. Lowering the Medicare age is popular, with one poll indicating 85% of Democrats and 69% of Republicans support lowering the eligibility age to as young as 50.<ref name="Biden_Medicare60">{{Cite web |date=November 11, 2020 |title=Biden Wants To Lower Medicare Eligibility Age To 60, But Hospitals Push Back |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2020/11/11/933522346/biden-wants-to-lower-medicare-eligibility-age-to-60-but-hospitals-push-back |access-date=January 23, 2021 |publisher=npr.org}}</ref>

The number of uninsured under age 65 fell from 31.2 million in 2020 under President Trump, to 27.0 million during the first half of 2022 under President Biden, a reduction of 3.2 million or 13%. The percentage of uninsured fell from 11.5% to 9.9% during that time.<ref name="NCHS_H122"/>

== Cryptocurrency ==
In January 2021, Biden suspended any federal regulatory proposal related to [[cryptocurrency]] until they can be reviewed by the new administration. This change was part of a freeze for all last-minute regulations put in place by the Trump administration.<ref name="GmbH">{{Cite web|last=Nagarajan|first=Shalini|title=Biden freezes all federal regulatory proposals, including Mnuchin's controversial crypto wallet legislation, until his new administration can review them|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/biden-freezes-new-regulatory-proposals-including-proposed-crypto-rule-2021-1|access-date=January 24, 2021|website=Business Insider|language=en-us}}</ref> On November 23, [[United States Senate|U.S. Senator]] [[Sherrod Brown]] ([[Senate Democratic Caucus|D]]–[[List of United States senators from Ohio|OH]]), Chairman of the [[United States Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs|U.S. Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs]], sent a letter to [[Tether (cryptocurrency)|Tether]] issuer [[Bitfinex]] requesting information about company operations due to concerns that the company was engaged in [[fraud]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Novak|first=Matt|date=November 24, 2021|title=U.S. Senators Demand Answers From People Behind Crypto Stablecoin Tether|website=[[Gizmodo]]|publisher=[[G/O Media]]|url=https://gizmodo.com/u-s-senators-demand-answers-from-people-behind-crypto-1848115558|access-date=July 13, 2022}}</ref> On March 9, 2022, Biden issued [[Executive Order 14067]] to federal departments and agencies to assess the benefits and risks of cryptocurrencies,<ref>{{cite news|last=Browne|first=Ryan|date=March 9, 2022|title=Biden just put out an executive order on cryptocurrencies — here's everything that's in it|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/03/09/heres-whats-in-bidens-executive-order-on-crypto.html|access-date=July 10, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite [[Federal Reserve]] to continue its research, development, and assessment efforts for a [[central bank digital currency]] (CBDC) for the [[United States dollar|U.S. dollar]].<ref>{{cite 22, 2022}}</ref> On June 6, the [[United States Office of Government Ethics|U.S. Office of Government Ethics]] issued a directive barring federal employees from working on any regulation that could influence the value of digital currencies that they hold.<ref>{{cite news|last=Rozen|first=Courtney|date=June 6, 2022|title=Crypto Holders Banned from Writing Rules on US Digital began investigating marketing claims made by Voyager that its customer dollar [[deposit account]]s were [[Deposit insurance|insured]] by the agency.<ref>{{cite news|last=Benoit|first=David|date=July
