[[Elizabeth Warren]]'s anti-cryptocurrency stance faced significant opposition within her party in 2024, as dozens of Democrats, including [[Chuck Schumer]], supported efforts to overturn SEC guidelines restricting banks from holding digital assets. This defiance also opposed Biden's veto threat. Amidst 2024 campaign dynamics, with Trump courting crypto supporters, crypto super PACs planned major spending to influence elections and policy. Despite concerns over money laundering and financial risks, key Democrats, including [[Maxine Waters]], remained opposed to the pro-crypto legislation.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Goodman |first1=Jasper|last2=Mueller |first2=Eleanor |title='I wanted to send a message': Democrats break with Warren, Biden on crypto |date=May 17, 2024 |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/05/17/crypto-congress-democrats-00158630 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518004943/https://www.politico.com/news/2024/05/17/crypto-congress-democrats-00158630 |archive-date=May 18, 2024 |access-date=May 18, 2024}}</ref>

===CFTC===
On January 3, 2022, the [[Commodity Futures Trading Commission]] (CFTC) issued an order requiring Blockratize, Inc. pay a $1.4 million fine for failing to [[Registration statement|register]] as a [[Swap Execution Facility|swap execution facility]], for offering illegal [[Binary option|binary]] [[Option (finance)|option contracts]] using cryptocurrency on its [[prediction market]] website Polymarket, and to close betting markets in violation of the [[Commodity Exchange Act]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Bain|first=Benjamin|date=January 3, 2022|title=Event-Betting Platform Polymarket to Pay $1.4 Million U.S. Fine|work=[[Bloomberg News]]|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-01-03/event-betting-platform-polymarket-to-pay-1-4-million-cftc-fine|access-date=July 13, 2022}}</ref> On February 9, CFTC Chairman [[Rostin Behnam]] asked the [[117th United States Congress|117th U.S. Congress]] for the authority to regulate certain cryptocurrencies in testimony before the [[United States Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry|U.S. Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Kiernan|first=Paul|date=February 9, 2022|title=CFTC Chair Asks Congress for Authority to Regulate Some Cryptocurrencies|work=The Wall Street Journal|publisher=News Corp|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/cftc-chair-to-testify-on-cryptocurrencies-as-congress-weighs-legislation-11644414710|access-date=July 13, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Senate Hearing on 2022}}</ref> On June 2, the CFTC filed a lawsuit against [[Gemini (company)|Gemini]] alleging that the executive staff of the cryptocurrency exchange made [[False statements of fact|false]] and [[Misrepresentation|misleading statements]] and [[Omission (law)|omissions]] in communications with regulators about [[market manipulation]] of a [[bitcoin]] [[futures contract]] the company proposed offering in 2017.<ref>{{cite news|last=Brandom|first=Russell|date=June 2, 2022|title=Regulators sue Winklevoss crypto firm over futures contracts|website=The Verge|publisher=Vox On June 7, U.S. Senators [[Kirsten Gillibrand]] (D–[[List of United States senators from New York|NY]]) and [[Cynthia Lummis]] ([[Senate Republican Conference|R]]–[[List of United States senators from Wyoming|WY]]) introduced a bill to create a regulatory framework for cryptocurrencies that would treat most digital assets as commodities subject to oversight from the CFTC and would not have cryptocurrencies subject to oversight from the SEC unless a cryptocurrency's holders were entitled to the same privileges as corporate investors.<ref>{{cite news|last=Franck|first=Thomas|date=June 7, oversight|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/06/07/bipartisan-crypto-bill-lummis-and-gillibrand-want-to-empower-cftc-treat-digitals-assets-like-commodities.html|access-date=July 10, 2022}}</ref> On June 8, Behnam announced support for the bill.<ref>{{cite news|last=Versprille|first=Allyson|date=June 8, 2022|title=CFTC Chairman Signals Support for Lummis-Gillibrand Crypto Plan|publisher=[[Bloomberg Law]]|url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/banking-law/cftc-chairman-signals-support-for-lummis-gillibrand-crypto-plan|access-date=July 13, 2022}}</ref> At a conference hosted by ''The Wall Street Journal'' on June 14, [[U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission]] (SEC) Chairman [[Gary Gensler]] expressed concern that the Lummis-Gillibrand bill could inadvertently undermine stock market and mutual fund protections, noted that cryptocurrency companies were already engaging in behaviors overseen by the SEC, and argued that some digital assets are securities necessitating oversight from the SEC rather than commodities (even if the overwhelming majority of tokens offered by cryptocurrency exchanges are commodities).<ref>{{cite news|last=Kiernan|first=Paul|date=June 14, 2022|title=Crypto Legislation Could Undermine Market Regulations, Gensler Says|work=The Wall Street Journal|publisher=News ===Federal Reserve===
At a conference held by the [[Bank for International Settlements]] on March 22, 2021, [[Chair of the Federal Reserve|Federal Reserve Chairman]] [[Jerome Powell]] stated that the Federal Reserve would not issue a [[central bank digital currency]] (CBDC) without explicit congressional authorization.<ref>{{cite news|last=Smialek|first=Jeanna|date=March 22, 2021|title=Jerome Powell says the Fed won't issue a digital currency without congressional approval|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/03/22/business/jerome-powell-says-the-fed-wont-issue-a-digital-currency-without-congressional-approval.html|access-date= July 22, 2022}}</ref> On April 28, Powell stated in a press conference following a [[Federal Open Market Committee]] (FOMC) policy meeting that the CBDC system that exists in [[China]] could not exist in the United States due to [[Privacy laws of the United States|privacy concerns]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Marte|first=Jonnelle|date=April 28, 2021|title=Fed's Powell: China's approach to digital currency would not work here|website=[[Yahoo! News]] |publisher=Yahoo, Inc.|url=https://news.yahoo.com/feds-powell-chinas-approach-digital-194313236.html|access-date=July 22, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Kenyon|first=Henry|date=November 16, 2021|title=Privacy issues seen reducing appeal of central bank digital currencies|website=[[Roll Call]]|publisher=[[FiscalNote]] |url=https://rollcall.com/2021/11/16/privacy-issues-seen-reducing-appeal-of-central-bank-digital-currencies/|access-date=July 22, 2022}}</ref> On May 20, Powell issued a press statement announcing that the Board of Governors would release a [[white paper]] on a CBDC for the U.S. dollar.<ref>{{cite report |title=Federal Reserve Chair Jerome H. Powell outlines the Federal Reserve's response to technological advances driving rapid change in the global payments landscape|date=May 20, 2021|publisher=Federal Reserve |url=https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/other20210520b.htm|access-date=July 22, 2022}}</ref> On July 14, Powell testified before the [[United States House Committee on Financial Services|U.S. House Financial Services Committee]] about CBDC, stated that the white paper on creating a CBDC for the U.S. dollar would be released in a few months, and that [[stablecoin]]s and cryptocurrencies would not be needed if there was a CBDC for the U.S. dollar.{{refn|name=PowellHearing|<ref>{{cite news|last=Marte|first=Jonnelle|date=July 14, 2021|title=Powell says a Fed digital currency could undercut need for cryptocurrencies|website=Reuters |publisher=Thomson Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/business/feds-powell-says-stablecoins-need-appropriate-regulatory-framework-2021-07-14/|access-date=July 20, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Sigalos|first=MacKenzie|date=July 16, 2021|title=Why the Fed hates cryptocurrencies and especially stablecoins|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/07/16/jerome-powell-promotes-cbdc-digital-dollar-warns-against-stablecoins.html|access-date=July 20, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite report|title=Monetary Policy and the State of the Economy|date=July 14, 2021|id=Serial No. 117-37|publisher=[[United States House Committee on Financial Services|U.S. House Committee on Financial Services]] / [[United States Government Publishing Office|U.S. Government Printing Office]]|pages=9–10; 17–18, 43–44|url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-117hhrg45384/pdf/CHRG-117hhrg45384.pdf|access-date=July 20, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Monetary Policy and the Economy|date=July 14, 2021|publisher=[[C-SPAN]]|url=https://www.c-span.org/video/?513257-1/fed-chair-inflation-remain-elevated-months-ahead-moderating|access-date=July 20, 2022}}</ref>}} At a press conference following an FOMC policy meeting on September 22, Powell stated that the Federal Reserve was continuing work on the white paper.<ref>{{cite news|last=Cox|first=Jeff|date=September 22, 2021|title=The Fed is evaluating whether to launch a digital currency and in what form, Powell says|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/09/22/the-fed-is-evaluating-whether-to-launch-a-digital-currency-and-in-what-form-powell-says.html|access-date=July 22, 2022}}</ref> On October 14, [[United Wholesale Mortgage]] announced that it would cease a company pilot to accept [[Mortgage loan|mortgage loan repayments]] in bitcoin.<ref>{{cite news|last=Sigalos|first=MacKenzie |date=October 14, 2021|title=Second-largest U.S. mortgage lender ditches its plan to accept payments in bitcoin|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/10/14/united-wholesale-mortgage-ditches-its-plan-to-accept-bitcoin-ethereum.html|access-date=July 19, 2022}}</ref>

On January 18, 2022, [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. Representative]] [[Tom Emmer]] ([[House Republican Conference|GOP]]; [[Minnesota's 6th congressional district|MN-6]]) introduced a bill (HR 6415) to prohibit Federal Reserve Banks from issuing a CBDC.<ref>{{cite news|last=Kupiec|first=Paul|date=February 24, 2022|title=How politics are affecting the design of a Fed digital ===Justice and homeland security departments===
On March 5, 2021, [[McAfee|McAfee Corp.]] founder [[John McAfee]] was indicted in the Southern New York U.S. District Court for promoting a cryptocurrency pump-and-dump scheme on his Twitter account that he made $23 million from (after being indicted by the Justice Department for tax evasion on money earned from the scheme and sued by the SEC for promoting the scheme the previous October).<ref>{{cite news|last1=Breuninger|first1=Kevin|last2=Mangan|first2=Dan|date=March 5, 2021|title=Antivirus software creator John McAfee indicted on cryptocurrency fraud charges|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/03/05/john-mcafee-indicted-on-cryptocurrency-fraud-charges.html|access-date=July 21, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=SEC sues John McAfee over promoting cryptocurrency offerings on Twitter|date=October 5, 2020|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2020/10/05/sec-sues-john-mcafee-over-promoting-cryptocurrency-offerings-on-twitter.html|access-date=July 21, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=U.S. indicts anti-virus software creator John McAfee for tax evasion|date=October 6, 2020|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2020/10/06/us-indicts-anti-virus-software-creator-john-mcafee-for-tax-evasion.html|access-date=July 21, 2022}}</ref> On May 13, [[Binance]] was reportedly under investigation by the [[United States Department of Justice|U.S. Justice Department]] and the [[Internal Revenue Service]] for usage by users for [[money laundering]] and [[tax evasion]].<ref name="Reuters 5-13-2021">{{cite news|title=Binance under investigation by Justice Department, IRS – Bloomberg News|date=May 13, 2021|website=[[Reuters]]|publisher=[[Thomson Reuters]]|url=https://www.reuters.com/technology/binance-under-investigation-by-justice-department-irs-bloomberg-news-2021-05-13/|access-date=July 11, 2022}}</ref> On February 8, 2022, the U.S. Justice Department arrested businessman [[Ilya Lichtenstein]] and rapper [[Heather R. ===Treasury and labor departments===
{{Main|United States Department of the Treasury|United States Department of Labor}}
During [[Janet Yellen]]'s confirmation hearing for Secretary of the Treasury, U.S. Senator [[Maggie Hassan]] (D-[[List of United States senators from New Hampshire|NH]]) asked about the use of cryptocurrency by terrorists and other criminals. "Cryptocurrencies are a particular concern," Yellen responded. "I think many are used—at least in a transactions sense—mainly for illicit financing." She said she wanted to "examine ways in which we can curtail their use and make sure that [money laundering] doesn't occur through those channels."<ref>{{Cite web|last=Lee|first=Timothy B.|date=January 20, 2021|title=Treasury nominee Yellen is looking to curtail use of cryptocurrency|url=https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2021/01/biden-treasury-pick-yellen-favors-new-restrictions-on-cryptocurrency/|access-date=January 24, 2021|website=Ars Technica|language=en-us}}</ref> On May 13, 2021, [[Binance]] was reportedly under investigation by the [[United States Department of Justice|U.S. Justice Department]] and the [[Internal Revenue Service]] (IRS) for usage by users for [[money laundering]] and [[tax evasion]].<ref name="Reuters 5-13-2021" /> On August 4, IRS officials stated that the agency had seized $1.2 billion worth of bitcoin during fiscal year 2021.<ref>{{cite news|last=Sigalos|first=MacKenzie|date=August 4, 2021|title=The IRS has seized $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency this fiscal year – here's what happens to it|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/08/04/irs-has-seized-1point2-billion-worth-of-cryptocurrency-this-year-.html|access-date=July 19, 2022}}</ref>

senators from Virginia|VA]]) rather than the amendment proposed by U.S. Senators Cynthia Lummis (R–WY), [[Pat Toomey]] (R–[[List of United States senators from Pennsylvania|PA]]), and [[Ron Wyden]] (D–[[List of United States senators from Oregon|OR]]).<ref>{{cite news|last1=Sigalos|first1=MacKenzie|last2=Wilkie|first2=Christina|date=August 6, 2021|title=White House backs senators pushing for ==Unions==
On January 22, 2021, Biden issued [[List of executive actions by Joe Biden|Executive Order 14003]] that removed [[Schedule F appointment|Schedule F]], overturning a number of Trump's policies that limited the [[collective bargaining]] power of federal unions.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wagner |first1=Erich |title=Biden to Sign Executive Order Killing Schedule F, Restoring Collective Bargaining Rights |url=https://www.govexec.com/management/2021/01/biden-sign-executive-order-killing-schedule-f-restoring-collective-bargaining-rights/171569/ |access-date=January 22, 2021 |work=Government Executive |date=January 22, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Ogrysko |first1=Nicole |title=Biden to repeal Schedule F, overturn Trump workforce policies with new executive order |url=https://federalnewsnetwork.com/workforce/2021/01/biden-to-repeal-schedule-f-overturn-trump-workforce-policies-with-new-executive-order/ |access-date=January 22, 2021 |work=Federal News Network |date=January 22, 2021}}</ref> He called on Amazon workers to vote for union representation in a closely watched election in Alabama. This was stronger support than any president has given unions in decades. However the workers defeated the proposal 71% to 29%, enhancing Amazon's reputation as a leading bulwark against unionization. Labor activists said Biden's advocacy would build his support in the working class, fighting off Republican inroads there.<ref>Sean Sullivan, "Biden took a chance in promoting the Amazon union push. What does its failure mean for him?" [https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/biden-union-amazon-failure/2021/04/09/1e1110f4-9945-11eb-a6d0-13d207aadb78_story.html ''Washington Post'' April 10, 2021].</ref>

He was criticized by some union activists for signing a bill to force an end to the [[2022 United States railroad labor dispute]] that did not contain the union's target of paid sick leave.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gordon |first=Aaron |date=December 2, 2022 |title=More than 500 Labor Historians Condemn Biden's Intervention in Freight Rail Dispute |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/more-than-500-labor-historians-condemn-bidens-intervention-in-freight-rail-dispute/ |access-date=November 21, 2023 |website=Vice |language=en}}</ref> However, the Biden administration was also influential in securing a later deal to provide paid sick leave to those rail workers.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wilkins |first=Brett |title=Biden pushed to seal the deal on paid sick leave for rail workers |url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/politics/biden-pushed-to-seal-the-deal-on-paid-sick-leave-for-rail-workers/ar-AA14OS6n |access-date=November 21, 2023 |website=Salon on MSN.com}}</ref>

Biden appointed two of the five members of the [[National Labor Relations Board]], which enacted many policies that boosted unions during his presidency. These were seen as a factor in an increase in labor strikes in 2023, which won unions several wins, such as increased pay and better working conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NLRB Board Continues Pro Union Agenda |url=https://www.natlawreview.com/article/labor-board-maintains-course-pro-union-agenda |access-date=November 21, 2023 |website=www.natlawreview.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Kaori Gurley |first=Lauren |title=The lawyer who could deliver on Biden's wish to be the most pro-union president |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2022/10/15/jennifer-abruzzo-union-biden-nlrb/ |newspaper=Washington Post}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Meyerson |first=Harold |date=August 28, 2023 |title=Biden's NLRB Brings Workers' Rights Back From the Dead |url=https://prospect.org/api/content/54e6445e-43a3-11ee-8651-12163087a831/ |access-date=November 21, 2023 |website=The American Prospect |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Isidore |first=Chris |date=September 30, 2023 |title=America is on strike. Here's the progress unions have made {{!}} CNN Business |url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/09/30/business/us-labor-unions-strike-surge/index.html |access-date=November 21, 2023 |website=CNN |language=en}}</ref>

In September 2023, Biden became the first United States president to ever march in a picket line with a union, when he joined [[2023 United Auto Workers strike|a strike]] with the [[United Auto Workers]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 26, 2023 |title=WATCH: Biden makes historic visit to UAW picket line, tells union to 'stick with it' |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-biden-makes-historic-visit-to-uaw-picket-line-tells-union-to-stick-with-it |access-date=November 21, 2023 |website=PBS NewsHour |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Isidore |first1=Chris |last2=Yurkevich |first2=Vanessa
|date=September 26, 2023 |title=Joe Biden is the first sitting president to join a picket line |url=https://www.cnn.com/business/live-news/michigan-picket-biden-uaw-strike-09-26-2023/h_5ec6c4d3563be9234b43af7816ec9280 |access-date=November 21, 2023 |website=CNN |language=en}}</ref>

== Taxation and deficits ==

===Individual taxes===
Biden has pledged to raise taxes only on individual persons earning over $200,000, or $400,000 for married couples filing jointly.<ref name="Biden_Wants"/> Treasury Secretary nominee [[Janet Yellen]] reiterated Biden's pledge in her answers during her Senate confirmation hearing process in January 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fortune.com/2021/01/21/janet-yellen-biden-tax-plans-treasury-secretary-taxes-fed-china-debt-climate-change-foreign-sanctions-iran-deal/|title=What Janet Yellen is saying about raising taxes on wealthy Americans – and other key issues – as Biden's Treasury Secretary-designate|publisher=fortune.com|date=January 21, 2021|access-date=January 22, 2021}}</ref> The individual tax cuts in President Trump's [[Tax Cuts and Jobs Act]] are scheduled to expire after 2025, for all income levels. This means they automatically revert to the higher rates of the Obama administration, in the absence of new legislation.

===Corporate taxes===
Biden has proposed raising the corporate tax rate from 21% to 28%.<ref name="Biden_Wants"/> This rate was lowered by the Republican's 2017 [[Tax Cuts and Jobs Act]] from 35% to 21%, so Biden's proposal represents a partial reversal. The 21% tax rate does not expire, in contrast to the individual rates, so legislation would be required to raise it.<ref>Garrett Watson and William McBride, [https://files.taxfoundation.org/20210224151522/Evaluating-Proposals-to-Increase-the-Corporate-Tax-Rate-and-Levy-a-Minimum-Tax-on-Corporate-Book-Income1.pdf "Evaluating Proposals to Increase the Corporate Tax Rate and Levy a Minimum Tax on Corporate Book Income,"  ''Fiscal Fact'' (Tax Foundation, No. 751 Feb. 2021) ]</ref>

===International taxation===
Finance officials from 130 countries agreed on July 1, 2021, to plans for a new international taxation policy. All the major economies agreed to pass national laws that would require corporations to pay at least 15% income tax in the countries they operate. This new policy would end the practice of locating world headquarters in small countries with very low taxation rates. Governments hope to recoup some of the lost revenue, estimated at $100 billion to $240 billion each year. The new system was promoted by the Biden administration and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development ([[OECD]]). Secretary-General [[Mathias Cormann]] of the OECD said, "This historic package will ensure that large multinational companies pay their fair share of tax everywhere."<ref>Paul Hannon and Kate Davidson, "U.S. Wins International Backing for Global Minimum Tax." [https://www.wsj.com/articles/u-s-wins-international-backing-for-global-minimum-tax-11625153698?mod=hp_lead_pos1 ''Wall Street Journal'' July 1, 2021]</ref>

==Budget deficit==
The first year that President Biden budgeted is fiscal 2022, which runs from October 1, 2021, to September 30, 2022. CBO forecast in July 2021 that the budget deficit in fiscal year 2022 will be $1.2 trillion, or 4.7% GDP.<ref name="CBO_July2021">{{cite web|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/57263|title=Additional information about the updated budget and economic outlook: 2021 to 2031|date=November 14, 2021|website=cbo.gov|access-date=November 14, 2021}}</ref> This would be a significant reduction to the budget deficits of $3.1 trillion (15.0% GDP) in FY2020 (the last fiscal year fully budgeted by President Trump) and $2.8 trillion (12.4% GDP) in FY2021. Those two record annual budget deficits were unusually high, primarily due to response measures to the Coronavirus pandemic.<ref name="CBO_MBRFY2021">{{cite web|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/57539|title=Monthly Budget Review: Summary for Fiscal Year 2021|date=November 8, 2021|website=cbo.gov|access-date=November 14, 2021}}</ref>

During February 2021, the CBO forecast budget deficits for 2021–2031, based on legislation in effect as of January 12, 2021, prior to the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA). This represents the deficit trajectory inherited by Biden; the deficit impact of his policies may be measured against that baseline. CBO later published a baseline including the impact of ARPA.<ref name="CBO_Letter">{{cite web|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/57239|title=Three Scenarios for the Budget as Specified by Senator Graham|date=May 21, 2020|website=cbo.gov|access-date=May 31, 2021}}</ref> OMB then published its forecast for Biden's fiscal 2022 budget, which includes ARPA plus Biden's American Jobs Plan and American Families Plan.<ref name="OMB_FY2022">{{Cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/omb/budget/|title=President's Budget|publisher=[[White House]]|date=May 28, 2021|access-date=May 31, 2021}}</ref> These amounts are shown in the following table:

Deficits in fiscal 2021 and 2022 will be significantly increased by ARPA, although the impact falls thereafter. The budget deficit is expected to fall mid-decade as pandemic-related spending fades and the economy returns to normal. Thereafter, deficits rise due to the long-term trends of an aging country (e.g., fewer workers per retiree) and healthcare costs rising faster than GDP growth.<ref name="CBO_BEO21"/>

== Theoretical economic perspectives==
In terms of theoretical economic perspectives, Bidenomics stands in striking contrast to the previously dominant economic model, known globally as the [[Washington consensus]], or (among its opponents) as [[neoliberalism]].<ref>People rarely call themselves "neoliberal" says [[Oliver Marc Hartwich]],  "Neoliberalism: The genesis of a political swearword." (CIS Occasional Paper 114. 2009) [https://www.ppesydney.net/content/uploads/2020/05/Contesting-actually-existing-neoliberalism.pdf online].</ref> [[Milton Friedman]] was the intellectual godfather, with a base in the [[Chicago school of economics]]. It was the dominant economic policy of Western nations from [[Presidency of Ronald Reagan|Ronald Reagan]] in the United States in the 1980s<ref>Monica Prasad,  "The popular origins of neoliberalism in the Reagan tax cut of 1981." ''Journal of Policy History'' 24.3 (2012): 351–383.</ref> through the presidencies of [[Presidency of George H.W. Bush|George H.W. Bush]], [[Presidency of Bill Clinton|Bill Clinton]], [[Presidency of George W. Bush|George W. Bush]], and [[Presidency of Barack Obama|Barack Obama]], as well as the British leaders [[Margaret Thatcher]], [[Tony Blair]] and [[David Cameron]].<ref name="Ip 2021" /><ref>Wesley Widmaier, "The power of economic ideas–through, over and in–political time: the construction, conversion and crisis of the neoliberal order in the US and UK." ''Journal of European Public Policy'' 23.3 (2016): 338–356.</ref> According to [[Greg Ip]] of the ''[[Wall Street Journal]]'', "Bidenomics Seeks to Remake the Economic Consensus: Declaring end to neoliberalism, new thinkers play down constraints of deficits, inflation and [[economic development incentive|incentives]]"<ref name="Ip 2021" />

Bidenomics draws on an even older economic heritage going back to [[John Maynard Keynes]] in the 1930s, and including Americans [[Walter Heller]], [[James Tobin]], and [[Arthur Okun]] in the 1960s. Versions of [[Keynesianism]] were the dominant American and British [[economic theory]] before the 1970s.<ref>Thomas I. Palley, "From Keynesianism to Neoliberalism: Shifting Paradigms in Economics" in Alfredo Saad-Filho, and Deborah Johnston, eds., ''Neoliberalism – A Critical Reader'' (Pluto Press, 2004) pp 20–29.</ref> Politically, [[modern liberalism in the United States|American liberals]] and Democrats have leaned toward Keynes;<ref>Margaret Weir, "Ideas and Politics: The Acceptance of Keynesianism in Britain and the United States." in ''The Political Power of Economic Ideas'' (Princeton UP, 2020) pp. 53–86.</ref> Republicans and [[American conservatism|conservatives]] favored the Chicago School, though Trump also [[First Trump tariffs|widely used tariffs]], which are at odds with conventional wisdom among the advocates of Chicago School.<ref>Daniel Stedman Jones, ''Masters of the Universe: Hayek, Friedman and the Birth of Neoliberal Politics'' (2012) pp. x, 146; [https://www.amazon.com/Masters-Universe-Friedman-Neoliberal-Politics/dp/0691161011/ excerpt].</ref>

=== Macroeconomics===
The traditional view is that the economy is built around scarcity, because the demand for labor and capital and everything else is unlimited. To achieve full employment and faster growth, more work is needed and more incentives to work. [[Monetary policy of the United States|Monetary]] and [[Fiscal policy of the United States|fiscal policy]] is seldom needed, since the market system naturally produces optimum results.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Xenos | first=Nicholas | title=Liberalism and the Postulate of Scarcity | journal=[[Political Theory]] | volume=15 | issue=2 | year=1987 | jstor=191676 | pages=225–243 | doi=10.1177/0090591787015002004 | s2cid=144596059 | url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/191676| url-access=subscription }}</ref> Bidenomics argues that slack is the main problem, not scarcity. The market system is typically stuck below optimal levels. Full employment and growth is held back by a lack of demand, and needs the stimulation of aggressive fiscal policies such as deficit spending, as well as monetary policies to keep cash flowing.<ref name="Ip 2021">{{cite news | last=Ip | first=Greg | title=How Bidenomics Seeks to Remake the Economic Consensus | work=[[Wall Street Journal]] | date=April 7, 2021 | url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/how-bidenomics-seeks-to-remake-the-economic-consensus-11617796981}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last=Mason | first=J.W | title=Aggregate Demand and Employment | chapter=Macroeconomic lessons from the past decade | publisher=[[Edward Elgar Publishing]] | year=2020 | pages=11–33 | doi=10.4337/9781786432056.00009| isbn=9781786432056 | s2cid=216194019 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | last=Rainey | first=Michael | title=A Quick Guide to 'Bidenomics' | work=[[The Fiscal Times]] | date=April 8, 2021 | url=https://www.thefiscaltimes.com/2021/04/08/Quick-Guide-Bidenomics | access-date=November 13, 2022}}</ref>

=== Budget deficits===
''Bidenomics'' holds that the developed world is awash in surplus savings, which has produced very low interest rates. Absorbing some of this huge pool of savings through large deficits will not divert private investments, and will not raise interest rates. As for tax rates, the very low interest rates makes covering the [[National debt of the United States|national debt much easier]].<ref name="Ip 2021" />{{Update inline|date=July 2024}}

=== Welfare state===
Bidenomics says the government should be promoting the national welfare, and a critical ingredient in our society is caring for dependents – especially children and elderly parents. It is a technical flaw in the definition of [[Gross Domestic Product]] that unpaid household care is not included, even though it is so important. The [[American Rescue Plan Act of 2021|Biden American Rescue Plan]] that became law in March 2021 includes a greatly expanded [[Child tax credit (United States)|child tax credit]].<ref name="Ip 2021" /><ref>Shalal, Andrea (April 6, 2021). [https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-biden-infrastructure-care-idUSKBN2BU02A "Top White House economist defends 'care economy{{'"}}]. [[Reuters]].</ref>

===Taxation and globalization ===
The old view strongly emphasized the wisdom of lowering income taxes, arguing that high rates discourage work, discourage investment, slow growth, and render the U.S. less competitive in a globalized world. Furthermore, the minimum wage reduces employment. The new view is that more danger comes from monopoly power, especially as exerted by the giant high tech companies such as Facebook, Google, and Amazon. Taxation, regulation and [[United States antitrust law|anti-trust laws]] should be used to control them.<ref name="Baker-2024" /> Furthermore, the status quo is creating many [[list of wealthiest Americans by net worth|multi-billionaires]], who largely evade taxation. The result is rapidly growing inequality that is politically and socially destabilizing.<ref>Oxford Analytica. "Biden's top picks to shape 'big tech' antitrust agenda." ''Emerald Expert Briefings oxan-db'' (2021) {{doi|10.1108/OXAN-DB258983}}</ref>

The old view warns that labor unions were the monopolies to worry about and fight against; Biden has been a strong supporter of [[labor union]]s.
The new view cites research to show that people paying higher tax rates do not make less effort, and high minimum wages do not reduce employment. However the minimum wage does pull millions of families out of poverty.<ref name="Ip 2021" /> As for globalization, the new view warns that while globalization raises total world output, it also moves American jobs to China and elsewhere; the new view warns against China as a threat to long-term American economic interests. Tariffs, which were strongly opposed in the old view, now become a useful weapon.

Regarding China, Bidenomics is somewhat parallel to the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration policy]].<ref>Thomas Gift, "Joe Biden's approach to China will not differ greatly from Donald Trump's." ''USApp–American Politics and Policy'' (2020) [https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/107764/ online].</ref> The old view called for lowering American tax rates to remain competitive internationally, while in April 2021 Biden proposed a different approach: the United States would work with the European Community, Britain, Japan and other friendly nations to form a standardized international minimum income tax. The goal is to stop the [[globalization]] process whereby companies relocate headquarters into the international host with the lowest tax.<ref>Paul Hannon and Richard Rubin, "Tax Talks Gain Momentum as U.S. Offers New Proposal Toward Global Deal: Proposal focuses on how to tax corporate income whose location is difficult to pin down," [https://www.wsj.com/articles/u-s-proposes-new-plan-for-global-pact-to-tackle-tax-avoidance-11617906458 ''Wall Street Journal'' April 8, 2021]</ref>

=== Unemployment===
Unemployment has had its longest run under 4% in 70 years, leading to wage growth at the bottom of the income distribution and reversing some income inequality.<ref name="Baker-2024" />

==Public perceptions of economy ==
[[2021-2022 inflation surge|Inflation]] peaked at 9.0% in June 2022 began swiftly abating and by November 2023 the inflation rate stood at 3.2% and summer 2024 had returned near target levels.<ref name="Baker-2024" /> GDP growth, job creation and wage growth remained strong under Biden, with a sustained nearly 50-year-low unemployment rate. Polls, however, indicated broad public discontent with the Biden economy, though data showed consumers continued spending, taking vacations and changing jobs as though they believed the economy was good.<ref>{{cite news |title=The Great Disconnect: Why Voters Feel One Way About the Economy but Act Differently |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/11/20/upshot/economy-voters-poll.html |work=The New York Times |date=November 20, 2023|author1=Claire Cain Miller|author2=Francesca Paris}}</ref>

A March 2024 CBS News poll found that 65% of Americans viewed the economy under Biden's predecessor, Donald Trump, as good, whereas only 38% expressed a similar positive opinion of the current economy under Biden.<ref name="Anne Marie Lee-2024">{{cite news |title=Voters remember Trump's economy as being better than Biden's. Here's what the data shows.|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-biden-economy-gdp-wages-inflation/ |work=CBS News |date=March 3, 2024|author1=Aimee Picchi|author2=Anne Marie Lee}}</ref>

People tend to see their own economic reality and that of their local and state economies as doing better than the national economy,<ref name="Ip-2024">{{cite news |last1=Ip |first1=Greg |title=What's Wrong With the Economy? It's You, Not the Data |url=https://www.wsj.com/economy/consumers/whats-wrong-with-the-economy-its-you-not-the-data-cfa911e6 |work=The Wall Street Journal |date=April 4, 2024}}</ref> hinting at a disconnect fueled more by media narrative.<ref name="Baker-2024" />

In the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]], two thirds of voters called the economy "not-so-good" or "poor" in exit polls, with 69% of them voting for Donald Trump, who defeated Biden's vice president, [[Kamala Harris]].<ref>{{Cite news|title=Voter anger over economy boosts Trump in 2024, baffling Democrats|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2024/11/06/economy-biden-trump-voters/|work=Washington Post|date=2024-11-06|access-date=2025-11-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250219015301/https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2024/11/06/economy-biden-trump-voters/|archive-date=2025-02-19|language=en}}</ref> An exit poll found 45% of voters stated their personal finances were in worse shape than four years prior.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Exit polls 2024: Deep economic discontent with Biden drove voters to Trump|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/2024-exit-polls-fears-american-democracy-economic-discontent/story?id=115529546|website=ABC News|access-date=2025-11-30|language=en|first=Gary|last=Langer}}</ref> The high inflation under Biden, compared to Trump, has been credited for Trump's victory.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Charting the Biden economy: Despite all the growth and jobs, a deeply unpopular president|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2025/01/19/charting-the-biden-economy-deeply-unpopular-despite-growth-and-jobs.html|website=CNBC|date=2025-01-19|access-date=2025-11-30|language=en|first=Jeff|last=Cox}}</ref>

[[Sweden]] has a highly developed [[Social democracy|social democratic economy]], aided by timber, [[hydropower]], and [[iron ore]]. These constitute the resource base of an economy oriented toward foreign trade. The main industries include [[motor vehicle]]s, [[telecommunication]]s, [[pharmaceutical drug|pharmaceutical]]s, industrial machines, precision equipment, chemical goods, home goods and appliances, [[forestry]], iron, and steel. Traditionally, [[Sweden]] relied on a modern [[agricultural economy]] that employed over half the domestic workforce. Today, industries such as engineering, mining, steel, and pulp have been further developed, and have given rise to multi-national companies such as [[Ericsson]], [[Allmänna Svenska Elektriska Aktiebolaget|ASEA]]/[[ABB Group|ABB]], [[SKF]], [[Alfa Laval]], [[AGA AB|AGA]], and [[Dyno Nobel]].<ref>[http://www.ekonomifakta.se/en/Swedish-economic-history/Agricultural-toward-Industrial/ Agricultural toward Industrial|Swedish economic history] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120809013438/http://www.ekonomifakta.se/en/Swedish-economic-history/Agricultural-toward-Industrial/|date=9 August 2012 }}. Ekonomifakta.se (28 September 2012). Retrieved on 29 January 2013.</ref>

Sweden is a competitive open [[mixed economy]]. There is a strong [[welfare state]], with public-sector spending accounting up to three-fifths of GDP.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://sweden.se/business/how-sweden-created-a-model-economy/|title= How Sweden Created a Model Economy|date= 2 November 2018|website= Sweden.se|access-date= 3 October 2019|quote= Today, Sweden has a diverse and highly competitive and successful economy. The World Economic Forum ranks Sweden among the top ten most competitive countries in the world. Sweden is also one of the easiest countries in the world to do business with, according to the World Bank. A key feature of the Swedish economy is its openness and liberal approach to trade and doing business.|archive-date= 3 September 2019|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190903125737/https://sweden.se/business/how-sweden-created-a-model-economy/|url-status= dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.britannica.com/place/Sweden/Economy|title= Sweden - Economy|website= Encyclopedia Britannica|access-date= 3 October 2019|quote= Most enterprises are privately owned and market-oriented, but when transfer payments—such as pensions, sick pay, and child allowances—are included, roughly three-fifths of gross domestic product (GDP) passes through the public sector. Education, health care, and child care costs are primarily met by taxation. Government involvement in the distribution of national income, however, diminished over the last two decades of the 20th century.}}</ref> In 2014, the percent of national wealth owned by the government was 24%.<ref>[https://www.peoplespolicyproject.org/2018/11/08/public-wealth-in-the-us-and-nordic-countries/ Public Wealth in the US and Nordic Countries]</ref>

Due to Sweden being one of the [[neutral powers during World War II]], it did not have to rebuild its economic base, the banking system, and country as a whole, as did many other European countries. Sweden has achieved a high [[standard of living]] under a mixed system of [[high-tech]] capitalism and extensive welfare benefits. Sweden has the second highest [[List of countries by tax rates|total tax revenue]] as a share of GDP, behind only Denmark. {{As of|2012}}, the total tax revenue was 44.2% of GDP, down from 48.3% in 2006.<ref>[http://www.ekonomifakta.se/sv/Fakta/Skatter/Skattetryck/ Skattetrycket| Skattetryck| Skatter| Fakta och statistik] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923235006/http://www.ekonomifakta.se/sv/Fakta/Skatter/Skattetryck/ |date=23 September 2015 }}. Ekonomifakta.se. Retrieved on 29 January 2013.</ref>

In 2014 the National Institute of Economic research predicted GDP growth of 1.8%, 3.1% and 3.4% in 2014, 2015 and 2016 respectively.<ref>{{cite web|title=Swedish economy marking time|url=http://www.konj.se/1088.html|publisher=NIER|access-date=19 October 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20141019211149/http://www.konj.se/1088.html|archive-date=19 October 2014}}</ref>{{update inline|date=August 2019}} A comparison of upcoming economic growth rates of [[European Union]] countries revealed that the [[Baltic states]], [[Poland]], and [[Slovakia]] are the only countries that are expected to keep comparable or higher growth rates.<ref>{{cite news|title=Taking Europe's Pulse|url=https://www.economist.com/blogs/graphicdetail/2014/03/european-economy-guide|newspaper=The Economist|access-date=5 May 2014}}</ref>

==History==
{{main|Economic history of Sweden}}
{{further|Industrialization in Sweden}}

In the 19th century Sweden evolved from a largely [[agricultural economy]] into the beginnings of an industrialized, urbanized country. Poverty remained widespread, prompting a large portion of the country to emigrate, mainly to the United States<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sweden – Economic Growth and Structural Change, 1800-2000 – EH.net |url=https://eh.net/encyclopedia/sweden-economic-growth-and-structural-change-1800-2000/ |access-date=2026-05-17 |language=en-US}}</ref>. Economic reforms and the creation of a modern economic system, banks and corporations were enacted during the later half of the 19th century. During that time Sweden was in a way the "powerhouse" of the Scandinavian region with a strong industrialization process commencing in the 1860s. Moreover, the [[Riksdag|Swedish Riksdag]] had developed into a very active Parliament already during the ''[[Age of Liberty]]'' (1719–72), and this tradition continued into the nineteenth century, laying the basis for the transition towards modern democracy at the end of said century. Apart from relatively high levels of human capital formation, the result of the Reformation and related government policies, such local democratic traditions were the other asset that made the "catching up" of the Scandinavian countries, including Sweden, possible and this economic rise was probably the most remarkable phenomenon in that region during the nineteenth century.<ref>{{cite book|author=Baten, Jörg|title=A History of the Global Economy. From 1500 to the Present.|date=2016|publisher=Cambridge University Press|page=22f|isbn=9781107507180}}</ref>

By the 1930s, Sweden had what ''[[Life magazine|Life]]'' [[Life magazine|magazine]] called in 1938 the "world's highest standard of living".<ref name="life19380711">{{cite news| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f08EAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA31| title=King Gustaf of Sweden| magazine=Life| date=11 July 1938| access-date=12 October 2012| page=31}}</ref> Sweden declared itself neutral during both world wars, thereby avoiding much physical destruction and instead, especially after the First World War, profiting from the new circumstances – such as booming demand for raw materials and foodstuffs and the disappearance of international competition for its exports.<ref name="baten history">{{cite book|author=Baten, Jörg|title=A History of the Global Economy. From 1500 to the Present.|date=2016|publisher=Cambridge University Press|page=25|isbn=9781107507180}}</ref> The postwar boom, that was the continuation of strong inflationary tendencies during the war itself,<ref name="baten history"/> propelled Sweden to greater economic prosperity. Beginning in the 1970s and culminating with the deep recession of the early 1990s, Swedish standards of living developed less favorably than many other industrialized countries. Since the mid-1990s, the economic performance has improved.{{Citation needed|date=February 2022}}

In 2009, Sweden had the world's tenth highest GDP per capita in nominal terms and the fourteenth highest by [[purchasing power parity]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.economist.com/countries/Sweden/profile.cfm?folder=History%20in%20brief|newspaper=The Economist|title=Economist.com – Country Briefings: Sweden}}</ref>

===Crisis of the 1990s===
{{main|1990–1994 Swedish financial crisis}}

Sweden has had an economic model in the post-[[World War II]] era characterized by close cooperation between the government, labour unions, and corporations. The Swedish economy has extensive and universal social benefits funded by high taxes, close to 50% of GDP.<ref name="steinmo" /> In the 1980s, a real estate and financial bubble formed, driven by a rapid increase in lending. A restructuring of the tax system, in order to emphasize low inflation combined with an international economic slowdown in the early 1990s, caused the bubble to burst. Between 1990 and 1993 GDP went down by 5% and unemployment skyrocketed, causing the worst economic crisis in Sweden since the 1930s. According to an analysis published in ''[[Computer Sweden]]'' in 1992, the investment level decreased drastically for information technology and computing equipment, except in the financial and banking sector, the part of the industry that created the crisis.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.scribd.com/doc/43589771/Computer-Sweden-1992|title=Computer Sweden 1992|access-date=3 March 2015|archive-date=20 October 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171020162121/https://www.scribd.com/doc/43589771/Computer-Sweden-1992|url-status=dead}}</ref> The investment levels for IT and computers were restored as early as 1993.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.scribd.com/doc/43605646/Computer-Sweden-1993|title=Computer Sweden 1993|access-date=3 March 2015|archive-date=20 October 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171020163124/https://www.scribd.com/doc/43605646/Computer-Sweden-1993|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1992 there was a run on the [[Swedish Krona|currency]], the [[Riksbank|central bank]] briefly jacking up interest to 500% in an unsuccessful effort to defend the currency's fixed exchange rate.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.iht.com/articles/1992/11/20/swed_2.php|title=Krona's Fall Threatens a New Currency Crisis in Europe – International Herald Tribune|access-date=19 August 2007|archive-date=13 May 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080513095115/http://www.iht.com/articles/1992/11/20/swed_2.php|url-status=dead }}</ref> Total employment fell by almost 10% during the crisis.

A real estate boom ended in a bust. The government took over nearly a quarter of banking assets at a cost of about 4% of the nation's GDP. This was known colloquially as the "Stockholm Solution". In 2007, the [[Federal Reserve System|United States Federal Reserve]] noted, "In the early 1970s, Sweden had one of the highest income levels in Europe; today, its lead has all but disappeared...So, even well-managed financial crises don't really have a happy ending".<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ergungor|first=O. Emre|title=On the Resolution of Financial Crises: The Swedish Experience|journal=Policy Discussion Papers|number=21|date=June 2007|issn=1528-4344|url=http://www.clevelandfed.org/research/POLICYDIS/pdp21.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131021152019/http://www.clevelandfed.org/research/POLICYDIS/pdp21.pdf|archive-date=21 October 2013|access-date=3 March 2015}}</ref>

The welfare system that had been growing rapidly since the 1970s could not be sustained with a falling GDP, lower employment and larger welfare payments. In 1994 the [[government budget deficit]] exceeded 15% of GDP. The response of the government was to cut spending and institute a multitude of reforms to improve Sweden's competitiveness. When the international economic outlook improved combined with a rapid growth in the IT sector, which Sweden was well positioned to capitalize on, the country was able to emerge from the crisis.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ssn.flinders.edu.au/scanlink/nornotes/vol6/articles/holgersson2.html|title=Celsius Centre for Scandinavian Studies|access-date=19 August 2007|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071028111324/http://www.ssn.flinders.edu.au/scanlink/nornotes/vol6/articles/holgersson2.html|archive-date=28 October 2007  }}</ref>

The crisis of the 1990s was by some viewed as the end of the much buzzed welfare model called "Svenska modellen", literally "The Swedish Model", as it proved that governmental spending at the levels previously experienced in Sweden was not long-term sustainable in a global open economy.<ref>{{in lang|sv}} [http://www.regeringen.se/sb/d/7672/a/99800 Anförande vid the Economists konferens om Sverige] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090705042527/http://www.regeringen.se/sb/d/7672/a/99800|date=5 July 2009 }}. Regeringen.se. Retrieved on 29 January 2013.</ref> Much of the Swedish Model's acclaimed advantages actually had to be viewed as a result of the post WWII special situation, which left Sweden untouched when competitors' economies were comparatively weak.<ref>[http://www.ekonomifakta.se/en/Swedish_economic_history/From_War_to_the_Swedish_Model/ From War to the Swedish Model| Swedish economic history] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090723174543/http://www.ekonomifakta.se/en/Swedish_economic_history/From_War_to_the_Swedish_Model/|date=23 July 2009 }}. Ekonomifakta.se (28 September 2012). Retrieved on 29 January 2013.</ref>

However, the reforms enacted during the 1990s seem to have created a model in which extensive welfare benefits can be maintained in a global economy.<ref name="steinmo">{{Cite journal |last=Steinmo |first=Sven |date=2003 |title=Bucking the Trend? The Welfare State and the Global Economy: The Swedish Case Up Close |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1356346032000078714 |journal=New Political Economy |language=en |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=31–48 |doi=10.1080/1356346032000078714 |issn=1356-3467|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In recent years, the Swedish welfare state model has been weakened. Massive privatizations have been carried out since the 1990s, including in public services such as health and education. Inequality has risen sharply, in particular because of a tax system that does not tax wealth and inheritance.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://oxfam.se/en/nyheter/globalt-index-visar-sverige-samst-i-norden-pa-att-bekampa-ojamlikhet/| title=Global index shows Sweden worst in the Nordic countries at fighting inequality - Oxfam Sweden }}</ref>

===Great Recession===
{{Excerpt|Great Recession in Europe|Sweden|paragraphs=3}}

==Contemporary economy==
[[File:Natural resources of Sweden.png|thumb|250px|left|Natural resources of Sweden. Fe – [[iron ore]], PY – [[pyrite]], Cu – [[copper]], Zn – [[zinc]], As – [[arsenic]], Ag – [[silver]], Au – [[gold]], Pb – [[lead]], U – [[uranium]]; in red: C – [[coal]], OS – [[oil shale]].]]

Sweden is an export-oriented [[mixed economy]] featuring a modern distribution system, excellent internal and external communications, and a skilled [[Workforce|labor force]]. Timber, [[hydropower]] and iron ore constitute the resource base of an economy heavily oriented toward [[foreign trade]]. Sweden's engineering sector accounts for 50% of output and exports. Telecommunications, the automotive industry and the pharmaceutical industries are also of great importance. Agriculture accounts for 2 percent of GDP and employment. The armaments industry has a technologically highly advanced reputation.<ref>
{{cite book
| last1 = Pierre
| first1 = Andrew J.
| year = 1982
| title = The Global Politics of Arms Sales
| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=2rX_AwAAQBAJ
| series = Princeton Legacy Library
| location = Princeton, New Jersey
| publisher = Princeton University Press
| publication-date = 2014
| page = 121
| isbn = 9781400854271
| access-date = 30 September 2020
| quote = [...] Sweden considers its relatively self-sufficient defense industry to be a cornerstone of its neutrality policy. [...] Its arms industry is highly advanced technologically [...].
}}
</ref>

The 20 largest Sweden-registered companies by turnover {{as of| 2013| lc = on}} were [[Volvo]], [[Ericsson]], [[Vattenfall]], [[Skanska]], [[Hennes & Mauritz]], [[Electrolux]], [[Volvo Personvagnar]], [[Preem]], [[TeliaSonera]], [[Sandvik]], [[ICA AB|ICA]], [[Atlas Copco]], [[Nordea]], [[Svenska Cellulosa Aktiebolaget]], [[Scania (company)|Scania]], [[Securitas AB|Securitas]], [[Nordstjernan]], [[SKF]], [[ABB Group|ABB Norden Holding]], and [[Sony Mobile Communications AB]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Top list: The largest companies in the Nordic countries by turnover (excl. national subsidiaries) |url=http://www.largestcompanies.com/default%24/cc-SE/lev2-TopList/lev2Desc-The_largest_companies_in_the_Nordic_countries_by%A0turnover%A0%28excl._national_subsidiaries%29/AdPageId-102/list-2/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140422112941/http://www.largestcompanies.com/default%24/cc-SE/lev2-TopList/lev2Desc-The_largest_companies_in_the_Nordic_countries_by%A0turnover%A0%28excl._national_subsidiaries%29/AdPageId-102/list-2/ |archive-date=2014-04-22 |website=Largest Companies}}</ref>

Some 4.5 million residents are working, out of which around a third have a tertiary education. GDP per hour worked is the world's 9th-highest at US$31 in 2006, compared to US$22 in Spain and US$35 in United States.<ref name="oecd2007"/> According to the OECD, deregulation, globalization, and technology-sector growth have been key drivers of productivity.<ref name="oecd2007"/> GDP per hour worked is growing {{frac|2|1|2}} per cent a year for the economy as a whole and trade-terms-balanced productivity growth 2%.<ref name="oecd2007"/> Sweden is a world leader in privatized pensions, and pension-funding problems are small compared to many other Western European countries.<ref>{{unfit|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20100113085905/http://www.heritage.org/Research/SocialSecurity/bg1381.cfm Pension Reform in Sweden: Lessons for American Policymakers]}} by Goran Normann, PhD and Daniel J. Mitchell, PhD 29 June 2000.</ref> The Swedish labor market has become more flexible, but it still has some widely acknowledged problems.<ref name="oecd2007"/> The typical worker receives only 40% of their income after the [[tax wedge]]. The slowly declining overall taxation, 51% of GDP in 2007, is still nearly double of that in the United States or Ireland. Civil servants amount to a third of Swedish workforce, multiple times the proportion in many other countries. Overall, GDP growth has been fast since reforms in the early 1990s, especially in manufacturing.<ref name="oecd2005">OECD Economic Surveys: Sweden – Volume 2005 Issue 9 by OECD Publishing</ref>

[[World Economic Forum]] 2012–2013 competitiveness index ranks Sweden 4th most competitive.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://reports.weforum.org/global-competitiveness-report-2012-2013/|title=The Global Competitiveness Report 2012 - 2013|work=Africa Competitiveness 2013|access-date=3 March 2015}}</ref> The [[Index of Economic Freedom]] 2012 ranks Sweden the 21st most free out of 179 countries, or 10th out of 43 European countries.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.heritage.org/index/country/sweden|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090115143232/http://www.heritage.org/index/country/Sweden|url-status=unfit|archive-date=15 January 2009|title=Sweden|access-date=3 March 2015}}</ref> Sweden ranked 9th in the IMD Competitiveness Yearbook 2008, scoring high in private sector efficiency.<ref name="imd">{{cite web|url=http://www.imd.ch/research/publications/wcy/index.cfm|title=WCC - Home|work=IMD|access-date=3 March 2015}}</ref> According to the book, ''The Flight of the Creative Class'', by the U.S. urban studies, Professor [[Richard Florida]] of [[University of Toronto]], Sweden is ranked as having the best [[creativity]] in Europe for business and is predicted to become a talent magnet for the world's most purposeful workers. The book compiled an index to measure the kind of creativity it claims is most useful to business – talent, technology and tolerance.<ref>"[http://www.isa.se/templates/News____59355.aspx "Sweden most creative country in Europe & top talent hotspot"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070521053538/http://www.isa.se/templates/News____59355.aspx|date=21 May 2007 }}, Invest in Sweden Agency, 25 June 2005.</ref> Sweden's investment into [[research and development]] stood, in 2007, at over 3.5% of GDP. This is considerably higher than that of a number of [[MEDC]]s, including the United States, and is the largest among the OECD members.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.oecd.org/dataoecd/49/45/24236156.pdf|title=Main Science and Technology Indicators|publisher=Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development|access-date=7 September 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100215172528/http://www.oecd.org/dataoecd/49/45/24236156.pdf|archive-date=15 February 2010}}</ref>

Sweden rejected the [[Euro]] in a [[2003 Swedish euro referendum|referendum]] in 2003, and Sweden maintains its own currency, the [[Swedish krona]] (SEK). The Swedish [[Sveriges Riksbank|Riksbank]]{{snd}}founded in 1668 and thus making it the oldest central bank in the world{{snd}}is currently focusing on price stability with its inflation target of 2%. According to ''Economic Survey of Sweden 2007'' by OECD, the average inflation in Sweden has been one of the lowest among European countries since the mid-1990s, largely because of deregulation and quick utilization of globalization.<ref name="oecd2007">[http://www.oecd.org/document/37/0,3343,en_2649_34569_38048997_1_1_1_1,00.html Economic survey of Sweden 2007] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110426123744/http://www.oecd.org/document/37/0,3343,en_2649_34569_38048997_1_1_1_1,00.html|date=26 April 2011 }}</ref>

The largest trade flows are with Germany, United States, Norway, United Kingdom, Denmark and Finland.

The Swedish economic picture has brightened significantly since the severe [[recession]] in the early 1990s. Growth has been strong in recent years, and even though the growth in the economy slackened between 2001 and 2003, the growth rate has picked up since with an average growth rate of 3.7% in the last three years. The long-run prospects for growth remain favorable. The inflation rate is low and stable, with projections for continued low levels over the next 2–3 years.{{update inline|date=August 2019}}

Since the mid-1990s the export sector has been booming, acting as the main engine for economic growth. Swedish exports also have proven to be surprisingly robust. A marked shift in the structure of the exports, where services, the IT industry, and telecommunications have taken over from traditional industries such as steel, paper and [[Wood pulp|pulp]], has made the Swedish export sector less vulnerable to international fluctuations. However, at the same time the Swedish industry has received less money for its exports while the import prices have gone up. During the period 1995–2003 the export prices were reduced by 4% at the same time as the import prices climbed by 11%. The net effect is that the Swedish terms-of-trade fell 13%.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sn.svensktnaringsliv.se/sn/Press.nsf/0/C2946EB9F1400D0EC1256FB6004F7CE6/$File/prm050228.pdf|title=Archived copy|website=sn.svensktnaringsliv.se|access-date=14 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060219114738/http://sn.svensktnaringsliv.se/sn/Press.nsf/0/C2946EB9F1400D0EC1256FB6004F7CE6/$File/prm050228.pdf|archive-date=19 February 2006|url-status=dead}}</ref>

By 2014, legislators, economists and the IMF were warning of a bubble with residential property prices soaring and the level of personal mortgage debt expanding. Household debt-to-income rose above 170% as the IMF called on legislators to consider zoning reform and other means of generating a greater supply of housing as demand was outstripping supply. By August 2014, 40% of home borrowers had interest-only loans while those that didn't were repaying principal at a rate that would take 100 years to fully repay.<ref name="SwedenProperty">{{cite news|title=Sweden facing possible property bubble warns IMF|url=http://www.swedennews.net/index.php/sid/225058369|date=24 August 2014|access-date=26 August 2014|website=Sweden News.Net|archive-date=27 August 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140827112345/http://www.swedennews.net/index.php/sid/225058369|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Government===
{{main|Monetary policy of Sweden}}

[[File:Sweden bonds.webp|thumb|300px|Sweden bonds
{{legend-line|#004B87 solid 3px|20 year}}
{{legend-line|#61D836 solid 3px|10 year}}
{{legend-line|#929292 solid 3px|5 year}}
{{legend-line|#73FDEA solid 3px|2 year}}
{{legend-line|#FF2600 solid 3px|6 month}}
{{legend-line|#D41876 solid 3px|3 month}}
{{legend-line|#FFCD00 solid 3px|1 month}}
]]

The [[Government of Sweden|government]] budget has improved dramatically from a record deficit of more than 12% of GDP in 1993. In the last decade, from 1998 to present, the government has run a surplus every year, except for 2003 and 2004. The surplus for 2011 is expected to be 99 billion ($15b) [[Swedish kronor|kronor]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://en.riksgalden.se/Dokument_eng/press/reports/borrowing/2011/central_government_borrowing_2011_1.pdf|title=Archived copy|access-date=11 July 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110728115957/https://en.riksgalden.se/Dokument_eng/press/reports/borrowing/2011/central_government_borrowing_2011_1.pdf|archive-date=28 July 2011  }}</ref> The new, strict [[budget]] process with spending ceilings set by the [[Riksdag]], and a [[Constitution of Sweden|constitutional]] change to an independent [[Sveriges Riksbank|Central Bank]], have greatly improved policy credibility.

From the perspective of longer-term [[fiscal sustainability]], the long-awaited reform of old-age pensions entered into force in 1999. This entails a far more robust system vis-à-vis adverse [[Demographics of Sweden|demographic]] and economic trends, which should keep the ratio of total pension disbursements to the aggregate wage bill close to 20% in the decades ahead. Taken together, both fiscal consolidation and pension reform have brought public finances back on a sustainable footing. Gross public debt, which jumped from 43% of GDP in 1990 to 78% in 1994, stabilised around the middle of the 1990s and started to come down again more significantly beginning in 1999. In 2000 it fell below the key level of 60% and had declined to a level of 35% of GDP as of 2010.<ref>
{{cite web|url=https://en.riksgalden.se/aboutsndo/Central-government-debt-and-finances/Debt_facts/|title=Debt facts - Riksgalden.se|access-date=11 July 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170227073710/https://en.riksgalden.se/aboutsndo/Central-government-debt-and-finances/Debt_facts/|archive-date=27 February 2017  }}
</ref>

===Companies===
{{see also|List of Swedish companies|List of largest Swedish companies}}

In 2022, the sector with the highest number of companies registered in Sweden was the services sector with 457,044 companies followed by finance, [[insurance industry|insurance]], and real estate with 184,377 companies.{{cn|date=October 2024}} The [[construction industry|construction sector]] is well-developed in Sweden, with significant development in the level of [[sub-contracting]] within the industry since the 1980s.

Other major companies headquartered in Sweden include [[Spotify]], [[IKEA]], [[Mojang]], [[Volvo]], [[Ericsson]], [[H&M]], and [[Scandinavian Airlines]].<ref>Dubois, A. and Gadde, L., [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0969701200000162 Supply strategy and network effects — purchasing behaviour in the construction industry], ''European Journal of Purchasing & Supply Management'', Volume 6, Issues 3–4, December 2000, page 207, accessed on 11 October 2024</ref>

==Economic and monetary union==
{{main|Sweden and the euro}}

Current economic development reflects a quite remarkable improvement of the Swedish economy since the crisis in 1991–93, so that Sweden could easily qualify for membership in the third phase of the [[Economic and Monetary Union of the European Union]], adopting the [[euro]] as its currency. In theory, by the rules of the EMU, Sweden is obliged to join, since the country has not obtained exception by any protocol or treaty (as opposed to Denmark and the United Kingdom). Nevertheless, the Swedish government decided in 1997 against joining the common currency from its start on 1 January 1999. This choice was implemented by exploiting a legal loophole, deliberately staying out of the [[European Exchange Rate Mechanism]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/Documents/college-social-sciences/business/economics/2010-papers/economics-papers-2010/10-13.pdf|title=Too Much to Lose, or More to Gain? Should Sweden Join the Euro?|last=J. James Reade, Ulrich Volz|date=April 2010|website=University of Birmingham|access-date=6 August 2018|archive-date=4 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211104220104/https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/Documents/college-social-sciences/business/economics/2010-papers/economics-papers-2010/10-13.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> This move is currently tolerated by the [[European Central Bank]], which however has warned that this would not be the case for newer EU members.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.economics-sociology.eu/files/ES_8_2_Palankai.pdf|title=THE INTRODUCTION OF THE EURO AND CENTRAL EUROPE|last=Palankai|first=Tibor|date=July 2015|website=Journal of Scientific Papers ECONOMICS & SOCIOLOGY}}</ref>

In the first years of the twenty-first century, a majority for joining emerged in the governing Social Democratic party, although the question was subject of heated debate, with leading personalities in the party on both sides. On 14 September 2003, a [[Referenda in Sweden|national referendum]] was held on the euro. A 56% majority of Swedes rejected the common currency, while 42% voted in favour of it.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/3108616.stm| work=BBC News| title=Sweden turns back on euro| date=15 September 2003| access-date=1 May 2010}}</ref>
Currently no plans for a new referendum or parliamentary vote on the matter are being discussed, though it has been implied that another referendum may take place in around ten years.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://braveneweurope.com/lars-syll-my-finest-hour-swedens-euro-referendum|title=Lars Syll: My Finest Hour – Sweden´s Euro Referendum|last=Syll|first=Lars|date=July 2018|website=Brave New Europe}}</ref>

===Water supply and sanitation===
Sweden provides safe drinking water and advanced sanitation to nearly 100% of its population. Local municipalities manage and own the public water and wastewater infrastructure, funding operations through user fees. Water sources comprise surface water from lakes and rivers, natural groundwater and artificially infiltrated groundwater.<ref>{{cite web |title=Department of Economic and Social Affairs |url=https://sdgs.un.org/basic-page/sweden-34141 |access-date=2026-08-29 |website=Sweden |ref={{sfnref|Sweden}}}}</ref>

==Labour force==
{{see also|Swedish labour movement}}

The traditionally low wage differential has increased in recent years as a result of increased flexibility as the role of wage setting at the company level has strengthened somewhat. Still, Swedish unskilled employees are well paid while well educated Swedish employees are low-paid compared with those in competitor countries in Western Europe and the US. The average increases in real wages in recent years have been high by historical standards, in large part due to unforeseen price stability. Even so, nominal wages in recent years have been slightly above those in competitor countries. Thus, while private-sector wages rose by an average annual rate of 3.75% from 1998 to 2000 in Sweden, the comparable increase for the EU area was 1.75%. In the year 2000 the total labour force was around 4.4 million people.<ref name=":0" />

==Unemployment==
{{see also|Unemployment benefits in Sweden|Ministry of Employment (Sweden)}}

In contrast with most other European countries, Sweden maintained an unemployment rate around 2% or 3% of the work force throughout the 1980s.<ref>{{cite web|title=Sweden Unemployment Rate|url=http://www.indexmundi.com/sweden/unemployment_rate.html|work=Index Mundi|access-date=12 December 2011}}</ref> This was, however, accompanied by high and accelerating inflation.{{Citation needed|reason=This contradicts the data table included in this article which indicates inflation dropped from 17.5% in 1980 to 3.2% in 1990|date=February 2022}} It became evident that such low unemployment rates were not sustainable, and in the severe crisis of the early 1990s the rate increased to more than 8%. In 1996 the government set out a goal of reducing unemployment to 4% by 2000. During 2000 employment rose by 90,000 people, the greatest increase in 40 years, and the goal was reached in the autumn of 2000. The same autumn the government set out its new target: that 80% of the working age population will have a regular job by 2004. Some have expressed concern that meeting the employment target may come at a cost of too high a rate of wage increases hence increasing inflation. However, as of August 2006, roughly 5% of working age Swedes were unemployed, over the government-established goal. However, some of the people who cannot find work are put away in so-called "labour market political activities", referred to as "AMS-åtgärder".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://stefanmikarlsson.blogspot.com/2006/05/denmarks-overrated-flexicurity.html|title=Stefan Karlsson's blog|access-date=3 March 2015}}</ref>

According to [[Jan Edling]], a former trade-unionist, the actual number of unemployed is far higher, and those figures are being suppressed by both the government and the [[Swedish Trade Union Confederation]]. In Edling's report he added that a further 3% of Swedes were occupied in state-organised job schemes, not in the private sector. He also claimed a further 700,000 Swedes are either on long-term sick leave or in early retirement. Edling asks how many of these people are in fact unemployed. According to his report, the "actual unemployment" rate hovers near 20%.<ref>[http://www.timbro.se/pdf/Alla_behovs_2.pdf Alla behövs] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060526083207/http://www.timbro.se/pdf/Alla_behovs_2.pdf|date=26 May 2006 }} Pdf file</ref> Some critics disagree with this concept of "actual" unemployment, also termed "broad unemployment", since they do not see e.g. students who rather want a job, people on sick leave and military conscripts as "unemployed".<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://nordichouse.pl/index.php/s/tresci/idk/10/d/60/pd//id/281|title=Swedish Market|website=nordichouse.pl|access-date=6 August 2018|archive-date=21 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211121015152/http://nordichouse.pl/index.php/s/tresci/idk/10/d/60/pd//id/281|url-status=dead}}</ref>

According to Swedish Statistics, unemployment in June 2013 was 9.1% in the general population and 29% amongst 15- to 25-year-olds.<ref name=LabourForceSurvey>{{cite web|title=Labour Force Survey|url=http://www.scb.se/Pages/Product____23276.aspx|publisher=Statistics Sweden|access-date=11 July 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110708162254/http://www.scb.se/Pages/Product____23276.aspx|archive-date=8 July 2011}}</ref>

==Trade unions==
{{see also|Saltsjöbaden Agreement}}

Around seventy percent of the Swedish labour force is unionised.<ref>[https://www.dn.se/ekonomi/arbetsgivarna-starkare-an-fackforeningarna/ Arbetsgivarna starkare än fackföreningarna]. DN.SE (18 June 2009). Retrieved on 29 January 2013.</ref><ref>Kjellberg, Anders (2023) [https://lucris.lub.lu.se/ws/portalfiles/portal/141188161/The_Nordic_model_of_industrial_relations_comparing_Denmark_Finland_Norway_and_Sweden.pdf ''The Nordic Model of Industrial Relations: comparing Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden'']. Department of Sociology, Lund University and  Max Planck Institute for the Study of Societies, Cologne.</ref> For most [[trade union|union]]s there is a counterpart employer's organization for businesses. The unions and employer organisations are independent of both the government and political parties, although the largest confederation of unions, the [[National Swedish Confederation of Trade Unions]] or ''LO'' (organising [[blue-collar]] workers), maintains close links to one of the three major parties, the [[Socialdemokratiska arbetarpartiet|Social Democrats]].

The [[Union density|unionisation rate]] among [[White-collar worker|white-collar]] workers is exceptionally high in Sweden – since 2008 higher than for blue-collar workers. In 2023, blue-collar density was 58%, and white-collar density was 73% (full-time students working part-time excluded).<ref>Anders Kjellberg (2025) [https://lucris.lub.lu.se/ws/portalfiles/portal/218634009/nord2025-001_Kjellberg_union_density.pdf ”Changes in union density in the Nordic countries”], ''Nordic Economic Policy Review'', pp. 124-129 (Nordregio and the Nordic Council of Ministers).</ref> Just before the considerably raised fees to union unemployment funds in January 2007, blue-collar and white-collar union density was the same (77% in 2006).<ref>Anders Kjellberg (2020) [https://portal.research.lu.se/portal/en/publications/kollektivavtalens-tackningsgrad-samt-organisationsgraden-hos-arbetsgivarfoerbund-och-fackfoerbund(384bb031-c144-442b-a02b-44099819d605).html ''Kollektivavtalens täckningsgrad samt organisationsgraden hos arbetsgivarförbund och fackförbund''], Department of Sociology, Lund University. Studies in Social Policy, Industrial Relations, Working Life and Mobility. Research Reports 2020:1, Appendix 3 (in English) Table A (updated 2023); see also Anders Kjellberg (2017) [http://portal.research.lu.se/portal/en/publications/the-membership-development-of-swedish-trade-unions-and-union-confederations-since-the-end-of-the-nineteenth-century(f155826a-fa3c-41c7-9e34-19c7fc94a8dc).html ''The Membership Development of Swedish Trade Unions and Union Confederations Since the End of the Nineteenth Century''] (Studies in Social Policy, Industrial Relations, Working Life and Mobility). Research Reports 2017:2 (updated 2020). Lund: Department of Sociology, Lund University</ref><ref>Anders Kjellberg (2011) [http://portal.research.lu.se/portal/files/3462138/2064087.pdf "The Decline in Swedish Union Density since 2007"] ''Nordic Journal of Working Life Studies'' (NJWLS) Vol. 1. No 1 (August 2011), pp. 67-93</ref> The average union density was 70% in the years 2011–2014, 69% in 2015-2017 and 68% in 2018 and 2019. There are two major confederations that organise professionals and other qualified employees: the [[Swedish Confederation of Professional Employees]] (''Tjänstemännens Centralorganisation'' or TCO) and the [[Swedish Confederation of Professional Associations]] (''Sveriges Akademikers Centralorganisation'' or SACO). They are both independent from Sweden's political parties and never endorse candidates for office in political elections.

There is no [[minimum wage]] that is required by legislation. Instead, minimum wage standards in different sectors are normally set by collective bargaining. About 90% of all workers are covered by collective agreements, in the private sector 83% (2018).<ref>Anders Kjellberg (2020) [https://portal.research.lu.se/portal/en/publications/kollektivavtalens-tackningsgrad-samt-organisationsgraden-hos-arbetsgivarfoerbund-och-fackfoerbund(384bb031-c144-442b-a02b-44099819d605).html ''Kollektivavtalens täckningsgrad samt organisationsgraden hos arbetsgivarförbund och fackförbund''], Department of Sociology, Lund University. Studies in Social Policy, Industrial Relations, Working Life and Mobility. Research Reports 2020:1, Appendix 3 (in English) Table F</ref><ref>Anders Kjellberg (2019) [https://portal.research.lu.se/portal/sv/publications/sweden-collective-bargaining-under-the-industry-norm(11510a6d-057c-4a81-b69b-a82670685caa).html "Sweden: collective bargaining under the industry norm"], in  Torsten Müller & Kurt Vandaele & Jeremy Waddington (eds.) ''Collective bargaining in Europe: towards an endgame'', European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) Brussels 2019. Vol. III (pp. 583-604)</ref> The high coverage of collective agreements is achieved despite the absence of state mechanisms extending  collective agreements to whole industries or sectors. This reflects the dominance of self-regulation (regulation by the labour market parties themselves) over state regulation in Swedish industrial relations.<ref>Anders Kjellberg (2017) [https://web.archive.org/web/20170418083350/http://portal.research.lu.se/ws/files/23904978/Kjellberg_FSNumhauserHenning_Self_Regulation_State_Regulation.pdf ”Self-regulation versus State Regulation in Swedish Industrial Relations”] In Mia Rönnmar and Jenny Julén Votinius (eds.) ''Festskrift till Ann Numhauser-Henning''. Lund: Juristförlaget i Lund 2017, pp. 357-383</ref><ref>Kjellberg, Anders (2023) [https://portal.research.lu.se/sv/publications/trade-unions-in-sweden-still-high-union-density-but-widening-gaps "Trade unions in Sweden: still high union density, but widening gaps by social category and national origin"]. In Jeremy Waddington & Torsten Mueller & Kurt Vandaele (eds.) Trade unions in the European Union. Picking up the pieces of the neoliberal challenge. Brussels: Peter Lang and Etui. Series: Travail et Société / Work and Society, Volume 86, 2023, chapter 28, pp. 1051-1092.</ref>

Sweden has not joined the EMU (the Economic and Monetary Union / the Euro) and will not in the foreseeable future. When the issue was at the agenda, the Swedish union movement was very split.<ref>Kjellberg, Anders (2000) [http://lup.lub.lu.se/luur/download?func=downloadFile&recordOId=583528&fileOId=3972107 "The Multitude of Challenges Facing Swedish Trade Unions"], in Jeremy Waddington & Reiner Hoffmann (eds.) ''Trade Unions in Europe: Facing Challenges and Searching For Solutions'', Bryssels: European Trade Union Institute, pp. 529-573, in particular pp. 544-547. {{ISBN|2-930143-36-3}}</ref> In contrast to the very positive attitude of employers' associations, the union rank-and file opinion was so split that several unions, as well as the confederations LO, TCO and SACO, abstained from taking an official position.
