Greenhouse, The Guardian, 21 May 2015</ref> A report by U.S. Senator [[Elizabeth Warren]] said that there was a huge gap between the labor standards of past US free trade agreements and the actual enforcement of those provisions.<ref name="TG21May2015SLOTPP" /> However, PIIE analysts note that research shows that the presence of "sticks" (a possible suspension of trade benefits) and "carrots" (technical assistance) in trade deals increase the likelihood that labor obligations in trade deals have a positive effect; there are both sticks and carrots present in TPP.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://piie.com/publications/piie-briefings/assessing-trans-pacific-partnership-volume-2-innovations-trading-rules|title=Assessing the Trans-Pacific Partnership, Volume 2: Innovations in Trading Rules {{!}} PIIE|website=piie.com|date=21 March 2016|access-date=22 July 2016}}</ref>

=== Regulatory cooperation ===
Even though the TPP had not been passed, the agreement had already introduced forms of regulatory cooperation for agriculture beyond that found in the WTO.<ref name=":31">{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/monkey-cage/wp/2016/08/30/the-sky-fell-on-the-u-s-poultry-industry-last-year-but-nafta-and-the-tpp-helped-protect-u-s-exports/|title=The sky fell on the U.S. poultry industry last year. But NAFTA and the TPP helped protect U.S. exports.|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=30 August 2016}}</ref> This means that regulators in different TPP signatories have been engaging with each other and building trust.<ref name=":31" /> Chad P. Bown, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, argues that this regulatory cooperation meant that the US poultry industry was not as hard-hit by the [[2015 United States H5N2 outbreak|2015 bird flu outbreak]], as regulators in TPP countries cooperated and continued to accept US exports of poultry.<ref name=":31" />

== Economic impact ==
The [[United States International Trade Commission|U.S. International Trade Commission]], the [[Peterson Institute for International Economics]], the [[World Bank]] and the Office of the Chief Economist at Global Affairs Canada found that the final agreement would, if ratified, lead to net positive economic outcomes for all signatories.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2"/><ref name=":12" />

=== Effects on economic equality ===
In 2013, [[Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences|Nobel]] Memorial prize-winning economist [[Joseph Stiglitz]] warned that, based on leaked drafts of the TPP, it "serves the interests of the wealthiest."<ref name="NYT-20140315">{{cite news|url=http://opinionator.blogs.nytimes.com/2014/03/15/on-the-wrong-side-of-globalization|title=On the Wrong Side of Globalization|last=Stiglitz|first=Joseph E.|date=15 March 2014|work=[[The New York Times]]|author-link=Joseph Stiglitz|access-date=17 March 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.smh.com.au/national/secrecy-surrounds-transpacific-partnership-talks-20131208-2yzea.html|title=Secrecy surrounds Trans-Pacific Partnership talks|date=9 December 2013|newspaper=The Sydney Morning Herald|access-date=9 December 2013}}</ref> Organised labour in the U.S. argued, during the negotiations, that the trade deal would largely benefit corporations at the expense of workers in the manufacturing and service industries.<ref>[https://www.msnbc.com/the-ed-show/watch/fighting-tpp-to-protect-workers-rights-87825475756 "Fighting TPP to protect workers' rights"]. ''[[The Ed Show]]''. 11 December 2013. Retrieved 17 December 2013.</ref> The [[Economic Policy Institute]] and the [[Center for Economic and Policy Research]] have argued that the TPP could result in job losses and declining wages in the U.S.<ref>[http://www.epi.org/publication/trade-pacts-korus-trans-pacific-partnership/ "No Jobs from Trade Pacts: The Trans-Pacific Partnership Could Be Much Worse than the Over-Hyped Korea Deal"]. [[Economic Policy Institute]]. 18 July 2013</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Rosnick |first1=David |title=Gains from Trade? The Net Effect of the Trans-Pacific Partnership Agreement on US. Wages |url=http://www.cepr.net/index.php/publications/reports/net-effect-of-the-tpp-on-us-wages |website=[[Center for Economic and Policy Research]] |access-date=September 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130910145111/http://www.cepr.net/index.php/publications/reports/net-effect-of-the-tpp-on-us-wages |archive-date=2013-09-10 |date=September 2013 }}</ref>

Economists Peter A. Petri and Michael G. Plummer challenge the view that TPP will primarily benefit the wealthy. Their analysis finds that "the gains from TPP appear to be fairly distributed—labour will gain relative to capital, and cost reductions will favour low-income households. Some workers will need to change jobs, but they constitute a small fraction of normal job churn in any given year, and the national benefits argue for generous compensation for their adjustment costs. The agreement will also benefit workers in TPP's poorest member countries."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://voxeu.org/article/economics-tpp-winners-and-losers|title=Economics of the Trans-Pacific Partnership: Distributional impact|website=VoxEU.org|date=30 April 2016|access-date=22 May 2016}}</ref> Research by Harvard economist Robert Z. Lawrence finds that the "percentage gains for labor income from the TPP will be slightly greater than the gains to capital income. Households in all quintiles will benefit by similar percentages, but once differences in spending shares are taken into account, the percentage gains to poor and middle-class households will be slightly larger than the gains to households at the top."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://piie.com/publications/working-papers/adjustment-and-income-distribution-impacts-trans-pacific-partnership|title=Adjustment and Income Distribution Impacts of the Trans-Pacific Partnership {{!}} PIIE|website=piie.com|date=23 March 2016|access-date=24 May 2016|archive-date=17 May 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160517232445/https://piie.com/publications/working-papers/adjustment-and-income-distribution-impacts-trans-pacific-partnership}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Why the TPP has benefits for workers that far outweighs its costs |url=https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2016/04/why-the-tpp-has-benefits-for-workers-that-far-outweigh-its-costs/ |publisher=World Economic Forum |access-date=24 May 2016}}</ref> An opinion piece by Ed Gerwin in ''The Wall Street Journal'' argues that the TPP agreement benefits small businesses in the US.<ref name="WSJ11272015" />

Economists [[David Autor]], David Dorn and [[Gordon Hanson|Gordon H. Hanson]], who have extensively studied US labor markets adjustments to [[China shock|trade competition shocks caused by China]],<ref>{{cite journal |first1=David H. |last1=Autor |first2=David |last2=Dorn |first3=Gordon H. |last3=Hanson |year=2016 |title=The China Shock: Learning from Labor Market Adjustment to Large Changes in Trade |journal=Annual Review of Economics |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=205–240 |doi=10.1146/annurev-economics-080315-015041 |s2cid=1415485 |url=http://www.nber.org/papers/w21906.pdf }}</ref> support TPP.<ref name=":10">{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/posteverything/wp/2015/03/12/why-obamas-key-trade-deal-with-asia-would-actually-be-good-for-american-workers/|title=Why Obama's key trade deal with Asia would actually be good for American workers|newspaper=The Washington Post|access-date=24 May 2016}}</ref> They argue that TPP "would promote trade in knowledge-intensive services in which U.S. companies exert a strong comparative advantage", note that "killing the TPP would do little to bring factory work back to America" and argue that it would pressure China to raise regulatory rules and standards to those of TPP members.<ref name=":10" />

According to the [[United States International Trade Commission|U.S. International Trade Commission]], the TPP will have positive effects on the U.S. economy as a whole, with unskilled labor reaping 25% of the gains, skilled workers 41% and business owners 34%.<ref name=":25">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/07/27/business/economy/why-dropping-the-trans-pacific-partnership-may-be-a-bad-idea.html|title=Why Dropping the Trans-Pacific Partnership May Be a Bad Idea|last=Porter|first=Eduardo|date=26 July 2016|newspaper=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|access-date=27 July 2016}}</ref>

===Macroeconomics===
==== World Bank report ====
[[World Bank]] found that if ratified by signatories, the TPP "agreement could raise GDP in member countries by an average of 1.1 percent by 2030. It could also increase member countries' trade by 11 percent by 2030, and represent a boost to regional trade growth, which had slowed to about 5 percent, on average, during 2010-14 from about 10 percent during 1990-07."<ref name=":1">{{cite web|url=http://www.worldbank.org/content/dam/Worldbank/GEP/GEP2016a/Global-Economic-Prospects-January-2016-Implications-Trans-Pacific-Partnership-Agreement.pdf|title=Potential Macroeconomic Implications of the Trans-Pacific Partnership|publisher=World Bank}}</ref> The World Bank finds that the agreement will raise real wages in all signatories: "In the United States, for example, changes in real wages are expected to be small as unskilled and skilled wages increase by 0.4 and 0.6 percent, respectively, by 2030. In contrast, in Vietnam, TPP could increase the real wages of unskilled workers by more than 14 percent by 2030, as production intensive in unskilled labor (e.g. textiles) shifts to Vietnam."<ref name=":1" />

==== U.S. International Trade Commission estimate ====
The [[United States International Trade Commission|U.S. International Trade Commission]] estimates that "TPP would have positive effects, albeit small as a percentage of the overall size of the U.S. economy".<ref name=":2"/> There will be 128,000 more full-time jobs.<ref name=":25" /> By 2032, U.S. annual real income would increase by 0.23%, real GDP would be $42.7 billion or 0.15% higher, employment would be 0.07% higher, US exports would increase 1%, and imports would increase 1.1%.<ref name=":2"/> The report added, "TPP would generally establish trade-related disciplines that strengthen and harmonize regulations, increase certainty, and decrease trade costs for firms that trade and invest in the TPP region."<ref name=":2"/> Vietnam is often seen as the biggest beneficiary of TPP.<ref name=":4">{{cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2015-10-08/more-shoes-and-shrimp-less-china-reliance-for-vietnam-in-tpp|title=The Biggest Winner From TPP Trade Deal May Be Vietnam|last=svwriter|first=John Boudreau|website=Bloomberg.com|date=8 October 2015|access-date=24 May 2016}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{cite web|url=https://thediplomat.com/2016/03/why-vietnam-loves-the-trans-pacific-partnership/|title=Why Vietnam Loves the Trans-Pacific Partnership|last=Diplomat|first=Dien Luong, The|website=The Diplomat|access-date=24 May 2016}}</ref><ref name=":9">{{Cite journal|last1=Green|first1=Michael J.|last2=Goodman|first2=Matthew P.|date=2 October 2015|title=After TPP: the Geopolitics of Asia and the Pacific|journal=The Washington Quarterly|volume=38|issue=4|pages=19–34|doi=10.1080/0163660X.2015.1125827|s2cid=155763676|issn=0163-660X}}</ref> The U.S. International Trade Commission identifies the following US industries as net beneficiaries of TPP: Passenger cars; Apparel, Dairy production; Retailers and Wholesalers; and Business services; and as net losers: Auto parts; Textiles; Soybean production; Transportation and tourism; and Chemicals and drugs.<ref name=":2"/><ref>{{cite news|url=https://blogs.wsj.com/economics/2016/05/19/ten-winning-and-losing-industries-from-the-pacific-trade-deal/|title=Ten Winning and Losing Industries from the Pacific Trade Deal|last=Mauldin|first=William|newspaper=Wall Street Journal|date=19 May 2016|access-date=24 May 2016}}</ref>

==== Office of the Chief Economist at Global Affairs Canada report ====
According to a report by the Office of the Chief Economist at Global Affairs Canada, ratification of TPP would increase Canada's GDP by $4.3 billion by 2040.<ref name=":32"/><ref name=":33">{{cite news|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/not-joining-tpp-will-cost-canada-billions-in-economic-growth-report/article31809986/|title=Not joining TPP will cost Canada billions in economic growth: report|access-date=10 September 2016}}</ref> This is primarily due to the preferential access it would receive to markets in the Asia-Pacific rim.<ref name=":32"/><ref name=":33" />  According to the report, ratification by the other TPP signatories but a failure by Canada to ratify the agreement would lead Canada to face estimated GDP losses of $5.3 billion by 2040.<ref name=":32"/><ref name=":33" />

==== Peterson Institute for International Economics report ====
Economists Peter A. Petri and Michael G. Plummer of the [[Peterson Institute for International Economics]] project that the TPP would increase incomes in the U.S. by $131 billion annually, or 0.5 percent of GDP.  Exports from the U.S. would increase by $357 billion annually, or 9.1 percent, as a result of the agreement.<ref name=":12">{{cite news|last1=Hufbauer|first1=Gary Clyde|title=Column: Why the Trans-Pacific Partnership isn't a bum deal|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/column-why-the-trans-pacific-partnership-isnt-a-bum-deal|publisher=PBS|date=5 February 2016|access-date=7 February 2016}}</ref>  However, two [[Tufts University]] economists argue that the research by Petri relies on unrealistic assumptions such as full employment: lost jobs will be immediately replaced in other industrial sectors.<ref name="TUJC16Jan20162" /> According to Harvard economist [[Dani Rodrik]], "Petri and Plummer assume that labor markets are sufficiently flexible that job losses in adversely affected parts of the economy are necessarily offset by job gains elsewhere. Unemployment is ruled out from the start – a built-in outcome of the model that TPP proponents often fudge."<ref name=":3"/> Rodrik notes that "the Petri-Plummer model is squarely rooted in decades of academic trade modeling, which makes a sharp distinction between microeconomic effects (shaping resource allocation across sectors) and macroeconomic effects (related to overall levels of demand and employment). In this tradition, trade liberalization is a microeconomic "shock" that affects the composition of employment, but not its overall level."<ref name=":3"/>

==== Tufts University report ====
[[Tufts University]] researchers project the TPP would have a negative impact on employment: 450,000 US jobs, 75,000 Japanese jobs, 58,000 Canadian jobs and 5,000 New Zealand jobs would be lost by 2025.<ref name="TUJC16Jan20162">[http://www.ase.tufts.edu/gdae/Pubs/wp/16-01Capaldo-IzurietaTPP.pdf Trading Down:Unemployment, Inequality and Other Risks of the Trans-Pacific Partnership Agreement] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190817001710/http://www.ase.tufts.edu/gdae/Pubs/wp/16-01Capaldo-IzurietaTPP.pdf |date=17 August 2019 }} J. Capaldo and A. Izurieta, Global Development and Environment Institute, Working Paper No. 16–1 Jan (2016)</ref> According to the report, 771,000 jobs would be lost in total and positive economic effects would be negligible for participating countries.<ref name="TUJC16Jan20162" /><ref name=nytimes01Feb2016JC>[https://www.nytimes.com/2016/02/02/business/international/economists-sharply-split-over-trade-deal-effects.html Economists Sharply Split Over Trade Deal Effects] J. Calmes, The New York Times, 1 February 2016</ref>

Harvard economist [[Robert Z. Lawrence]] says that the model used by the Tufts researchers "is simply not suited for credibly predicting the effects of the TPP" and argues that the model used by Petri and Plummer is superior.<ref name=":0"/> Lawrence argues that the model used by the Tufts researchers "does not have the granularity that allows it to estimate variables such as exports, imports, foreign direct investment, and changes in industrial structure. As a result, its predictions ignore the benefits to the TPP economies that occur through increased specialization, the realization of scale economies, and improved consumer choice."<ref name=":0"/> Lawrence also notes that the model used by the Tufts researchers finds that the TPP will cause GDP to fall by 5.24% in non-TPP developing countries, such as China, India, and Indonesia, which Lawrence is highly skeptical of: "It is not believable that a trade agreement of this magnitude could cause the rest of the world to plummet into recession."<ref name=":0"/> Harvard economist [[Dani Rodrik]], a well-known skeptic of globalization, says that the Tufts researchers do "a poor job of explaining how their model works, and the particulars of their simulation are somewhat murky... the Capaldo framework lacks sectoral and country detail; its behavioral assumptions remain opaque; and its extreme Keynesian assumptions sit uneasily with its medium-term perspective."<ref name=":3"/>

Fredrik Erixon and Matthias Bauer of the [[ECIPE|European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE)]] write that the Tufts analysis has such serious flaws "that its results should neither be regarded reliable nor realistic."<ref name=":30"/> They write that Tufts model is "by and large a demand-driven model that does not make efforts to capture the supply-side effects of trade, which are the effects that are proven to be the core positive effects of trade liberalisation. Equally problematic, the model is not designed to assess the effect on trade from trade agreements – in fact, the model is profoundly ill suited for such an exercise. No trade economist, regardless what school of thought he or she comes from, has ever used this model to make estimates of trade. The reason is simple: if a model cannot predict the effects on the flows and profile of trade as a consequence of trade liberalisation, it is of no use at all."<ref name=":30"/> They add, "In Capaldo's analysis, structural change and the emergence of new industries do not play a role at all. Capaldo implicitly assumes that an economy with its labour and capital does not respond and adjust to new circumstances. New competition only leads to new unemployment. In addition, the impact of lower barriers on international commerce on product and process innovation is neglected. Finally, Capaldo does not account for the impact of competition on the cost of production and final consumer prices."<ref name=":30"/>

According to the Congressional Research Service, "The Tufts study has drawn particular criticism as an unconventional framework for analyzing trade agreements, whereas Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) models, such as that used in the Peterson study are standard in trade policy analysis."<ref name=":8"/> Fabio Ghironi, Professor in Economics at the [[University of Washington]], describes the models used by the World Bank and the Peterson Institute in more favorable terms than the Tufts analysis.<ref name="auto1"/>

=== Effects on the European Union ===
The EU is trying to form trade agreements with each country that is part of the TPP: since 2013, there have been talks of a free trade agreement between the EU and Japan, and in 2015 the EU presented its new strategy to improve trade in the Asia-Pacific entitled "Trade for All."<ref name="European Parliamentary Research Service">{{cite web|url=http://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/BRIE/2016/582028/EPRS_BRI(2016)582028_EN.pdf|title=The Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) Potential regional and global impacts|author= Krisztina Binder|date=May 2016}}</ref>

=== Liberalization ===
According to an analysis by the Cato Institute of the chapters of the TPP, 15 chapters have a liberalizing impact, 5 have a protectionist impact, and 2 have a neutral impact.<ref name=":34">{{cite web|url=http://www.cato.org/publications/working-paper/should-free-traders-support-trans-pacific-partnership-assessment-americas|title=Should Free Traders Support the Trans- Pacific Partnership? An Assessment of America's Largest Preferential Trade Agreement|date=12 September 2016|access-date=13 September 2016}}</ref> Considered as a whole, the terms of the TPP are net liberalizing.<ref name=":34" />

There have been conflicting arguments on whether or not the TPP aims to increase the liberalization of trade. For arguments that propose that the TPP succeeds at liberalizing trade among the participating nations, there is a question of whether or not this causes a positive or a negative net change. Some scholars argue that participatory members of the TPP believe that such membership is a utilitarian and practical method toward new trade liberalization.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lewis|first=Meredith|year=2011|title=The Trans-Pacific Partnership: New Paradigm or Wolf in Sheep's Clothing?|ssrn=1908411|journal=Boston College International & Comparative Law Review|volume=34}}</ref> Scholars Peter Petri and Michael Plummer describe the TPP as a "dynamic process - and example of competitive liberalization," and this liberalization described can result in a new type of governance for the Asia-Pacific, as well as transnational trade.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Petri|first1=Peter|last2=Plummer|first2=Michael|year=2012|title=The Trans-Pacific Partnership and Asia-Pacific Integration: Policy Implications|journal=Peterson Institute for International Economics Policy Brief}}</ref>

According to analyst and economist B.R. Williams, the United States has a large role in the reduction of trade barriers and increased U.S. investment. Williams explains that the U.S. aims to create a "broader platform for trade liberalization, particularly throughout the Asia-Pacific region."<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Williams|first=B.R.|year=2013|title=Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) countries: Comparative trade and economic analysis|journal=Washington, D.C.: Congressional Research Service}}</ref> Scholars C. Li and J. Whalley explore a numerical approach in explaining the liberalizing effects of the TPP. Li and Whalley uses a quantitative equilibrium simulation to explore the effects of the TPP on the liberalization of trade and new markets.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Li|first1=C|last2=Whalley|first2=J|year=2014|title=China and the Trans-Pacific Partnership: A Numerical Simulation Assessment of the Effects Involved|journal=World Economics|volume=37|issue=2|pages=169–192|doi=10.1111/twec.12123|s2cid=154672692}}</ref>

=== China ===
According to a 2020 study, the TPP pushed [[China]] to introduce its own internal liberal market reforms. Reform-minded elites in China used the TPP to justify reform.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lin|first1=Alex Yu-Ting|last2=Katada|first2=Saori N.|date=2020-08-07|title=Striving for greatness: status aspirations, rhetorical entrapment, and domestic reforms|journal=Review of International Political Economy|volume=29 |pages=175–201|doi=10.1080/09692290.2020.1801486|s2cid=225371407|issn=0969-2290}}</ref> In anticipation of China's exclusion from the agreement, exposed Chinese firms began investing in production in TPP member states.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gulotty|first1=Robert|last2=Li|first2=Xiaojun|date=2019-07-30|title=Anticipating exclusion: Global supply chains and Chinese business responses to the Trans-Pacific Partnership|journal=Business and Politics|volume=22|issue=2|pages=253–278|doi=10.1017/bap.2019.8|s2cid=201359183}}</ref>

In May 2020, Chinese Premier [[Li Keqiang]] said that China has a positive and open attitude toward joining the [[Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership|CPTPP]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scmp.com/economy/china-economy/article/3092143/chinas-interest-trans-pacific-trade-deal-met-scepticism-those|title=China's interest in trans-Pacific trade deal met with scepticism by those who helped negotiate it|first=Finbarr|last=Bermingham|work=South China Morning Post|date=2020-07-08}}</ref>

In November 2020, China and fourteen Asia-Pacific nations signed a trade deal, the [[Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/11/16/economy/rcep-trade-agreement-intl-hnk/index.html|title=China signs huge Asia Pacific trade deal with 14 countries|first1=Jill |last1=Disis |first2=Laura |last2=He|website=CNN|date=16 November 2020 }}</ref>

== Geopolitics ==
TPP would have increased the likelihood that Japan would undertake economic reforms to revive its economy, which coupled with potential South Korean accession to the TPP, could have had an economic impact on China. By making the Chinese economy less competitive and Chinese leadership less likely to write the rules of trade in East and Southeast Asia, the Chinese government would have been under great internal and external pressure to liberalize its economy.<ref name=":6"/> Japan's former prime minister, [[Shinzō Abe|Shinzo Abe]], believed that future Chinese accession to the TPP would have a major pacifying impact on the Asia-Pacific region.<ref name=":7"/> U.S. Trade Representative [[Michael Froman]] said that a failure to ratify the TPP would give China the opportunity to boost its exports and set labor and environmental standards in the fast-growing Asia Pacific region through the [[Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership]] (RCEP).<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-trade-idUSKCN1090QZ |title=Killing TPP would hand China 'keys to the castle': U.S. trade representative |date=29 July 2016 |newspaper=Reuters |access-date=29 July 2016}}</ref>

South Korea did not participate in the TPP "largely out of a concern to maintain balance in its economic relations with China and the United States" but showed greater interest in joining after Japan, its biggest economic competitor, decided to participate.<ref name=":9" /> The Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand, and Taiwan also reportedly considered and implemented various domestic reforms to improve their prospects for eventually joining.<ref name=":29" />

Since formal TPP negotiations began in 2010, China's attitude towards TPP has:

<blockquote>swung from disdain to suspicion to cautious embrace... Conclusion of a TPP agreement in early October has sparked a lively debate in Beijing, with the weight of elite opinion seeming to tilt toward eventual membership; for example, the head of the Chinese-sponsored Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), Jin Liqun, announced his support during a speech in Washington shortly after the TPP deal was announced.<ref name=":9" /></blockquote>

The TPP may give renewed impetus to trade negotiations among China, Japan, and Korea, and increase the likelihood of [[Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership]] (RCEP) which could provide a possible pathway to a [[free trade area]] of the Asia-Pacific.<ref name=":9" /> The 2017 decision by United States President Donald Trump to withdraw from the TPP strengthened China's alternative model of the RCEP.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mitter |first=Rana |title=China's good war: how World War II is shaping a new nationalism |date=2020 |publisher=The Belknap Press of [[Harvard University Press]] |isbn=978-0-674-98426-4 |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |page=8 |oclc=1141442704}}</ref>

In January 2016, the United States [[National Association of Manufacturers]] announced its support for TPP, saying "without such an agreement, the United States would be ceding economic leadership to other global powers, letting them set the rules of economic engagement in the region".<ref>{{cite news |url=https://thehill.com/policy/finance/264631-manufacturers-endorse-tpp/ |title=Big Endorsement for Obama Trade Deal |newspaper=The Hill |last1=Needham |first1=Vicki |access-date=4 January 2016}}</ref>

A 2016 study by [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland]] political scientists Todd Allee and Andrew Lugg suggested that if the TPP became standard legal text, it would shape future trade cooperation and agreements.<ref name=":24" />

An October 2016 survey of 746 [[international relations]] scholars showed that 71% supported the TPP, 18% opposed the TPP, 9% were neutral, and 2% were undecided.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://trip.wm.edu/charts/#/bargraph/42/6771 |title=TRIP Data Viewer |website=trip.wm.edu |access-date=26 October 2016}}</ref>

=== United States considerations ===
The original TPP was thought by some to likely bring China's neighbours closer to the United States and reduce their dependence on Chinese trade.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /><ref name=":9" /><ref name=":6">{{cite web |url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2015/10/07/china-tpp-trans-pacific-partnership-obama-us-trade-xi/ |title=What Will the TPP Mean for China? |website=Foreign Policy |date=7 October 2015 |access-date=24 May 2016}}</ref><ref name=":7">{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/10/07/world/asia/trans-pacific-partnership-china-australia.html |title=U.S. Allies See Trans-Pacific Partnership as a Check on China |last=Perlez |first=Jane |date=6 October 2015|newspaper=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 |access-date=24 May 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://belfercenter.hks.harvard.edu/publication/26627/trade_is_a_national_security_imperative.html |title=Trade Is a National Security Imperative - Harvard - Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs |website=belfercenter.hks.harvard.edu |access-date=24 May 2016 |archive-date=7 August 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160807185910/http://belfercenter.hks.harvard.edu/publication/26627/trade_is_a_national_security_imperative.html }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.commentarymagazine.com/foreign-policy/asia/geopolitical-necessity-trade/ |title=The Geopolitical Necessity of Trade |last=Boot |first=Max |date=29 April 2016 }}</ref><ref name=":26">{{Cite news |url=http://nationalinterest.org/feature/the-death-tpp-the-best-thing-ever-happened-china-19232?page=show |title=The Death of TPP: The Best Thing That Ever Happened to China |last=Magnusson |first=Earl Anthony Wayne, Oliver |newspaper=The National Interest |language=en |access-date=31 January 2017}}</ref><ref name="foreignpolicy.com">{{Cite web |url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2017/05/03/this-isnt-realpolitik-this-is-amateur-hour/|title=This Isn't Realpolitik. This Is Amateur Hour. |website=Foreign Policy|date=3 May 2017 |access-date=4 May 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2017/11/06/trump-will-be-haunted-by-the-ghost-of-tpp-in-asia/ |title=Trump Will Be Haunted by the Ghost of TPP |website=Foreign Policy |date=6 November 2017 |access-date=22 November 2017}}</ref> If ratified, the TPP would have strengthened American influence on future rules for the global economy. US Secretary of Defense [[Ash Carter]] claimed the passage of the TPP to be as valuable to the United States as the creation of another aircraft carrier.<ref name=":9" /> President Obama has argued "if we don't pass this agreement—if America doesn't write those rules—then countries like China will".<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/11/06/business/international/trans-pacific-trade-deal-tpp-vietnam-labor-rights.html |title=Trans-Pacific Partnership Text Released, Waving Green Flag for Debate |last=Calmes |first=Jackie |date=5 November 2015 |newspaper=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 |access-date=24 May 2016}}</ref> According to the Congressional Research Service, "many Asian policymakers—correctly or not—could interpret a failure of TPP in the United States as a symbol of declining U.S. interest in the region and inability to assert leadership... failure to conclude TPP could, in effect, allow China to shape regional rules of commerce and diplomacy through its own trade and investment initiatives, potentially creating regional rules and norms less beneficial for U.S. interests."<ref name=":8"/> [[Michael Green (political expert)|Michael J. Green]] and Matthew P. Goodman argue that "history will be unforgiving if TPP fails... If Congress rejects TPP, trying to negotiate a similar arrangement in Asia would reopen demands on the United States—and in the meantime, would likely give impetus to alternative arrangements like RCEP that exclude the United States. Momentum behind the U.S.-led international order would shift to momentum against it. Future generations of historians will take note of U.S. leadership at this moment."<ref name=":9" /> Dan Ikenson, director of Cato's Herbert A. Stiefel Center for Trade Policy Studies, argued in July 2016 that the "failure of Congress to ratify the Trans-Pacific Partnership this year would do more to subvert U.S. regional and global interests than anything China is capable of doing."<ref name=":29">{{cite web |url=http://www.cato.org/publications/commentary/the-trans-pacific-partnership-is-essential-to-regional-peace |title=The Trans-Pacific Partnership Is Essential to Regional Peace and Global Prosperity |date=14 July 2016 |access-date=20 July 2016}}</ref> [[Stephen Walt|Stephen M. Walt]], professor of international relations at Harvard University, writing after the Trump Administration abandoned the TPP, described the TPP as "a key institution that would have bound a number of Asian countries more tightly to the United States".<ref name="foreignpolicy.com"/>

=== Non-TPP party opinions ===
On 30 January 2015 [[Philip Hammond]], the former [[Foreign Secretary of the United Kingdom]], described the Trans-Pacific Partnership and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership as "potentially important liberalising steps forward".<ref>Hammond, P., [https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/foreign-secretarys-speech-on-the-uk-in-asia-pacific "Foreign Secretary's speech on the UK in Asia Pacific"] Foreign & Commonwealth Office, UK, 30 January 2015, accessed 8 October 2015</ref>

The [[European Centre for International Political Economy]] (ECIPE), a think tank on European policies, predicted in 2012 that the TPP would be a "deadly threat to European exporters of agricultural products in TPP countries".<ref>Messerlin, Patrick, [http://www.ecipe.org/media/publication_pdfs/Messerlin_TPP-EU_EN05212.pdf The TPP and the EU policy in East Asia], ECIPE Policy Brief, no.11/2012, European Centre for International Political Economy, {{ISSN|1653-8994}}.</ref> ECIPE has said in 2014 that TPP "[would] be the first 'competing' [[economic integration]] that is large enough to have a considerable negative impact on Europe. In the long-term, the negative effects [would] come from dynamic impact, e.g. on investment, productivity and competitiveness".<ref name=ecipe14>Matthias Bauer, Fredrik Erixon, Martina Ferracane and Hosuk Lee-Makiyama [http://www.ecipe.org/app/uploads/2014/12/PB09_1.pdf TRANS-PACIFIC PARTNERSHIP: A challenge to Europe] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160315115352/http://www.ecipe.org/app/uploads/2014/12/PB09_1.pdf |date=15 March 2016 }} ECIPE Policy Briefs, No.9/2014, page 1-13, European Centre for International Political Economy, {{ISSN|1653-8994}}</ref>
[[Pascal Lamy]] called the TPP "the last of big old-style trade agreements".<ref name=ecipe14/>{{rp|2}}

== Criticism{{anchor|Protests}} ==
{{Commons category|Demonstrations and protests against the TPP}}
{{Commons category|Demonstrations and protests against the TTIP}}
In 2014, Nobel Memorial Prize-winning economist [[Paul Krugman]] said "there isn't a compelling case for this deal, from either a global or a national point of view."<ref name="NYT-20140227">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/02/28/opinion/krugman-no-big-deal.html|title=No Big Deal|last=Krugman|first=Paul|date=27 February 2014|work=[[The New York Times]]|author-link=Paul Krugman|access-date=28 February 2014}}</ref>

=== Currency manipulation ===
Some critics and even supporters of the TPP wanted the deal to contain measures that would crack down on nations who engage in alleged [[currency manipulation]], notably China.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/chinas-impact-looms-large-u-s-debates-trade-deals|title=China's impact looms large as U.S. debates its own trade deals|website=[[PBS]]|date=20 May 2015|language=en-US|access-date=22 July 2016}}</ref> However, [[Daniel W. Drezner|Daniel Drezner]], professor of international politics at Tufts University, has argued that the trade deal was never likely to include restrictions on currency manipulation, as it would have restricted U.S. monetary policy.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/posteverything/wp/2015/10/08/is-hillary-clinton-right-about-the-trans-pacific-partnership/|title=Is Hillary Clinton right about the Trans-Pacific Partnership?|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=22 July 2016}}</ref> Harvard economist [[Jeffrey Frankel]] has argued that the inclusion of currency manipulation language in TPP would be a mistake.<ref name=":22">{{cite web|url=http://econbrowser.com/archives/2015/06/the-top-ten-reasons-why-trade-agreements-should-not-cover-currency-manipulation|title="The Top Ten Reasons Why Trade Agreements Should Not Cover Currency Manipulation" {{!}} Econbrowser|website=econbrowser.com|date=12 June 2015 |access-date=22 July 2016}}</ref> Frankel noted that currency manipulation would be hard to enforce (in part because it is impossible to tell whether a currency is overvalued or undervalued); "currency manipulation" can often be legitimate; China, often alleged to be a major currency manipulator, is not party to the TPP; currency manipulation accusations are often meritless; and because it would restrict U.S. monetary policy.<ref name=":22" />

=== Length and complexity ===
In his [[Donald Trump 2016 presidential campaign|2016 presidential campaign]], then-candidate [[Donald Trump]] criticized the TPP agreement for being too long and complicated, saying "[i]t's 5,600 pages long, so complex that nobody's read it."<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/donald-trump-is-upset-1447374770 |title=Donald Trump Is Upset |date=13 November 2015 |newspaper=The Wall Street Journal |issn=0099-9660 |access-date=2 August 2016}}</ref> Vermont U.S. Senator [[Bernie Sanders]] claimed that the "TPP is much more than a 'free trade' agreement."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://feelthebern.org/bernie-sanders-on-trade/ |title=Bernie Sanders on Trade |last=FeelTheBern.org |language=en-US |access-date=2 August 2016}}</ref>

However, [[Georgetown University]] Professor Marc L. Busch and [[McGill University]] Professor Krzysztof J. Pelc note that modern trade deals are long and complex because they often tackle [[non-tariff barriers to trade]], such as different standards and regulations, in addition to [[tariff]]s. Due to steadily decreasing tariff barriers since WWII, countries have become increasingly likely to enact trade barriers in the form of non-tariff barriers. National firms often lobby their own governments to enact regulations that are designed to keep out foreign firms. The TPP addresses many of these "disguised restrictions on trade" by, for instance, "basing these measures on agreed-upon science; making the process of formulating regulations more transparent; and giving foreign exporters opportunities to offer substantive input in the formulation of these measures."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/monkey-cage/wp/2016/08/02/yes-the-tpp-agreement-is-over-5000-pages-long-heres-why-thats-a-good-thing/|title=Yes, the TPP agreement is over 5,000 pages long. Here's why that's a good thing.|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=2 August 2016}}</ref>

=== Secrecy of negotiations ===
Until being finalized, negotiations for the TPP were conducted with significant secrecy. Drafts of the agreement were kept [[classified information|classified]] during negotiations, and access to the working text was significantly restricted even for government officials, including the [[United States Congress]]; and business representatives involved in the talks.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2015/05/secrecy-eroding-support-for-trade-pact-critics-say-117581|title=Extreme secrecy eroding support for Obama's trade pact|publisher=Politico|author=Edward-Isaac Dovere|author-link=Edward-Isaac Dovere|date=4 May 2015|access-date=22 July 2016}}</ref> Despite this, some sections of TPP drafts were leaked to the public by [[WikiLeaks]], which published an intellectual property chapter draft in 2013.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2013/nov/13/wikileaks-trans-pacific-partnership-chapter-secret |title=WikiLeaks publishes secret draft chapter of Trans-Pacific Partnership |first=Steven |last=Musil |work=The Guardian (UK) |date=12 November 2013 |access-date=15 November 2013}}</ref>

In 2012, critics such as Public Citizen's [[Global Trade Watch]], a consumer advocacy group, called for more open negotiations in regard to the agreement. U.S. Trade Representative [[Ron Kirk]] responded that he believed the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) conducted "the most engaged and transparent process as we possibly could", but that "some measure of discretion and confidentiality" are needed "to preserve negotiating strength and to encourage our partners to be willing to put issues on the table they may not otherwise."<ref name="reuters_1">{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-trade-kirk-idUSBRE84C0AQ20120514?feedType=RSS&feedName=everything&virtualBrandChannel=11563|title=Some secrecy needed in trade talks: Ron Kirk|work=[[Reuters]]|date=13 May 2012|last=Palmer|first=Doug|access-date=2 July 2017|archive-date=19 October 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151019110203/http://www.reuters.com/article/2012/05/14/us-usa-trade-kirk-idUSBRE84C0AQ20120514?feedType=RSS&feedName=everything&virtualBrandChannel=11563|url-status=live}}</ref> He dismissed the "tension" as natural and noted that when the [[Free Trade Area of the Americas]] drafts were released, negotiators were subsequently unable to reach a final agreement.<ref name="reuters_1" />

On 23 May 2012, U.S. Senator [[Ron Wyden]], Democrat of Oregon, introduced {{USBill|112|s|3225}}, which would have required the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative to disclose its TPP documents to all members of Congress.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.govtrack.us/congress/bills/112/s3225| title=S. 3225 (112th)| access-date=30 May 2012| author=112th Congress (2012)| date=23 May 2012| work=Legislation| publisher=GovTrack.us| quote=A bill to require the United States Trade Representative to provide documents relating to trade negotiations to Members of Congress and their staff upon request, and for other purposes.}}</ref> Had it passed, Wyden said that the bill would increase Congressional access to information about USTR activity.<ref name="Wyden20120523">{{USCongRec|2012|S3517|date=23 May 2012}}</ref>

Michael R. Wessel, former commissioner on the U.S. Trade Deficit Review Commission claimed in May 2015 that "cleared advisors" like himself were "prohibited from sharing publicly the criticisms we've lodged about specific proposals and approaches". He claimed that only portions of the text had been provided, "to be read under the watchful eye of a USTR official", that access on secure government-run website did not contain the most-up-to-date information, and that for cleared advisors to get that information, he had "to travel to certain government facilities and sign in to read the materials" and "even then, the administration determines what we can and cannot review and, often, they provide carefully edited summaries rather than the actual underlying text, which is critical to really understanding the consequences of the agreement."<ref>Michael Wessel [https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2015/05/tpp-elizabeth-warren-labor-118068/ I've Read Obama's Trade Deal. Elizabeth Warren is Right to be Concerned.] Politico.com 19 May 2015, accessed 8 October 2015</ref>

In June 2015, U.S. Senator [[Rand Paul]], Republican of Kentucky, opposed the bill to [[Fast track (trade)|fast-track]] the congressional ratification of the TPP on the basis of the trade agreement's secrecy.<ref>{{cite news|title=Rand Paul demands White House release trade deal text immediately|last=Shabad|first=Rebecca|date=6 June 2015|work=The Hill|url=https://thehill.com/policy/finance/244220-rand-paul-demands-white-house-release-trade-deal-text-immediately/}}</ref>

===Indigenous rights===
In late June 2015, several prominent Māori figures including Dr Papaarangi Reid, [[Moana Jackson]], Rikirangi Gage, Angeline Greensill, [[Hone Harawira]] and [[Moana Maniapoto]] filed an urgent claim with the [[Waitangi Tribunal]],<ref name="Te Ao June 2015">{{cite news |title=High profile Māori file Waitangi Tribunal claim over TPPA |url=https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2015/06/25/high-profile-maori-file-waitangi-tribunal-claim-over-tppa/ |access-date=21 May 2024 |work=Te Ao Māori News |publisher=[[Whakaata Māori]] |date=25 June 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518035525/https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2015/06/25/high-profile-maori-file-waitangi-tribunal-claim-over-tppa/ |archive-date=18 May 2024}}</ref> a standing commission of inquiry established in 1975 to investigate the [[New Zealand Crown]]'s breaches of the [[Treaty of Waitangi]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ruru |first1=Karanama |title=The Waitangi Tribunal, explained |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/350201186/waitangi-tribunal-explained |access-date=21 May 2024 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=9 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240403031616/https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/350201186/waitangi-tribunal-explained |archive-date=3 April 2024|url-status=live}}</ref> The plaintiffs claimed that the way the New Zealand Government was negotiating the TPP breached the [[Treaty of Waitangi]] because its ratification  would not require the consent of the [[New Zealand Parliament]], the lack of Māori involvement in the negotiation process and the lack of any legal obligation to assess the TPP's implications for the Treaty of Waitangi.<ref name="Te Ao June 2015"/> In response to the claim, the Government argued that the secret nature of the TPP negotiations would allow it to negotiate in the national interest, had taken steps to consider Māori interests under the Treaty and that it has been consulting with Māori in relation to the TPP.<ref>{{cite web |title=Waitangi Tribunal claim over New Zealand's participation in the TPPA |url=https://www.ajpark.com/insights/waitangi-tribunal-claim-over-new-zealands-participation-in-the-tppa/ |publisher=AJ Park |access-date=21 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231206101126/https://www.ajpark.com/insights/waitangi-tribunal-claim-over-new-zealands-participation-in-the-tppa/ |archive-date=6 December 2023 |date=20 July 2015 |url-status=live}}</ref> In early May 2016, the Waitangi Tribunal backed the inclusion of a Treaty of Waitangi clause in the finalised TPP trade deal. However, the Tribunal expressed concern that a clause allowing foreign investors to bring claims against the New Zealand Government could affect the Crown's willingness or ability to meet its Treaty obligations.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Haunui-Thompson |first1=Shannon |title=Waitangi Tribunal backs TPP treaty clause |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/303148/waitangi-tribunal-backs-tpp-treaty-clause |access-date=21 May 2024 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=5 May 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518035228/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/303148/waitangi-tribunal-backs-tpp-treaty-clause |archive-date=18 May 2024|url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Industry influence ===
U.S. Senator [[Elizabeth Warren]], Democrat of Massachusetts, has alleged that corporations and industry exert disproportionate influence on U.S. trade negotiators.<ref name=":13">{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/fact-checker/wp/2016/07/18/warrens-claim-that-advisory-committees-formed-during-drafting-of-trans-pacific-partnership/|title=Warren's claim that advisory committees 'formed' during drafting of Trans-Pacific Partnership|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=20 July 2016}}</ref> She asserted in July 2016 that 85% of seats on U.S. trade advisory committees were held by "senior corporation executives or industry lobbyists", and that the members of the committees "whisper in the ear" of negotiators.<ref name=":13" />

Michelle Ye Hee Lee, a fact-checker for ''The Washington Post'', wrote that Warren used "misleading language" in describing the TPP. While Warren implied that "28 trade advisory committees were formed" specifically to influence the TPP, the advisory committees were actually created as part of the [[Trade Act of 1974]]; only the membership of the trade committees had changed during the Obama administration and the early phases of the TPP. Regarding Warren's claim that trade advisers secretly "whisper in the ear of our trade negotiators", Lee wrote: "while the direct meetings take place in private, committees still have to submit written reports to Congress and provide written recommendations and advice that are made public."<ref name=":13" /> Furthermore, Lee wrote, "it is true that industry representatives make up a large number of the total membership, but it is worth noting that there is a labor committee in the second tier, labor representatives in the first tier and that the industry groups have a narrow focus (to give technical advice)."<ref name=":13" />

In response to criticisms about transparency and the large representation from industry representatives, USTR announced it would create a Public Interest Trade Advisory Committee.<ref name=":13" />

In June 2026, after the Argentine government announced its intention to accede to the Trans-Pacific treaty, the [[Province of Buenos Aires]], led by Governor [[Axel Kicillof]], and in particular his chief of staff, Carlos Bianco, harshly criticized Argentina’s accession to the treaty, arguing that it imposes disadvantageous conditions on domestic industry (small and medium-sized enterprises, industrial employment, and domestic production) and that, with the [[United Kingdom]] as a member state of the treaty, it would jeopardize Argentina’s historic claim to sovereignty over the [[Falkland Islands]].<ref>{{cite web|access-date=2026-06-04 |date=2026-06-03 |title=Bianco acusó a Milei de “entregar la industria” y poner en riesgo Malvinas |url=https://laletrachica.com.ar/nota/25582/bianco-acuso-a-milei-de-entregar-la-industria-y-poner-en-riesgo-malvinas/ |website=laletrachica.com.ar}}<!-- auto-translated from Spanish by Module:CS1 translator --></ref>

=== Non-compete clause ===
[[Dean Baker]] argued that Article 18.78, under which countries should ensure that they protect [[trade secrets]] and impose criminal procedures for violators, could be used to enforce [[non-compete agreement]]s.<ref name=":16" /> Baker points out that [[California]]'s success can partly be attributed to the fact that the state did not allow for the enforcement of non-compete agreements, making it easy for tech workers to quit their jobs and start to work for another company.<ref name=":16">[https://www.huffingtonpost.com/dean-baker/will-the-trans-pacific-pa_b_9878794.html Will the Trans-Pacific Partnership Turn Silicon Valley Into Detroit?] D. Baker, The Huffington Post, 9 May 2016</ref>

=== Criticisms from politicians and activists ===
In 2014, linguist and political activist [[Noam Chomsky]] warned that the TPP is "designed to carry forward the [[Neoliberalism|neoliberal]] project to maximize profit and domination, and to set the working people in the world in competition with one another so as to lower wages to increase insecurity."<ref>Zach Carter and Ryan Grim (13 January 2014). [https://www.huffingtonpost.com/2014/01/13/noam-chomsky-obama-trans-pacific-partnership_n_4577495.html?ref=topbar "Noam Chomsky: Obama Trade Deal A 'Neoliberal Assault' To Further Corporate 'Domination'"]. ''[[The Huffington Post]]''. Retrieved 13 January 2014.</ref> Senator [[Bernie Sanders]] ([[Independent politician|I]]-[[Vermont|VT]]) argues that trade agreements like the TPP "have ended up devastating working families and enriching large corporations."<ref>[https://www.msnbc.com/the-ed-show/watch/preventing-tpp-essential-to-all-u-s-workers-118892611809 "Preventing TPP essential to all U.S. workers"]. ''[[The Ed Show]]'', 16 January 2014. Retrieved 23 January 2014.</ref> [[AFL-CIO]] head [[Richard Trumka]] criticized the trade deal.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/2015/4/20/8445991/afl-cio-tpp-obama-trumka|title=AFL-CIO head Richard Trumka explains why labor unions hate Obama's trade deal|website=Vox|date=April 20, 2015}}</ref>
